How to use a hypo page

  1. 1
    Read the facts and the Assume list. Each hypo has a base and one to three twists, like Prof Chong's “how would your answer differ” questions.
  2. 2
    Round 1: which Menu boxes? Note the boxes you would tick, then open the green box to compare. It lists the boxes to write from, the decoys with the reason each is wrong, and boxes that are fair but not needed.
  3. 3
    Answer the application questions. Pick an option and press Check. Every option then shows a line on why it is right or wrong; below it are the law-reviewed explanation and the pre-write block, word for word.
  4. 4
    How the answer runs. The violet box gives the answer in plain English, step by step, in the order an exam answer would write it, with both routes wherever a point is open.
  5. 5
    What the check changed. The end of each page lists what was wrong in Gemini's version and what was filled in, so you can see the traps.

“Answers: Always shown” at the top of each hypo opens every answer at once, for fast revision. Your answers and that setting stay in this browser.

LAW302 · META GAME · ★ DO FIRST · QUESTION 1 · HYPO q1-10 · GEMINI PROMPT V2 · LAW REVIEWED 17 NOV · 13 QUESTIONS

Bramwell Bio v Kaldor Labs

Gemini wrote this hypo with prompt v2. Claude reviewed it in three passes and made 33 changes before it went into the drill. Gemini's file: law302_drill_q1_10_bramwell_bio_v_kaldor_labs.ht.

Answers:

1Base facts

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Bramwell Bio v Kaldor Labs

Bramwell Bio Pte Ltd, a Singapore incorporated company, makes diagnostic test kits in Jurong. Kaldor Labs SA is the Arcadian arm of the Kaldor group, incorporated in Arcadia, where it runs clinical laboratories. Kaldor Labs has no office, staff or assets in Singapore. The two companies made three contracts.

Under the Reagent Supply Agreement, signed on 15 June 2016 and governed by Singapore law, Bramwell Bio supplies reagents to Kaldor Labs in Arcadia. Clause 14 reads:

“The High Court of Singapore shall have exclusive jurisdiction over any dispute arising out of or in connection with this Agreement.”

Under the Equipment Servicing Agreement, signed on 10 March 2021 and governed by Arcadian law, Kaldor Labs’s engineers service Bramwell Bio’s calibration rigs in Singapore. Clause 19 reads:

“All disputes arising out of or in connection with this Agreement shall be submitted exclusively to the courts of Arcadia.”

Under the Joint Validation Agreement, signed on 5 November 2023 and governed by Singapore law, Bramwell Bio validates test kits for Kaldor Labs. Clause 11 reads:

“Any dispute arising out of or in connection with this Agreement shall be resolved by the Singapore International Commercial Court.”

Disputes have arisen on all three contracts. On the Supply Agreement, Kaldor Labs has not paid S$2.4 million for reagents, alleging transit damage. On the Servicing Agreement, Bramwell Bio claims S$900,000 for damage to a rig in Singapore. On the Validation Agreement, Bramwell Bio claims S$1.5 million in unpaid fees. Bramwell Bio wants all three claims heard together in Singapore, in the General Division or the Singapore International Commercial Court. Kaldor Labs will contest Singapore jurisdiction on all three.

Advise Bramwell Bio whether the General Division or the Singapore International Commercial Court has jurisdiction over each claim, and whether it will hear it.

ℹ ASSUME
  1. Arcadia is a Contracting State to the Hague Convention on Choice of Court Agreements. The Convention entered into force for Arcadia on 1 July 2018.
  2. None of the three contracts says how legal process may be served.
  3. Kaldor Labs’s laboratory technicians and testing records for the Supply Agreement are all in Arcadia.
  4. A civil trial takes about four years in Arcadia and about 14 months in Singapore.
  5. Under Singapore law and Arcadian law, clauses 14, 19 and 11 are all valid and cover the respective claims.
✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • A2
    Says "exclusive": Singapore courts. Clause 14 is an express exclusive clause for the Singapore High Court, so Kaldor Labs’s objection to Singapore is a breach.
  • B1
    CCAA gate: five conditions. Run the CCAA gate for each contract. The Supply Agreement fails on its pre-1 October 2016 date; the Servicing and Validation Agreements pass all five conditions.
  • B2
    CCAA applies and Singapore is the chosen court (s 11). Clause 11 names only the SICC, so s 3(2) deems it exclusive, and it post-dates 1 October 2016. Per s 11 the SICC must hear the Validation claim, with no Spiliada and no strong cause.
  • B3
    CCAA applies and a foreign court is chosen (s 12). The Servicing Agreement is inside the CCAA with Arcadia chosen, so s 12 requires a stay or dismissal unless an exception applies; delay and fragmentation fail.
  • D8
    Singapore clause, defendant abroad. Kaldor Labs is abroad with no service clause, so Bramwell Bio serves out on the Supply Agreement using clause 14 as nexus and showing a serious question separately.
  • E7
    Strong cause: starter and nature of the test. If Kaldor Labs contests the Supply Agreement claim in Singapore, it breaks clause 14 and bears strong cause; its Arcadian witnesses were foreseeable.
  • F2
    Primary jurisdiction under a written jurisdiction agreement. Clause 11 is a written jurisdiction agreement naming the SICC, and the Validation claim is international and commercial. So the SICC has primary jurisdiction over it under O 2 r 1(1), and no transfer is needed.
  • F3
    "Singapore High Court" clause: check the date. Clause 14 predates 1 October 2016 so it reaches the SICC only by transfer; clause 11 names the SICC only, so the General Division cannot rely on it alone.
  • F6
    SCORECARD · Transfer from the General Division: is the SICC "more appropriate"?. Because clause 14 gives no primary SICC jurisdiction, Bramwell Bio must seek a transfer from the General Division under O 2 r 4(1)(c).

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • E4
    SCORECARD · Spiliada stage 1: connecting factors. The Arcadian technicians and records look like Spiliada stage 1 factors, but no claim here runs Spiliada: Supply uses strong cause, Servicing s 12 and Validation s 11.
  • E5
    SCORECARD · Spiliada stage 2: substantial justice. The four-year wait in Arcadia looks like Spiliada stage 2. But s 12 displaces Spiliada on the Servicing claim, and mere delay is not manifest injustice and does not mean the clause “cannot reasonably be performed”.
  • A4
    Says "non-exclusive": Singapore courts. Clause 14 expressly states “exclusive jurisdiction”, so it is an exclusive clause rather than a non-exclusive submission.
  • D10
    Foreign clause, defendant abroad. D10 is for suing at common law despite a foreign clause, whereas the Servicing Agreement is governed by CCAA s 12.

Fair to tick but not needed: A1 Any jurisdiction clause: what it promises, A3 Says "exclusive": a foreign court, B4 Outside the CCAA: say why, then the common law, D4 Defendant abroad: service out and the three requirements, D5 Gateway: name the sub-limb of PD para 63(3), D7 Serious question to be tried, E1 Which test, and who bears the burden, E8 SCORECARD · Strong cause: the Eleftheria factors, F1 International and commercial, F4 Serving the defendant abroad from the SICC, F5 Exercise in the SICC: O 2 r 3, no Spiliada

Application questions · base facts

⚡ Base facts · 1 of 7B1
Does the CCAA apply to the Supply Agreement (clause 14)?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

The temporal gate tests the date the clause was concluded against the Convention’s entry into force for the chosen court’s State. Clause 14 was signed on 15 June 2016, before Singapore’s date of 1 October 2016, so the common law governs.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J1.2.2 :: Temporal Scope

[State of chosen court] is a Contracting State, and [clause X] was concluded on [date], after the HCCCA entered into force for it (Singapore: 1 October 2016). [Check the HCCH status table.]

  • UK clauses (±): the HCCCA applied to the UK via the EU from 1 October 2015 and in its own right from 1 January 2021; continuity across Brexit is contested, so [an English clause] concluded on [a date between them] is arguable either way.
⚡ Base facts · 2 of 7D8
Bramwell Bio sues on the Supply Agreement in the General Division. What must it show in practice to serve Kaldor Labs out of Singapore?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Because clause 14 says nothing on service, approval under O 8 r 1(1) is required. In practice, clause 14 supplies the nexus under PD para 63(3)(d)(iv) and (r), the serious question is shown separately, and forum shifts to strong cause on Kaldor Labs if it objects.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J3.2 :: Singapore EJC or NEJC: In Principle v In Practice (must write)

Per Week 9 slides, [claimant] relies on [the Singapore clause] against [defendant]:

  • In principle, [claimant] must still make out all three requirements against [defendant], even inter partes.
  • Nexus: [the clause] itself, under para 63(3)(r) ([defendant] "agreed to submit") or (d)(iv) (Shanghai Turbo (CA); J3.1.2).
  • In practice, [claimant] need only show a good arguable case that [the clause] is valid, binds [defendant] and covers [the dispute] (J1.5–J1.6), plus a serious question, shown separately because (d)(iv) and (r) are neutral (J3.1.4).
  • Forum: need not be proved. If [defendant] contests it, that breaches its promise, so per Shanghai Turbo (CA) [defendant] bears strong cause (J4.3), whether it challenges existence or exercise; if [defendant] never raises it, [claimant] need prove nothing.
⚡ Base facts · 3 of 7E7
Kaldor Labs applies to set aside service of the Supply Agreement claim on forum grounds. Who bears the burden, and of what?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

The burden lies on the party seeking release from its promise. By objecting to Singapore, Kaldor Labs breaks clause 14 and must show strong cause; its Arcadian witnesses and records were foreseeable at contracting.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J4.3.0 :: Starter (must write)

Presently, [claimant] sues here in breach of [the EJC for X] / [defendant] seeks a stay or set-aside in breach of [the Singapore EJC / NEJC]. Per Vinmar (restating The Eleftheria), the court holds the parties to their bargain unless [the party in breach] shows strong cause, whether on a stay or a set-aside (Shanghai Turbo).

⚡ Base facts · 4 of 7F3
Can Bramwell Bio file the Supply Agreement claim directly in the SICC?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Under O 2 r 2(2), a Singapore High Court clause concluded before 1 October 2016 does not of itself submit to the SICC. Bramwell Bio must start in the General Division and apply for a transfer.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J5.2.3 :: Pre-2016 Clause (−)

Per O 2 r 2(2), [clause X], concluded on [date] before 1 October 2016, "does not of itself" submit to the SICC. Per Chong (sample-final answer scheme), there is no primary jurisdiction, so [claimant] sues in the General Division and seeks [a transfer] (J5.4).

⚡ Base facts · 5 of 7F6
If Bramwell Bio asks the General Division to transfer the Supply Agreement claim to the SICC, will the transfer succeed?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Outside the CCAA, transfer under O 2 r 4(1)(c) needs the SICC to be more appropriate, and Kaldor Labs’s consent is not required. Per Chong (seminar), the test turns on how international and commercial the dispute is, not its complexity. The Arcadian buyer and evidence point to the SICC. But Singapore law governs, so no SICC feature such as deciding foreign law on submissions is needed. The links to Singapore are strong, and Kaldor Labs contests jurisdiction instead of consenting. So a General Division judge can resolve the claim expeditiously.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J5.4.1 :: Not More Appropriate (−)

[The dispute] is [a straightforward Singapore-law debt claim / largely domestic], and [a General Division judge] can resolve it expeditiously (cf C&Y on SICC → General Division transfers), so no SICC feature makes transfer more appropriate.

⚡ Base facts · 6 of 7B3
Bramwell Bio sues on the Servicing Agreement in Singapore, arguing that the four-year wait in Arcadia and splitting the three claims are manifest injustice under s 12(1)(c) of the CCAA. Will that succeed?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per the Hartley–Dogauchi Report, s 12(1)(c) and (d) apply only in the most exceptional circumstances. Per 6DM, even the risk that a related party could not be joined abroad fell far short of manifest injustice, so splitting these claims fails, and mere delay is not enough.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J1.4.2 :: (c) Fragmentation (−)

Similar to 6DM, where the risk that a related individual could not be joined in England failed s 12(1)(c), [claimant]'s argument that [third party] cannot be joined in [State B] fails. The test is "very different" from, and far higher than, fragmentation as strong cause at common law (Vinmar), and [claimant] led no evidence of [State B law].

⚡ Base facts · 7 of 7F3
Can Bramwell Bio rely on clause 11 of the Validation Agreement alone to sue Kaldor Labs in the General Division?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Under O 2 r 2(3), a clause naming only the SICC is not of itself submission to the General Division. Bramwell Bio should file the Validation Agreement claim directly in the SICC, where clause 11 gives primary jurisdiction and s 11 CCAA applies.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J5.2.3 :: SICC-Only Clause (−)

Per O 2 r 2(3), [clause X], naming [the SICC] alone, is not "of itself" submission to the General Division, so [claimant] suing there cannot rely on it alone (C&Y).

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
⚡ BIG IDEA

Three contracts with three clauses go to three different regimes, so run the CCAA gate and the SICC rules contract by contract before any forum question. The June 2016 Supply Agreement fails the CCAA date row: Bramwell Bio serves out on clause 14, Kaldor Labs bears strong cause, and the pre-2016 “High Court” clause reaches the SICC only by a transfer that is unlikely. Inside the CCAA, s 12 sends the Servicing claim to Arcadia, and s 11 makes the SICC, chosen by clause 11, hear the Validation claim. The twists add a contractual anti-suit injunction that delay probably defeats, then common law enforcement of the Elbonian default judgment, which turns on the open question whether a stay application is a submission (IGCF against Henry v Geoprosco).

  1. 1
    Characterise the clauses first A2

    What each clause promises decides who, if anyone, is in breach. Clause 14 says “exclusive jurisdiction” and sits in a Singapore-law contract, so it is an express exclusive clause for the Singapore High Court. An exclusive clause holds three promises: to submit to the chosen court, not to object to its exercise of jurisdiction, and not to sue elsewhere. So if Kaldor Labs objects to Singapore on the Supply claim, it breaks clause 14. Clause 19 is an express exclusive clause for Arcadia, and clause 11 names only the SICC; the CCAA gate decides what follows from them.

  2. 2
    The CCAA gate, contract by contract B1

    Run every row for each clause. Clause 14 chooses Singapore but was concluded on 15 June 2016, before the Convention entered into force for Singapore, the chosen court’s State, on 1 October 2016, so the Supply Agreement fails the date row and the common law decides. Clause 19 expressly chooses the courts of Arcadia, a Contracting State, and was concluded on 10 March 2021, after Arcadia’s date of 1 July 2018. Clause 11 does not say “exclusive”, but nothing provides otherwise, so s 3(2) deems it exclusive, and it was concluded on 5 November 2023, after Singapore’s date. Both cases are international, as Kaldor Labs resides in Arcadia and Bramwell Bio in Singapore (ss 4(1) and 6), and commercial; the rig claim arises under the Servicing Agreement, so the s 9(2) exclusion of non-contractual property damage does not apply. So the Servicing Agreement is a CCAA case with Arcadia chosen (s 12), and the Validation Agreement one with Singapore chosen (s 11).

  3. 3
    Supply claim: serving Kaldor Labs out on clause 14 D8

    Kaldor Labs has no office, staff or assets in Singapore, so it must be served out. None of the contracts says how process may be served, so O 8 r 1(3) does not help, and Bramwell Bio needs approval under O 8 r 1(1), on the “appropriate court” ground as the case is outside the CCAA. In principle it must meet all three requirements; in practice it shows a good arguable case that clause 14 is valid, binds Kaldor Labs and covers the dispute, which supplies the nexus under para 63(3)(d)(iv) or (r). Those factors say nothing about the merits, so it shows a serious question on the unpaid S$2.4 million separately. Forum need not be proved: if Kaldor Labs contests it, it breaks clause 14 and must show strong cause.

  4. 4
    Supply claim: strong cause on Kaldor Labs E7

    Kaldor Labs will apply to set aside service or for a stay on forum grounds, which breaks its promise in clause 14. Per Vinmar, restating The Eleftheria, the court holds the parties to their bargain unless the party in breach shows strong cause, on a set-aside as on a stay (Shanghai Turbo). This is not Spiliada: it is a higher hurdle, because the court is asked to sanction a breach. Kaldor Labs’s Arcadian technicians and testing records were foreseeable when it agreed to clause 14, so per Vinmar they carry little weight, and Singapore law governs the contract. Nothing suggests abuse by Bramwell Bio or real prejudice to Kaldor Labs in defending here, so there is no strong cause and the General Division will hear the Supply claim.

  5. 5
    Supply claim: the SICC only by transfer, which is unlikely F3F6

    Clause 14 names the High Court and predates 1 October 2016, so per O 2 r 2(2) it does not of itself submit to the SICC; per Chong (sample-final answer scheme) the SICC has no primary jurisdiction, and Bramwell Bio starts in the General Division. It may seek a transfer under O 2 r 4(1): the action must be international and commercial, seek no prerogative relief, and the SICC must be more appropriate. The case is outside the CCAA, so Kaldor Labs’s consent is not needed (O 2 r 4(4) is for CCAA “High Court” clauses), and its objection is only a factor. Per Chong (seminar), the test is how international and commercial the dispute is, not its complexity, and the Arcadian buyer and evidence point to the SICC. But Singapore law governs, so no SICC feature such as deciding foreign law on submissions is needed, the links to Singapore are strong and Kaldor Labs does not consent. So a General Division judge can resolve the claim, and a transfer is unlikely.

  6. 6
    Servicing claim: s 12 sends it to Arcadia B3

    Per s 12(1), “despite any other written law or rule of law”, Singapore must stay or dismiss unless an exception applies, so even if Bramwell Bio founds jurisdiction by serving Kaldor Labs out, the claim stops here. Per 6DM, Kaldor Labs needs only a good arguable case that clause 19 is an exclusive agreement not designating a Singapore court, which it plainly is. Exception (a) fails, as clause 19 is valid under Arcadian law, the chosen court’s law. Per the Hartley–Dogauchi Report, exceptions (c) and (d) apply only in the most exceptional circumstances: per 6DM even the risk that a related party could not be joined abroad fell far short of manifest injustice, so splitting the three claims fails, and a four-year trial is mere delay, which is not enough under (c) or (d). So the Servicing claim is stayed or dismissed and Bramwell Bio must sue in Arcadia; the common law test for a foreign clause (strong cause on Bramwell Bio) would arise only if an exception applied.

  7. 7
    Validation claim: primary jurisdiction in the SICC F2F3

    Clause 11 is a written jurisdiction agreement naming the SICC (O 2 r 1(7)). The action is international, as Kaldor Labs’s place of business is in Arcadia, and commercial, arising from a commercial relationship, and it seeks no prerogative relief, so per O 2 r 1(1) the SICC has primary jurisdiction. Per Chong (AY23-24 mid-term feedback), primary jurisdiction ends the inquiry, so no transfer is needed, and Kaldor Labs, a party to clause 11, may be served abroad without permission (O 5 r 6(2)(a)). But per O 2 r 2(3), a clause naming only the SICC is not of itself submission to the General Division (C&Y), so Bramwell Bio cannot rely on clause 11 alone to sue there and should file in the SICC.

  8. 8
    Validation claim: the SICC must hear it B2

    The Validation Agreement is inside the CCAA with the SICC chosen, so per s 11(1) the SICC must not decline unless clause 11 is null and void under Singapore law, including its choice of law rules; the Assume list says it is valid. Per s 11(2) it cannot decline in favour of Arcadia, so neither Spiliada nor strong cause applies, and Kaldor Labs’s links to Arcadia and its objection are irrelevant. The SICC’s own rules point the same way: it may not decline merely because the action is connected with Arcadia (O 2 r 3(3)). So the SICC will hear the Validation claim.

  9. 9
    Advice to Bramwell Bio

    Bramwell Bio cannot have all three claims heard together in Singapore. Supply: the General Division has jurisdiction once Kaldor Labs is served out with approval on clause 14, and will hear the claim, as Kaldor Labs cannot show strong cause; the SICC has no primary jurisdiction, and a transfer is possible but unlikely. Servicing: Singapore must stay or dismiss under s 12, so Bramwell Bio must sue in Arcadia. Validation: Bramwell Bio should file in the SICC, which has primary jurisdiction under clause 11 and must hear the claim under s 11.

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes: a contractual anti-suit injunction G1

    Jurisdiction over the three base claims stays as it was. What is new: Kaldor Labs, served in the Singapore Supply action, sued Bramwell Bio in Elbonia on the Supply Agreement, and after eight months contesting jurisdiction there and losing, Bramwell Bio asks the General Division for an anti-suit injunction, with the Elbonian trial due next month. Per SNIA and Lakshmi, such an injunction interferes indirectly with the foreign court, so it issues only where the ends of justice require; Bramwell Bio bears the burden and must name its basis (Cooperative Muratori). The basis is contractual: amenability, breach of clause 14 and no strong reasons, with natural forum dropping out. Vexation could be pleaded in the alternative (Kaldor Labs sued abroad two weeks after service instead of counterclaiming here, similar to Lakshmi), but kept apart: breaking clause 14 is not itself vexation (Cooperative Muratori).

  2. 2
    Amenability: valid service out, with Akai against it G2

    Amenability is always required: Kaldor Labs must be within the court’s personal jurisdiction (Cooperative Muratori). It was validly served out in Arcadia with approval in the Supply action, and per Prof Chong’s answer scheme the injunction can be sought as relief in that action, so no fresh permission is needed. The settled view (C&Y; Cooperative Muratori) is that valid service makes it amenable, and its lack of assets here goes only to whether the injunction bites. Kaldor Labs will cite Akai, where a respondent served out with no presence or assets here, which only opposed the injunction, was held not amenable. So Kaldor Labs is amenable in principle; if it ignored an injunction, contempt would bite only on assets or a presence here, but a judgment obtained in breach would be refused recognition here as contrary to public policy (Nimbus).

  3. 3
    Breach of clause 14, and no strong reasons G3

    Breach is a question of interpretation under the clause’s proper law (C&Y): clause 14 is an express exclusive clause in a Singapore-law contract, and the Elbonian claim for defective reagents arises out of the Supply Agreement, so suing in Elbonia breaks the promise not to sue elsewhere. Per Westbridge v Mittal and Cooperative Muratori, clause 14 itself supplies Singapore’s connection, so natural forum does not arise; the Supply Agreement is outside the CCAA and Elbonia is not a Contracting State, so this is an ordinary contractual injunction. Per Sun Travels and Cooperative Muratori, it ordinarily issues unless Kaldor Labs shows strong reasons, in practice the strong cause test (C&Y), and the facts give none: no third parties, no claims outside clause 14, and its Arcadian evidence was foreseeable and points to Arcadia, not Elbonia. Kaldor Labs may add that Bramwell Bio waived clause 14 by applying for a stay in Elbonia (UniCredit); per IGCF a stay application is a protest, not submission, though on Henry v Geoprosco’s logic it is submission, and the delay decides the injunction either way.

  4. 4
    Delay and comity: the injunction is probably refused G3

    Per Sun Travels, comity re-enters with delay even in contractual cases, and how far the foreign proceedings have progressed matters more than the length of the delay. Bramwell Bio waited eight months and the Elbonian merits trial is next month; similar to Hilton, where the Maldivian proceedings were too far advanced, an injunction now would waste the Elbonian court’s work. Contesting jurisdiction in Elbonia first is no excuse: per Sun Travels there are no “two bites at the cherry”, and Bramwell Bio should have objected there and applied here at the same time. The Elbonian refusal of the stay is not itself a bar (Lakshmi), and whether delay belongs to strong reasons or to the discretion is open, but either way the delay defeats the injunction. So the injunction is probably refused.

Application questions · twist 2

⚡ Twist 2 · 1 of 3H1
Which regime governs Kaldor Labs’s application to enforce the Elbonian default judgment in Singapore?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

CCAA Part 3 covers only judgments of the chosen court of a Contracting State, and Elbonia is neither. So Kaldor Labs sues on the judgment debt at common law. Per C&Y, Singapore tests the Elbonian court’s international jurisdiction by its own rules, and that court’s own ruling creates no estoppel.

⚡ Twist 2 · 2 of 3H4
Did Bramwell Bio submit to the Elbonian court by applying for a stay on jurisdiction?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Giant Light Metal, Singapore law decides, with Elbonian procedure only as context. As in Nimbus, objecting, losing and then taking no part is not submission. But on Henry v Geoprosco’s logic a stay accepts the jurisdiction it asks the court not to use, and Nimbus assumed Henry without deciding. Per IGCF, Henry should not be followed, and Bramwell Bio sought nothing more than the stay. So submission is probably not made out and, with no presence in Elbonia, the Elbonian court probably lacked international jurisdiction. If Henry is followed, Bramwell Bio submitted.

On this route Bramwell Bio submitted to the Elbonian court, and per C&Y a debtor that submitted loses the objection, so the defence probably fails. Even apart from that it is undecided: per C&Y, damages for the breach could cancel the sum and REFJA s 5(4)(b) gives an analogue, but no Singapore authority recognises the defence.

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes: enforcing the Elbonian default judgment H1

    Keep Twist 1, with no injunction granted. What is new: Bramwell Bio took no further part in Elbonia, the Elbonian court gave a default judgment for US$500,000 in damages, and Kaldor Labs sues on it in the General Division. CCAA Part 3 covers only a judgment of the court chosen in an exclusive agreement within the CCAA; Elbonia is not a Contracting State and its court was not chosen (clause 14 chose Singapore), so the common law governs. Kaldor Labs sues on the judgment debt, serving Bramwell Bio, a Singapore company, here as of right, and Bramwell Bio gets leave to defend only with a real defence, never on the merits (C&Y). Per C&Y, Singapore tests the Elbonian court’s international jurisdiction by its own rules, and the Elbonian refusal of the stay creates no estoppel.

  2. 2
    On the merits, final and for a definite sum H2H5

    Per C&Y, Kaldor Labs must show that the judgment is on the merits, given by a court with international jurisdiction over Bramwell Bio, final and conclusive, and for a definite sum that is not a tax, fine or penalty. A default judgment is on the merits although Bramwell Bio did not appear (C&Y); staying away goes only to fraud or natural justice, nothing suggests fraud, and Bramwell Bio had notice and a chance to defend, so letting the default judgment go by is no breach of natural justice (Sang Cheol Woo). Per Humpuss and Eleven v Boxsentry, a default judgment is final if given final effect until set aside, and the Assume list says Elbonian law does so. US$500,000 in damages is a definite sum. So the fight is international jurisdiction.

  3. 3
    International jurisdiction: was the stay application a submission? H4

    Per Republic of India v Deutsche Telekom, Bramwell Bio must have been present in Elbonia, or have claimed there, voluntarily appeared, or agreed in advance to submit. It had no office, staff or assets in Elbonia, so it was not present (Adams v Cape); it made no claim there; and clause 14 chose Singapore, so it never agreed to Elbonia. That leaves the stay application, judged by Singapore law with Elbonian procedure only as context (Giant Light Metal). On Henry v Geoprosco’s logic, asking for a stay accepts the jurisdiction it asks the court not to use, and Nimbus assumed Henry without deciding; but per IGCF Henry should not be followed, a stay is a protest unless more is sought, and Bramwell Bio sought only the stay and then, as in Nimbus, took no further part. So there was probably no submission and no international jurisdiction, and the judgment is probably not enforced; if Henry is followed, Bramwell Bio submitted and all four requirements are met.

  4. 4
    If the stay was a submission: the clause 14 defence H7

    Per Prof Chong’s March 2026 answer scheme, the defence needs a breach, so the clause must be promissory: clause 14 is expressly exclusive, and Kaldor Labs broke it by suing in Elbonia. But on this route Bramwell Bio submitted, and per C&Y a debtor that submitted loses the objection, so the defence is probably lost. It is undecided anyway: per C&Y damages for the breach could cancel the sum and REFJA s 5(4)(b) gives an analogue, but no Singapore authority recognises the defence. No anti-suit injunction was granted, so the public policy bar for a judgment obtained in breach of one (Nimbus) does not arise. So on this route the judgment would probably be enforced, unless Bramwell Bio’s Supply claim here ends in an inconsistent Singapore judgment, which bars recognition whether it comes earlier or later (Merck). Whether a judgment given while that Singapore claim was pending is recognised at all is open (Merck): Prof Yeo would recognise it, but art 7(2) of the Hague Judgments Convention allows refusal where, as here, Singapore was seised first and the dispute is closely connected with Singapore.

4Remember

🧠 FOR THE EXAM
  • Run the CCAA gate clause by clause: the date row compares when the clause was concluded with when the Convention entered into force for the chosen court’s State (Singapore: 1 October 2016).
  • A Singapore exclusive clause outside the CCAA: serve out on the clause (valid, binds, covers, plus a separate serious question); a forum objection by the defendant needs strong cause, never Spiliada.
  • A pre-1 October 2016 “High Court” clause gives the SICC no primary jurisdiction (O 2 r 2(2)), only a transfer on “more appropriate”, which outside the CCAA does not need every party’s consent; an SICC-only clause is not submission to the General Division (O 2 r 2(3)).
  • Inside the CCAA, s 11 makes the chosen Singapore court hear the case and s 12 makes Singapore stay for a chosen foreign court; delay and fragmentation do not meet s 12(1)(c) or (d).
  • A contractual anti-suit injunction needs no natural forum, but comity re-enters with delay: contesting jurisdiction abroad first is no excuse, and on the eve of trial relief is probably refused.
  • Whether a stay application abroad is a submission is open (Henry v Geoprosco against IGCF): give both routes, and on the submission route the breach-of-clause defence is probably lost too.

LAW302 · META GAME · ★ DO FIRST · QUESTION 1 · HYPO q1-16 · GEMINI PROMPT V2 · LAW REVIEWED 17 NOV · 16 QUESTIONS

Banyan Logistics v Caspian ColdTech and Mr Novak

Gemini (prompt v2) sent only a guide for this hypo, with no usable file. Claude rebuilt the full hypo from it (30 gaps filled or errors fixed), then reviewed it in three passes (21 changes). Gemini's file: q1_16_banyan_logistics_v_caspian_coldtech_and_mr.

Answers:

1Base facts

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Banyan Logistics v Caspian ColdTech and Mr Novak

Banyan Logistics Pte Ltd, a Singapore incorporated cold-chain operator, runs a pharmaceutical warehouse at Changi. Caspian ColdTech SA is incorporated in Ruritania, where it builds industrial compressors. Caspian has no office, staff or assets in Singapore.

Under an Equipment Supply Contract signed on 15 June 2016 and expressly governed by Ruritanian law, Caspian agreed to install compressors at the Changi warehouse and to service them there for ten years. Clause 14 reads:

“The parties submit to the jurisdiction of the Singapore High Court in respect of any dispute arising out of this contract.”

Mr Goran Novak, Caspian's chief technical officer, who lives in Ruritania, signed a separate personal guarantee of Caspian's performance. The guarantee is governed by Ruritanian law and has no jurisdiction clause.

In 2025 the compressors failed and medicines worth US$4.5 million spoiled. Caspian says that the warehouse's power supply caused the failure. Banyan sued Caspian for breach of contract, and Mr Novak on his guarantee, in the General Division. It obtained approval and served Caspian in Ruritania. Caspian applied to set aside service and, in the alternative, for a stay. Banyan served Mr Novak personally at his hotel in Singapore while he attended a three-day trade conference. Mr Novak has applied for a stay in favour of Ruritania. Banyan also asks for the action to be transferred to the Singapore International Commercial Court (SICC).

Advise Banyan whether the Singapore courts have jurisdiction over each defendant, whether they will hear the claims, and whether the case can go to the SICC.

ℹ ASSUME
  1. The Hague Convention on Choice of Court Agreements entered into force for Ruritania on 1 January 2016 and for Singapore on 1 October 2016.
  2. Under Ruritanian law, clause 14 is valid and gives the Singapore High Court jurisdiction. But Ruritanian law treats a jurisdiction clause as procedural only: it contains no promise of any kind.
  3. Ruritanian contract law is a civil law system, quite unlike Singapore's. One of the SICC's International Judges is a retired Ruritanian appeal judge.
  4. Neither contract says how legal process may be served.
  5. The independent engineers who inspected the failed compressors live in Singapore and cannot be made to give evidence in Ruritania. Caspian's engineers who built them live in Ruritania and will give evidence by video link.
  6. A civil trial takes about four years in Ruritania and about 12 months in Singapore.
  7. No claim is time-barred under any relevant law.
✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • A6
    No label: "the parties submit to the jurisdiction of ...". Clause 14 has no label and names the Singapore High Court. Note its date and the law that governs it: construed under Ruritanian law, it holds no promise.
  • B1
    CCAA gate: five conditions. Run the gate. As an unlabelled clause, clause 14 would be deemed exclusive, but it fails the date row: it predates 1 October 2016, when the Convention entered into force for Singapore.
  • D8
    Singapore clause, defendant abroad. Caspian is abroad and clause 14 names Singapore, so the clause gives the nexus. With no promise under Ruritanian law, Caspian's forum objection breaks nothing, so D8 leads to E3, not to strong cause.
  • E3
    Forum conveniens on service out: burden on the claimant. Caspian was served out and attacks service, and no promise is broken. So the forum conveniens burden stays on Banyan.
  • E4
    SCORECARD · Spiliada stage 1: connecting factors. Mark the stage 1 factors: clause 14 still points to Singapore, Ruritanian law points away, and the witness facts must be weighed.
  • D1
    Defendant can be served in Singapore. Mr Novak was personally served while present in Singapore, so jurisdiction over him exists as of right.
  • E2
    Stay after service in Singapore: Spiliada starter. Mr Novak, served here and outside clause 14, asks for a stay: plain Spiliada with stage 1 on him. The trial delay is Banyan's stage 2 point.
  • F3
    "Singapore High Court" clause: check the date. Banyan wants the SICC, and clause 14 names the Singapore High Court. It predates 1 October 2016, so it does not of itself reach the SICC.
  • F6
    SCORECARD · Transfer from the General Division: is the SICC "more appropriate"?. With no primary jurisdiction, the SICC is reached only by transfer. The Ruritanian International Judge goes to whether the SICC is more appropriate.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • B2
    CCAA applies and Singapore is the chosen court (s 11). Tempting because clause 14 names Singapore and was signed after Ruritania's Convention date. But the test date is that of the chosen court's State, and clause 14 predates 1 October 2016.
  • E7
    Strong cause: starter and nature of the test. Tempting because a Singapore clause usually puts strong cause on a defendant who objects. Here proved Ruritanian law finds no promise in clause 14, so Caspian breaks nothing.
  • A4
    Says "non-exclusive": Singapore courts. Tempting because Singapore law reads “submit” as a waiver of objection, which A4 turns into strong cause on the defendant. But clause 14 is read under proved Ruritanian law, which finds no promise in it.
  • D9
    The contract says how process may be served. D9 is for a contract that allows service abroad without approval. Neither contract deals with service, so Banyan needed approval.
  • D2
    Foreign company never registered here, with an office or agent here. Tempting because Caspian's chief technical officer was served in Singapore. But D2 needs a company with an office or agent here, and Caspian has neither. Serving an officer on a visit is doubtful when the company itself is absent, and Banyan served Caspian abroad instead.

Fair to tick but not needed: B4 Outside the CCAA: say why, then the common law, D4 Defendant abroad: service out and the three requirements, D5 Gateway: name the sub-limb of PD para 63(3), D7 Serious question to be tried, D11 How to serve abroad, and the set-aside, E1 Which test, and who bears the burden, E5 SCORECARD · Spiliada stage 2: substantial justice, E6 Second bite: claimant fails stage 1 on service out, E9 The SICC as a Spiliada factor, A9 Is this claim, or this party, inside the clause?, F1 International and commercial

Application questions · base facts

⚡ Base facts · 1 of 7B1
Is Banyan's claim against Caspian a CCAA case?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Temporal scope turns on the State of the chosen court. Clause 14 chooses Singapore, where the Convention entered into force on 1 October 2016, and it was signed on 15 June 2016. Ruritania's date is irrelevant to a Singapore clause. Had the date fitted, s 3(2) would deem the unlabelled clause exclusive, whatever Ruritanian law says about promises.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J1.2.2 :: Temporal Scope

  • UK clauses (±): the HCCCA applied to the UK via the EU from 1 October 2015 and in its own right from 1 January 2021; continuity across Brexit is contested, so [an English clause] concluded on [a date between them] is arguable either way.
⚡ Base facts · 2 of 7A6
Does Caspian break a promise in clause 14 by asking the court to set aside service?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

A jurisdiction clause may contain a promise not to object to the chosen court. Whether clause 14 does is a matter of construction under its proper law, here Ruritanian law. That law is proved and finds no promise, so Caspian breaks nothing by objecting, whether it sets aside or seeks a stay. The narrow waiver in Shanghai Turbo is how Singapore law reads “submit”, so it applies where Singapore law governs or the foreign law is not proved.

If [Ruritanian law] is proved and implies no waiver, [clause X] contains only (1A), so [defendant]'s FNC objection is no breach and Spiliada applies (J4.1; J4.2).

Who bears the forum burden on Caspian's set-aside, and on Mr Novak's stay?

Per Chong's answer scheme, where clause 14 read under Ruritanian law contains no promise, Caspian breaks nothing by objecting, so the test is plain forum conveniens with the burden on Banyan, which served Caspian out. Mr Novak was served here as of right, so he bears stage 1 on his stay. Caspian's fall-back stay is not submission, but per Zoom it takes on the stage 1 burden that the set-aside leaves with Banyan.

  • Then: [the Singapore clause] is only a factor; weigh [the governing law] against the possibility of transfer to the SICC (J4.4), and raise the Konamaneni stage 2 issue if stage 1 points to [X] (J3.1.3).
⚡ Base facts · 4 of 7D1
Mr Novak says that jurisdiction founded on a three-day conference visit is arbitrary. What is the answer?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per s 16(1)(a)(i) SCJA, Mr Novak was personally served at his hotel as of right under O 7 r 2(1)(a). Per Maharanee of Baroda v Wildenstein and Colt Industries v Sarlie, presence on a short visit suffices, with no other connection needed. Only presence induced by fraud may be set aside (Watkins v North American Land), and he came for a conference. Per C&Y, the fleeting visit goes to the natural forum, not to existence.

⚡ Base facts · 5 of 7E4

⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Chong's answer scheme, where a clause naming Singapore contains no promise under its own law, Spiliada applies, but the clause still points to Singapore at stage 1. It is only one factor, weighed with the governing law, the possible transfer to the SICC and the rest. It does not move the burden, which stays on Banyan as the party that served out.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J4.1.2 :: Singapore Clause Without a Promise (+)

Per Chong's answer scheme, where [clause X] naming [Singapore] contains no promise under [law X], Spiliada applies, but the clause still points to Singapore at stage 1.

⚡ Base facts · 6 of 7F3
Could Banyan have filed its claim against Caspian directly in the SICC?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per O 2 r 2(2), a clause concluded before 1 October 2016 that names the High Court “does not of itself” submit to the SICC. Per Chong (sample-final answer scheme), there is then no primary jurisdiction, so Banyan sues in the General Division and seeks a transfer. Only a clause concluded on or after that date includes the SICC.

⚡ Base facts · 7 of 7F6
What must Banyan show to have the action transferred to the SICC?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per O 2 r 4(1), the General Division may transfer if the action is international and commercial when the order is made, no prerogative relief is sought, and the SICC is more appropriate. Outside the CCAA, the court may transfer without every party's consent. Per Chong (seminar), the test turns on how international and commercial the case is, not its complexity. Per Chong (AY23-24 mid-term feedback), an International Judge with expertise in the governing law, here the retired Ruritanian judge, favours the SICC.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J5.4.1 :: Requirements (must write)

Per O 2 r 4(1), it may transfer if (a) [the action] is international and commercial when the order is made; (b) no prerogative relief is sought; and (c) the SICC is more appropriate.

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
⚡ BIG IDEA

An unlabelled “Singapore High Court” clause, governed by Ruritanian law and signed before 1 October 2016, is outside the CCAA, and proved Ruritanian law gives it no promise. So Caspian, served out, breaks nothing by objecting: plain forum conveniens with the burden on Banyan, the clause only one stage 1 factor, and the SICC only by transfer, while Mr Novak, served on a short visit and outside the clause, bears stage 1 on his own stay. Twist 1 leaves Ruritanian law unpleaded, so Singapore law reads in the waiver and strong cause falls on Caspian. Twist 2 dates the clause 2019: s 11 removes forum discretion over the claim against Caspian, the SICC gains primary jurisdiction over that claim, and the injunction argues breach of a deemed exclusive clause as open, then vexation.

  1. 1
    Clause 14: no label, Ruritanian law A6

    Clause 14 says the parties “submit to the jurisdiction of the Singapore High Court”, with no word “exclusive”. Whether it holds a promise not to object to Singapore is construction under its proper law, Ruritanian law (Shanghai Turbo). Ruritanian law is proved: clause 14 is valid and gives Singapore jurisdiction, but holds no promise of any kind. So Caspian breaks nothing by objecting, whether it sets aside service or seeks a stay; had neither party pleaded Ruritanian law, Singapore law would apply by default and read the waiver into “submit” (Twist 1). Note the date, 15 June 2016, for the CCAA and the SICC.

  2. 2
    The CCAA gate fails on the date B1

    Unlabelled, clause 14 would be deemed exclusive under s 3(2), whatever Ruritanian law says. But the CCAA covers only a clause concluded after the Convention entered into force for the State of the chosen court. Clause 14 chooses Singapore, whose date is 1 October 2016, and it was signed on 15 June 2016. Ruritania's earlier date, 1 January 2016, is irrelevant, and one failed row is enough. So the common law decides.

  3. 3
    Caspian: service out, with clause 14 as the nexus D8

    Caspian has no office, staff or assets here, so Banyan needed approval to serve it in Ruritania (O 8 r 1(1)); neither contract deals with service, so O 8 r 1(3) does not help. Outside the CCAA, approval goes on the “appropriate court” ground, with the three PD para 63(2) requirements (Chong's answer scheme). The nexus is clause 14 itself, under para 63(3)(r) or (d)(iv) (Shanghai Turbo). These factors are neutral, so Banyan must also show a serious question: the compressors failed, the medicines spoiled and Caspian blames the power supply, and nothing is time-barred. With no promise broken, the forum limb stays: it is forum conveniens, not strong cause.

  4. 4
    Forum conveniens: the burden stays on Banyan E3

    Per Chong's answer scheme, where clause 14 read under Ruritanian law holds no promise, Caspian breaks nothing by objecting, so the test is plain forum conveniens with the burden on Banyan. Per Zoom, it is the Spiliada test with the burden reversed, and on a set-aside the burden stays on Banyan for all three requirements (Li Shengwu). Banyan must show Singapore is clearly the more appropriate forum (Spiliada), not merely as appropriate as Ruritania (Sudarga); per Oro Negro, “on balance” suffices, so argue both. Caspian should argue forum inside its set-aside: its fall-back stay is not submission, but per Zoom it takes on the stage 1 burden that the set-aside leaves with Banyan.

  5. 5
    Stage 1 factors, and stage 2 if needed E4

    Clause 14 still points to Singapore, but only as one factor (Chong's answer scheme). Ruritanian law, expressly chosen and very different, points away, but it weighs most where the dispute turns on law, and this one turns on why the compressors failed (Rickshaw; JIO). Banyan may name the SICC feature, a retired Ruritanian appeal judge (Rappo), but that at most discounts the weight of Ruritanian law, depending on how far it differs and how complex the issues are, and never decides alone (IM Skaugen). Performance is disputed at Changi, and the independent engineers, who live in Singapore, cannot be made to testify in Ruritania, while Caspian's own engineers will use video and the party links cancel out, so Singapore is probably the more appropriate forum, all the more on the Oro Negro “on balance” test. Had stage 1 pointed to Ruritania, whether Banyan gets a second bite at stage 2 is open: no per Konamaneni and Allenger, yes per Spiliada, Yeo and Shen Sophie. Even on the second route, a four-year trial is delay, disregarded unless egregious (C&Y; Grains and Industrial), so service would be set aside either way.

  6. 6
    Mr Novak: presence founds jurisdiction D1

    Mr Novak was personally served at his hotel while present here, so jurisdiction exists as of right (s 16(1)(a)(i) SCJA; O 7 r 2(1)(a)). Presence on a short visit is enough, with no other link (Maharanee of Baroda v Wildenstein; Colt Industries v Sarlie). Service is set aside only where presence was induced by fraud (Watkins v North American Land), and he came for a conference. If he calls this arbitrary, jurisdiction is territorial (Sirdar Gurdyal Singh), and per Chong (seminar) forum non conveniens corrects the fortuity at the exercise stage.

  7. 7
    Mr Novak's stay: plain Spiliada E2

    Mr Novak signed only the guarantee, which has no jurisdiction clause, so clause 14 cannot saddle him with a burden (Chong, AY23-24 feedback). Served here, he bears stage 1: he must show Ruritania is clearly or distinctly more appropriate (Spiliada; JIO). His brief visit (C&Y) and the Ruritanian law of the guarantee help him, while his home in Ruritania only cancels out Banyan's in Singapore. But his liability turns on the same failure at Changi, and with the claim against Caspian staying here, a stay would split one dispute between two courts (C&Y; Mulacek), so it probably fails. The four-year Ruritanian trial would be Banyan's stage 2 point, but delay counts only if egregious (C&Y; Grains and Industrial).

  8. 8
    The SICC: only by transfer F3F6

    Clause 14 names the Singapore High Court and predates 1 October 2016, so per O 2 r 2(2) it “does not of itself” submit the parties to the SICC, and there is no primary jurisdiction (Chong, sample-final answer scheme). Banyan rightly sued in the General Division and must seek a transfer. Per O 2 r 4(1), the court may transfer if the action is international and commercial when the order is made, no prerogative relief is sought, and the SICC is more appropriate; outside the CCAA it may do so without every party's consent (C&Y). The test turns on how international and commercial the dispute is, not its complexity (Chong, seminar), and here the parties are in different States and the claims are commercial. An International Judge expert in the governing law, here the retired Ruritanian appeal judge, favours the SICC (Chong, AY23-24 mid-term feedback), though nothing suggests the defendants consent, which would make the court lean towards transfer (C&Y). So Banyan has a fair case for a transfer of the whole action, but it remains a discretion.

  9. 9
    Result

    Service on Caspian probably stands: clause 14 gives the nexus, there is a serious question, and Singapore is probably the more appropriate forum. Mr Novak is within jurisdiction by presence, and his stay probably fails. The case can reach the SICC only by a transfer from the General Division, for which Banyan has a fair case.

Application questions · twist 1

⚡ Twist 1 · 1 of 4A4
With Ruritanian law on clause 14 neither pleaded nor proved, does Caspian break a promise by objecting to Singapore?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Whether clause 14 contains the promise not to object is for its proper law. If that law is not proved, the presumption of similarity reads in the same waiver as Singapore law. Here neither party even pleads Ruritanian law on the point, so Singapore law applies by default (Brownlie; EFT Holdings), which C&Y also call a presumption. The limit on presuming a civil law system similar to Singapore's (C&Y) is for law that is pleaded but not proved, so it does not arise. Per Shanghai Turbo, “submit” means consenting to the named court and waiving any objection to its exercise of jurisdiction. So Caspian's set-aside and its stay are both attempts to escape clause 14. The date is unchanged, so the CCAA still does not apply.

Per O 2 r 2(1) and s 2(2) to (3) CCAA, a “Singapore High Court” clause concluded on or after 1 October 2016 includes the SICC unless a contrary intention appears. Whether that rule applies where foreign law governs the clause is open, but per Chong (seminar) a foreign law with no rule of its own falls back on O 2 r 2(1), and Ruritanian law has none, so the result is the same either way. Moving it from the General Division would be a CCAA transfer, needing every party's consent, which clause 14 is deemed to give, though per C&Y it is unclear whether that is enough. The SICC has no primary jurisdiction over the claim against Mr Novak.

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes

    Two things change. Clause 14 is now dated 15 June 2019, and a week after being served Caspian sued Banyan in Ruritania for a declaration that the compressors met the contract and that it owes nothing; Banyan at once applied to restrain that action. The Ruritanian action is at an early stage, and Ruritanian law has no rule on which Singapore court a “Singapore High Court” clause covers. What stays: proved Ruritanian law still finds no promise in clause 14, and Mr Novak, outside it, keeps his Spiliada stay, which probably fails as in the base; Caspian's new action adds little to it, as it is at an early stage and he is not a party (Lakshmi; C&Y).

  2. 2
    Inside the CCAA: s 11 and the SICC B2F2

    Clause 14 now postdates 1 October 2016, Singapore's date; s 3(2) deems it exclusive whatever Ruritanian law says; and the case is international and commercial, so the CCAA applies. Per s 11, Singapore must hear the claim against Caspian and cannot decline in favour of Ruritania: no Spiliada, no strong cause, and Caspian's witnesses, Ruritanian law and Ruritanian suit are irrelevant (C&Y). Approval to serve Caspian out goes on the “has the jurisdiction” ground (Chong's answer scheme), with no nexus or forum conveniens inquiry (C&Y). A High Court clause concluded on or after 1 October 2016 includes the SICC (O 2 r 2(1); s 2(2) to (3) CCAA). Whether that forum rule reaches a clause governed by Ruritanian law is open, but the result is the same either way, as Ruritanian law has no rule of its own and so falls back on O 2 r 2(1) (Chong, seminar). Caspian may cite a query in Prof Chong's answer scheme that a more specific reference to the SICC is needed, which would leave only a transfer, but the scheme itself gave primary jurisdiction under a clause worded like clause 14. So Banyan could file the Caspian claim in the SICC. Moving it from the General Division instead is a CCAA transfer needing every party's consent: clause 14 deems Caspian's (O 2 r 4(7)), but C&Y find it unclear whether that is enough, given the art 8(5) risk of refused recognition in Ruritania if Caspian objects in time, and if actual consent is needed, Caspian's refusal blocks the transfer.

  3. 3
    The injunction: amenability, then breach G2G9

    An injunction indirectly interferes with the Ruritanian court, so it issues only where the ends of justice require, with caution (SNIA; Lakshmi), and Banyan must name its basis (Cooperative Muratori). Sought as ancillary relief in Banyan's action (Chong's answer scheme), it rests on the valid service out on Caspian, which suffices for amenability (Cooperative Muratori; C&Y); Caspian may cite Akai, but its lack of presence or assets here goes only to how well the order bites. Breach is open. For: per C&Y, s 3(2) makes clause 14 exclusive in effect, so a contractual injunction is arguable; it would ordinarily issue unless Caspian shows strong reasons (Sun Travels), and foreseeable points such as its Ruritanian witnesses are not enough (C&Y). Against: breach is a question of contract under the proper law, and Ruritanian law finds no promise, so deeming arguably settles only jurisdiction. Prof Chong's answer scheme leaves breach open, so argue it, then run vexation in the alternative.

  4. 4
    The vexation route G7

    Without breach, clause 14 still gives Singapore a sufficient interest (Prof Chong's answer scheme), so Banyan need not prove Singapore is the natural forum. Vexation must still be shown, in the clearest cases only (Kirkham; UBS v Telesto), and parallel proceedings alone are not enough. Here Caspian sued a week after being served, on a claim that mirrors its defence here (Lakshmi); the independent engineers, key witnesses on why the compressors failed, cannot be made to testify in Ruritania (UBS v Telesto); and the action abroad is at an early stage (Baker v BCS (SICC); C&Y). Any advantage Caspian loses counts for less as Ruritania is probably not the natural forum (UBS v Telesto), and undertakings can meet a genuine one (SNIA). Ruritania's court should itself decline under art 6, which gives the chosen court more leeway (C&Y). Per the scheme, Singapore “will likely grant the ASI”, so the injunction is probably granted, though it remains a discretion.

Prof Chong rewards applying facts to factor tests. Sort each fact, then answer the verdict question. These use the base facts unless a line says “Suppose”.

E4 Sort the factors: Stage 1 on Caspian's set-aside

Banyan must show that Singapore is the more appropriate forum. Where does each fact point at stage 1?

Clause 14 names the Singapore High Court, though Ruritanian law finds no promise in it.
Singapore. Per Chong's answer scheme, a clause naming Singapore with no promise under its own law still points to Singapore at stage 1. It is a factor, not a test. J4.1.2 :: Singapore Clause Without a Promise

Ruritania. An express choice of a very different law points to Ruritania. Its weight falls because the dispute turns mainly on fact: why the compressors failed. J4.1.2 :: Governing Law: When Weighty
Banyan points out that one of the SICC's International Judges is a retired Ruritanian appeal judge.
Singapore. Per IM Skaugen, the SICC route at most discounts the weight of Ruritanian law, depending on how far it differs from Singapore law and how complex the issues are. It is never decisive alone, and per Rappo Banyan must show a transfer is prima facie available. J4.4 :: At Most a Discount
The independent engineers who inspected the compressors live in Singapore and cannot be made to testify in Ruritania.
Singapore. Compellability matters more than convenience. Non-party witnesses who can be compelled only here point to Singapore. J4.2.2 :: Witnesses

Neutral or little weight. They are Caspian's own employees and will testify by video, so where they live carries little weight. J4.1.2 :: Compellability Reduced

Neutral or little weight. A claimant here and a defendant there cancel out. J4.1.2 :: Parties: Neutral or Counterbalancing

Singapore. The place of performance is neutral unless performance is disputed. Here it is, and the evidence of the failure is at the warehouse. J4.1.2 :: Events: Contract

Neutral or little weight. Delay is not a connecting factor. It is a stage 2 point, and even there it is disregarded unless egregious. J4.1.3 :: Delay
⚡ Scorecard 1 · the verdictE4
On the base facts, what is the likely result?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

The clause, the disputed failure at the Changi warehouse and the independent engineers who can be compelled only here point to Singapore. Ruritanian law points away, but the dispute turns mainly on fact, and the SICC route may discount it. The party connections cancel out, and Caspian's own engineers will testify by video. Mr Novak bears stage 1 on much the same factors, and staying his claim would split one dispute between two courts. Delay is a stage 2 point, not reached here.

5Remember

🧠 FOR THE EXAM
  • Date a Singapore clause against Singapore's Convention date, 1 October 2016; the other party's State's date is irrelevant.
  • Outside the CCAA, whether an unlabelled clause holds a promise not to object is for its proper law: proved foreign law with no promise means plain forum conveniens, with the burden on a claimant that served out and the clause as one stage 1 factor.
  • If the foreign law is not pleaded, Singapore law reads the narrow waiver into “submit”, so an objecting defendant bears strong cause, and foreseeable witnesses or foreign law will not make it out.
  • Presence when served founds jurisdiction however short the visit; the fortuity goes to the stay, and a stranger to the clause served here stays on plain Spiliada with stage 1 on him.
  • A “Singapore High Court” clause concluded before 1 October 2016 reaches the SICC only by transfer under O 2 r 4(1); one concluded on or after that date includes the SICC.
  • Inside the CCAA, s 11 removes forum discretion; for an injunction, breach of a clause exclusive only by s 3(2), with no promise under its proper law, is open, so argue breach, then vexation, with the clause giving sufficient interest.
