LAW302 · META GAME · ★ DO FIRST · QUESTION 1 · HYPO q1-07 · GEMINI PROMPT V1 · 15 QUESTIONS

Galen v Brask

Written by Claude for the drill and law reviewed. Gemini (prompt v1) rebalanced the option lengths and wrote a note on each question; both were checked (6 corrections) and feed the notes here.

Answers:

1Base facts

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Galen v Brask

Galen Ferries Pte Ltd, a Singapore incorporated company, runs passenger ferries from Singapore. Brask Yard Ltd is incorporated in Elbonia, where it builds ships. Brask has no office, staff or assets in Singapore.

Under a Shipbuilding Contract signed on 14 February 2022 and governed by Singapore law, Brask built two electric ferries and delivered them to Galen in Singapore. Clause 27 reads:

“Brask may bring proceedings against Galen only in the courts of Elbonia, and Galen submits to the jurisdiction of those courts. Galen may bring proceedings against Brask in the courts of any country, and Brask submits to the jurisdiction of any court so chosen.”

The ferries' batteries overheat. Galen has refused to pay the final instalment of US$7 million. In May 2026 Brask sued Galen in Elbonia for the instalment.

Galen denies that it owes anything. It wants a Singapore court to declare that it is not liable to pay the instalment, and it would prefer the Singapore International Commercial Court. It also wants the Elbonian action stopped. Brask says that it will contest any Singapore proceedings.

Advise Galen whether a Singapore court will hear its claim, and whether it can stop the Elbonian action.

ℹ ASSUME
  1. The Hague Convention on Choice of Court Agreements entered into force for Elbonia on 1 January 2019.
  2. Under Singapore law, both sentences of clause 27 are valid and are read together.
  3. The Elbonian action is at an early stage. Galen has been served and has taken no step in it.
  4. Brask's designers and welders live in Elbonia. The engineers who examined the batteries live in Singapore. Both courts take evidence by video link.
  5. A civil trial takes about six years in Elbonia and about one year in Singapore.
  6. An Elbonian court will not recognise a Singapore declaration.
  7. The contract does not say how legal process may be served.
✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • A7
    Asymmetric clause: one side may sue anywhere. Clause 27 is asymmetric. Brask may sue only in Elbonia. Galen may sue anywhere, and Brask submits. Work out who promised what before anything else.
  • B1
    CCAA gate: five conditions. Elbonia is a Contracting State and the dates fit, so run the gate. The contract fails on one row: a clause that lets one side sue anywhere is not exclusive under the CCAA.
  • D6
    The Singapore claim is for a negative declaration. Galen is the natural defendant and wants a declaration that it is not liable. A negative declaration needs its own nexus and a serious question shown separately.
  • D8
    Singapore clause, defendant abroad. Brask is abroad, and it agreed to submit to any court Galen chose, including Singapore. In practice Galen shows that this limb is valid, binds Brask and covers the dispute.
  • E7
    Strong cause: starter and nature of the test. Brask will contest Singapore's jurisdiction. That breaks its promise to submit, so the test is strong cause and the burden is on Brask.
  • E8
    SCORECARD · Strong cause: the Eleftheria factors. The witness, delay and recognition facts are there to be marked on the strong cause scorecard. They were foreseeable when the clause was signed.
  • G1
    ASI starter, and the basis. Galen wants the Elbonian action stopped. That is an anti-suit injunction, and Galen must name its basis.
  • G5
    Twist: the applicant's own ASI application breaks a clause. The clause sends Brask to Elbonia, so its action breaks nothing. Galen promised to submit there, so its own application for an injunction is a breach.
  • F2
    Primary jurisdiction under a written jurisdiction agreement. Galen wants the SICC. Ask whether Brask's agreement to submit to “any court so chosen” is a written jurisdiction agreement for the SICC.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • B3
    CCAA applies and a foreign court is chosen (s 12). Tempting because Elbonia is a Contracting State and Galen submits to its courts. Wrong because the clause is asymmetric: per CHLOE V it is not exclusive under the CCAA, so s 12 cannot be engaged.
  • G3
    Contractual ASI: a Singapore clause is breached. A contractual injunction needs a respondent who broke a promise by suing abroad. Elbonia is the only court Brask is allowed to use.
  • E3
    Forum conveniens on service out: burden on the claimant. A negative declaration served out with no clause is won or lost on forum conveniens, with the burden on the claimant. Here Brask promised to submit, so its objection is a breach and the test is strong cause.
  • A3
    Says "exclusive": a foreign court. A3 is for a claimant who sues here in breach of a foreign exclusive clause. The Elbonia-only promise binds Brask alone. Galen is free to sue in any country.
  • G9
    ASI in a CCAA case. G9 is for an injunction in a contract inside the CCAA. This contract is outside it.

Fair to tick but not needed: B4 Outside the CCAA: say why, then the common law, A1 Any jurisdiction clause: what it promises, D4 Defendant abroad: service out and the three requirements, D5 Gateway: name the sub-limb of PD para 63(3), D7 Serious question to be tried, G2 Amenability, G6 Vexation ASI: sufficient interest, G7 SCORECARD · Vexation or oppression, and injustice to the respondent, F1 International and commercial, F4 Serving the defendant abroad from the SICC, F5 Exercise in the SICC: O 2 r 3, no Spiliada, E10 Parallel foreign proceedings, and time bars

Application questions · base facts

⚡ Base facts · 1 of 7B1
Is the Shipbuilding Contract a CCAA case?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per CHLOE V, following the Hartley–Dogauchi Report, an asymmetric clause is not an exclusive choice of court agreement under the CCAA, so s 12 cannot be engaged. The Contracting State, date, international and commercial rows are all met. Per C&Y, at common law the clause stays exclusive against the restricted party, so the promises in it still decide who is in breach.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per CHLOE V, following the Hartley–Dogauchi Report, an asymmetric clause that lets one party sue in any court is not an exclusive choice of court agreement under the CCAA, so s 12 cannot be engaged. Per Etihad (EWCA) (obiter), the Convention probably excludes such clauses; earlier first-instance dicta reading it more widely (Commerzbank v Liquimar; Etihad (EWHC)) are weak after CHLOE V. The other rows pass: Elbonia has been a Contracting State since 1 January 2019, clause 27 was signed on 14 February 2022, the parties are in different States, and a shipbuilding contract is commercial. Per C&Y, at common law the clause stays exclusive against the restricted party, Brask, so its promises still decide who is in breach.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J1.2.1 :: Asymmetric Clause (−)

Presently, [clause X] gives [State B] exclusive jurisdiction but lets [the lender] sue [the borrower] [anywhere]. Per CHLOE V, following the Hartley–Dogauchi Report (VCLT art 32), such a clause is not exclusive under the CCAA, so s 12 cannot be engaged even on [the court's own motion], and even though [defendant] conceded the point.

  • Support: Per Etihad (EWCA) (obiter), the Convention probably excludes [asymmetric clauses] like [clause X], the Diplomatic Session having rejected a Swiss proposal to cover clauses exclusive "for some or all of the parties".
  • Counter (+): Earlier first-instance dicta (Commerzbank v Liquimar; Etihad (EWHC)) read the Convention's wording as wide enough for [clause X], but [the lender]'s reliance on them is weak after CHLOE V.
  • Consequence: At common law [clause X] stays exclusive against [the restricted party] (per C&Y), so J1.1 applies.
⚡ Base facts · 2 of 7E7
Galen sues in Singapore and serves Brask in Elbonia. Brask applies to set service aside and says that Elbonia is the proper forum. Who bears the burden, and of what?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Under an asymmetric clause with a submission limb, if the favoured party sues here the other party has agreed to submit, so it bears strong cause. The burden lies on the party seeking release from its promise, on a stay or a set-aside. Galen made no promise to sue only in Elbonia. Spiliada is never the strong cause test.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Under an asymmetric clause with a submission limb, if the favoured party sues here, the other party has agreed to submit, so it bears strong cause (handout clause bank). By analogy with Shanghai Turbo (CA), under Singapore law, the contract's law, “submits” means consenting to the court's jurisdiction and waiving any objection to its exercise. So Brask's challenge breaks that promise, and the burden lies on the party seeking release from its promise, on a stay or a set-aside, even though Galen served out (Shanghai Turbo (CA)). If Brask instead attacked the clause itself (no agreement, void, outside its scope), the burden on that point would stay on Galen. Spiliada is never the strong cause test.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J1.1.4 :: Asymmetric, With Submission

["[A] may sue [B] in any court, [B] submitting to it; [B] may sue [A] only in [Y]"]. If [A] sues here, [B] agreed to submit, so [B] bears strong cause to stay; if [B] sues here, [B] breaches its [Y]-only promise and bears strong cause.

⚡ Base facts · 3 of 7D8
What must Galen show to serve its claim on Brask in Elbonia from the General Division?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Outside the CCAA, service goes on the “appropriate court” ground. In principle Galen must make out all three requirements. In practice it need only show that the clause is valid, binds Brask and covers the dispute. The clause is a neutral nexus, so the serious question is shown separately. Forum need not be proved: if Brask raises it, Brask bears strong cause. Approval is still needed because the contract says nothing about service.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

The contract says nothing about service, so O 8 r 1(3) does not apply and Galen needs approval under O 8 r 1(1). Outside the CCAA the ground is “appropriate court”, as the answer scheme uses for its asymmetric clause; “has the jurisdiction” is arguably kept for CCAA cases. In principle (Week 9 slides) Galen must make out all three requirements, with sentence two as the nexus under para 63(3)(r), as Brask “agreed to submit”, or (d)(iv). In practice (Chong's answer scheme; C&Y) it need only show that the clause is valid, binds Brask and covers the dispute, plus a serious question, shown separately because (r) and (d)(iv) are neutral. If Brask contests forum, that breaks its promise, so Brask bears strong cause (Shanghai Turbo (CA)).

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J3.2 :: Singapore EJC or NEJC: In Principle v In Practice (must write)

Per Week 9 slides, [claimant] relies on [the Singapore clause] against [defendant]:

  • In principle, [claimant] must still make out all three requirements against [defendant], even inter partes.
  • Nexus: [the clause] itself, under para 63(3)(r) ([defendant] "agreed to submit") or (d)(iv) (Shanghai Turbo (CA); J3.1.2).
  • In practice, [claimant] need only show a good arguable case that [the clause] is valid, binds [defendant] and covers [the dispute] (J1.5–J1.6), plus a serious question, shown separately because (d)(iv) and (r) are neutral (J3.1.4).
  • Forum: need not be proved. If [defendant] contests it, that breaches its promise, so per Shanghai Turbo (CA) [defendant] bears strong cause (J4.3), whether it challenges existence or exercise; if [defendant] never raises it, [claimant] need prove nothing.
⚡ Base facts · 4 of 7D6
Galen is the natural defendant and claims only a declaration that it is not liable. What does that change?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

The pre-write block is written for a declaration that no contract exists, but the same steps apply to a declaration of no liability under an admitted contract, and the answer scheme runs them that way. A negative declaration needs a nexus like any other claim, and here the clause supplies it. That nexus does not engage the merits, so the serious question is stated separately. With no clause the case would be won or lost on forum conveniens. With Brask's promise to submit, as in Bunge, its forum objection is a breach and needs strong cause.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

The pre-write pattern is written for a declaration that no contract exists, but the answer scheme runs the same steps for a declaration of no breach under an admitted contract. A negative declaration needs a nexus like any other claim; here sentence two supplies it, with Singapore governing law ((d)(iii)) in the alternative. Neither engages the merits, so the serious question is shown separately. With no clause, the case would be won or lost on forum conveniens, with the burden on Galen as the party serving out. Because Brask promised to submit, its forum objection is a breach requiring strong cause, as in Bunge.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J3.1.2 :: Pattern: Negative Declaration that No Contract Exists

Presently, [claimant] seeks a declaration that no contract was concluded with [defendant], which is suing on it in [X].

  • Usable (1): (d)(i), as [the negotiations were conducted and concluded here], needing only a good arguable case of the connection; (d)(iii), if the putative proper law of [the alleged contract] is Singapore law (Lew v Nargolwala; C2).
  • Usable (2): (p), arguably, reading "cause of action" generously, [the formation events] having occurred here; (n), through para 14 of the First Schedule (Li Shengwu) for [the declaration].
  • Not usable: (e) ([claimant] alleges no breach; [the breach claim] is [defendant]'s, in [X]); (c) (no anchor defendant); (b) (an ASI against [the X proceedings] is separate: J6); (s) (no Singapore statute).
  • Then: none of these engages the merits of [the declaration], so state the serious question separately (J3.1.4), and [the case] is won or lost on forum (J4.2).
  • Clause in a related contract: where [a concluded contract between the parties] has a Singapore EJC wide enough to catch [the dealings], [defendant]'s forum objection is a breach requiring strong cause (Bunge; J3.2).
  • Infection: but [claimant] who says no contract was concluded must meet the infection point before relying on [that contract's clause] (J1.6).
⚡ Base facts · 5 of 7E8
Brask says that its witnesses are in Elbonia, that its Elbonian action came first, and that Elbonia will not recognise a Singapore declaration. Is that strong cause?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Vinmar, where only the parties to the clause are involved, strong cause is generally abuse of process or denial of justice. Witnesses abroad were foreseeable and can use video link. A clause that lets Galen sue anywhere while Brask must sue in Elbonia makes parallel actions foreseeable, and related foreign proceedings were not enough in Shanghai Turbo. That a Singapore judgment may not be recognised abroad was foreseeable too.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Vinmar, factors foreseeable at contracting carry little weight, and here both courts take evidence by video link. A clause that lets Galen sue anywhere while Brask must sue in Elbonia makes parallel actions foreseeable, and in Shanghai Turbo related foreign proceedings were not strong cause. Per C&Y, that a Singapore judgment may not be enforced where the defendant's assets are was foreseeable, so it weighs little. As Brask objects to a forum it agreed to, factors (d) and (e) are flipped: is Galen's suit here abusive, or would Brask be prejudiced defending here? Nothing on these facts suggests either.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J4.3.1 :: Two Grounds

Per Vinmar, where only [the clause's parties] are involved, strong cause is generally [abuse of process] or [denial of justice]; with [non-parties], fragmentation may suffice (J4.3.4). The list is not closed.

⚡ Base facts · 6 of 7G5
Is Brask's Elbonian action a breach of clause 27, and what about Galen's application to stop it?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Prof Chong's answer scheme, where the clause lets the respondent sue abroad and the applicant promised to submit there, the application for the injunction is the applicant's own breach. So ask who bears strong cause: arguably the applicant, as the party in breach. A six year wait in Elbonia was foreseeable and would not release Galen. Whether the “any country” limb gives Singapore a sufficient interest is also open, because the injunction is not founded on a breach by Brask.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Chong (answer scheme), where the clause lets the respondent sue in the foreign court and the applicant promised to submit there, seeking the injunction is the applicant's own breach, so ask who bears strong cause. Arguably Galen does, as the party in breach, and a six year trial in Elbonia was foreseeable when it signed (Vinmar), so it would not be released. If the burden is not put on Galen, it still needs a basis: the rule that an injunction issues unless the respondent shows strong reasons assumes a respondent who sued in breach (Sun Travels), and Brask did not, so Galen is left with vexation, where parallel proceedings alone are not enough (UBS v Telesto). Either way the injunction is unlikely. Sufficient interest is open too: per Cooperative Muratori it is not needed where the injunction rests on breach of agreement, but this one rests on no breach by Brask.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J6.3.1.4 :: Applicant Itself in Breach (−)

Presently, [clause X] lets [respondent] sue in [foreign court], so its suit breaches nothing, but [applicant] promised to submit there. Per Chong (answer scheme), seeking the ASI is then [applicant]'s own breach, so ask who bears strong cause: arguably [applicant], as the party in breach.

⚡ Base facts · 7 of 7F2
Can Galen file its claim directly in the SICC?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Chong (sample-final answer scheme), an “any court” limb can give the SICC primary jurisdiction over an international and commercial claim, with service as of right and the SICC's own test for exercising jurisdiction. The scheme adds the counter: arguably the clause needs a more specific reference to the SICC to qualify as a written jurisdiction agreement for it. If it does not qualify, Galen sues in the General Division and asks for a transfer.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Chong (sample-final answer scheme), an “any court” limb can give the SICC primary jurisdiction over an international and commercial claim. The claim is international, as Brask's place of business is in Elbonia, and commercial, as it arises from a shipbuilding contract. Brask, a party to the written agreement, is then served out without permission (O 5 r 6(2)(a)), and the SICC may decline only under O 2 r 3, with no Spiliada and no strong cause. The scheme adds the counter: arguably the clause needs a more specific reference to the SICC to qualify as a written jurisdiction agreement for it. If it does not, Galen files in the General Division, serves out with approval, and seeks a transfer under the O 2 r 4(1)(c) “more appropriate” test.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J5.2.3 :: Post-2016 High Court Clause Includes the SICC (+)

Presently, [clause X], concluded on [date] (on or after 1 October 2016), names [the Singapore High Court / the General Division]. Per O 2 r 2(1) and s 2(2)–(3) CCAA, it includes the SICC unless [a contrary intention] appears, so [claimant] may file directly in the SICC.

  • Critique (−): Per C&Y, O 2 r 2(1) seems to bar evidence that [the parties] [never contemplated the SICC], contrary to Singapore's contextual interpretation and to party autonomy.
  • Reply (+): Per C&Y, the lost autonomy buys HCCCA enforceability of [the SICC judgment] in [State] and fits the SICC's international template; per Hartley–Dogauchi, "the courts of France" lets French law allocate internally.
  • Specific Reference Needed? (−): Per Chong (sample-final answer scheme), arguably [clause X] needs a more specific reference to the SICC to qualify as a written jurisdiction agreement for it, so [defendant] resists [primary jurisdiction].
📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
⚡ BIG IDEA

Clause 27 is asymmetric: Brask may sue only in Elbonia, while Galen may sue anywhere and Brask submits to the court Galen picks. That takes it outside the CCAA (CHLOE V), but at common law its promises still decide who is in breach. The deciding move is to find who breaks which promise: Brask breaks its promise to submit if it objects to Singapore, so it bears strong cause and fails, while Galen breaks its promise to submit to Elbonia by seeking an injunction, so the two actions probably run side by side. The twists test an open estoppel from the Elbonian ruling and a clause without Brask's submission words, which on the handout answer turns the test into forum conveniens with the burden on Galen.

  1. 1
    Read clause 27: who promised what A7

    Write this first, because what clause 27 promises decides who, if anyone, is in breach. Brask may sue Galen only in Elbonia, and Galen submits to the Elbonian courts. Galen may sue Brask in any country, and Brask submits to the court Galen chooses. Under Singapore law, the contract's law, both sentences are valid and read together. Per the handout clause bank, if Galen sues here, Brask agreed to submit and bears strong cause if it objects; if Brask sued here, it would break its Elbonia-only promise.

  2. 2
    The CCAA gate fails on one row B1

    Elbonia has been a Contracting State since 1 January 2019 and clause 27 was signed on 14 February 2022, so the date row passes for the chosen court's State. The parties are in different States, and a shipbuilding contract is commercial. But per CHLOE V, following the Hartley–Dogauchi Report, a clause that lets one side sue anywhere is not exclusive under the CCAA, so s 12 cannot be engaged; Etihad (EWCA), obiter, agrees. Per C&Y, at common law the clause stays exclusive against Brask, the restricted party, so its promises still decide who is in breach.

  3. 3
    Serving Brask out: the clause in practice D8

    Brask has no office, staff or assets here, so Galen must serve it in Elbonia. The contract says nothing about service, so O 8 r 1(3) does not apply and Galen needs approval under O 8 r 1(1) on the “appropriate court” ground (“has the jurisdiction” is arguably kept for CCAA cases). Per the Week 9 slides, in principle Galen must make out all three requirements, with sentence two as the nexus under para 63(3)(r), as Brask agreed to submit, or (d)(iv). In practice (Chong's answer scheme; C&Y), it need only show a good arguable case that sentence two is valid, binds Brask and covers the dispute, plus a serious question, shown separately because (r) and (d)(iv) are neutral. Forum need not be proved: if Brask raises it, that breaks its promise, so Brask bears strong cause (Shanghai Turbo (CA)).

  4. 4
    A negative declaration changes little D6

    Galen is the natural defendant: it wants a declaration that it does not owe the US$7 million instalment that Brask claims in Elbonia. The pre-write pattern is written for a declaration that no contract exists, but the answer scheme runs the same steps for a declaration of no breach. A declaration needs a nexus like any other claim; here sentence two supplies it, with Singapore governing law ((d)(iii)) in the alternative. Neither engages the merits, so Galen states the serious question separately (Bradley Lomas). With no clause the case would be won or lost on forum conveniens, but because Brask promised to submit, its forum objection is a breach needing strong cause, as in Bunge.

  5. 5
    The test: strong cause, on Brask E7

    Brask says it will contest any Singapore proceedings, and whether it applies to set service aside or for a stay, it is trying to escape its promise to submit. Per Vinmar (restating The Eleftheria), the court holds the parties to their bargain unless the party in breach shows strong cause, on a stay or a set-aside (Shanghai Turbo). The burden lies on the party seeking release from its promise, so it is on Brask, although Galen served out. Strong cause is a higher hurdle than Spiliada, which applies only where no one is in breach, so never call Spiliada the strong cause test.

  6. 6
    Mark the strong cause facts E8

    Per Vinmar, where only the clause's parties are involved, strong cause is generally abuse of process or denial of justice, and factors foreseeable at signing carry little weight. Brask's designers and welders live in Elbonia, but that was foreseeable and both courts take evidence by video link. Its earlier Elbonian action fails too: a clause that lets Galen sue anywhere while Brask must sue in Elbonia makes parallel actions foreseeable, and related foreign proceedings were not enough in Shanghai Turbo. Per C&Y, that Elbonia will not recognise a Singapore declaration was foreseeable, so it weighs little; Singapore law governs, a trial here is far quicker, and the merits are not entertained (Vinmar). With (d) and (e) flipped, nothing suggests that Galen's suit here is abusive or that Brask would suffer concrete prejudice defending here, so Brask shows no strong cause and Singapore hears the claim.

  7. 7
    The SICC: arguably primary jurisdiction F2

    Galen prefers the SICC. Per Chong's sample-final answer scheme, an “any court” limb like sentence two can give the SICC primary jurisdiction: the claim is international, as Brask's place of business is in Elbonia, and commercial, as it arises from a shipbuilding contract. Brask, a party to the written agreement, is then served out without permission (O 5 r 6(2)(a)), and the SICC may decline only under O 2 r 3, so Brask's links with Elbonia count for nothing. The scheme adds the counter: arguably the clause needs a more specific reference to the SICC to be a written jurisdiction agreement for it. If so, Galen sues in the General Division as above and seeks a transfer, which turns on whether the SICC is “more appropriate” (O 2 r 4(1)(c)).

  8. 8
    The injunction: name the basis G1

    Galen wants the Elbonian action stopped, so it seeks an anti-suit injunction and must name its basis (Cooperative Muratori). Per Chong's answer scheme, it asks for the injunction as ancillary relief in its declaration action, so Brask is amenable once validly served out; Brask may cite Akai, as it has no assets here, but that goes only to whether the order would be effective (C&Y; Cooperative Muratori). The contractual basis needs a respondent who sued in breach, and Brask did not: sentence one sends its claims to Elbonia, the only court it may use. The Elbonian action is at an early stage and Galen has taken no step in it, so delay does not count against Galen and it has not submitted there by conduct.

  9. 9
    Galen's own breach, and the result G5

    Galen promised in sentence one to submit to the Elbonian courts, so per Chong's answer scheme its application to stop the Elbonian action is its own breach. Who bears strong cause is then open, arguably Galen as the party in breach, and a six year trial in Elbonia was foreseeable when it signed (Vinmar), so it is not released. If the burden is not put on Galen, it still needs a basis, and with no breach by Brask that is vexation, where parallel proceedings alone are not enough (UBS v Telesto). Sufficient interest is open too: per Cooperative Muratori it is not needed where the injunction rests on breach of agreement, but this one rests on no breach by Brask, so Galen may have to show that Singapore is the natural forum. Result: the injunction is unlikely on either route, and the two actions probably run side by side, as clause 27 allows.

But Galen may argue that there is no estoppel on this point, because each Contracting State court decides for itself whether the Convention applies. Then Singapore applies CHLOE V and the contract is outside the CCAA.

Per Prof Chong (March 2026 answer scheme), Galen may argue that no estoppel arises, because each Contracting State court decides for itself whether the Convention applies. ⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

If it is a CCAA case, Singapore is a non-chosen court and must decline unless an exception applies. The exceptions are read narrowly, and mere delay or expense is not enough. A later Elbonian judgment would then be a chosen court's judgment under Part 3.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per s 12(1), “despite any other written law or rule of law”, a non-chosen court must stay or dismiss unless one of exceptions (a) to (e) applies. Per 6DM, the court asks whether there is an exclusive agreement for another court, then whether an exception applies. Per the Hartley–Dogauchi Report (and C&Y), the exceptions are read narrowly: under (d) mere delay or expense is not enough, and manifest injustice under (c) must be clear, extremely serious and highly probable (Brand & Herrup, in 6DM). As in the answer scheme, none applies. A later Elbonian judgment would be a chosen court's judgment, recognised and enforced to the extent it has effect in Elbonia (s 13(2)).

What the clause promises is a question of contract under its governing law, Singapore law, under which both sentences are valid and read together.

The Elbonian question was what effect sentence two has in Elbonian civil procedure; the Singapore question is what Galen and Brask promised each other under Singapore law. Even on the narrow reading per Chong (seminar), identity fails where Singapore's rules select Singapore law, as they do here. 5Remember

🧠 FOR THE EXAM
  • Read an asymmetric clause promise by promise: whoever objects to a court it agreed to, or sues where it promised not to, bears strong cause.
  • An asymmetric clause is outside the CCAA (CHLOE V), but at common law it stays exclusive against the restricted party.
  • Served out under a submission limb, in practice the claimant shows only that the clause is valid, binds the defendant and covers the dispute, plus a separate serious question; if the defendant raises forum, it bears strong cause.
  • An applicant that promised to submit abroad breaks that promise by seeking an injunction (answer scheme): arguably it bears strong cause, and a foreseeable delay will not release it.
  • A foreign ruling that the Convention applies binds only through issue estoppel, which is open: give the s 12 route and the base answer.
  • Without the submission words, on the handout answer the test becomes forum conveniens with the burden on the claimant who served out, and the SICC has no primary jurisdiction.

LAW302 · META GAME · ★ DO FIRST · QUESTION 1 · HYPO q1-01 · NO GEMINI · 15 QUESTIONS

Sunmark v Brightline

Written by Claude for the drill and law reviewed. There is no Gemini output for this hypo.

Answers:

1Base facts

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Sunmark v Brightline

Sunmark Pte Ltd, a Singapore incorporated company, makes solar inverters at its plant in Tuas. Brightline Ltd is incorporated in Ruritania, where it runs solar farms. Brightline has no office, staff or assets in Singapore. The two companies made two contracts.

Under the Supply Contract, signed on 4 May 2018 and governed by Singapore law, Sunmark sold Brightline 900 inverters, delivered to Port Ruri. Clause 15 reads:

“Each party submits to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the Singapore High Court.”

Under the Maintenance Contract, signed on 1 March 2017 and governed by Ruritanian law, Sunmark's engineers service the inverters at Brightline's farms in Ruritania. Brightline was to pay the fees into Sunmark's account at a Singapore bank. Clause 22 reads:

“The courts of Ruritania shall have exclusive jurisdiction over any dispute arising out of or in connection with this contract.”

Brightline has not paid US$3 million of the price under the Supply Contract. It says that the inverters overheat. It has also refused to pay US$400,000 in fees under the Maintenance Contract, and says that Sunmark's engineers damaged its control room.

Sunmark wants to sue Brightline in Singapore for the price and for the fees. Its lawyers would prefer the Singapore International Commercial Court for the Supply Contract claim. Brightline has said that it will “contest any Singapore proceedings at every stage”.

Advise Sunmark whether the Singapore courts have jurisdiction over each claim, and whether they will hear it.

ℹ ASSUME
  1. Ruritania is a Contracting State to the Hague Convention on Choice of Court Agreements. The Convention entered into force for Ruritania on 1 January 2018.
  2. Neither contract says how legal process may be served.
  3. Brightline's engineers who inspected the inverters all live in Ruritania. They are willing to give evidence by video link.
  4. A civil trial takes about five years in Ruritania and about 18 months in Singapore.
  5. Under Ruritanian law, clause 22 is valid and covers every claim arising from the Maintenance Contract.
✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • A4
    Says "non-exclusive": Singapore courts. Clause 15 is a Singapore clause that calls itself non-exclusive, and Brightline will resist Singapore. Singapore takes the contractual approach: “submits” waives any objection to the named court.
  • A3
    Says "exclusive": a foreign court. Clause 22 names the Ruritanian courts exclusively, yet Sunmark wants to sue on the Maintenance Contract here. Sunmark would be the party in breach.
  • B1
    CCAA gate: five conditions. Clause 22 is an express exclusive clause for a Contracting State, so run the gate. It fails on the date row: 1 March 2017 is before the Convention entered into force for Ruritania.
  • B4
    Outside the CCAA: say why, then the common law. Both contracts are outside the CCAA, each for a different reason, so say why and go to the common law.
  • D8
    Singapore clause, defendant abroad. Brightline is abroad and the Supply Contract has a Singapore clause. The clause supplies the nexus, and in practice Sunmark shows the clause is valid, binds Brightline and covers the dispute.
  • D10
    Foreign clause, defendant abroad. On the Maintenance Contract the clause points away from Singapore, so Sunmark needs a nexus through another factor and bears every limb.
  • E7
    Strong cause: starter and nature of the test. A promise is broken on each contract, so the test is strong cause on both. The burden sits on a different party each time.
  • E8
    SCORECARD · Strong cause: the Eleftheria factors. The witness and delay facts are there to be marked on the strong cause scorecard. Both were foreseeable when the clauses were signed.
  • F3
    "Singapore High Court" clause: check the date. Sunmark wants the SICC, and clause 15 names the Singapore High Court. Its date decides whether the clause reaches the SICC.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • B2
    CCAA applies and Singapore is the chosen court (s 11). Tempting because clause 15 is a post-2016 Singapore clause. Wrong because it says “non-exclusive”, so s 3(2) deeming is displaced and s 11 is never reached. Prof Chong has called this a recurring exam error.
  • B3
    CCAA applies and a foreign court is chosen (s 12). Tempting because Ruritania is a Contracting State and clause 22 is exclusive. Wrong on these dates: the clause was concluded before the Convention entered into force for Ruritania, so s 12 does not apply.
  • E4
    SCORECARD · Spiliada stage 1: connecting factors. Witnesses and trial delay look like Spiliada stage 1 facts. But a promise is broken on both contracts, so the test is strong cause. Never run the Spiliada scorecard under a strong cause heading.
  • A6
    No label: "the parties submit to the jurisdiction of ...". A6 is for a clause with no label. Clause 15 labels itself “non-exclusive”, so the label gets its ordinary meaning.
  • E3
    Forum conveniens on service out: burden on the claimant. Forum conveniens with the burden on the claimant is the service out test where no promise is broken. Here each contract has a clause that someone is breaking.

Fair to tick but not needed: D4 Defendant abroad: service out and the three requirements, D5 Gateway: name the sub-limb of PD para 63(3), E1 Which test, and who bears the burden, F2 Primary jurisdiction under a written jurisdiction agreement, F5 Exercise in the SICC: O 2 r 3, no Spiliada, D7 Serious question to be tried

Application questions · base facts

⚡ Base facts · 1 of 7B1
Is the Supply Contract a CCAA case?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Deeming under s 3(2) applies unless the parties expressly provide otherwise. “Non-exclusive” is an express provision otherwise, so the CCAA does not apply and the common law decides. Ruritania's date is irrelevant to a Singapore clause.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J1.2.1 :: Deemed Exclusive (+)

Per s 3(2), [clause X] (["the parties submit to the jurisdiction of the [State] courts"]) is deemed exclusive unless the parties expressly provide otherwise. At common law the same unlabelled clause could go either way under [its proper law] (J1.1).

  • Rebuttal (−): [clause X] [says "non-exclusive" / allows suit "in any other competent court"], so s 3(2) is displaced and [the CCAA] does not apply.
  • Trap: per Chong (seminar), where the facts call [clause X] [non-exclusive], do not invoke s 3(2): [the CCAA] does not apply, a recurring exam error.
⚡ Base facts · 2 of 7B1
Clause 22 was signed on 1 March 2017. Singapore's Convention date is 1 October 2016 and Ruritania's is 1 January 2018. Does s 12 of the CCAA require a stay of the Maintenance Contract claim?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

The test date belongs to the State of the chosen court. Clause 22 was concluded ten months before the Convention entered into force for Ruritania, so the CCAA does not apply and the stay is decided at common law.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J1.2.2 :: Temporal Scope

[State of chosen court] is a Contracting State, and [clause X] was concluded on [date], after the HCCCA entered into force for it (Singapore: 1 October 2016). [Check the HCCH status table.]

  • UK clauses (±): the HCCCA applied to the UK via the EU from 1 October 2015 and in its own right from 1 January 2021; continuity across Brexit is contested, so [an English clause] concluded on [a date between them] is arguable either way.
⚡ Base facts · 3 of 7E7
Brightline applies to set aside service of both claims. Who bears the burden, and of what?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

The burden lies on the party seeking release from its promise. Brightline's objection escapes its submission in clause 15, even though the clause is non-exclusive. On the Maintenance Contract Sunmark is in breach by suing here, so it bears strong cause although Brightline brings the application.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J4.0.2 :: General Rule

Per C&Y and Shanghai Turbo, the burden lies on [the party seeking release] from its promise on where to sue, whether in [a stay] or [a set-aside].

⚡ Base facts · 4 of 7D8
For service out on the Supply Contract claim, what must Sunmark show in practice?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

The clause is the nexus (the submission and jurisdiction-term limbs). Those limbs are neutral on the merits, so the serious question is shown separately. Forum need not be proved: if Brightline contests it, Brightline bears strong cause. Approval is still needed because neither contract deals with service.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J3.2 :: Singapore EJC or NEJC: In Principle v In Practice (must write)

Per Week 9 slides, [claimant] relies on [the Singapore clause] against [defendant]:

  • In principle, [claimant] must still make out all three requirements against [defendant], even inter partes.
  • Nexus: [the clause] itself, under para 63(3)(r) ([defendant] "agreed to submit") or (d)(iv) (Shanghai Turbo (CA); J3.1.2).
  • In practice, [claimant] need only show a good arguable case that [the clause] is valid, binds [defendant] and covers [the dispute] (J1.5–J1.6), plus a serious question, shown separately because (d)(iv) and (r) are neutral (J3.1.4).
  • Forum: need not be proved. If [defendant] contests it, that breaches its promise, so per Shanghai Turbo (CA) [defendant] bears strong cause (J4.3), whether it challenges existence or exercise; if [defendant] never raises it, [claimant] need prove nothing.
⚡ Base facts · 5 of 7D10
How does Sunmark get the Maintenance Contract claim served on Brightline in Ruritania?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Clause 22 points away from Singapore, so the nexus must come from elsewhere, here the breach by non-payment in Singapore. Because Sunmark sues in breach, strong cause replaces forum conveniens and the burden on every limb stays on Sunmark.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J3.2 :: Foreign EJC: Strong Cause on Claimant Throughout

[Claimant] sues here despite [the EJC for X], so it is in breach. Without notice: it needs a nexus through another factor ([defendant]'s residence or property here / a breach or tort here), a serious question, and strong cause in place of forum conveniens.

  • Inter partes: per C&Y and Week 9 slides, the burden on every limb stays on [claimant], and the same holds if [defendant] seeks a stay instead of a set-aside.
  • Note the reversal when served in: [defendant] applies for the stay, yet [claimant] must show strong cause (J4.3).
⚡ Base facts · 6 of 7E8
Sunmark says a five year wait for trial in Ruritania is strong cause to keep the Maintenance Contract claim here. Will that work?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Parties are taken to know the chosen court's procedure and delays. Strong cause exists where the chosen court is dissolved or unavailable, or trial would be so difficult as to deny justice, if that was unforeseeable. Stage 2 belongs to Spiliada, not to this test.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J4.3.3 :: Chosen Court Unavailable

Per Vinmar, strong cause exists where [X's chosen court] is dissolved or unavailable through [war], or trial there would be so overwhelmingly difficult as to deny justice, if unforeseeable; notorious delay in [X] is foreseeable and insufficient.

⚡ Base facts · 7 of 7F3
Can Sunmark file the Supply Contract claim directly in the SICC?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Clause 15 is dated 4 May 2018, so it reaches the SICC. Both exclusive and non-exclusive clauses count as written jurisdiction agreements. Once the SICC has jurisdiction under one, it must not decline only because the action is connected to another country.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J5.2.3 :: Post-2016 High Court Clause Includes the SICC (+)

Presently, [clause X], concluded on [date] (on or after 1 October 2016), names [the Singapore High Court / the General Division]. Per O 2 r 2(1) and s 2(2)–(3) CCAA, it includes the SICC unless [a contrary intention] appears, so [claimant] may file directly in the SICC.

  • Critique (−): Per C&Y, O 2 r 2(1) seems to bar evidence that [the parties] [never contemplated the SICC], contrary to Singapore's contextual interpretation and to party autonomy.
  • Reply (+): Per C&Y, the lost autonomy buys HCCCA enforceability of [the SICC judgment] in [State] and fits the SICC's international template; per Hartley–Dogauchi, "the courts of France" lets French law allocate internally.
  • Specific Reference Needed? (−): Per Chong (sample-final answer scheme), arguably [clause X] needs a more specific reference to the SICC to qualify as a written jurisdiction agreement for it, so [defendant] resists [primary jurisdiction].
📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
⚡ BIG IDEA

Two contracts between the same parties, each with its own clause, and each must be tested on its own. Clause 15 is a Singapore clause that says “non-exclusive”, so it is outside the CCAA, and Brightline breaks its promise by objecting to Singapore. Clause 22 is a Ruritanian exclusive clause, so Sunmark is the party in breach by suing here; the clause misses the CCAA only because it was signed before the Convention entered into force for Ruritania, the chosen court's State. The move that decides it: find who breaks which promise and put strong cause on that party, contract by contract.

  1. 1
    Read each clause: who promised what? A4A3

    Clause 15 is a Singapore clause that calls itself non-exclusive, in a contract governed by Singapore law. Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), Singapore takes the contractual approach: “submits” means Brightline waives any objection to the Singapore court, so any forum objection by Brightline, on a set-aside or a stay, breaks clause 15. Clause 22 names the Ruritanian courts exclusively, and we are told that under Ruritanian law, its proper law, it is valid and covers every Maintenance Contract claim. So Sunmark breaks clause 22 by suing here. Each contract has a party in breach, but a different one.

  2. 2
    The CCAA gate, clause by clause B1B4

    Clause 15 fails the exclusivity row: s 3(2) deems a clause exclusive only unless the parties expressly provide otherwise, and “non-exclusive” does exactly that. So the CCAA does not apply to clause 15 and s 11 is never reached; per Chong (seminar), invoking s 3(2) for such a clause is a recurring exam error. Clause 22 is expressly exclusive and Ruritania is a Contracting State, but it fails the date row. The date that counts is the date the Convention entered into force for the chosen court's State (Ruritania: 1 January 2018), and clause 22 was signed on 1 March 2017. So s 12 is not engaged either, and both contracts go to the common law, each for a different reason.

  3. 3
    Supply Contract: serving Brightline out D8

    Brightline has no presence in Singapore and neither contract says how process may be served, so Sunmark needs approval under O 8 r 1(1), on the “appropriate court” ground. In principle it must make out all three requirements. In practice (Per Chong's answer scheme and C&Y), it shows a good arguable case that clause 15 is valid, binds Brightline and covers the price claim. The clause itself is the nexus (para 63(3)(r) or (d)(iv)); those limbs are neutral on the merits, so Sunmark also shows a serious question to be tried. Forum need not be proved: if Brightline contests it, Brightline bears strong cause (Per Shanghai Turbo (CA)).

  4. 4
    Maintenance Contract: serving Brightline out D10

    Clause 22 points away from Singapore, so it cannot be the nexus, and Sunmark sues in breach of it. Sunmark needs another factor: the fees were payable into its account at a Singapore bank, so non-payment is a breach in Singapore (para 63(3)(e)). That gateway engages the merits, so a good arguable case of breach also clears the serious question (Per Bradley Lomas). In place of forum conveniens, Sunmark must show strong cause. On Brightline's set-aside the burden on every limb stays on Sunmark (Per C&Y and the Week 9 slides).

  5. 5
    Which test, and who bears it E7

    A promise is broken on each contract, so the test on both is strong cause, never Spiliada. Per Vinmar (restating The Eleftheria), the court holds the parties to their bargain unless the party in breach shows strong cause, on a stay or a set-aside. Per Shanghai Turbo, the burden lies on the party seeking release from its promise. Supply Contract: Brightline bears it, because its challenge escapes its submission, and strong cause means the same for a Singapore non-exclusive clause. Maintenance Contract: Sunmark bears it, as the party suing in breach, although Brightline brings the application.

  6. 6
    Mark the strong cause facts E8

    Per Vinmar, factors foreseeable at contracting carry little weight. Brightline's engineer witnesses live in Ruritania, but that was foreseeable and they can give evidence by video link; for clause 15 the abuse and prejudice factors are flipped, and Brightline shows neither abuse by Sunmark nor real prejudice in defending here. Sunmark's five-year wait in Ruritania fails too: parties are taken to know the chosen court's delays (Per Shanghai Turbo), and delay becomes strong cause only through something unforeseeable, such as a dissolved or unavailable court (Per Vinmar). Sunmark's point that Brightline has no real defence to the fees is irrelevant, as the merits are not entertained (Per Vinmar). Result: no strong cause on either side, so the Supply Contract claim is heard here and the Maintenance Contract claim is stayed or service is set aside.

  7. 7
    The SICC for the Supply Contract claim F3

    Clause 15 names the Singapore High Court and was signed on 4 May 2018, after 1 October 2016. Per O 2 r 2(1), it includes the SICC unless a contrary intention appears, and per C&Y a non-exclusive clause is still a written jurisdiction agreement. The claim is international, as Brightline's place of business is in Ruritania, and commercial (O 2 r 1(3)). So Sunmark may file directly in the SICC and serve Brightline without permission (O 5 r 6(2)(a)), and the SICC must not decline only because the case is connected to Ruritania (O 2 r 3(3)): no Spiliada, no strong cause. Brightline may reply, per Chong's answer scheme, that arguably a more specific reference to the SICC is needed. If that won, the SICC would have no primary jurisdiction, and Sunmark would sue in the General Division and seek a transfer, which turns on whether the SICC is “more appropriate” (O 2 r 4(1)(c)).

2Twist 1

🧩 TWIST 1

Now add these facts.

Sunmark issues its Supply Contract claim in the General Division. It obtains approval and serves Brightline in Ruritania. A week later Brightline sues Sunmark in Ruritania for damages for the overheating inverters. In the same action it asks the Ruritanian court for an order restraining Sunmark from continuing the Singapore claim.

Sunmark asks what it can do in Singapore to stop Brightline.

ℹ ASSUME
  1. The Ruritanian action is three weeks old. No defence is due yet.
  2. Ruritanian law gives a buyer of defective energy equipment three times its loss. Singapore law gives no such damages.
✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • G1
    ASI starter, and the basis. Sunmark wants an anti-suit injunction, and there are two foreign proceedings to restrain: the damages claim and the Ruritanian restraining application. Each gets its own analysis and its own basis.
  • G2
    Amenability. Brightline must be within the court's personal jurisdiction. It has been served out, but it has no presence or assets here.
  • G4
    Singapore non-exclusive clause: is suing abroad a breach?. Clause 15 is a Singapore non-exclusive clause. Suing abroad is not ordinarily a breach, but asking a foreign court to stop the Singapore action arguably is.
  • G6
    Vexation ASI: sufficient interest. With no breach in the damages claim, Sunmark needs Singapore to have a sufficient interest before running vexation.
  • G7
    SCORECARD · Vexation or oppression, and injustice to the respondent. The early stage of the foreign action and the triple damages are scorecard facts: vexation on one side, what Brightline would lose on the other.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • G9
    ASI in a CCAA case. G9 is for a contract inside the CCAA. The Supply Contract is outside it, because clause 15 is expressly non-exclusive.
  • G8
    Clause for a foreign court, or Singapore is neither forum. G8 is for an applicant asking Singapore to protect a clause for another court. The Ruritanian action is on the Supply Contract, whose clause names Singapore.
  • G5
    Twist: the applicant's own ASI application breaks a clause. G5 applies where the applicant promised to submit to the foreign court. Sunmark made no such promise in clause 15, so its application breaks nothing.
  • H10
    Anti-enforcement injunction: the judgment already exists. An anti-enforcement injunction needs a foreign judgment. The Ruritanian action is three weeks old.

Fair to tick but not needed: G3 Contractual ASI: a Singapore clause is breached

Application questions · twist 1

⚡ Twist 1 · 1 of 4G1
How should the answer be organised?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Analyse each foreign proceeding separately. Under a Singapore non-exclusive clause, suing abroad is no breach, but seeking a foreign order against the Singapore action is in substance an objection to Singapore's jurisdiction.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J6.0.1 :: One ASI per foreign proceeding

Per Chong (seminar), analyse [foreign claim] and [foreign ASI application] separately: under [a Singapore NEJC], suing abroad is no breach (vexation, J6.3.2), but seeking [a foreign ASI against Suit X] is (contractual, J6.3.1.2).

⚡ Twist 1 · 2 of 4G4
Is Brightline's damages claim in Ruritania a breach of clause 15?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

The contractual approach reads “submits” as a promise not to object to Singapore's jurisdiction. It is not a promise to sue only in Singapore. Only a challenge to Singapore's jurisdiction needs strong cause.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J6.3.1.2 :: No Breach (−)

Presently, [clause X] is a Singapore NEJC. Per C&Y and Shanghai Turbo, suing in [foreign court] is not ordinarily a breach, the parties having accepted parallel proceedings; only a challenge to [Singapore]'s jurisdiction, e.g., [a stay application in [Suit X]], needs strong cause. So [applicant] relies on vexation (J6.3.2) or abuse (J6.3.3).

⚡ Twist 1 · 3 of 4G2
Is Brightline amenable to the Singapore court?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Amenability means being within the court's in personam jurisdiction, by submission or valid service in or out. The counter is the case where a respondent served out, with no presence or assets here, was held not amenable. The reply is the settled view that valid service or submission is enough, and that a lack of assets goes only to whether the order would bite. Amenability and sufficient interest are separate requirements.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J6.1 :: Submission or Valid Service (+)

Presently, [respondent] is amenable, having [submitted by [appearing / defending / counterclaiming] in [Suit X]] or been validly served [in / out of] Singapore (Koh Kay Yew; Westbridge v Mittal; C&Y). Per Cooperative Muratori, being within the court's in personam jurisdiction is what amenability requires.

⚡ Twist 1 · 4 of 4G7
Brightline says an injunction would cost it triple damages. How is that weighed?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Vexation and injustice to the respondent are two sides of the same coin. The court weighs the advantage lost against the injustice to the applicant, and the advantage counts for less where the foreign court is not the natural forum. A claim unknown in Singapore is not vexatious for that reason alone.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J6.4 :: Balancing (must write)

Per Kirkham, vexation and injustice to [respondent] are "two sides of the same coin"; the injustice "feeds into" vexation (Cooperative Muratori). Per SNIA and C&Y, the court weighs [respondent]'s loss of [legitimate juridical advantage] against the injustice to [applicant] if the ASI is refused.

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes: two injunctions, not one G1

    The jurisdiction analysis for both contracts stays as it was. What is new is the anti-suit injunction, and there are two Ruritanian proceedings to restrain. Per Chong (seminar), analyse each separately, and per Cooperative Muratori, Sunmark must name its basis for each, as the elements differ. The damages claim breaks no promise in clause 15, so the basis is vexation; the restraining application is arguably a breach, so the basis is contractual. Either way the injunction interferes indirectly with the Ruritanian court, so it issues only where the ends of justice require it, with caution (Per SNIA and Lakshmi).

  2. 2
    Amenability G2

    Amenability is always required, whatever the basis. Brightline was validly served out with the Supply Contract claim; Sunmark seeks the injunction as ancillary relief in that action, so amenability comes from that service (Per Chong's answer scheme), and on the base analysis Brightline cannot show strong cause to set it aside. Brightline will cite Akai, where a respondent served out, with no presence or assets here, was held not amenable. The reply is the settled view (C&Y; Cooperative Muratori) that valid service is enough. The lack of assets goes only to whether the order bites, since breach is contempt; and a Ruritanian judgment obtained in breach of it would be refused recognition here (Per Nimbus).

  3. 3
    The restraining application: arguably a breach G4

    Per the handout, Shanghai Turbo's narrow-waiver reading implies a promise not to object to Singapore's jurisdiction. Asking the Ruritanian court to stop the Singapore claim is in substance such an objection, much as in Sabah Shipyard, where the English CA called a similar foreign injunction “clearly a breach of contract”. Route 1, breach: a contractual injunction needs amenability, breach and no strong reasons from Brightline, and natural forum drops out (Per Cooperative Muratori); Brightline shows no strong reason, and at three weeks old the application is at an early stage, so the injunction should issue. Route 2, no breach: per UBS v Telesto and C&Y, Sabah is really a vexation case, so Sunmark pleads vexation in the alternative, and per Airbus and C&Y Singapore may restrain a foreign application aimed at its own proceedings on the usual requirements. On that route the injunction probably still issues, as Brightline is trying to stop Sunmark enforcing its rights here, the Sabah pattern that UBS v Telesto treats as vexation; but Sunmark must then also show sufficient interest and no undue injustice to Brightline.

  4. 4
    The damages claim: vexation G6G7

    With no breach, Sunmark first needs sufficient interest. Arguably clause 15 supplies it (Per Shanghai Turbo and C&Y); if not, Sunmark must show Singapore is clearly the more appropriate forum (Per Lakshmi), which is arguable: Singapore law governs and the inverters were made here, but they and the engineer witnesses are in Ruritania, though video links reduce the weight of where witnesses are (Per Lakshmi). If Sunmark fails on interest, the injunction against the damages claim fails there. Vexation needs the clearest of circumstances (Per Kirkham): a parallel suit under a non-exclusive clause is not enough alone (Per UBS v Telesto), and a triple damages claim unknown here is not vexatious for that reason (Per British Airways v Laker). Brightline's loss of triple damages is weighed as injustice to it, counting for less if Ruritania is not the natural forum. Sunmark's best point is that Brightline sued a week after service instead of counterclaiming here (similar to Lakshmi), and the action is only three weeks old. Result: doubtful; the injunction issues only if the court accepts that point, otherwise it is refused as a mere parallel suit, so the restraining application is Sunmark's stronger target.

3Twist 2

🧩 TWIST 2

Go back to the base facts and change one date.

How would your advice on the Maintenance Contract differ if it had been signed on 1 March 2019?

✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • B3
    CCAA applies and a foreign court is chosen (s 12). Clause 22 is now concluded after the Convention entered into force for Ruritania. The CCAA applies, a foreign court is chosen, and s 12 governs.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • B2
    CCAA applies and Singapore is the chosen court (s 11). Section 11 is for a clause choosing Singapore. Clause 22 chooses Ruritania.
  • E5
    SCORECARD · Spiliada stage 2: substantial justice. The five year delay looks like a substantial justice point. But there is no Spiliada here: s 12 leaves no general discretion, and its exceptions are narrower than stage 2.
  • B5
    The foreign court has already ruled that the HCCCA applies. B5 needs a foreign court that has already ruled that the Convention applies. No court has ruled on anything.

Application questions · twist 2

⚡ Twist 2 · 1 of 3B3
What is the test for the Maintenance Contract claim now?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Section 12(1) applies despite any other rule of law. The court asks whether there is an exclusive agreement that does not designate a Singapore court, then whether an exception applies. Only if one does is the stay decided at common law.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J1.4 :: Must Stay or Dismiss (must write)

[Claimant] sued here, and [defendant] seeks a stay because [clause X] designates [the courts of State B]. Per s 12(1), "despite any other written law or rule of law", [Singapore] must stay or dismiss unless exception (a)–(e) applies; per s 12(2), a stay on other grounds remains possible.

⚡ Twist 2 · 2 of 3B3
Sunmark argues that a five year wait for trial in Ruritania is a manifest injustice. Is that likely to succeed?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Manifest injustice must be clear, extremely serious and highly probable. The examples are a court that cannot give a fair trial, reasons special to a party that prevent suit there, or an agreement procured by fraud. Mere delay or expense does not meet the neighbouring exception either.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J1.4.2 :: (c) Manifest Injustice: Rule (−)

Per 6DM, adopting the Hartley–Dogauchi Report, manifest injustice covers, e.g., [no fair trial for bias or corruption in State B], [party-specific reasons precluding suit there] or [an agreement procured by fraud]. Per Brand & Herrup (in 6DM), it must be clear, extremely serious and highly probable, not speculative.

⚡ Twist 2 · 3 of 3B3
What stays the same?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Each contract is tested on its own clause. Clause 15 is expressly non-exclusive, so it stays outside the CCAA whatever the dates.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J1.4.1 :: Clause Covers Singapore or Is Outside the CCAA (−)

[Claimant] answers that [clause X] [designates Singapore / is asymmetric / is non-exclusive]. Then s 12 is not engaged (CHLOE V), and [the stay] is decided at common law: [strong cause for an EJC / Spiliada for a foreign NEJC] (J4).

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes, and what stays

    Only the date of the Maintenance Contract changes, to 1 March 2019. Clause 22 is now concluded after the Convention entered into force for Ruritania (1 January 2018), and the other rows still pass: an express exclusive clause for one Contracting State, an international case (the parties are in different States) and a commercial contract. So the CCAA applies, a foreign court is chosen, and s 12 governs, not s 11. The Supply Contract does not change: clause 15 is still expressly non-exclusive, so it stays outside the CCAA, with strong cause on Brightline if it objects.

  2. 2
    Section 12: stay or dismiss B3

    Per s 12(1), despite any other written law or rule of law, Singapore must stay or dismiss unless an exception in (a) to (e) applies. Per 6DM the court asks two questions: is there an exclusive agreement that does not designate a Singapore court (yes, clause 22), and does an exception apply. So strong cause, and the scorecard on it, falls away for this contract: there is no general discretion and no Spiliada. Only if an exception applied would the stay go back to the common law, with strong cause on Sunmark.

  3. 3
    Sunmark's delay argument fails B3

    Per the Hartley–Dogauchi Report (and C&Y), exceptions (c) and (d) apply only in the most exceptional circumstances and are read narrowly. Per 6DM, manifest injustice covers cases such as no fair trial for bias or corruption, reasons special to a party that prevent suit there, or a clause procured by fraud, and per Brand & Herrup (in 6DM) it must be clear, extremely serious and highly probable. A five-year wait is none of these, and under (d) mere delay or expense is not enough either. Result: no exception applies, so the Maintenance Contract claim is stayed or dismissed under s 12(1).

4Scorecards: weigh the factors

Prof Chong rewards applying facts to factor tests. Sort each fact, then answer the verdict question. These use the base facts unless a line says “Suppose”.

E8 Sort the factors: Strong cause on the base facts

Each line is a fact that a party offers as strong cause to escape its clause. Does it work? Lines marked “Suppose” are extra facts for this card only.

Brightline: our engineer witnesses all live in Ruritania.
Fails. Where the witnesses live was foreseeable at contracting, and they can give evidence by video link. J4.3.1 :: Foreseeable Factors
Sunmark: a trial takes five years in Ruritania.
Fails. Parties are taken to know the chosen court's delays. Notorious delay is foreseeable and is not enough. J4.3.3 :: Chosen Court Unavailable
Sunmark: Brightline has no real defence to the fee claim.
Fails. The merits are not entertained. Parties choose a forum to win or lose there. J4.3.3 :: Merits Irrelevant
Suppose: Ruritania's commercial courts were dissolved by decree last month.
Works. A chosen court that is dissolved or unavailable, where that was not foreseeable, is strong cause. J4.3.3 :: Chosen Court Unavailable
Suppose: the fee claim is now time-barred in Ruritania, and Sunmark never filed a protective claim there.
Fails. A time bar counts only if the claimant shows very good reasons for not filing a protective writ. Otherwise it is self-induced. J4.3.3 :: Time Bar
Suppose: Brightline has also sued the maker of the inverters' cooling fans, a stranger to both contracts, in Ruritania over the overheating. It says the price claim should be heard with that case.
Could go either way. With a non-party involved, splitting the overheating dispute between two courts may be strong cause for Brightline, unless that was foreseeable at contracting. A related case with different parties and claims may also be dismissed as limited overlap. J4.3.4 :: Fragmentation
Suppose: Brightline admits it owes the fees in full and says only that it cannot pay yet. Sunmark says that relying on clause 22 is then abusive.
Works. The abuse factor asks whether the party relying on the clause is acting abusively. The threshold is very high, but a defendant that admits liability and quantum and simply cannot pay is the example given of conduct that meets it. J4.3.3 :: Abuse Reformulated
⚡ Scorecard 1 · the verdictE8
On the base facts alone, what is the likely result?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Neither party can show strong cause on facts that were foreseeable when the clauses were signed. So each clause is enforced: clause 15 keeps the Supply Contract claim here, and clause 22 sends the Maintenance Contract claim to Ruritania.

5Remember

🧠 FOR THE EXAM
  • Test each clause on its own: one hypo can have two regimes and a different party in breach on each contract.
  • The CCAA date is the date the Convention entered into force for the chosen court's State, set against the date the clause was concluded.
  • A clause that says “non-exclusive” is never deemed exclusive under s 3(2), so the CCAA does not apply to it.
  • Strong cause sits on the party breaking its promise, not on the applicant: Brightline for clause 15, Sunmark for clause 22.
  • Foreseeable facts (witnesses abroad, a slow chosen court) and the merits are not strong cause, and the s 12 exceptions are narrower still.
  • Under a Singapore non-exclusive clause, suing abroad is no breach (vexation), but asking a foreign court to stop the Singapore action arguably is (contractual): one analysis per foreign proceeding.

6What the check changed

✓ THE CHECK

There is no Gemini output in this hypo, so there was nothing of Gemini's to correct. The notes and walkthrough on this page were written for this page and checked against the pre-writes (18 fixes in that check).
