LAW302 · META GAME · ★ DO FIRST · QUESTION 1 · HYPO q1-05 · GEMINI PROMPT V1 · 18 QUESTIONS

Fairhaven v Kestor

Written by Claude for the drill and law reviewed. Gemini (prompt v1) rebalanced the option lengths and wrote a note on each question; both were checked (10 corrections) and feed the notes here.

Answers:

1Base facts

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Fairhaven v Kestor

Fairhaven Pte Ltd, a Singapore incorporated company, makes filtration membranes for desalination plants. Kestor Utilities Ltd is incorporated in Elbonia, where it runs three plants. Kestor has no office, staff or assets in Singapore. The two companies made two contracts.

Under the Licence Contract, signed on 5 August 2016, Fairhaven licensed its plant monitoring software to Kestor. Clause 9 was printed in small type on the back of Kestor's order form. It reads:

“Any dispute arising out of or in connection with this contract shall be decided only by the courts of Arcadia.”

Under the Supply Contract, signed on 12 June 2019 and expressly governed by Elbonian law, Fairhaven sold Kestor 4,000 membranes. Clause 18 reads:

“The parties agree to submit to the jurisdiction of the Singapore High Court in respect of all disputes arising under this contract.”

Kestor has not paid US$6 million of the price or US$900,000 in licence fees. It says that the membranes clog. Fairhaven wants to bring both claims in Singapore, in the Singapore International Commercial Court if it can. Kestor replies that every witness and every membrane is in Elbonia, and that the licence fee claim belongs in Arcadia. Fairhaven says that it would be unjust to split one dispute between two countries.

Advise Fairhaven whether a Singapore court will hear each claim, and whether the Singapore International Commercial Court can hear it.

ℹ ASSUME
  1. The Hague Convention on Choice of Court Agreements entered into force for Arcadia on 1 October 2015. Elbonia is not a Contracting State.
  2. Under Elbonian law, a clause by which parties “submit” to a court gives that court jurisdiction but contains no promise not to sue elsewhere.
  3. Under Arcadian law, clause 9 is valid and binding. Under Singapore law, assume that a term printed in that way is not part of the contract.
  4. A civil trial takes about four years in Arcadia and about 18 months in Singapore.
  5. One of the International Judges of the Singapore International Commercial Court is trained in Elbonian law.
  6. Neither contract says how legal process may be served.
✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • A6
    No label: "the parties submit to the jurisdiction of ...". Clause 18 has no label. Note its date and its governing law. At common law its meaning would turn on Elbonian law, so first ask whether the CCAA takes over.
  • B1
    CCAA gate: five conditions. Run the gate for each clause. Clause 18 is tested against Singapore's date. Clause 9 is tested against Arcadia's date. Both pass.
  • B2
    CCAA applies and Singapore is the chosen court (s 11). The Supply Contract is inside the CCAA and names a Singapore court. Section 11 applies: the court must hear the claim, and Kestor is served abroad on the “has the jurisdiction” ground.
  • B3
    CCAA applies and a foreign court is chosen (s 12). The Licence Contract is inside the CCAA and names a foreign court. Section 12 applies. Fairhaven's points on small print, split proceedings and delay must each be tested as an exception.
  • F2
    Primary jurisdiction under a written jurisdiction agreement. Fairhaven wants the SICC. Clause 18 is a written agreement to submit, so ask whether it gives the SICC primary jurisdiction.
  • F3
    "Singapore High Court" clause: check the date. Clause 18 names the Singapore High Court, not the SICC. Its date, 12 June 2019, decides whether it reaches the SICC.
  • F5
    Exercise in the SICC: O 2 r 3, no Spiliada. Kestor points to Elbonian witnesses and goods. In the SICC under a written jurisdiction agreement, foreign connections alone are no ground to decline.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • D8
    Singapore clause, defendant abroad. Tempting because there is a Singapore clause and the defendant is abroad. But D8 is the common law route (clause as nexus, then strong cause). In a CCAA case service goes on the “has the jurisdiction” ground under B2.
  • E4
    SCORECARD · Spiliada stage 1: connecting factors. Witnesses and goods in Elbonia look like Spiliada stage 1 facts. But neither contract has a Spiliada stage: s 11 forbids declining, and s 12 requires a stay or dismissal.
  • E9
    The SICC as a Spiliada factor. The International Judge matters only where the General Division runs Spiliada and the SICC is offered as a factor. No Spiliada is run on either contract.
  • F6
    SCORECARD · Transfer from the General Division: is the SICC "more appropriate"?. The transfer scorecard is for a case with no primary jurisdiction, such as a clause signed before 1 October 2016. Clause 18 is dated 2019, and primary jurisdiction ends the inquiry.
  • A4
    Says "non-exclusive": Singapore courts. A4 is for a clause that says “non-exclusive”. Clause 18 has no label at all, which is why s 3(2) can deem it exclusive.

Fair to tick but not needed: A1 Any jurisdiction clause: what it promises, A2 Says "exclusive": Singapore courts, A3 Says "exclusive": a foreign court, F1 International and commercial, F4 Serving the defendant abroad from the SICC, D4 Defendant abroad: service out and the three requirements, D5 Gateway: name the sub-limb of PD para 63(3), D7 Serious question to be tried, E7 Strong cause: starter and nature of the test

Application questions · base facts

⚡ Base facts · 1 of 7B1
Under Elbonian law, clause 18 contains no promise not to sue elsewhere. Is the Supply Contract still a CCAA case?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Deeming applies unless the parties expressly provide otherwise, and clause 18 says nothing. It was concluded after 1 October 2016, Singapore's date, in an international commercial case. What Elbonian law makes of the clause matters at common law, and later for an injunction, but not at the gate. The forum conveniens route is right only for a clause outside the CCAA, such as one signed before 1 October 2016.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per s 3(2), a clause designating the courts of one Contracting State is deemed exclusive unless the parties expressly provide otherwise, so it does not matter that Elbonian law finds no promise in clause 18. Clause 18 was concluded on 12 June 2019, after the Convention entered into force for Singapore on 1 October 2016. The case is international, as Kestor resides in Elbonia (s 4(1)), and a price claim under a supply contract is commercial. At common law the same unlabelled clause could go either way under its proper law, but here the CCAA displaces that inquiry. Elbonian law matters again for breach, if an anti-suit injunction is sought.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J1.2.1 :: Deemed Exclusive (+)

Per s 3(2), [clause X] (["the parties submit to the jurisdiction of the [State] courts"]) is deemed exclusive unless the parties expressly provide otherwise. At common law the same unlabelled clause could go either way under [its proper law] (J1.1).

  • Rebuttal (−): [clause X] [says "non-exclusive" / allows suit "in any other competent court"], so s 3(2) is displaced and [the CCAA] does not apply.
  • Trap: per Chong (seminar), where the facts call [clause X] [non-exclusive], do not invoke s 3(2): [the CCAA] does not apply, a recurring exam error.
⚡ Base facts · 2 of 7B1
Clause 9 was signed on 5 August 2016. Singapore's Convention date is 1 October 2016 and Arcadia's is 1 October 2015. Is the Licence Contract inside the CCAA?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

The test date belongs to the State of the chosen court. Clause 9 chooses Arcadia and was concluded ten months after the Convention entered into force there. Singapore's own date matters only for a clause that chooses Singapore. Each contract is tested on its own clause.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

The CCAA applies only to an exclusive choice of court agreement concluded after the Convention entered into force for the State of the chosen court. Clause 9 says disputes “shall be decided only by the courts of Arcadia”, so it is expressly exclusive (s 3(1)), and Arcadia's date is 1 October 2015. Singapore's date of 1 October 2016 governs only clauses choosing Singapore. The case is international and the licence fee claim is commercial. Each contract is tested on its own clause.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J1.2.2 :: Temporal Scope

[State of chosen court] is a Contracting State, and [clause X] was concluded on [date], after the HCCCA entered into force for it (Singapore: 1 October 2016). [Check the HCCH status table.]

  • UK clauses (±): the HCCCA applied to the UK via the EU from 1 October 2015 and in its own right from 1 January 2021; continuity across Brexit is contested, so [an English clause] concluded on [a date between them] is arguable either way.
⚡ Base facts · 3 of 7B2
Kestor is in Elbonia. How does Fairhaven serve the Supply Contract claim from the General Division?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per C&Y, the “has the jurisdiction” ground was created partly for CCAA cases, where the chosen court must hear the case. The “appropriate court” ground with the clause as nexus is the common law route for a Singapore clause outside the CCAA. Approval is still needed because the contract does not deal with service.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per C&Y, the “has the jurisdiction” ground in O 8 r 1(1) ROC 2021 was created partly for CCAA cases, where the chosen court must hear the case and cannot decline for forum non conveniens (s 11). Per Chong (answer scheme), a CCAA contract goes on this ground, so there is no nexus and no forum conveniens inquiry. Per C&Y, it is unclear why approval is needed when the court already has jurisdiction, but O 8 r 1(1) still asks for it. Approval is dispensed with only where the contract allows service out (O 8 r 1(3)), and per Yeo agreeing to General Division jurisdiction alone does not do that, even in a Hague case.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J1.3 :: Serving Abroad: General Division (+)

[Claimant] seeks approval on the "has the jurisdiction" ground (O 8 r 1(1) ROC 2021), created partly for CCAA cases, so [no nexus] and [no forum conveniens] inquiry arises (per C&Y; J3.1.1). If [contract] permits service out, no approval is needed (O 8 r 1(3); J3.1.5).

  • Open (±): whether [defendant] may still argue [the claim] is outside the CCAA, and so resist "has the jurisdiction", should be raised inter partes (J3.1.1).
⚡ Base facts · 4 of 7F5
Fairhaven files the Supply Contract claim in the SICC. Kestor asks the SICC to decline because every witness and every membrane is in Elbonia. What is the answer?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

The SICC may decline only if hearing the case is contrary to its international and commercial character or an abuse of its process. There is no Spiliada balancing and no strong cause. Under s 11 the chosen court cannot decline in favour of another State, so Kestor's only answer is that clause 18 is null and void under Singapore law, including its choice of law rules.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per O 2 r 3(2) SICC Rules, the SICC may decline only if exercising jurisdiction is contrary to its international and commercial character or an abuse of its process. Per O 2 r 3(3), as there is a written jurisdiction agreement, it must not decline solely because the action is connected to a jurisdiction other than Singapore. Per C&Y and Chong (AY23-24 mid-term feedback), there is no Spiliada balancing and no strong cause. Per Chong (same feedback), an objectively international and commercial action, with the defendant abroad, gives little ground to decline. Separately, per s 11(1) Singapore must not decline unless clause 18 is null and void under Singapore law, including its choice of law rules, and per s 11(2) it cannot decline in favour of another State.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J5.3 :: Foreign Connections Irrelevant (+)

Per O 2 r 3(3), as there is [a written jurisdiction agreement], the SICC must not decline "solely on the ground that the action … is connected to a jurisdiction other than Singapore". Per C&Y and Chong (AY23-24 mid-term feedback), there is no Spiliada balancing, Australian test or strong cause, so [defendant]'s links to [State] count for nothing.

⚡ Base facts · 5 of 7B3
Fairhaven says that s 12 does not stop the Licence Contract claim, because splitting one dispute between Singapore and Arcadia is manifestly unjust and an Arcadian trial takes four years. Will that work?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per 6DM, the manifest injustice test is very different from, and far higher than, fragmentation as strong cause at common law. It covers cases such as no fair trial for bias or corruption. Mere delay or expense does not show that the agreement cannot reasonably be performed. So the court must stay or dismiss, and the two claims cannot be tried together here.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per the Hartley–Dogauchi Report (and C&Y), exceptions (c) and (d) apply only in the most exceptional circumstances and are read narrowly. Per 6DM, manifest injustice covers cases such as no fair trial for bias or corruption, and per Brand & Herrup (in 6DM) it must be clear, extremely serious and highly probable, not speculative. In 6DM the risk that a related individual could not be joined in England failed, as the test is very different from, and far higher than, fragmentation as strong cause at common law (Vinmar). Under (d), mere delay or expense is not enough. So no exception applies, and Singapore must stay or dismiss the Licence Contract claim.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J1.4.2 :: (c) Fragmentation (−)

Similar to 6DM, where the risk that a related individual could not be joined in England failed s 12(1)(c), [claimant]'s argument that [third party] cannot be joined in [State B] fails. The test is "very different" from, and far higher than, fragmentation as strong cause at common law (Vinmar), and [claimant] led no evidence of [State B law].

⚡ Base facts · 6 of 7B3
Fairhaven also says that clause 9 does not bind it because, under Singapore law, small print on the back of a form is not part of the contract. Which law decides?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Under s 12(1)(a) the question is whether the agreement is null and void under the law of the State of the chosen court. Per the Hartley–Dogauchi Report, whether a party consented to the clause is for the same law. Per 6DM, a clause is not disregarded merely because it would not bind under Singapore domestic law. Singapore law decides validity only under s 11, where Singapore is the chosen court.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per s 12(1)(a), Singapore must stay or dismiss unless the agreement is null and void under the law of the State of the chosen court, including its choice of law rules. Per the Hartley–Dogauchi Report (and C&Y), whether a party consented to the clause is also for that law, avoiding a split between validity and existence. Under Arcadian law clause 9 is valid and binding, so the attack fails. Nor can Fairhaven re-run the point as public policy under (c): per 6DM, a clause is not disregarded merely because it would not bind under Singapore domestic law.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J1.4.2 :: (a) Null and Void (±)

[Claimant] argues [clause X] is null and void for [ground] under [State B]'s law, including its choice of law rules, not Singapore law. [Claimant] must prove [State B law] as fact, or the presumption of similarity applies (C1.6.3); by analogy, [the s 12(1)(c) argument] in 6DM failed for want of evidence of English law.

⚡ Base facts · 7 of 7F3
Can Fairhaven file the Supply Contract claim directly in the SICC?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Clause 18 is dated 12 June 2019. A Singapore High Court clause of that date includes the SICC unless a contrary intention appears, and the CCAA says the same. Where foreign law governs the clause, it is open in principle whether this is a forum rule or a matter of construction for the proper law. Per Chong (seminar), the foreign law probably has no rule on the point, so the clause includes the SICC unless it expressly excludes it. The answer scheme reaches the same result for a clause of this kind governed by foreign law: the SICC has primary jurisdiction. Kestor is then served without permission as a party to the written jurisdiction agreement.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per O 2 r 2(1) SICC Rules and s 2(2) to (3) CCAA, a clause naming the Singapore High Court or the General Division, concluded on or after 1 October 2016, includes the SICC unless a contrary intention appears. Clause 18 is governed by Elbonian law, so it is open in principle whether O 2 r 2(1) applies: Fairhaven says it is a forum rule on internal allocation, for the lex fori, so the SICC is included; Kestor says construing the clause is for its proper law, and if Elbonian law read it as excluding the SICC, Fairhaven could reach the SICC only by transfer. Per Chong (seminar), Elbonian law probably has no rule on construing a reference to the Singapore High Court, so it falls back on O 2 r 2(1), and the clause includes the SICC unless it expressly excludes it. Kestor may also argue that a more specific reference to the SICC is needed (Chong, sample-final answer scheme), but the scheme gave the SICC primary jurisdiction on a High Court clause of this kind. Kestor, a party to the written jurisdiction agreement, is then served out without permission (O 5 r 6(2)(a)).

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J5.2.3 :: Post-2016 High Court Clause Includes the SICC (+)

Presently, [clause X], concluded on [date] (on or after 1 October 2016), names [the Singapore High Court / the General Division]. Per O 2 r 2(1) and s 2(2)–(3) CCAA, it includes the SICC unless [a contrary intention] appears, so [claimant] may file directly in the SICC.

  • Critique (−): Per C&Y, O 2 r 2(1) seems to bar evidence that [the parties] [never contemplated the SICC], contrary to Singapore's contextual interpretation and to party autonomy.
  • Reply (+): Per C&Y, the lost autonomy buys HCCCA enforceability of [the SICC judgment] in [State] and fits the SICC's international template; per Hartley–Dogauchi, "the courts of France" lets French law allocate internally.
  • Specific Reference Needed? (−): Per Chong (sample-final answer scheme), arguably [clause X] needs a more specific reference to the SICC to qualify as a written jurisdiction agreement for it, so [defendant] resists [primary jurisdiction].
📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
⚡ BIG IDEA

Each contract is tested on its own clause: two in the base, a third in Twist 1. Clause 18 has no label and Elbonian law gives it no promise, but s 3(2) deems it exclusive, so Singapore must hear the price claim under s 11, and as a 2019 High Court clause it probably opens the SICC too. Clause 9 is an Arcadian exclusive clause inside the CCAA on Arcadia's earlier date, so s 12 makes Singapore stay or dismiss the licence claim, and Fairhaven's small print, split and delay points all fail. The twists test a floating clause before election, transfer and joinder into the SICC, and an injunction where breach of a deemed exclusive clause is open.

  1. 1
    Clause 18: no label, Elbonian law A6

    Clause 18 says the parties “agree to submit to the jurisdiction of the Singapore High Court”, with no word “exclusive”. At common law it is construed under its governing law, Elbonian law (Shanghai Turbo (CA)), which finds no promise not to sue elsewhere. But it is dated 12 June 2019, so first ask whether the CCAA takes over. What Elbonian law says matters again for an injunction.

  2. 2
    The CCAA gate, clause by clause B1

    Test each contract on its own clause. Clause 18 names one Contracting State's courts, Singapore, and has no label, so s 3(2) deems it exclusive unless the parties expressly provide otherwise, whatever Elbonian law says; it is later than Singapore's date of 1 October 2016. Clause 9 says “only by the courts of Arcadia”, an express exclusive choice (s 3(1)), and its test date is Arcadia's, as the chosen court's State: 1 October 2015, which 5 August 2016 passes. Both cases are international, as Kestor resides in Elbonia (s 4(1)), and both claims are commercial. That Elbonia is not a Contracting State does not matter, as the test looks at the chosen court's State.

  3. 3
    Supply Contract in the General Division: s 11 B2

    Per s 11(1), Singapore must not decline unless clause 18 is null and void under Singapore law, including its choice of law rules, and nothing suggests it is. Per s 11(2), it cannot decline in favour of Elbonia, so there is no Spiliada and no strong cause, and the Elbonian witnesses and membranes are irrelevant. Kestor is abroad, so Fairhaven seeks approval to serve out on the “has the jurisdiction” ground (O 8 r 1(1) ROC 2021), created partly for CCAA cases, with no nexus or forum conveniens inquiry (C&Y; answer scheme). Approval is needed because neither contract deals with service (O 8 r 1(3)).

  4. 4
    Supply Contract in the SICC: probably primary jurisdiction F2F3

    Per O 2 r 1(1), the SICC has jurisdiction if the action is international and commercial, each party submitted under a written jurisdiction agreement, and no prerogative relief is sought. Clause 18 names the Singapore High Court, not the SICC, but per O 2 r 2(1) and s 2(2) to (3) CCAA a High Court clause concluded on or after 1 October 2016 includes the SICC unless a contrary intention appears. Open point: Fairhaven says O 2 r 2(1) is a forum rule, so it applies; Kestor says construing clause 18 is for Elbonian law, and if that law excluded the SICC, Fairhaven could reach it only by transfer, which in a CCAA case also needs every party's consent. Per Chong (seminar), Elbonian law probably has no rule on the point, so the clause includes the SICC. Kestor may also argue that a more specific reference to the SICC is needed (Chong, sample-final answer scheme), but the scheme gave the SICC primary jurisdiction on a High Court clause like this one. Kestor is then served out without permission as a party to the agreement (O 5 r 6(2)(a)), and transfer need not be discussed.

  5. 5
    Kestor asks the SICC to decline F5

    Per O 2 r 3(2), the SICC may decline only if hearing the case is contrary to its international and commercial character or an abuse of its process. Per O 2 r 3(3), with a written jurisdiction agreement it must not decline solely because the action is connected to another country, so there is no Spiliada and no strong cause. The action is objectively international and commercial, with Kestor in Elbonia, so there is little ground to decline (Chong, AY23-24 mid-term feedback). Section 11 points the same way, so Kestor's witnesses and membranes count for nothing.

  6. 6
    Licence Contract: s 12 and Fairhaven's three points B3

    Per s 12(1), Singapore must stay or dismiss unless an exception applies; clause 9 is an exclusive agreement that does not designate Singapore, so per 6DM the next question is the exceptions, and (c) and (d) are read narrowly (Hartley–Dogauchi Report). Small print fails under (a): validity is for Arcadian law, including its choice of law rules, and so is whether Fairhaven consented (Hartley–Dogauchi Report); Arcadian law holds clause 9 valid and binding. Nor can Fairhaven re-run the point as public policy under (c): per 6DM, a clause is not disregarded merely because it would not bind under Singapore domestic law. The split fails under (c), as manifest injustice is very different from, and far higher than, fragmentation as strong cause at common law (6DM), and the four year wait is neither manifest injustice under (c) nor, as mere delay, enough under (d). So the licence claim is stayed or dismissed in favour of Arcadia.

  7. 7
    Result

    Singapore must hear the Supply Contract claim, and Fairhaven can probably file it directly in the SICC, where Kestor's Elbonian links count for nothing. The Licence Contract claim must be stayed or dismissed in favour of Arcadia. The SICC is no way round this: it is a division of the General Division, and clause 9 is not an agreement to submit to it. So the two claims cannot be tried together here, because the parties chose different courts in their two clauses.

2Twist 1

🧩 TWIST 1

Now add these facts.

A third contract, the Maintenance Contract, was signed on 2 February 2022 and is governed by Singapore law. Kestor owes US$300,000 under it. Clause 14 reads:

“The courts of Singapore or the courts of Arcadia, as Kestor may elect by written notice to Fairhaven, shall have exclusive jurisdiction over any dispute arising out of this contract.”

Kestor has given no notice. Fairhaven wants to add the maintenance claim to its Singapore action.

✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • A8
    Floating clause, or two courts named. Clause 14 is a floating jurisdiction clause: two courts are named and one party picks by notice. Ask whether it is valid at common law and whether it has been exercised.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • A7
    Asymmetric clause: one side may sue anywhere. Tempting because only Kestor may elect. But an asymmetric clause lets one side sue anywhere and ties the other to one court. After an election clause 14 ties both parties to the same court.
  • A2
    Says "exclusive": Singapore courts. Tempting because the clause names Singapore and says “exclusive”. But no court is exclusive until Kestor elects, and Kestor may elect Arcadia.

Fair to tick but not needed: B4 Outside the CCAA: say why, then the common law, A1 Any jurisdiction clause: what it promises, D8 Singapore clause, defendant abroad

Application questions · twist 1

⚡ Twist 1 · 1 of 3B1
Kestor has not elected. Is the Maintenance Contract inside the CCAA?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per C&Y, CCAA coverage of a floating clause is unclear. Before election there is no chosen court, so arguably no exclusive agreement. Once notice is served, the clause crystallises into an exclusive choice of one court and is probably within the CCAA. It is arguable that an election by Kestor alone is enough, because both parties agreed that Kestor could elect. The two States row is for a clause that names two courts with no way to pick one.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per C&Y, CCAA coverage of a floating clause is unclear. Before election there is no chosen court, so arguably no s 3(1) agreement, and the common law governs. Once notice is served, the clause crystallises into an exclusive choice of the elected court and is probably within the CCAA: s 11 if Kestor elects Singapore, s 12 if it elects Arcadia. Both States' dates are met, as the contract was signed on 2 February 2022. Section 3 requires agreement between the parties, but arguably Kestor's election suffices because both parties agreed that Kestor could elect.

⚡ Twist 1 · 2 of 3A8
At common law, is clause 14 a valid jurisdiction clause?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Shanghai Turbo and C&Y, a floating jurisdiction clause is valid at common law if not too uncertain, unlike a floating choice of law clause. It needs an election mechanism, and one party's option is one. Two named courts are read as non-exclusive for both only where there is no mechanism. Letting the claimant elect by suing was rejected as encouraging a race to sue.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Shanghai Turbo (CA) and C&Y, a floating jurisdiction clause is valid at common law if not too uncertain, unlike a floating choice of law clause, which is void because a contract cannot exist “in a legal vacuum” (Amin Rasheed). It needs an election mechanism, such as one party's right to choose, and Kestor's right to elect by written notice is one. Two named courts are read as a non-exclusive clause for both only where there is no mechanism. Letting the claimant elect at the moment of suing was rejected as encouraging a race to sue.

If the CCAA did not apply, the common law points the same way: Fairhaven would be suing in breach of a foreign exclusive clause and would have to show strong cause.

If the CCAA applies, s 12 requires a stay or dismissal unless an exception applies, and none is suggested. If it does not, the common law points the same way: Fairhaven would be suing in breach of a foreign exclusive clause and would have to show strong cause.

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes

    The Supply and Licence answers stay the same. A third contract, the Maintenance Contract, signed on 2 February 2022 and governed by Singapore law, has clause 14: the courts of Singapore or Arcadia, “as Kestor may elect by written notice”, shall have exclusive jurisdiction. Kestor has given no notice, and Fairhaven wants to add the US$300,000 claim to its Singapore action.

  2. 2
    Clause 14 is a valid floating clause A8

    Per Shanghai Turbo (CA) and C&Y, a floating jurisdiction clause is valid at common law if not too uncertain, unlike a floating choice of law clause, which is void. It needs an election mechanism, and Kestor's right to elect by written notice is one, so clause 14 is not read as non-exclusive for both courts. The election is Kestor's alone: letting a claimant elect by suing was rejected as encouraging a race to sue. Nor is the clause asymmetric, as after election both parties are tied to the same court.

  3. 3
    Inside the CCAA? Unclear until Kestor elects B1

    Per C&Y, CCAA coverage of a floating clause is unclear. Against: before election there is no chosen court, so arguably no s 3(1) agreement, and the common law governs, with clause 14 binding as a valid floating clause. For: once Kestor serves notice, the clause crystallises into an exclusive choice of one court and is probably within the CCAA, as both States' dates are earlier than 2 February 2022. Section 3 requires agreement between the parties, but arguably Kestor's election suffices because both parties agreed that Kestor could elect.

  4. 4
    Where the maintenance claim goes B2B3

    If Kestor elects Singapore, clause 14 probably comes inside the CCAA and s 11 makes Singapore hear the claim; outside it, clause 14 is an exclusive Singapore clause at common law, so Kestor would bear strong cause to resist Singapore. If it elects Arcadia, s 12 probably requires a stay or dismissal; even outside the CCAA, Fairhaven would be suing in breach of an exclusive Arcadian clause and would bear strong cause. Until Kestor elects, Fairhaven cannot be sure the maintenance claim stays here, and the licence claim must go to Arcadia anyway, so the three claims can never all be tried together in Singapore.

Application questions · twist 2

⚡ Twist 2 · 1 of 3F7
The CCAA applies and clause 18 names the Singapore High Court. Kestor objects. Can the General Division still transfer the claim to the SICC?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

In a CCAA case with a High Court clause, transfer needs every party's consent on top of the usual requirements. Where the clause names the receiving court each party is treated as consenting, and a 2019 High Court clause includes the SICC, so consent is doubly deemed. The counter, per C&Y: it is unclear whether deemed consent meets the Convention's threshold. Kestor objected in time, so a court in another Contracting State might refuse to recognise the SICC judgment against it. Arguably the court should insist on actual consent. Filing in the SICC at the start avoids the problem.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per O 2 r 4(1), transfer needs an international and commercial action, no prerogative relief, and the SICC being more appropriate; an International Judge trained in Elbonian law, the governing law, favours the SICC (Chong, AY23-24 mid-term feedback). As the CCAA applies and clause 18 names the Singapore High Court, O 2 r 4(4) also requires every party's consent. Per O 2 r 4(7), a clause naming the receiving court counts as each party's consent, and per O 2 r 2(1) a 2019 High Court clause includes the SICC, so Kestor's consent is doubly deemed (C&Y). But per C&Y it is unclear whether deemed consent meets the Convention's threshold: Kestor objected in time, so a court in another Contracting State might refuse to recognise the SICC judgment (art 8(5)), and arguably the court should insist on actual consent, in which case Kestor's refusal blocks the transfer. Filing directly in the SICC at the start avoids the problem.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J5.4.2 :: Deemed Consent (+)

  • Counter (−): Per C&Y, it is unclear whether deemed consent meets the CCAA threshold. [Defendant] objected in time, so [the SICC judgment] risks refusal under art 8(5) in [State], where its assets are; arguably the General Division should insist on actual consent.

⚡ Twist 2 · 2 of 3F8
How does Fairhaven bring Kestor Holdings, which is in Utopia and outside clause 18, into the SICC action?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Once the SICC has jurisdiction over an international and commercial action, it may hear claims against additional parties if the action as a whole stays international and commercial. The joined party need not have submitted in writing. A party abroad who is outside the agreement is served with permission, given if the SICC has jurisdiction and the case is appropriate for it. Per C&Y, forum non conveniens does not apply. The claim on the guarantee shares a common question with the price claim.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per s 18D(3) to (4) SCJA, once the SICC has jurisdiction over an international and commercial action, it may hear claims against additional parties if the action as a whole stays international and commercial. Per O 10 r 5(2), the added party need not have submitted under a written jurisdiction agreement. Joinder generally needs the SICC's permission (O 10 r 7(1)), and the guarantee claim shares a common question with the price claim, so joining it lets the court resolve connected matters (O 10 r 6(1)). A party abroad outside the agreement is served with permission under O 5 r 6(1), given if the SICC “has the jurisdiction” and “it is appropriate”; per C&Y, forum non conveniens does not apply.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J5.6 :: Service on [C] Abroad (±)

Per O 5 r 6(2), [C] in [State] is served without permission if party to a written jurisdiction agreement or [an agreement allowing service out]; otherwise, per O 5 r 6(1), with permission if the SICC "has the jurisdiction" and "it is appropriate". Per C&Y, FNC does not apply, unlike the General Division's test (J3.1).

⚡ Twist 2 · 3 of 3F8
Kestor Holdings asks the SICC to decline because it has no link with Singapore. Kestor made the same point and failed. Must Kestor Holdings fail too?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Kestor Holdings applies under the same rule: the SICC declines only where hearing the case is contrary to its international and commercial character or an abuse of process. But the rule that foreign connections alone are no ground protects only where the parties agreed in writing. Kestor Holdings did not, so the SICC may weigh its links with Utopia. That is still not a Spiliada analysis.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Kestor Holdings applies under the same rule as Kestor: per O 2 r 3(2), the SICC may decline only where hearing the case is contrary to its international and commercial character or an abuse of its process. But per the slides, the bar in O 2 r 3(3) on declining solely for foreign connections protects only parties to a written jurisdiction agreement. The User Guide ignores connections because the parties agreed in writing; Kestor Holdings did not, so the SICC may weigh its links with Utopia. That is still not a Spiliada analysis, and arguably Fairhaven bears the burden of showing that the claim against Kestor Holdings is appropriate for the SICC (O 10 r 5(1)(b)(ii)).

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes

    Whether Singapore must hear the Supply Contract claim does not change: s 11 still applies. What changes is the route into the SICC: Fairhaven started in the General Division and served Kestor in Elbonia, so it now needs a transfer, which Kestor opposes. Fairhaven also wants to join Kestor Holdings, the Utopian parent, which guaranteed the price by a separate letter with no jurisdiction clause.

  2. 2
    Transfer: consent is deemed, but is that enough? F7

    Per O 2 r 4(1), transfer needs an international and commercial action, no prerogative relief, and the SICC being more appropriate, which an International Judge trained in Elbonian law, the governing law, supports (Chong, AY23-24 mid-term feedback). As the CCAA applies and clause 18 names the Singapore High Court, O 2 r 4(4) also needs every party's consent. Per O 2 r 4(7), a clause naming the receiving court counts as consent, and a 2019 High Court clause includes the SICC (O 2 r 2(1)), so Kestor's consent is doubly deemed (C&Y). Against, per C&Y: Kestor objected in time, so it is unclear whether deemed consent is enough, as a court in another Contracting State might refuse to recognise the SICC judgment (art 8(5)); arguably the court should insist on actual consent, and Kestor's refusal would then block the transfer. Result: transfer is probably allowed; the risk matters only for enforcement in a Contracting State, and Elbonia, where Kestor trades, is not one.

  3. 3
    Kestor Holdings is outside clause 18 A9

    Kestor Holdings is not a party to clause 18, and its guarantee letter has no jurisdiction clause. A clause cannot be used to saddle a non-party with a burden (Chong, AY23-24 feedback), and in keeping with privity it usually does not reach a non-party without a quite clear indication (Asiana). So Kestor Holdings takes neither the burden of clause 18 nor its protection: it cannot be served as of right as a party to the agreement, and the bar on relying on foreign connections does not cover it.

  4. 4
    Joining Kestor Holdings in the SICC F8

    Per s 18D(3) to (4) SCJA, once the SICC has jurisdiction over an international and commercial action, it may hear claims against added parties if the action as a whole stays international and commercial, and per O 10 r 5(2) they need not have submitted in writing. The guarantee claim shares a common question with the price claim, so joining Kestor Holdings lets the court resolve connected matters (O 10 r 6(1)), generally with the SICC's permission (O 10 r 7(1)). It is served abroad with permission under O 5 r 6(1), given if the SICC has jurisdiction and the case is appropriate for it; per C&Y, forum non conveniens does not apply. If it then asks the SICC to decline, the foreign-connections bar in O 2 r 3(3) protects only parties to a written jurisdiction agreement, so its Utopian links may be weighed under O 2 r 3(2), still without Spiliada. Arguably Fairhaven bears the burden of showing that the claim is appropriate for the SICC (O 10 r 5(1)(b)(ii)). Result: Kestor Holdings can probably be joined and served, but its own application to decline is less sure to fail than Kestor's.

Application questions · twist 3

⚡ Twist 3 · 1 of 4G9
Is Kestor's Elbonian action a breach of clause 18?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per C&Y, deeming makes the clause exclusive in effect, and the chosen court's injunction against a suit in a non-chosen court upholds the agreement, so a contractual injunction is arguable. The reply is that breach is contract interpretation under the proper law, and Elbonian law gives the clause no promise, so deeming arguably settles only jurisdiction. Prof Chong's answer scheme leaves breach open and runs vexation.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per C&Y, s 3(2) deems clause 18 “exclusive in effect”, and the chosen court's injunction against a suit in a non-chosen court in breach of the agreement upholds it, so a contractual injunction is arguable; if breach is shown, it ordinarily issues unless Kestor shows strong reasons (Sun Travels). The reply: per C&Y, breach is a question of contract interpretation under the proper law; under Elbonian law “submit” carries no promise not to sue elsewhere, so deeming arguably settles only jurisdiction. Prof Chong's answer scheme leaves breach open and runs the injunction on vexation.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J6.5.3 :: Deemed-Exclusive Singapore Clause (±)

Presently, [clause X] is exclusive only by s 3(2) CCAA and, under [law X], arguably has no promissory content. Per Chong (answer scheme), [clause X] still supplies sufficient interest and the ASI is run on vexation or oppression (J6.3.2); as the chosen court, Singapore "will likely grant the ASI".

  • Breach arguable (+): per C&Y, s 3(2) deems [clause X] "exclusive in effect", and the chosen court's ASI against a suit in [a non-chosen court] in breach of the agreement upholds it, so a contractual ASI is arguable (J6.3.1).

⚡ Twist 3 · 2 of 4G9
If breach is not shown, must Fairhaven prove that Singapore is the natural forum before the court looks at vexation?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Chong (answer scheme), a deemed exclusive Singapore clause still supplies sufficient interest even if it carries no promise under its own law. The injunction is then run on vexation or oppression. The natural forum is the usual proxy for sufficient interest where there is no Singapore clause at all.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

For an injunction not founded on breach, Singapore usually shows sufficient interest by being the natural forum, but natural forum is only a proxy (BCS v Baker). Per Chong (answer scheme), a deemed exclusive Singapore clause still supplies sufficient interest even if it carries no promise under its own law, and the injunction is then run on vexation or oppression. So Fairhaven need not show that Singapore is clearly more appropriate than Elbonia, and Kestor's Elbonian witnesses and goods do not block the application.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J6.5.3 :: Deemed-Exclusive Singapore Clause (±)

Presently, [clause X] is exclusive only by s 3(2) CCAA and, under [law X], arguably has no promissory content. Per Chong (answer scheme), [clause X] still supplies sufficient interest and the ASI is run on vexation or oppression (J6.3.2); as the chosen court, Singapore "will likely grant the ASI".

  • Breach arguable (+): per C&Y, s 3(2) deems [clause X] "exclusive in effect", and the chosen court's ASI against a suit in [a non-chosen court] in breach of the agreement upholds it, so a contractual ASI is arguable (J6.3.1).
  • Reply (−): per C&Y, breach is contract interpretation under [the proper law]; if [law X] gives [clause X] no promise, s 3(2) arguably settles only [jurisdiction] (analysis). Chong's scheme leaves breach open: "no promissory content?" (J7.2.6).

How is the vexation route likely to end?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Parallel proceedings alone do not usually show vexation, so Fairhaven should say what is oppressive on these facts. But per the answer scheme, as the chosen court under the Convention Singapore “will likely grant” the injunction. The early stage of the Elbonian action points the same way, and Fairhaven applied promptly. One caution: in the scheme the foreign court was in a Contracting State, which should itself have declined, and that gives the chosen court more leeway. Elbonia is not a Contracting State, so that support is missing and the result is less sure than in the scheme. It is still a discretion, and vexation must be shown.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Parallel proceedings alone do not usually show vexation (UBS v Telesto), so Fairhaven must point to something more on these facts. Per Prof Chong's answer scheme, as the chosen court under the Convention Singapore “will likely grant” the injunction. Separately, an early stage points to the injunction (Baker v BCS (SICC); C&Y): the Elbonian action is six weeks old and Fairhaven has taken no step in it. One caution: in the scheme the foreign court was in a Contracting State, which should itself have declined, and per C&Y that gives the chosen court more leeway. Elbonia is not a Contracting State, so that support is missing and the result is less sure.

⚡ Twist 3 · 4 of 4G10
Fairhaven's claim is in the SICC under clause 18. Which test governs the injunction application there?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per BCS v Baker, the same framework governs an injunction from the SICC. Per Chong (sample-final answer scheme), if the SICC has primary jurisdiction under the clause, its own test arguably governs the application: it declines only where hearing the matter is contrary to its international and commercial character or an abuse of its process.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per BCS v Baker and C&Y, the same framework governs an injunction sought from the SICC. Seised under a written SICC agreement, the SICC modifies sufficient interest: per C&Y, Spiliada is irrelevant and O 2 r 3 supplies the connection test, unless the claim is not international and commercial or suing in the SICC is abusive. Per Chong (sample-final answer scheme), if the SICC has primary jurisdiction under the clause, its O 2 r 3(2) test arguably governs the application: it declines only where hearing the matter is contrary to its international and commercial character or an abuse of its process.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J5.7 :: ASI Sought From the SICC

Per Chong (sample-final answer scheme), if [the SICC] has primary jurisdiction under [clause X], the O 2 r 3(2) test arguably governs [the ASI application]. For HCCCA cases see J6.5.3; s 10 CCAA leaves interim measures outside the Act.

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes

    The jurisdiction answers stay the same: s 11 applies, and the SICC probably has primary jurisdiction under clause 18. What is new is Kestor's Elbonian action on the Supply Contract, now six weeks old, in which Fairhaven has taken no step; Elbonia took jurisdiction under its own rules and is not a Contracting State. Fairhaven has filed its price claim in the SICC, served Kestor in Elbonia, and wants an anti-suit injunction.

  2. 2
    Starter, the SICC and amenability G1G10G2

    An injunction indirectly interferes with the Elbonian court, so it issues only where the ends of justice require, with caution (SNIA; Lakshmi); Fairhaven bears the burden (Kirkham) and must name its basis (Cooperative Muratori). Per BCS v Baker the same framework governs in the SICC, but as the SICC has primary jurisdiction under clause 18, its O 2 r 3(2) test arguably governs the application (answer scheme). Kestor is amenable: it was validly served out as a party to clause 18, and valid service suffices (Cooperative Muratori; C&Y). Kestor may cite Akai, where a respondent with no presence or assets here was not amenable, but its lack of assets goes only to how well the order bites, as breach is contempt (SNIA; C&Y).

  3. 3
    Breach of clause 18: open G9

    Argue breach first. For: per C&Y, s 3(2) makes clause 18 “exclusive in effect”, and the chosen court's injunction against a suit in a non-chosen court upholds the agreement, so a contractual injunction is arguable. Elbonia is outside the Convention, so it would run as an ordinary contractual injunction with no natural forum inquiry, issued unless Kestor shows strong reasons (Sun Travels); as the SICC is seised under clause 18, per C&Y that test arguably does not apply at all, or applies modified by O 2 r 3(2). Against: per C&Y, breach is contract interpretation under the proper law; Elbonian law gives clause 18 no promise not to sue elsewhere, so deeming arguably settles only jurisdiction. The answer scheme leaves breach open, so run vexation in the alternative.

  4. 4
    No breach: sufficient interest, then vexation G9G7

    Without breach, clause 18 still gives Singapore a sufficient interest (Chong, answer scheme), and in the SICC its O 2 r 3 test points the same way, so natural forum is not needed and the Elbonian witnesses do not block the application. Vexation must still be shown, in the clearest cases only (Kirkham), and parallel proceedings alone are not enough (UBS v Telesto). The early stage helps: the action is six weeks old and Fairhaven has taken no step in it (Baker v BCS (SICC); C&Y). On injustice, Kestor can still raise the clogging as its defence here, and an undertaking can meet any genuine advantage it loses (SNIA). Per the scheme, as the chosen court Singapore “will likely grant” the injunction, but there the foreign court was in a Contracting State that should itself have declined; Elbonia is not, so the result is probable, not certain.

5Scorecards: weigh the factors

Prof Chong rewards applying facts to factor tests. Sort each fact, then answer the verdict question. These use the base facts unless a line says “Suppose”.

B1 Sort the factors: The CCAA gate, clause by clause

Each line is a clause. Is the contract inside the CCAA? Lines marked “Suppose” change one fact for this card only.

Clause 18: “submit to the jurisdiction of the Singapore High Court”, signed 12 June 2019. Elbonian law gives it no promise.
Inside the CCAA. An unlabelled clause for one State's courts is deemed exclusive unless the parties expressly provide otherwise. Its own governing law does not matter at the gate. J1.2.1 :: Deemed Exclusive
Clause 9: “only by the courts of Arcadia”, signed 5 August 2016. Arcadia's date is 1 October 2015.
Inside the CCAA. The clause is later than the date the Convention entered into force for the chosen court's State. Singapore's date of 1 October 2016 is not the test for an Arcadian clause. J1.2.2 :: Temporal Scope
Clause 14: Singapore or Arcadia “as Kestor may elect by written notice”. No notice yet.
Unclear. Before election there is no single chosen court, so arguably no exclusive agreement. After election it probably comes inside. J1.2.1 :: Floating Clause
Suppose: clause 18 was signed on 12 June 2016.
Outside. A clause choosing Singapore must be concluded after 1 October 2016. This one is not, so the common law decides, and its meaning turns on Elbonian law. J1.2.2 :: Temporal Scope
Suppose: clause 18 said “submit to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the Singapore High Court”.
Outside. “Non-exclusive” is an express provision otherwise, so deeming is displaced. Invoking s 3(2) here is a recurring exam error. J1.2.1 :: Deemed Exclusive
Suppose: clause 14 said only “the courts of Singapore or the courts of Arcadia shall have jurisdiction”, with no election words.
Outside. It designates the courts of two States, not of one Contracting State, so it is outside the CCAA. J1.2.1 :: More Than One State
Suppose: clause 9 added “but Fairhaven may also sue Kestor in any other court”.
Outside. Per CHLOE V, an asymmetric clause is not exclusive under the CCAA. At common law it stays exclusive against the restricted party. J1.2.1 :: Asymmetric Clause
Suppose: clause 18 sat in Fairhaven's employment contract with an engineer based in Elbonia.
Outside. Employment agreements are excluded from the CCAA, so nothing is deemed and the common law decides. J1.2.4 :: Excluded
Kestor says that the whole Supply Contract is void for misrepresentation.
Inside the CCAA. The clause is independent of the contract. Its validity cannot be challenged only because the contract is said to be void. J1.2.1 :: Separability
⚡ Scorecard 1 · the verdictB1
On the base facts and Twist 1, where does each claim go?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Each contract is tested on its own clause. Clause 18 is inside the CCAA with Singapore chosen (s 11). Clause 9 is inside with Arcadia chosen and no exception applies (s 12). Clause 14 has no chosen court yet. So the three claims cannot all be tried together in Singapore.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Under the CCAA each contract's clause is tested separately. Clause 18 (Supply) chooses Singapore, is deemed exclusive and is dated after 1 October 2016, so s 11 requires Singapore to hear the claim. Clause 9 (Licence) chooses Arcadia exclusively, is dated after Arcadia's date of 1 October 2015, and no s 12 exception applies, so the claim is stayed or dismissed. Clause 14 (Maintenance) is a floating clause with no chosen court until Kestor elects: arguably outside the CCAA before then, probably inside after.

6Remember

🧠 FOR THE EXAM
  • Test each contract on its own clause, and date each clause against the chosen court's State: Singapore's 1 October 2016 is irrelevant to an Arcadian clause.
  • An unlabelled clause for one State's courts is deemed exclusive by s 3(2) whatever its governing law says; only express words such as “non-exclusive” displace it.
  • Singapore chosen inside the CCAA: s 11, no Spiliada or strong cause, and service out on the “has the jurisdiction” ground; a High Court clause from 1 October 2016 includes the SICC, probably even when foreign law governs it.
  • Foreign court chosen inside the CCAA: s 12; small print goes to the chosen court's law, and split proceedings and delay fall far short of the exceptions.
  • A floating jurisdiction clause with an election mechanism is valid at common law; before election it is arguably outside the CCAA, after election probably inside. A stranger to a clause takes neither its burden nor its protection.
  • Deemed exclusive with no promise under the proper law: breach is open, so argue it, then use the clause for sufficient interest and run vexation.

LAW302 · META GAME · QUESTION 1 · HYPO q1-09 · NO GEMINI · 16 QUESTIONS

Lakemont v Sora Dining

Written by Claude for the drill and law reviewed. There is no Gemini output for this hypo.

Answers:

1Base facts

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Lakemont v Sora Dining

Lakemont Brands Ltd, a company incorporated in Ruritania, owns a café brand. Sora Dining Pte Ltd, a Singapore incorporated company, runs the brand's cafés in Singapore. Sora has no office or staff in Ruritania. On 3 March 2021 the two companies signed two agreements.

The Franchise Agreement is governed by Ruritanian law. Clause 28 reads:

“The courts of Ruritania shall have exclusive jurisdiction over any dispute arising out of or in connection with this Agreement.”

The Supply Agreement, under which Lakemont sells ovens to Sora, is governed by Singapore law. Clause 15 reads:

“The courts of Singapore shall have exclusive jurisdiction over any dispute arising out of or in connection with this Agreement.”

In 2025 Sora stopped paying. Lakemont sued it in Ruritania under both agreements. Sora was served at its Singapore office in good time, but it did not appear. In February 2026 the Ruritanian court gave judgment in default. It ruled that clause 28 is an exclusive choice of court agreement under the Hague Convention. It also ruled that clause 15 is void under the Ruritanian Franchise Act.

It ordered Sora: (i) to pay royalties of US$2 million under the Franchise Agreement; (ii) to pay US$4 million in exemplary damages for deliberate breach of that Agreement; (iii) to remove the brand's signs from its cafés; and (iv) to pay US$1 million, the price of the ovens under the Supply Agreement.

Lakemont applies to the General Division to enforce all four orders. It says that both rulings bind Sora in Singapore.

Advise Sora.

ℹ ASSUME
  1. The Hague Convention on Choice of Court Agreements entered into force for Ruritania on 1 January 2019. No other treaty or statute on foreign judgments applies.
  2. The Ruritanian Franchise Act makes void any clause that sends a dispute with a Ruritanian franchisor to a foreign court. Under Singapore law clause 15 is valid.
  3. Under Ruritanian law exemplary damages punish a deliberate breach. They are paid to the claimant.
  4. In April 2026 Sora applied in Ruritania to set aside the default judgment. The application is pending. The judgment can be enforced in Ruritania in the meantime.
  5. Sora says that the royalties were wrongly calculated.
✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • H1
    Which regime. One judgment, two regimes. Test each order against the clause of its own contract: the Ruritanian court was the chosen court for the Franchise claims only.
  • B1
    CCAA gate: five conditions. Part 3 needs an exclusive agreement inside the CCAA. Clause 28 passes every row: express, international, commercial, and signed after the Convention entered into force for Ruritania.
  • H9
    CCAA Part 3: judgment of the chosen court. Orders (i) to (iii) come from the chosen court. They must be recognised and enforced unless a ground in ss 14 to 16 applies, and the facts plant several.
  • B5
    The foreign court has already ruled that the HCCCA applies. The Ruritanian court has ruled that the Convention applies, and Lakemont says that binds. The judgment was by default.
  • H8
    Issue estoppel from the foreign ruling. The ruling that clause 15 is void is pleaded as an issue estoppel. It was made under the Franchise Act, and clause 15 is governed by Singapore law.
  • H2
    Common law: the four requirements; on the merits. Order (iv) is outside the CCAA, so Lakemont needs the four common law requirements for it.
  • H4
    International jurisdiction: submission. For order (iv) the fight is international jurisdiction. Sora did not appear, and the only agreement to submit in the Supply Agreement points to Singapore.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • B3
    CCAA applies and a foreign court is chosen (s 12). Section 12 tells a Singapore court to stay an action brought here against a foreign chosen court clause. No one has sued here on the Franchise Agreement. The question is the effect of a judgment, which is Part 3.
  • H6
    Money judgment, or a declaration?. Order (iii) is not for money, which tempts the common law rule that only a fixed sum is enforced. But order (iii) is a Franchise order under Part 3, and Part 3 covers non-money judgments.
  • E7
    Strong cause: starter and nature of the test. Lakemont broke an exclusive Singapore clause, which sounds like strong cause. But strong cause is the test for a stay or a set-aside of a pending action. Here the breach matters only as a possible defence to recognition.
  • B2
    CCAA applies and Singapore is the chosen court (s 11). Section 11 is for a Singapore court asked to hear a claim under a Singapore clause. On the base facts no one has sued here on the Supply Agreement.
  • G3
    Contractual ASI: a Singapore clause is breached. A breach of a Singapore exclusive clause is the basis of a contractual anti-suit injunction. But the Ruritanian action has ended in judgment, so there is no action left to restrain.

Fair to tick but not needed: H3 International jurisdiction: presence, H5 Final and conclusive, H7 Defences to recognition and enforcement, B4 Outside the CCAA: say why, then the common law

Application questions · base facts

⚡ Base facts · 1 of 7H1
How many regimes apply to the Ruritanian judgment?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Only a judgment of the chosen court qualifies under Part 3. For the oven claim the Ruritanian court was not the chosen court, so that part is outside the CCAA. The CCAA does not bar its enforcement at common law, but the common law rules and defences then apply. A default judgment and a non-money order are both “judgments” under the CCAA.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J7.5.5 :: The Gap (±)

Presently, [the COCA] chose [X court 1], but [creditor] sued in [Y court] in breach. (+) Per C&Y, [the Y judgment] is outside the CCAA, which does not bar its enforcement under [REFJA / common law]. (−) Submitted that the common law should recognise a defence (J7.2.6); if [Y] is gazetted, s 5(4)(b) REFJA already applies (J7.4.3).

⚡ Base facts · 2 of 7B5
Lakemont says that the Ruritanian ruling that clause 28 falls within the Convention binds the Singapore court. Does it?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Run both sides. For Lakemont: the usual requirements for an estoppel look met, since Sora agreed to the Ruritanian court in clause 28. For Sora: per Prof Chong's answer scheme, the debtor may argue that such a ruling raises no estoppel, because each court decides for itself whether the Convention applies. Section 13(3)(b) binds the court to the chosen court's findings of fact on jurisdiction, but not where the judgment was by default, and never to the legal evaluation of those facts. Singapore then runs the gate itself. Clause 28 passes it, so the point does not save Sora.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J7.3.2.3 :: HCCCA Applicability

Per Prof Chong (March 2026 answer scheme), [debtor] may argue that [the X court]'s ruling that [clause] falls within the HCCCA raises no estoppel, each Contracting State court deciding for itself whether [the HCCCA] applies (J1).

⚡ Base facts · 3 of 7H9
Sora says that the royalties were wrongly calculated, and that a default judgment which may still be set aside is not final. Do these points work under Part 3?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per s 13(3)(a) the court may not review the merits. Per s 13(2) a judgment is enforced if it is enforceable in the State of origin, and the Assume list says it is. The grounds in ss 14 to 16 are exhaustive. Applying the common law requirements and defences to a CCAA judgment is a common error.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J7.5.2 :: No Review of the Merits (+)

Per s 13(3)(a), the court may not review [the X judgment]'s merits save to apply Part 3; per s 13(1), it recognises it as it would [a General Division judgment].

⚡ Base facts · 4 of 7H9
Which Part 3 ground is Sora's best answer, for now, to orders (i) to (iii) as a whole?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Sora was notified in good time and chose not to appear, so s 14(a) fails. The pending application to set aside is a review, and under s 15(2) the court may refuse or postpone. That is a discretion, not a duty. Exemplary damages go to s 16, and only to order (ii). Hong Pian Tee is a common law test.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J7.5.4 :: Pending Review or Appeal (±)

Per s 15(2)–(3), if [the X judgment] is under [appeal] in [X], or time to appeal has not expired, the court may refuse, set aside or postpone, but [creditor] may apply again once [the appeal] is decided.

⚡ Base facts · 5 of 7H9
What happens to order (ii), the exemplary damages?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Section 16 lets the court refuse a judgment so far as it awards damages, such as exemplary damages, beyond compensation for actual loss. It does not matter that the claimant receives them. The court considers whether the award covers the costs of the foreign proceedings. Under s 19 a severable part must be enforced. Who receives the money is the common law test, not the CCAA test.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J7.5.4 :: Excess Damages (±)

(−) Per s 16, the court may refuse [the X judgment] insofar as it awards damages, such as [punitive damages], exceeding compensation for actual loss. (+) It considers whether [the award] covers [costs and expenses of the X proceedings].

⚡ Base facts · 6 of 7H4
On the base facts, can order (iv) be enforced at common law?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

International jurisdiction needs presence or submission, by Singapore's rules. Sora has no place of business in Ruritania and took no step there. Clause 15 is an agreement to submit to Singapore. Clause 28 belongs to the Franchise Agreement and does not cover a claim under the Supply Agreement, which has its own clause. Proper service goes to natural justice, not to jurisdiction. The breach of clause 15 is a further answer, but that defence is unsettled.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J7.1.2 :: Four Grounds

Per Republic of India v Deutsche Telekom (SGCA), [debtor] must have been [present in [X]] or have [claimed or counterclaimed / voluntarily appeared / agreed in advance to submit]. Residence is not listed (J7.1.2.2).

⚡ Base facts · 7 of 7H8
Does the Ruritanian ruling that clause 15 is void bind Sora in Singapore on the base facts?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Merck, issue estoppel needs a foreign judgment capable of recognition, the same parties and the same issue. The first fails, as there was no international jurisdiction over Sora on the oven claim. The third fails too. Per Gonzalo Gil White the party relying on the estoppel bears the burden, and there is no identity where the issue arose under different laws. Singapore's rules test clause 15 by Singapore law, under which it is valid.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J7.3.2.1 :: Identity of Issue (−)

Per Gonzalo Gil White (SGCA), [the party relying] bears the burden, with special caution for foreign rulings. Ask (1) were [the issues] framed the same way; and (2) if so, did they arise under different laws? If so, no identity.

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
⚡ BIG IDEA

One Ruritanian judgment decides claims under two contracts, and each order must be tested against the clause of its own contract. Ruritania was the chosen court only for the Franchise claims, so orders (i) to (iii) go to Part 3 of the CCAA, where only ss 14 to 16 count, while the oven order (iv) goes to the common law and fails there, because Sora was not present in Ruritania and did not submit to it on the oven claim. The twists move the fight: a defence on the merits is a submission and probably costs Sora the clause 15 defence, but a clashing Singapore judgment bars order (iv) on its own; and stopping enforcement abroad after judgment needs exceptional circumstances, not just a breach.

  1. 1
    Which regime? Split the judgment by contract H1

    Test each order against the clause of its own contract. Per s 2(1), Part 3 of the CCAA covers only a judgment of the court chosen in an exclusive agreement inside the CCAA. Clause 28 chose the Ruritanian courts for Franchise disputes, so orders (i) to (iii) come from the chosen court. Lakemont may say the ovens serve the franchise, so the oven claim is “in connection with” the Franchise Agreement; but where contracts have competing clauses, per Bunge a dispute goes to the clause it is most closely connected with in its pith and substance, and the oven price is a Supply Agreement claim. Its clause 15 chose Singapore, so for order (iv) Ruritania was a non-chosen court and the order is outside the CCAA; per C&Y the CCAA does not bar its enforcement at common law, where the common law requirements and defences apply. Neither the default nor the non-money order (iii) changes the split, as both are “judgments” under s 2(1).

  2. 2
    The CCAA gate for clause 28 B1

    Run every row. Clause 28 is an express exclusive choice of the courts of one Contracting State, Ruritania (s 3(1)). It was signed on 3 March 2021, after the Convention entered into force for Ruritania, the chosen court's State, on 1 January 2019 (and for Singapore on 1 October 2016). The case is international, as Lakemont resides in Ruritania and Sora in Singapore (s 4(1)), and a franchise between two companies is a commercial matter, not a consumer or employment contract. So clause 28 is inside the CCAA. Clause 15 passes the same rows, but it chooses Singapore, so it cannot make Ruritania the chosen court for the oven claim.

  3. 3
    Does the Ruritanian ruling on the Convention bind? B5

    Lakemont says the ruling that clause 28 is an exclusive agreement under the Convention binds Singapore. For Lakemont: the usual requirements for an issue estoppel look met, as Sora agreed to the Ruritanian court in clause 28. For Sora: per Prof Chong's March 2026 answer scheme, it may argue that there is no estoppel, because each Contracting State court decides for itself whether the Convention applies. Section 13(3)(b) does not help Lakemont: it binds only the chosen court's findings of fact on jurisdiction, never their legal evaluation (per C&Y), and not at all where the judgment was by default. Result under both routes: Part 3 applies, either because the ruling binds or because Singapore runs the gate itself and clause 28 passes it, so the point does not save Sora.

  4. 4
    Part 3: no review of the merits, no common law tests H9

    Lakemont applies to the General Division under s 13(1) and O 37 ROC 2021, without a fresh action. Per s 13(4) the court must recognise and enforce orders (i) to (iii) unless a ground in ss 14 to 16 applies, and that list is exhaustive. Per s 13(3)(a) it may not review the merits, so Sora's complaint that the royalties were wrongly calculated goes nowhere. “Final and conclusive” is a common law requirement: per s 13(2) the judgment is enforced only if it is enforceable in Ruritania, and the Assume list says it is, despite the pending set-aside. Order (iii), to remove the signs, is a non-money “judgment” under s 2(1), so the common law rule that only a fixed sum is enforced has no place here.

  5. 5
    Part 3 grounds: two discretions are live H9

    The mandatory grounds fail: Sora was served at its office in good time and chose not to appear, so s 14(a) fails; nothing shows fraud in connection with procedure (s 14(b)); and nothing reaches the high “manifestly” bar of public policy in s 14(c). Section 15(1)(a) is not live either: nothing suggests clause 28 is void under Ruritanian law, as the Franchise Act voids only clauses that send disputes to a foreign court. Two discretions are live. Under s 15(2) the pending set-aside is a review in Ruritania, so the court may refuse or postpone for now, and Lakemont may apply again once it is decided. Under s 16 the court may refuse order (ii), US$4 million to punish a deliberate breach, as damages beyond compensation for actual loss, after asking whether any of it covers the costs of the Ruritanian proceedings; who receives the money does not matter. Under s 19 the court must enforce the severable rest, orders (i) and (iii).

  6. 6
    Order (iv): the four common law requirements H2

    Order (iv) is outside the CCAA and the Assume list rules out any other statute, so Lakemont sues on the judgment debt at common law; Sora is a Singapore company, so it is served here as of right. Per C&Y, Lakemont must show that the judgment is (a) on the merits, (b) given by a court with international jurisdiction over Sora, (c) final and conclusive, and (d) for a definite sum that is not a tax, fine or penalty. A default judgment is on the merits (per C&Y), and per Humpuss and Eleven v Boxsentry it is final if given final effect until set aside, which a judgment enforceable in Ruritania in the meantime probably is. US$1 million, the oven price, is a definite sum. So the fight is (b).

  7. 7
    Order (iv): no international jurisdiction H4

    International jurisdiction is tested by Singapore's rules, not Ruritania's (per C&Y). Per Republic of India v Deutsche Telekom, Sora must have been present in Ruritania, or have claimed there, voluntarily appeared, or agreed in advance to submit. Presence fails: per Adams v Cape a company needs a fixed place of business there, and Sora has no office or staff in Ruritania. Sora did not appear in the action, and its later application to set aside is not shown to argue the merits of the oven claim, so it did not submit by conduct; its only agreement to submit to Ruritania is clause 28, which covers Franchise disputes, while for the Supply Agreement it chose Singapore exclusively in clause 15. Proper service in good time goes to natural justice, not to jurisdiction. So order (iv) cannot be enforced; the breach of clause 15 is only a back-up, as no case decides that it is a defence, but if it is one, Sora keeps it, as it did not submit.

  8. 8
    The ruling that clause 15 is void binds nothing H8

    Lakemont pleads the ruling as an issue estoppel. Per Merck it must show (a) a foreign judgment capable of recognition, (b) the same parties and (c) the same issue; (a) fails, as Ruritania had no international jurisdiction over Sora on the oven claim. (c) fails too: per Gonzalo Gil White, Lakemont bears the burden, with special caution for foreign rulings, and there is no identity where the issue arose under different laws. Ruritania applied its Franchise Act, while Singapore's own rules pick Singapore law, clause 15's governing law, under which the clause is valid. Lakemont may reply, per First Laser, that different choice of law rules do not matter, but even on the narrow reading (per Chong (seminar)) identity fails where Singapore's rules select Singapore law, as here. So clause 15 stands in Singapore.

  9. 9
    Advice to Sora on the base facts

    Orders (i) to (iii): Sora cannot reopen the royalties or rely on the default, but it should ask the court to postpone under s 15(2) until the Ruritanian set-aside is decided. If the judgment stands, orders (i) and (iii) will be enforced, and the court may refuse order (ii) under s 16 and enforce the rest under s 19. Order (iv) cannot be enforced, because Ruritania had no international jurisdiction over Sora on the oven claim, and the ruling that clause 15 is void does not bind it here.

⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

A jurisdictional objection is not a submission, as in Nimbus. But filing a defence on the merits is. Had Ruritanian procedure required both together, and had Sora kept up its objection, there would be none.

⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

The defence needs a breach, so the clause must have promissory content. An exclusive clause has it. No Singapore case recognises the defence. For it: damages for the breach could cancel the judgment sum, the REFJA has an analogue, and convergence is favoured (Merck). Against it: no authority, and the Convention does not forbid recognising a non-chosen court's judgment. If the defence exists, the debtor loses it by submitting. 📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes, and Part 3 for orders (i) to (iii) H9

    Now Sora appeared in Ruritania: it objected to jurisdiction over the oven claim under clause 15, lost, then defended every claim on the merits and lost after a trial. No set-aside is pending, and a Singapore judgment of November 2025 holds that the ovens were defective and that Sora owes nothing for them. Part 3 still governs orders (i) to (iii), but Sora loses the points that came from the default: under s 13(3)(b) the chosen court's findings of fact on jurisdiction now bind (though not their legal evaluation), and s 15(2) is gone. Section 16 still lets the court refuse order (ii), and s 15(1)(d) does not reach these orders, because the Singapore judgment is about the ovens only and does not conflict with the Franchise orders. So orders (i) and (iii) are enforced, and order (ii) may still be refused.

  2. 2
    Order (iv): Sora has now submitted H4

    The clause 15 objection alone was a protest, as in Nimbus, where objecting, losing and then taking no further part was not a submission. But Sora then filed a defence on the merits. Per C&Y and Malaysia Marine a defence on the merits is a submission; per C&Y it is voluntary, and so a submission, where the foreign procedure permits but does not require a merits plea, as Ruritanian procedure did here. Had Ruritanian procedure required Sora to plead the merits with its challenge, and had Sora kept up its objection throughout, there would be none, unless it could have withdrawn the merits plea after losing on jurisdiction and did not. So the Ruritanian court had international jurisdiction, order (iv) now meets the four requirements, and Sora needs a defence.

  3. 3
    Defence 1: breach of clause 15, open on both steps H7

    Per Prof Chong's March 2026 answer scheme, the defence needs a breach, so the clause must be promissory: clause 15 is expressly exclusive, so Lakemont broke it by suing in Ruritania. Whether breach is a defence is open, as no case decides it. For Sora, per C&Y: damages for the breach could cancel the judgment sum, the REFJA has an analogue, and convergence is favoured (Merck); for Lakemont: no Singapore authority, and per C&Y the Convention does not forbid recognising a non-chosen court's judgment. If there is no such defence, the breach gives Sora nothing here; if there is, per C&Y a debtor that submits loses it, though Sora may answer that it defended only after Lakemont's breach, so the loss is probable, not certain. The Ruritanian ruling that clause 15 is void does not shut the point out, as the issue arose under a different law in each court (Gonzalo Gil White).

  4. 4
    Defence 2: the Singapore judgment decides order (iv) H7H8

    Per Merck, a foreign judgment is not recognised if it is inconsistent with a Singapore judgment between the same parties, whether that judgment came earlier or later. The General Division held that Sora owes nothing for the ovens, while order (iv) orders it to pay US$1 million for them, so order (iv) is refused. “The earlier prevails” is the rule for two competing foreign judgments, and s 15(1)(d) is the CCAA rule, which does not apply to order (iv). This defence does not depend on clause 15, so Sora's submission does not touch it. Nor does the clause 15 ruling now estop Sora: submission supplies international jurisdiction, but the issue is still not the same.
