📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes, and what stays

    Keep Twist 1. Recognition in Singapore does not change: order (iv) is refused here because of the Singapore judgment. What is new: Lakemont has started to enforce order (iv) in Arcadia, where Sora owns a central kitchen, and Sora asks the General Division to stop it before the Arcadian hearing next month. A judgment already exists, so this is an anti-enforcement injunction: run the ordinary anti-suit requirements as the floor, then the Sun Travels overlay.

  2. 2
    Amenability: Lakemont came here to sue G2

    Amenability is always required, whatever the basis: Lakemont must be within the court's in personam jurisdiction (Cooperative Muratori). It has no office or assets here, but it applied here to enforce this very judgment, and per Glencore a party that sues here submits to all the incidents of its action, including related relief such as an injunction. Lakemont may cite Akai, where a respondent served out, with no presence or assets here, that only opposed the injunction was held not amenable; but Lakemont came here as a claimant, and the settled view (C&Y; Cooperative Muratori) is that submission or valid service is enough, and the lack of assets goes only to whether the order bites. Clause 15 alone is not enough, as an agreement to submit is not a submission (Shanghai Turbo (CA)). Result: arguably amenable; if not, Sora needs permission to serve out under O 8 r 1 ROC 2021.

  3. 3
    The floor: a contractual basis from clause 15 G3

    The basis is contractual: clause 15 is an exclusive Singapore clause governed by Singapore law, and Lakemont broke it by suing in Ruritania on the oven claim. The clause itself supplies Singapore's interest (Westbridge v Mittal), so it does not matter that enforcement is in Arcadia, and natural forum does not arise. Sora breaks nothing by applying here, as its promise in clause 28 covers only Franchise disputes. Before judgment the injunction would ordinarily issue unless Lakemont showed strong reasons (Sun Travels; Cooperative Muratori). Two further points: Sora's defence on the merits in Ruritania may weigh against it in the discretion, as arguably waiving clause 15 (per UniCredit); and clause 15 is inside the CCAA, so Singapore is the chosen court and, per C&Y, may be given more leeway against a suit in another Contracting State such as Ruritania, though here that suit is over and the target is enforcement in Arcadia.

  4. 4
    The overlay: no exceptional circumstances H10

    Per Sun Travels, once a judgment exists Sora must also show exceptional circumstances tied to unconscionability; neither the breach nor vexation is enough alone, and caution is needed because the injunction would stop Arcadia deciding recognition for itself. The recognised cases are fraud in obtaining the judgment and a debtor that did not know it was being sought. Sora alleges no fraud, and it knew of the action from service in 2025, fought it in Ruritania and never asked the Singapore court to restrain it, even with its own action running here; contesting jurisdiction abroad does not excuse delay. The list is not closed, and Sora's best point is that Lakemont pressed on after the Singapore judgment of November 2025; but a new category needs the equities to favour Sora, and, similar to Sun Travels, where Hilton waited until after the Maldivian judgment, its delay with knowledge tells against it. Per Sun Travels such injunctions “should generally be refused”, and Sora can instead resist in Arcadia, where breach of a jurisdiction clause is a ground, and claim damages for the breach, so the injunction is probably refused.

H9 Sort the factors: Part 3: the grounds against orders (i) to (iii)

Each line is a point Sora might raise against the Franchise orders on the base facts. Sort it by what the court does with it under ss 14 to 16. Lines marked “Suppose” are extra facts for this card only.

Sora was served at its office in good time and chose not to appear.
No ground. Section 14(a) needs a debtor that was not notified in time to arrange its defence. A debtor that knew and stayed away has no ground. J7.5.3 :: No Timely Notice
Sora's application to set aside the judgment is pending in Ruritania.
May refuse or postpone. Under s 15(2) the court may refuse or postpone while a review is pending. Lakemont may apply again once it is decided. J7.5.4 :: Pending Review or Appeal

May refuse or postpone. Section 16 allows refusal so far as damages go beyond compensation for actual loss. Who receives them does not matter. The rest is severed and enforced under s 19. J7.5.4 :: Excess Damages
Sora: “The royalties were wrongly calculated.”
No ground. The court may not review the merits of the chosen court's judgment. J7.5.2 :: No Review of the Merits
Order (iii) is an order to remove signs, not to pay money.
No ground. A “judgment” under the CCAA includes a non-money judgment. This is a point students miss: the common law rule about a fixed sum has no place in Part 3. J7.5.1 :: Judgment
Sora: “A default judgment is never final and conclusive, so Part 3 cannot apply to it.”
No ground. Final and conclusive is the common law requirement. Part 3 covers a default judgment, and asks only whether it has effect and is enforceable in Ruritania. It is. The pending set-aside counts only through s 15(2). J7.5.2 :: Effect in the State of Origin
Suppose: Lakemont's lawyer deliberately gave Sora the wrong hearing date, and judgment was entered a week before it.
Must refuse. Deliberately misleading the debtor about the hearing is fraud in connection with a matter of procedure. Refusal under s 14(b) is mandatory. J7.5.3 :: Procedural Fraud

Must refuse. Sora was not notified in time to arrange its defence, and it did not appear. Refusal under s 14(a) is mandatory. J7.5.3 :: No Timely Notice
Suppose: the General Division had earlier held clause 28 void and given judgment for Sora on the royalties.
May refuse or postpone. Under s 15(1)(d) the court may refuse a judgment that conflicts with a Singapore judgment between the same parties, earlier or later. J7.5.4 :: Inconsistent Singapore Judgment

H8 Sort the factors: Does the foreign ruling bind? Issue estoppel

Lakemont pleads each ruling below against Sora in Singapore. Can it raise an issue estoppel? The requirements are a judgment capable of recognition, the same parties and the same issue. Lines marked “Suppose” are extra facts for this card only.

Base facts: the ruling that clause 15 is void, made in the default judgment on the oven claim.
No estoppel. The first requirement fails. The Ruritanian court had no international jurisdiction over Sora on that claim, so the judgment cannot be recognised. J7.3.2.1 :: §
Twist 1: the same ruling, after Sora defended on the merits. It applied the Ruritanian Franchise Act to a clause governed by Singapore law.
No estoppel. The judgment is now recognisable, but the issue is not the same. It arose under a different law in each court, and Singapore's own rules pick Singapore law for clause 15. J7.3.2.1 :: Identity of Issue
The ruling that clause 28 falls within the Hague Convention.
Arguable. Per Prof Chong's answer scheme the debtor may argue that there is no estoppel, since each Contracting State's court decides for itself whether the Convention applies. The other side points to a final ruling between the same parties. J7.3.2.3 :: HCCCA Applicability
Suppose: the Ruritanian court found that Sora's clause 15 objection was itself a submission to its jurisdiction.
No estoppel. Whether a debtor submitted is for Singapore's conflict rules. An estoppel would sub-contract that question to the foreign court. J7.3.2.3 :: International Jurisdiction
Twist 1: the finding after trial that Sora owes US$2 million in royalties under the Franchise Agreement.
Estoppel can arise. A judgment of the chosen court after a trial, between the same parties, on an issue that was necessary to the decision. J7.3.2.1 :: Necessary, Not Collateral
Suppose: at the trial the Ruritanian court ruled that Ruritanian law governs the Franchise Agreement.
Estoppel can arise. A ruling on the governing law can found an estoppel if it was decided at the final trial. It is not so sensitive that Singapore must decide it for itself. J7.3.2.4 :: Governing Law
Suppose: that governing law ruling was made only on a stay application, on a good arguable case.
No estoppel. Per First Laser a ruling on a stay application, decided on a good arguable case and open to change at trial, is not final on the issue. Students miss this: the same ruling binds or not depending on the stage. J7.3.2.4 :: Governing Law
Suppose: the Ruritanian court refused Sora a stay because Ruritania was the natural forum, and Lakemont pleads that against Sora's injunction application.
No estoppel. Per Lakshmi there is no identity of subject matter: an injunction turns on breach or vexation, not on the natural forum. Each court decides its own appropriateness. J7.3.2.3 :: Forum Non Conveniens
Suppose: the Arcadian court declares the Ruritanian judgment enforceable in Arcadia, and Lakemont pleads that as proof that Sora owes the oven price.
No estoppel. A judgment on a judgment decides only its effect in that country. It raises no estoppel on liability. Look to the Ruritanian judgment itself. J7.3.2.4 :: Judgment on a Judgment
⚡ Scorecard 2 · the verdictH8
In Twist 1, Lakemont says that the ruling on clause 15 stops Sora from relying on the clause in Singapore. Is that right?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Submission cures the first requirement only. Per Gonzalo Gil White the party relying on the estoppel bears the burden on identity of issue, with special caution for foreign rulings. The ruling does not bind. What hurts Sora in Twist 1 is its own submission, which probably costs it the clause 15 defence, not any estoppel.

5Remember

🧠 FOR THE EXAM
  • Split a foreign judgment by contract: Part 3 covers only orders from the court chosen in an exclusive clause inside the CCAA; the rest goes to the common law.
  • Under Part 3 the merits, common law finality and the non-money form do not matter: only ss 14 to 16, with s 15(2) for a pending review, s 16 for damages beyond actual loss and s 19 to sever.
  • A foreign ruling that the Convention applies arguably raises no estoppel (Prof Chong's answer scheme), and s 13(3)(b) binds nothing in a default judgment: run the gate yourself and show the result either way.
  • At common law, no presence and no submission means no enforcement; an objection is a protest, but a merits defence that procedure did not require is a submission and probably costs the breach-of-clause defence.
  • At common law a Singapore judgment between the same parties bars recognition of an inconsistent foreign judgment, earlier or later (Merck), whatever the debtor did abroad.
  • After judgment, an anti-enforcement injunction needs exceptional circumstances on top of the usual requirements (Sun Travels): fraud or no knowledge, the list not closed; delay with knowledge counts against the applicant, so resist where enforcement is sought instead.

6What the check changed

✓ THE CHECK

There is no Gemini output in this hypo, so there was nothing of Gemini's to correct. The notes and walkthrough on this page were written for this page and checked against the pre-writes (18 fixes in that check).

Parallels in the Meta Game material: H9 (a chosen court's default judgment under Part 3 and the ss 14 to 16 grounds, without the Mareva part); the judgment parts of H4 and H8 (a foreign ruling on the clause said to bind Singapore), H7 (a clashing Singapore judgment; an anti-enforcement injunction) and H20(b) (a judgment in breach of a clause after defending abroad); Set 2 “what if” 1 (a default judgment and a ruling that the Convention applies)

LAW302 · META GAME · QUESTION 1 · HYPO q1-03 · GEMINI PROMPT V1 · 15 QUESTIONS

Elmtree v Vanora and Sweetwell

Written by Claude for the drill and law reviewed. Gemini (prompt v1) rebalanced the option lengths and wrote a note on each question; both were checked (14 corrections) and feed the notes here.

Answers:

1Base facts

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Elmtree v Vanora and Sweetwell

Elmtree Pte Ltd, a Singapore incorporated company, makes ice cream at its factory in Senoko. In February 2025 it signed a Supply Agreement with Vanora Ltd, a company incorporated in Ruritania, for the whole 2025 vanilla crop of Vanora's farms. Both parties signed the Agreement at a food fair in Utopia. Vanora was to deliver the vanilla “FOB Port Ruri” in October 2025. Elmtree paid a deposit of US$2 million. If Vanora did not ship by 31 October 2025, it was to repay the deposit into Elmtree's bank account in Singapore. The Agreement has no jurisdiction clause. It provides:

“17. This Agreement is governed by Singapore law.”
“18. Any legal process may be served on the Supplier by courier at its head office in Ruritania.”

Vanora shipped nothing and has not repaid the deposit. It says that a cyclone destroyed the crop. Elmtree says that Vanora sold the crop to Sweetwell Inc, a Utopian company that competes with Elmtree. In September 2025, at a meeting in Ruritania, Sweetwell had offered Vanora double the price. Elmtree's factory stood idle and it lost its orders from Singapore supermarkets.

Elmtree sued in the General Division: Vanora for damages and the deposit, and Sweetwell for inducing a breach of contract. On 2 March 2026, on one application made without notice, it obtained approval to serve both defendants out of Singapore. It served Vanora on 9 March and Sweetwell on 16 March. Vanora has applied to set aside service. Sweetwell has applied only for a stay.

Advise Elmtree whether the General Division will take jurisdiction over each defendant for each claim.

ℹ ASSUME
  1. Neither defendant has an office, staff or assets in Singapore. Vanora's sales manager visits buyers in Singapore twice a year.
  2. Three weeks before Elmtree's application, Vanora sued Elmtree in Ruritania for a declaration that the cyclone released it from the Agreement. Elmtree's affidavit did not mention this. That action is at an early stage.
  3. Under Ruritanian law it is not a civil wrong to persuade a seller to break its contract. Under Singapore law it is a tort.
  4. Ruritanian port officials and crop inspectors know how much vanilla was harvested and shipped. They cannot be compelled to give evidence in Singapore.
  5. Both defendants can be sued in Ruritania.
  6. Vanora is owned by the Ruritanian Ministry of Agriculture. Elmtree's lawyers say that Ruritanian judges “never” find against state companies. Their only evidence is two newspaper articles.
✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • D4
    Defendant abroad: service out and the three requirements. Both defendants are abroad, with nothing here, and have not submitted. Open with service out and the three requirements, for each defendant.
  • D5
    Gateway: name the sub-limb of PD para 63(3). Each claim against each defendant needs its own gateway, and the sub-limb must be named. The place of signing, the delivery term, the repayment term and the place of the offer each open or close one.
  • D7
    Serious question to be tried. Some of Elmtree's gateways are neutral, so the serious question must be shown separately. The Ruritanian rule on inducing breach goes to whether there is a tort claim to try at all.
  • D9
    The contract says how process may be served. Clause 18 says how process may be served on Vanora abroad. Ask whether the contract allowed service out with no approval, before running the three requirements.
  • D11
    How to serve abroad, and the set-aside. Vanora applies to set aside, so Elmtree must make out all three requirements again. The silence of its affidavit about the Ruritanian action is a separate ground to set the approval aside.
  • E3
    Forum conveniens on service out: burden on the claimant. Nobody has broken a promise on forum, so the test is Spiliada. The burden is on Elmtree against Vanora's set-aside. Sweetwell asked only for a stay, which changes its burden.
  • E4
    SCORECARD · Spiliada stage 1: connecting factors. The witnesses who cannot be compelled, and the fact that both defendants can be sued in Ruritania, are stage 1 facts to be marked on the scorecard.
  • E6
    Second bite: claimant fails stage 1 on service out. If stage 1 points to Ruritania, Elmtree's complaint about Ruritanian judges is a stage 2 point. Whether a claimant who served out gets stage 2 at all is open.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • D8
    Singapore clause, defendant abroad. Tempting because clause 17 names Singapore. But it chooses Singapore law, not the Singapore courts. An agreement to submit is not inferred from a governing law clause, so there is no clause to found jurisdiction or to shift the burden.
  • D2
    Foreign company never registered here, with an office or agent here. Tempting because a Vanora officer comes to Singapore. Visits to buyers are not a fixed place of business, so Vanora is not present here. In any case it was served in Ruritania.
  • D6
    The Singapore claim is for a negative declaration. D6 is for a Singapore claim that is itself a negative declaration. Here the declaration is Vanora's claim in Ruritania. Elmtree's Singapore claims are for damages and a debt.
  • G1
    ASI starter, and the basis. Tempting because Vanora is suing in Ruritania. But the question asks only whether Singapore will take jurisdiction. The Ruritanian action is a stage 1 factor here, not something to restrain.

Fair to tick but not needed: E1 Which test, and who bears the burden, E5 SCORECARD · Spiliada stage 2: substantial justice, E10 Parallel foreign proceedings, and time bars, D3 Defendant has taken a step in the Singapore action, A1 Any jurisdiction clause: what it promises

Application questions · base facts

⚡ Base facts · 1 of 7D5
Elmtree relies on gateway (c): Sweetwell is a necessary or proper party to the claim against Vanora. What is the difficulty?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per AK Investment, ask whether both would be proper parties if both were here: one investigation, or claims closely bound up. Inducing the very breach sued on meets that. But the anchor must be duly served when the application is made, or approval is set aside unless the court gives retroactive leave. Elmtree applied against both on 2 March and served Vanora on 9 March. So it should lead with (f)(ii) and keep (c) as an alternative. Gateway (c) is neutral, so the serious question is shown separately.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per AK Investment (adopting Massey v Heynes), ask whether both defendants would have been proper parties had both been here: the claims must involve one investigation or be closely bound up. A claim that Sweetwell induced the very breach that Vanora is sued for meets that, and the claim against Vanora is not bound to fail. But per C&Y, if the anchor has not been duly served when the application is made, the application is dismissed, and approval wrongly given is set aside unless the claimant obtains retroactive leave. Elmtree applied against both on 2 March and served Vanora only on 9 March. So it should lead with (f)(ii) against Sweetwell and keep (c) as an alternative. Gateway (c) is neutral, so the serious question is shown separately.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J3.1.2 :: (c) The Anchor Claim

Per AK Investment, that D1 is sued only to bring in [D2] is not fatal (The Brabo; Derby v Larsson), but the claim against [D1] must not be "bound to fail" (otherwise D1's presence is a device). A point of law going to [jurisdiction] is normally decided now.

  • Duly served: per C&Y, if [D1] has not been duly served when the application is made, it is dismissed, and approval wrongly given is set aside unless [claimant] obtains retroactive leave; irregular service of [D1] may be curable.
  • Collapse: per Elan Impex, if the action against [D1] is struck out, [D2] ceases to be a necessary or proper party.
⚡ Base facts · 2 of 7D5
Under Ruritanian law, persuading a seller to break its contract is not a civil wrong. Does that matter at the gateway stage?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per the textbook, citing IM Skaugen (HC), which was not challenged on appeal, “tort” in gateway (f) is tested by Singapore's choice of law rule: double actionability with the flexible exception. Per Metall, inducing a breach is located where the contract was broken and the claimant injured, not where the inducement was made. Delivery failed at Port Ruri, so Sweetwell places the tort in Ruritania, where limb two fails. Elmtree then needs the exception. Its reply is that it was injured in Singapore. Nippon Catalyst treated the rule as irrelevant to service out, and Shen Sophie followed IM Skaugen but said no more about the gateway stage. So plead actionability under both laws and note that doubt in one line. The same point feeds the serious question.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per C&Y (citing IM Skaugen (HC), unchallenged on appeal), “tort” in gateway (f) is tested by Singapore's choice of law rule: double actionability with the flexible exception (Rickshaw). Per Metall, inducing a breach is located where the contract was broken and the claimant injured, not where the inducement was made. Sweetwell says the contract was broken at Port Ruri, so the tort is in Ruritania, limb two fails, and Elmtree needs the flexible exception, which Rickshaw applies strictly. Elmtree replies that it was injured in Singapore, so the tort is located here and both limbs point to Singapore law. Whether double actionability applies at the gateway at all is unresolved: Nippon Catalyst treated the rule as irrelevant to service out, and Shen Sophie followed IM Skaugen's broad approach but said no more about the gateway stage. So plead actionability under both laws and flag the doubt in one line. The same point feeds the serious question.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J3.1.2 :: (f) Tort: Characterisation

Per C&Y (citing IM Skaugen (HC), unchallenged on appeal), "tort" is tested by Singapore's choice of law rules: double actionability with the flexible exception (Rickshaw), for local and foreign torts alike. So [claimant] may use (f) though [the claim] fails under Singapore law, if the exception applies [law X] (C3).

  • Equitable claims: per Recovery Vehicle 1 (HC), [dishonest assistance / knowing receipt / breach of directors' duties] were described as torts; such claims may need (f) because (o) covers only restitution and claims against [trustees or fiduciaries] (C&Y).
⚡ Base facts · 3 of 7D7
For which of Elmtree's gateways must a serious question to be tried be shown separately?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Bradley Lomas, where the gateway itself engages the merits, as with a breach or tortious damage here, a good arguable case on it clears the lower merits bar. Where the gateway is a neutral connecting factor, such as the governing law or a necessary or proper party, the serious question is a distinct hurdle.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Bradley Lomas (adopted in Li Shengwu and C&Y), where the gateway itself engages the merits, a good arguable case on it clears the lower merits bar: (e) needs a good arguable case of a breach committed here, and (f) of a tortious act or damage here. Per Bradley Lomas and C&Y, where the gateway is a neutral connecting factor, the serious question is a distinct hurdle: (a) and (r) expressly, and on the same logic (d) and (c). The governing law and a co-defendant's link say nothing about breach or tort, so Elmtree shows the serious question separately for (d)(iii) and (c). The standard is a substantial question of fact or law that Elmtree bona fide wishes to try (Seaconsar).

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J3.1.4 :: When It Must Be Proved Separately (−)

Per Bradley Lomas and C&Y, where [the gateway] is a neutral connecting factor, (c) is a distinct hurdle: (a) and (r) expressly, and on the same logic (d) and (c) (J3.1.2); for [a negative declaration], (n) and (p) too.

  • Standard: per Seaconsar (cited in AK Investment), a substantial question of fact or law that [claimant] bona fide wishes to try, i.e., not frivolous or vexatious; here [prima facie evidence of breach / documented loss] suffices.
  • Time bar: per Recovery Vehicle 1, [a time-barred claim] cannot meet the merits requirement, so check [the applicable limitation period] (FLPA; C1).
⚡ Base facts · 4 of 7D9
Could Elmtree have served Vanora under clause 18 without asking for approval?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per O 8 r 1(3), approval is not needed if the contract allows service out. Per NW Corp, the rule was read widely, but there the clause referred disputes to the Singapore courts in the same breath. The textbook presumes that the parties have also submitted to Singapore. On the wider reading, Vanora could attack only exercise and would bear that burden. On the narrower one, Elmtree needs the three requirements. So seeking approval was the safe course. Sweetwell is not a party to the Agreement at all.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per O 8 r 1(3), approval is not required if service out is allowed under a contract between the parties. Per NW Corp, the rule was read widely: “out of” Singapore means that no place of service need be named, and a contract allows service out if it agrees to service of Singapore process on a foreign defendant. But there the clause also referred disputes to the Singapore courts in the same breath, so “service of process” could only mean Singapore process. Clause 18 names no court, and clause 17 chooses only a law, which is not an agreement to submit (Vizcaya Partners); per C&Y, r 1(3) presumably applies where the parties have also submitted to Singapore. Per Yeo, the most persuasive test is a method expressly or impliedly usable for service out, and clause 18 is one, so the point is arguable. On the wide reading, Vanora could attack only exercise and would bear that burden; on the narrow one, Elmtree needs the three requirements. So seeking approval was the safe course, and clause 18 cannot reach Sweetwell, which is not a party to the Agreement.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J3.1.5 :: NW Corp: Read Widely

Per NW Corp, [a clause] choosing [English law], referring disputes to the Singapore courts and providing for "service of process by registered mail" fell within r 1(3), so posting [the originating process] to [defendant] in Hong Kong needed no approval.

  • Reasons: the rule says "out of", not "outside", Singapore, so no place of [service] need be named; a contract "allows" service out if it agrees to service of Singapore process on [a foreign defendant] not ordinarily here.
  • Purpose: per NW Corp, r 1(3) spares [claimant] a redundant approval where [defendant] has consented to jurisdiction being founded by service, consistent with the Ideals of expedition and efficiency.
  • Context: the clause named the Singapore courts in the same breath, and [the contract] recorded [defendant]'s Hong Kong place of business, so "service of process" could only mean service of Singapore process abroad.
⚡ Base facts · 5 of 7D11
Elmtree's affidavit did not mention Vanora's Ruritanian action. What follows?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

A claimant applying without notice must disclose matters that count against approval, including foreign proceedings. Per Zoom, material non-disclosure can found a set-aside. It is a separate ground from the three requirements, so Elmtree should not rely on winning those.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per C&Y, on a without-notice application only the claimant is before the court, so it bears the burden and owes full and frank disclosure of matters against approval: the defendant's links with the foreign country, the foreign proceedings and any gateway weaknesses. Vanora's Ruritanian action was started three weeks before Elmtree applied and is about the same dispute, so it was material. Per Zoom and C&Y, material non-disclosure can found a set-aside unless the defendant waived it. It is a separate ground from the three requirements, so Elmtree cannot rely on winning those. It is a power to set aside, not automatic voidness.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J3.1.6 :: Full and Frank Disclosure

Per C&Y, because the application is without notice, [claimant] must disclose matters against approval ([defendant]'s connections with [X], the foreign proceedings, gateway weaknesses). Material non-disclosure can found [a setting aside] (Zoom).

⚡ Base facts · 6 of 7E3
Who bears the burden on the forum question?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Zoom, after service out the claimant bears the forum burden on a set-aside, and the defendant bears stage 1 on a stay. By asking only for a stay, Sweetwell took on a burden that it could have left with Elmtree. A stay sought alone also risks being a submission at common law, although under the Rules of Court 2021 stating an exercise challenge is not one.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

No one breaks a promise on forum, as clause 17 chooses only a law, so the test is Spiliada and the burden depends on how each defendant responds. Per Zoom, after service out the claimant bears the forum burden without notice and still on a set-aside (Spiliada; Oriental Insurance), while a stay puts stage 1 on the defendant. Against Vanora, Elmtree must show that Singapore is clearly the more appropriate forum; per Oro Negro “on balance” suffices, so argue both. By asking only for a stay, Sweetwell took on a burden that it could have left with Elmtree. A stay sought alone also ordinarily submits at common law (Zoom), though under O 6 rr 7(6) and 12(5) a defence or affidavit stating an exercise challenge is not submission. Whether a failed stay then becomes submission is unclear: yes per C&Y, no on the broad reading of the rules.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J4.0.2 :: No Breach: Spiliada

For [no clause / a foreign NEJC / a claim outside clause X (J1.5)], served in, [defendant] bears stage 1; served out, [claimant] bears it on a set-aside and [defendant] on a stay (Zoom).

⚡ Base facts · 7 of 7E6
Suppose that stage 1 points to Ruritania on Vanora's set-aside. Can Elmtree still argue that it would be denied justice there?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Oro Negro and IM Skaugen (CA), the second bite is open. Against: Konamaneni and Allenger. For: Spiliada was itself a service out case, and Shen Sophie relies on access to justice and even-handed treatment. Then run the substance on each view. An allegation that foreign courts favour state-linked parties needs cogent evidence, and the court is slow to impugn a foreign system. If it fails, the case goes to Ruritania with the allegation on record.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Oro Negro and IM Skaugen (CA), whether a claimant who served out may still show injustice abroad after failing stage 1 is open: Lewis v King and Metall for, Konamaneni and Fentiman against. Against: per Konamaneni, failing stage 1 “is the end of the matter”, and per Allenger, running stage 2 would confer jurisdiction where none was established. For: Spiliada was itself a service out case, and per Shen Sophie (adopting Yeo) and C&Y, access to justice and even-handed treatment apply both ways. Then run the substance on either view. An allegation that Ruritanian courts favour state-linked parties needs cogent evidence (AK Investment), and the court is slow to impugn a foreign system (The Hung Vuong-2), so two newspaper articles will fail. The allegation is also risky: if it fails, the case goes to Ruritania with the allegation on record.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J4.2.3 :: Claimant Fails Stage 1: Second Bite? (must write)

Presently [the factors point to X], so can [claimant] still show injustice there? Per Oro Negro and IM Skaugen (CA), this is open: Lewis v King and Metall for; Konamaneni and Fentiman against.

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
⚡ BIG IDEA

Both defendants are abroad and have not submitted, so everything runs through service out, with a gateway for each claim against each defendant. Vanora is caught by (d)(iii), with (e) for the deposit, but against Sweetwell (f)(ii) is only arguable, double actionability may bite, and (c) was not open when Elmtree applied, because Vanora had not yet been served. The deciding move is the forum burden: on Vanora's set-aside Elmtree must show that Singapore is clearly more appropriate, which probably fails because the evidence on the crop is in Ruritania, and the open second bite cannot be won on two newspaper articles. The twists change the route: a negative declaration runs on the neutral (d) limbs, and a Singapore non-exclusive clause with a service term removes approval and puts strong cause on Vanora.

  1. 1
    Threshold: both defendants are abroad D4

    Neither defendant has an office, staff or assets here, neither was served here, and neither has submitted, so state first that neither can be served in Singapore (per Chong (seminar)). Vanora's sales manager visits buyers twice a year, but visits are not a fixed place of business, so Vanora is not present here. Jurisdiction therefore rests on s 16(1)(a)(ii) SCJA with O 8. Per PD para 63(2), restating Zoom, Elmtree must show against each defendant a good arguable case of a gateway for each claim, that Singapore is forum conveniens, and a serious question to be tried. Clause 17 chooses only Singapore law, so there is no Singapore jurisdiction clause: no CCAA route, and no promise on forum for anyone to break.

  2. 2
    Clause 18: was approval needed for Vanora? D9

    Check this before the three requirements: per O 8 r 1(3), no approval is needed if a contract between the parties allows service out. Clause 18 fixes a method usable in Ruritania, which Yeo's preferred reading accepts, but it names no court. In NW Corp the clause also referred disputes to the Singapore courts in the same breath, and per C&Y the rule presumably applies where the parties also submitted to Singapore; clause 17 is no such submission (Vizcaya Partners). On the wide reading, Vanora could attack only exercise and would bear that burden; on the narrow one, Elmtree needs approval on the three requirements. So applying for approval was the safe course, and clause 18 cannot reach Sweetwell, which is not a party.

  3. 3
    Gateways against Vanora D5

    Name a gateway for each claim against each defendant: distinct claims cannot be pooled, and one per claim is enough (C&Y; IM Skaugen (CA); Li Shengwu). Both contract claims fit (d)(iii), as clause 17 chooses Singapore law. The deposit also fits (e): an express term made Singapore the place of repayment, so the failure to repay is a breach here. The damages claim does not fit (e): delivery was due FOB Port Ruri, so that breach was in Ruritania, and where the loss was felt is not the test. (d)(i) fails on these facts, as the parties signed in Utopia and nothing shows an essential step taken here, and (d)(iv) fails because a governing law clause is not an agreement to submit (Vizcaya Partners). (a) is at most arguable: carrying on business here needs no fixed place (C&Y), but two sales visits a year are thin.

  4. 4
    Gateways against Sweetwell D5

    (d) does not reach Sweetwell: whether the contract must be between the parties is unsettled, but Chen v BHNV held (d) plainly inapplicable against a non-party defendant, and the other view helps only someone who stands in a party's shoes, such as an assignee, which Sweetwell does not. (f)(i) fails, as the offer and the sale were in Ruritania. Lead with (f)(ii): the idle factory and the lost Singapore orders are arguably damage here, not merely trivial (IM Skaugen (CA)), though Sweetwell will say that Singapore felt only the effects. Plead (c) in the alternative: inducing the very breach sued on is one investigation (AK Investment), but per C&Y the anchor must be duly served when the application is made, and Vanora was served on 9 March, after the 2 March application, so approval on (c) is liable to be set aside unless the court gives retroactive leave. If the claim against Vanora is struck out, Sweetwell ceases to be a proper party (Elan Impex). End with the non-exhaustive list (CJC Report; C&Y).

  5. 5
    The Ruritanian rule: is there a “tort”? D5

    Per C&Y (citing IM Skaugen (HC)), “tort” in (f) is tested by double actionability with the flexible exception; per Nippon Catalyst the rule is irrelevant to service out, so on that view the Ruritanian rule does not block the gateway, though it still feeds the serious question; Shen Sophie left the split standing. Per Metall, inducing a breach is located where the contract was broken and the claimant injured. Route 1 (Sweetwell): the contract was broken at Port Ruri, so the tort is in Ruritania, where persuading a seller to break its contract is not a civil wrong; limb two fails, and Elmtree needs the flexible exception, which Rickshaw applies strictly; Ruritania, where the crop was grown and delivery was due, is hardly fortuitous, so on this route the tort claim probably fails. Route 2 (Elmtree): it was injured in Singapore, and per Metall the court need not turn a blind eye to damage caused here, though per Distillers the place of damage may be fortuitous; if the tort is here, both limbs point to Singapore law and the claim passes. Plead actionability under both laws and flag the doubt in one line.

  6. 6
    Serious question to be tried D7

    A good arguable case under (e) or (f) engages the merits and carries the serious question, but (d)(iii) and (c) are neutral, so for them it is shown separately (Bradley Lomas; C&Y). The bar is low: a substantial question that Elmtree bona fide wishes to try (Seaconsar). Against Vanora it is easily met, as Vanora shipped nothing and has not repaid the deposit. Against Sweetwell the Ruritanian rule is the live point: a co-defendant with a good defence cannot be a proper party (J H Rayner), so Elmtree must show a tort claim it can arguably win on one of the two routes.

  7. 7
    Vanora's set-aside, Sweetwell's stay D11E3

    Vanora applies to set aside, so Elmtree must make out all three requirements again, and per Zoom the legal burden, including on forum, stays on it. The affidavit's silence is a separate ground: on a without-notice application Elmtree had to disclose the foreign proceedings (C&Y), and per Zoom material non-disclosure can found a set-aside unless waived. Nobody breaks a promise on forum, so the test is Spiliada, not strong cause. Sweetwell asked only for a stay, so it bears stage 1 (Zoom), a burden it could have left with Elmtree. A stay sought alone ordinarily submits at common law (Zoom), but under O 6 rr 7(6) and 12(5) stating an exercise challenge is not submission; whether a failed stay then becomes submission is unclear (yes per C&Y, no on the broad reading).

  8. 8
    Stage 1: weigh quality, not number E4

    Per Rappo and JIO, only links relevant to the dispute count, and the dispute is whether a cyclone destroyed the crop or Vanora sold it to Sweetwell. The uncompellable Ruritanian port officials and crop inspectors are third parties whose evidence goes to that question, so they point to Ruritania (JIO), and the offer, the sale and the failure to ship all happened there. The tort claim is closely tied to the contract claim, and both defendants can be sued together in Ruritania, so the case need not be split. Clause 17 weighs little, as the dispute turns on fact; the repayment term is neutral, as nobody says the deposit was repaid; the parties' bases cancel out; and Elmtree's own staff raise no compellability problem. Vanora's Ruritanian action counts by progress and overlap, not by who sued first (Lakshmi), and it is at an early stage; Vanora's state ownership is irrelevant at stage 1. So Elmtree probably cannot show that Singapore is clearly, or even on balance (Oro Negro), the more appropriate forum.

  9. 9
    Second bite, then the result E6

    Whether a claimant who fails stage 1 may still show injustice abroad is open (Oro Negro; IM Skaugen (CA)): against, Konamaneni (“the end of the matter”) and Allenger; for, Spiliada itself, a service out case, and Shen Sophie with C&Y. On either view the substance fails: an allegation that Ruritanian judges favour state companies needs cogent evidence (AK Investment), the court is slow to impugn a foreign system (The Hung Vuong-2), two newspaper articles are not that, and the allegation is risky, as the case may then go to Ruritania with it on record. Result for Vanora: its set-aside will probably succeed on forum, with non-disclosure as a separate risk; even on the wide reading of clause 18, where Vanora would bear stage 1 on a stay, the same factors probably favour Ruritania. Result for Sweetwell: it sought only a stay, so it does not contest existence and bears stage 1; if the claim against Vanora goes to Ruritania, the closely tied tort claim tends to follow it (Oro Negro; Chen v BHNV), so the stay probably succeeds, and if that claim stays here, the stay probably fails. Approval against Sweetwell rests on (f)(ii), which is arguable, as (c) needs retroactive leave and would likely fall with service on Vanora (by analogy with Elan Impex).

Presently, [claimant] seeks a declaration that no contract was concluded with [defendant], which is suing on it in [X].

⚡ Twist 1 · 3 of 3E3
Vanora sued first, in Ruritania. Does that stop the Singapore claim, or force Elmtree to choose?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Each court decides for itself. Forum election applies to a common claimant, not where the defendant here is the claimant abroad. Reversed-party proceedings go to stage 1, where they are weighed by progress, parties and issues, not by who sued first. The overlap is complete, but the action is at an early stage.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Singapore has no first-seised rule: each court decides for itself, and a foreign action is no bar here, unlike under the EU rule. Forum election (Koh Kay Yew; Virsagi) applies where the same claimant sues the same defendant here and abroad on the same issues. Here Vanora is the claimant in Ruritania and Elmtree the claimant here, so the parties are reversed and election does not apply. The Ruritanian action goes to stage 1, weighed by progress, parties and issues, not by who sued first (Lakshmi). The overlap is complete, which raises the risk of inconsistent judgments, but the action is at an early stage.

1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per NW Corp, a defendant served under O 8 r 1(3) cannot dispute the existence of jurisdiction, only its exercise. Where the contract also names the Singapore courts, the forum challenge is itself a breach of the promise to submit, so per Shanghai Turbo the defendant must show strong cause. Treating a Singapore non-exclusive clause as a mere Spiliada factor is the old approach that was overruled.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per NW Corp, service under r 1(3) founds jurisdiction without approval, so Vanora cannot dispute its existence, only its exercise. Clause 18 also names the Singapore courts, so Vanora's forum objection is itself a breach. Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), Singapore takes the contractual approach: under Singapore law, which clause 17 chooses, “submits” means consenting to the court's jurisdiction and waiving any objection to its exercise. So Vanora's set-aside and its stay are both attempts to escape clause 18, and Vanora must show strong cause. Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), High Court cases treating a Singapore non-exclusive clause as a mere Spiliada factor were wrongly decided.

Strong cause is not Spiliada. Points to Singapore. They would be third party witnesses whom only Singapore can compel. They go to the amount of the loss, so they carry some weight, though less than the evidence on the crop. J4.1.2 :: Witness Compellability

Leave out the “Suppose” line. Has Elmtree shown at stage 1 that Singapore is clearly the more appropriate forum for its claims against Vanora?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

On a set-aside the burden stays on the claimant (Zoom), and being merely as appropriate as Ruritania is not enough (Sudarga). Even if “on balance” suffices (Oro Negro), the weighty factors point to Ruritania. A contract governed by Singapore law can still be refused service out where another forum is the appropriate one. So the second bite and the non-disclosure point matter.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

On Vanora's set-aside, Elmtree bears the burden of showing that Singapore is clearly the more appropriate forum (Zoom), and being merely as appropriate as Ruritania is not enough (Sudarga). Even if “on balance” suffices (Oro Negro), the weighty factors point to Ruritania: the dispute is about what happened to the crop, the uncompellable port officials and crop inspectors are there, the tort is closely tied to the contract claim, and both defendants can be sued together there. Clause 17 weighs little because the dispute turns on fact, and per Amin Rasheed a contract governed by the forum's law can still be refused service out where another forum is the appropriate one. So the second bite and the non-disclosure point matter.

5Remember

🧠 FOR THE EXAM
  • Check for a service clause before the three requirements: one that names the Singapore courts and allows service abroad removes approval (O 8 r 1(3); NW Corp), but a clause that only fixes a method of service abroad, naming no court, is only arguably enough, so apply.
  • One gateway per claim per defendant, sub-limb named: (e) asks where performance was due, not where the loss was felt; a governing law clause gives (d)(iii), never (d)(iv); (d) does not reach a stranger to the contract such as Sweetwell (Chen v BHNV).
  • Gateway (c) needs the anchor duly served when you apply, and a co-defendant with a good defence (here, perhaps, no tort under Ruritanian law) is not a proper party.
  • Neutral gateways ((c), (d), and for a negative declaration (n) and (p)) need a separate serious question; (e) and (f) carry it.
  • After service out the claimant bears the forum burden on a set-aside, the defendant bears stage 1 on a stay alone, and under a Singapore non-exclusive clause the defendant bears strong cause.
  • Disclose foreign proceedings on a without-notice application; the second bite after a failed stage 1 is open, but two newspaper articles are not the cogent evidence it needs.

LAW302 · META GAME · QUESTION 1 · HYPO q1-06 · GEMINI PROMPT V1 · 16 QUESTIONS

Hexa and Mr Imran v Zorin

Written by Claude for the drill and law reviewed. Gemini (prompt v1) rebalanced the option lengths and wrote a note on each question; both were checked (8 corrections) and feed the notes here.

Answers:

1Base facts

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Hexa and Mr Imran v Zorin

Hexa Studios Pte Ltd, a Singapore incorporated company, makes video games. Zorin Media Inc is incorporated in Utopia, where it publishes games. Zorin has no office or staff in Singapore, but it owns shares in a Singapore company.

Under a Licence Agreement of 2023, Hexa licensed its game Tidefall to Zorin for Utopia. Mr Imran, Hexa's creative director, who lives in Singapore, negotiated it but is not a party to it. Clause 30 reads:

“This Agreement is governed by Arcadian law. The courts of Arcadia have exclusive jurisdiction over any dispute arising out of or in connection with it.”

Under a Co-development Agreement of 2024, Hexa built an expansion for Zorin at its Singapore studio. That agreement is governed by Singapore law and has no jurisdiction clause.

In November 2025 Hexa sued Zorin in the General Division for unpaid fees under the Co-development Agreement, and served it in Utopia with approval. On 10 March 2026 Zorin's application for a stay failed. On 11 March 2026 Zorin sued in Utopia. Count 1, against Hexa and Mr Imran, claims damages for false sales forecasts given before the Licence Agreement. Count 2, against Hexa, claims damages for late delivery of the expansion. Count 3, against Hexa, claims compensation under the Utopian Online Sales Act for Hexa's direct sales to players in Utopia.

Hexa challenged the Utopian court's jurisdiction and took no other step. In August 2026 that court ruled that Utopia is the natural forum. In October 2026 Hexa and Mr Imran ask the General Division to stop the Utopian action.

Advise Hexa and Mr Imran.

ℹ ASSUME
  1. Neither Arcadia nor Utopia is a party to the Hague Convention on Choice of Court Agreements.
  2. Arcadian courts do not grant anti-suit injunctions. Zorin has no presence or assets in Arcadia.
  3. Under Arcadian law, clause 30 is valid and covers Count 1 against Hexa.
  4. The Utopian action has not gone beyond the jurisdiction ruling. No defence is due and no trial date is fixed.
  5. The expansion was tested by an independent Singapore laboratory. Its staff cannot be compelled to give evidence in Utopia.
  6. Utopian courts order wide pre-trial disclosure of documents. Singapore courts would order less.
  7. Only a Utopian court can apply the Online Sales Act.
✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • G1
    ASI starter, and the basis. There are three counts and two applicants. Each injunction needs its own basis: a clause for Count 1 against Hexa, and vexation for everything else.
  • G2
    Amenability. Zorin must be within the court's personal jurisdiction. It was served out in Hexa's Singapore action, and its Singapore shares mean an order would bite.
  • G8
    Clause for a foreign court, or Singapore is neither forum. Clause 30 names the courts of Arcadia, not Singapore. Hexa must explain why a Singapore court, and not the chosen court, should restrain Count 1.
  • A9
    Is this claim, or this party, inside the clause?. Mr Imran is sued on Count 1 but is not a party to the Licence Agreement. Ask whether clause 30 reaches a claim against him.
  • G6
    Vexation ASI: sufficient interest. Counts 2 and 3 break no clause. For Count 2 Singapore must be the natural forum. Count 3 is a single forum claim, which has its own questions.
  • G7
    SCORECARD · Vexation or oppression, and injustice to the respondent. The timing of the Utopian suit, the laboratory witnesses, the disclosure Zorin would lose and the stage of the Utopian action are all vexation scorecard facts.
  • H8
    Issue estoppel from the foreign ruling. The Utopian court has ruled that Utopia is the natural forum. Zorin will say that the ruling binds Hexa in Singapore.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • G9
    ASI in a CCAA case. G9 is for a contract inside the CCAA. Arcadia is not a Contracting State, so clause 30 is a common law clause.
  • G4
    Singapore non-exclusive clause: is suing abroad a breach?. G4 needs a Singapore non-exclusive clause. The Co-development Agreement has no jurisdiction clause at all, so no promise can be breached.
  • B3
    CCAA applies and a foreign court is chosen (s 12). Section 12 is for a claim brought in Singapore against a Contracting State clause. Nobody sues here on the Licence Agreement, and Arcadia is outside the Convention.
  • H10
    Anti-enforcement injunction: the judgment already exists. An anti-enforcement injunction needs a foreign judgment. The August ruling is on jurisdiction only, and no trial date is fixed.
  • E10
    Parallel foreign proceedings, and time bars. E10 is about staying the Singapore action. That stay has already been refused, a day before Zorin sued in Utopia, and nobody now asks for one. The parallel Utopian action matters only inside vexation, where alone it is not enough.

Fair to tick but not needed: G3 Contractual ASI: a Singapore clause is breached, G5 Twist: the applicant's own ASI application breaks a clause, G11 Relitigation after a Singapore judgment; third parties; if the ASI is ignored, B1 CCAA gate: five conditions, H4 International jurisdiction: submission, E4 SCORECARD · Spiliada stage 1: connecting factors, D4 Defendant abroad: service out and the three requirements, D5 Gateway: name the sub-limb of PD para 63(3)

Application questions · base facts

⚡ Base facts · 1 of 7G1
How should the answer be organised?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Cooperative Muratori, the applicant must name its basis, because the elements differ. Clause 30 covers only Count 1 against Hexa. Mr Imran is not a party to it. Counts 2 and 3 arise outside the Licence Agreement. Abuse of process protects Singapore's judgments and processes, and Singapore has decided nothing yet on the Co-development Agreement.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Cooperative Muratori, the applicant must name its basis, because the elements differ. A contractual injunction needs amenability, breach and no strong reasons, though with a clause for a foreign court sufficient interest stays live. A vexation injunction needs amenability, sufficient interest (usually the natural forum), vexation and no undue injustice (Per Kirkham). Abuse of process needs amenability and a self-evident interest (Per BCS v Baker). The strands are distinct, so Hexa should not argue that breaking clause 30 is itself vexatious (Per Cooperative Muratori). Clause 30 covers only Count 1 against Hexa. Mr Imran is not a party to the Licence Agreement, and Counts 2 and 3 arise outside it. Abuse of process protects Singapore's judgments and processes, and Singapore has decided nothing yet on the Co-development Agreement; with both actions pending, Hexa must show the natural forum (Per Baker v BCS (SICC)).

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J6.3 :: Choosing the Basis

Presently, [applicant] relies on [breach of [clause X] (J6.3.1) / vexation (J6.3.2) / abuse of process (J6.3.3) / public policy (J6.3.4)]. Per C&Y, the categories are not closed. Per BCS v Baker, abuse invokes the inherent power (disruption to [Singapore's processes]); vexation invokes equity (the personal equities); the overriding test is the interests of justice.

⚡ Base facts · 2 of 7G8
Count 1 against Hexa breaks an Arcadian clause, not a Singapore one. Will a Singapore court restrain it?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

A Singapore clause supplies the connection by itself. A foreign clause does not, so sufficient interest stays live. Per Akai and C&Y, the applicant should ordinarily go to the chosen court, and Singapore should not be an international busybody. Hexa's reasons are that Arcadian courts do not grant such orders and that it must shield its Singapore assets. Per C&Y, Singapore has generally declined even then, because a later judgment can be met by resisting recognition. The reply, per Chong (seminar), is that Akai is old and its busybody point may carry less force today, especially where the chosen court is in a Contracting State. Arcadia is not one, so the reply is weaker here. Hexa may add UniCredit by analogy (a party is held to its bargain by any court that has jurisdiction over it), but that is an arbitration case and only persuasive. State both sides, then go on to breach, strong reasons and delay.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

A Singapore clause supplies the connection by itself; a clause for Arcadia does not, so sufficient interest stays live. Per Akai and C&Y, Hexa should ordinarily seek the injunction from the Arcadian court, and Singapore should not be an “international busybody”. Hexa answers that Arcadian courts do not grant anti-suit injunctions, that Zorin has nothing in Arcadia for an order to bite on, and that it must shield its Singapore assets from a Utopian judgment. Per C&Y, Singapore has generally declined even then: as in Akai, later enforcement against the applicant's assets is “an entirely different matter”, met by resisting recognition. Per Chong (seminar), Akai is old and its busybody point may carry less force today, especially where the chosen court is in a Contracting State, which Arcadia is not. By analogy, UniCredit holds parties to their bargain in any court before which they can properly be brought, but it is an arbitration case, its link was that English law governed the agreement, and it left open whether personal jurisdiction alone suffices; here Arcadian law governs clause 30. State both sides, then go on to breach, strong reasons and delay.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J6.2.6 :: Reasons to Come Here (+)

[Applicant] argues [Court B] [does not grant ASIs / lacks the remedy], or that it must shield its [Singapore assets] from [Court A]'s judgment (C&Y). For HCCCA states, see J6.5.3.

  • Rebuttal (−): Per C&Y, Singapore has generally declined even then. As in Akai, where the insurer sued here only to protect its Singapore assets, any later enforcement against [applicant]'s [assets] is "an entirely different matter", met by resisting [recognition] then (J7).
⚡ Base facts · 3 of 7A9
Count 1 is also brought against Mr Imran. Can he rely on clause 30 to stop it?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Asiana, whether a clause reaches claims against third parties is a matter of construction, and in keeping with privity it usually does not without a quite clear indication. Whether a third party may rely on a clause is for its governing law, and the facts say only that Arcadian law makes clause 30 cover Count 1 against Hexa. If Arcadian law is taken to be the same as Singapore law, per VKC v VJZ a non-party cannot use the third party rights statute to enforce a jurisdiction clause. So Mr Imran falls back on vexation in his own right. Hexa's own injunction is separate, but Mr Imran's presence in the Utopian action may be a strong reason against it, as in Donohue. Per Asiana, that fragmentation point should not be overstated.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Asiana, adopting Team Y&R, whether a clause reaches claims against third parties is construction, and in keeping with privity it usually does not without a quite clear indication. Party scope is for the proper law of clause 30, Arcadian law, and the facts say only that it covers Count 1 against Hexa; on the rest, Singapore law applies by the presumption of similarity. Per VKC v VJZ, a non-party cannot use CRTPA s 2(1)(b) to enforce a jurisdiction clause, as Parliament extended the Act to arbitration agreements (s 9) but not to jurisdiction clauses. Per Chong (seminar), VKC's “procedural” label is wrong. Even so, the routes VKC left open (an express right under s 2(1)(a), s 2(3), or equity) need words or facts that are not here. So Mr Imran falls back on vexation to himself (Per Asiana). Separately, his presence in the Utopian action may be a strong reason against Hexa's own injunction (Per Donohue), though per Asiana fragmentation should not be overstated.

Per VKC v VJZ and C&Y, C cannot use CRTPA s 2(1)(b): Parliament deliberately extended the Act to [arbitration agreements] (s 9) but not [jurisdiction clauses], and an EJC confers no substantive benefit.

  • Critique (+): per Chong (seminar), the "procedural" label is wrong: if [an EJC] were merely procedural, its breach could not found [an ASI] or [damages].
  • Routes left open (+): C may "arguably" rely on s 2(1)(a) if [contract] expressly confers the right, or on s 2(3), or on equity as in Hai Jiang (VKC). Presently, [clause X] [expressly names [C / a class including C]].
  • Comparison (±): Contrast Global Partners v Babcock & Brown (NSWCA), where [group companies] that took part in the decisions complained of and were "Indemnified Persons" could rely on [the English clause] (J1.5.3).

⚡ Base facts · 4 of 7G6
For Count 2, what must Hexa show before the court looks at vexation, and is it enough on its own?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Where the dispute can be heard in either court, comity requires a sufficient interest, usually that Singapore is clearly the more appropriate forum. Here the work was done at Hexa's Singapore studio, Singapore law governs and the laboratory witnesses are here. Per SNIA, the natural forum alone is never enough, or Singapore would be imposing a mere difference of view. Hexa must also show vexation.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Where the dispute can be heard in either court, comity requires a sufficient interest, normally that Singapore is the natural forum (Per Airbus and BCS v Baker), and with Hexa's action and Count 2 both pending, Hexa must show it (Per Baker v BCS (SICC)). Per Lakshmi, Singapore must be “clearly the more appropriate forum”, weighing the quality, not the quantity, of the factors. Singapore law governs the Co-development Agreement, the expansion was built at Hexa's Singapore studio, and per Lakshmi third-party witnesses compellable here but not abroad matter where the dispute is factual, as the laboratory staff are. Per SNIA, the natural forum alone is never enough, or Singapore would impose a mere difference of view on the Utopian court, so Hexa must also show vexation.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J6.2.3 :: Natural Forum (+)

Presently, [the dispute] can be heard in Singapore or [foreign court]. Per BCS v Baker and Airbus, an ASI is normally granted where Singapore is the natural forum and the other requirements are met. Per Lakshmi, [applicant] must show Singapore is "clearly the more appropriate forum", weighing the quality, not quantity, of [the JIO factors] (J4.1.2).

⚡ Base facts · 5 of 7G6
Only a Utopian court can apply the Online Sales Act, and Count 3 concerns Hexa's own sales to players in Utopia. Will Count 3 be restrained?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Singapore can never be the natural forum for a claim that lies only in Utopia. The questions are whether Singapore still has a sufficient interest and whether pursuing the claim is unconscionable. An injunction is especially harsh because it denies Zorin its only redress. As in British Airways v Laker, a party that chose to trade in the foreign market accepted its law. It would differ if the dealings were overwhelmingly centred in Singapore, as in Midland Bank v Laker. Each count is tested separately. This is not the Spiliada availability question.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per C&Y, a single forum claim is one that Singapore law gives no cause of action for, so Singapore can never be the natural forum. Per Airbus and BCS v Baker, the questions are whether Singapore still has a sufficient interest and whether pursuing the claim is unconscionable, and per C&Y an injunction is especially harsh, as it denies Zorin its only redress. As in British Airways v Laker, where the airlines voluntarily submitted to US antitrust law by taking licences to fly between the UK and the US, Hexa voluntarily sold to players in Utopia and so accepted Utopian law. It would differ if the dealings were overwhelmingly centred in Singapore, as in Midland Bank v Laker, but direct sales to Utopian players are not. Each count is tested separately, and this is not the Spiliada availability question.

Per C&Y, the ASI is especially harsh, denying [respondent] its only redress.

  • Not Spiliada availability: Per C&Y, "single forum" means [Singapore law] gives no cause of action, so the question is [unconscionability], not [appropriateness]; Spiliada availability asks only whether [a court] can hear the claim.
⚡ Base facts · 6 of 7H8
The Utopian court has ruled that Utopia is the natural forum. Does that ruling bind the Singapore court?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Lakshmi, a foreign court's refusal to stay because it is the natural forum raises no issue estoppel against a Singapore anti-suit application. There is no identity of subject matter, and an estoppel would make the result turn on court scheduling. A foreign refusal of a stay is not decisive either: the injunction in SNIA was granted although Texas had refused a stay. Hexa only contested jurisdiction, which per IGCF is a protest, not a submission. Zorin may cite Henry v Geoprosco, as the challenge ended in a natural forum ruling, but per IGCF Henry should not be followed.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Lakshmi, a foreign court's refusal to stay because it is the natural forum raises no issue estoppel against a Singapore anti-suit application: there is no identity of subject matter, as the injunction also needs vexation or oppression, and an estoppel would make the result turn on court scheduling. Per C&Y, it is better explained as each court deciding its own appropriateness, so the Utopian view never binds Singapore, though per Lakshmi it may still bear on comity. A foreign refusal to stay is not decisive either: the injunction in SNIA was granted although Texas had refused a stay, and per Lakshmi a sufficient connection plus unconscionable conduct breaches no comity, absent exceptional circumstances. Hexa only contested jurisdiction, which per IGCF is a protest, not a submission. Zorin may cite Henry v Geoprosco, as the challenge ended in a ruling on the natural forum, but per IGCF Henry should not be followed. On either route there is no estoppel, as the forum ruling is not the issue the injunction raises (Per Lakshmi).

1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Sun Travels, comity is relevant to delay even in contractual cases, and how far the foreign proceedings have gone matters more than the length of the delay. Contesting jurisdiction abroad first does not excuse delay: there are no two bites at the cherry, and Hexa should have objected in Utopia and applied here at the same time. But where no merits hearing is imminent, the length of delay alone does not point against the injunction. It would be different if the trial had started.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Sun Travels (following Ecobank and Sea Powerful), comity is relevant to delay even in contractual cases, and how far the foreign proceedings have progressed matters more than the length of the delay, as a late injunction wastes more of the foreign court's resources (C&Y). Per Sun Travels, contesting jurisdiction abroad does not excuse delay: there are no “two bites at the cherry”, and per C&Y Hexa should have objected in Utopia and applied here at the same time. But the Utopian action has not gone beyond the jurisdiction ruling, and per ZHD v SQO (C&Y), where no merits hearing is imminent or held, the length of delay alone does not point against the injunction. Whether delay belongs under strong reasons or under discretion is open (C&Y) and makes little practical difference: either way, Hexa's delay does not defeat the injunctions. It would be different if the Utopian trial had started, as in Hilton, where the foreign action was “too far advanced”.

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
⚡ BIG IDEA

One Utopian action holds three counts against two applicants, so each injunction needs its own basis. Count 1 against Hexa breaks clause 30, but clause 30 names Arcadia, so the deciding question is why Singapore, not the chosen court, should act: arguable, but Singapore usually declines (Akai). Mr Imran is outside clause 30 and must show vexation himself, Count 2 is probably restrained on natural forum plus vexation if Hexa offers a disclosure undertaking, and Count 3, a single forum claim on Hexa's own Utopian sales, survives. The twists test an anti-enforcement injunction after judgment, the cost of submitting abroad, and an anti-anti-suit injunction.

  1. 1
    Map the counts and name each basis G1

    Hexa and Mr Imran ask the General Division to stop one Utopian action with three counts. The injunction interferes indirectly with the Utopian court, so it issues only where the ends of justice require it, with caution (Per SNIA and Lakshmi), and the applicant bears the burden (Per Kirkham). Per Cooperative Muratori, each applicant must name its basis, as the elements differ. Count 1 against Hexa rests on clause 30; Mr Imran, a non-party, and Counts 2 and 3, which break no clause, rest on vexation. Abuse of process does not fit: Singapore has decided nothing yet, and with both actions pending Hexa must show the natural forum (Per Baker v BCS (SICC)).

  2. 2
    Amenability G2

    Amenability is always required. Zorin was validly served out, with approval, in Hexa's Singapore action, and valid service is enough (Per Cooperative Muratori; C&Y). Unlike the respondent in Akai, Zorin owns shares in a Singapore company, so an order would bite, as breach is contempt (Per SNIA). Mr Imran is not a party to Hexa's action, so Zorin must also be validly served with his claim, which needs approval to serve out.

  3. 3
    The Utopian ruling does not bind Singapore H8

    Zorin will say the August ruling that Utopia is the natural forum settles the point. Per Lakshmi, a foreign refusal to stay raises no issue estoppel against an anti-suit application: the injunction also needs vexation, so the subject matter differs, and an estoppel would turn on court scheduling. Per C&Y, each court decides its own appropriateness; per Lakshmi the ruling may still bear on comity, but deference is weaker where, as arguably with Count 2, Zorin carved a dispute out of the pending Singapore action to sue abroad, and a foreign refusal is not decisive (as in SNIA). Zorin may add that Hexa submitted: Hexa only contested jurisdiction, which per IGCF is a protest, though on Henry v Geoprosco asking a court to decline a jurisdiction it has is submission, and per IGCF Henry should not be followed. On either route the result is the same: the forum ruling is not the issue the injunction raises (Per Lakshmi), so it does not bind Singapore.

  4. 4
    Count 1 for Hexa: why Singapore, not Arcadia? G8

    Clause 30 names Arcadia, so unlike a Singapore clause it does not give Singapore an interest by itself. Against Hexa: per Akai and C&Y, it should ordinarily go to the chosen court, and Singapore should not be an international busybody. For Hexa: Arcadian courts grant no anti-suit injunctions, Zorin has nothing in Arcadia, and Hexa must shield its Singapore assets; per Chong (seminar), Akai is old and its busybody point may carry less force today, especially where the chosen court is in a Contracting State, which Arcadia is not, so this reply is weaker here; UniCredit helps only by analogy. Per C&Y, Singapore has generally declined even then, leaving Hexa to resist recognition later. Route 1: interest is found, so go on to breach; Route 2, the likelier: no injunction on Count 1 for Hexa.

  5. 5
    Count 1 for Hexa: breach and strong reasons G8

    If Singapore has an interest, the injunction is contractual. Breach is for the proper law of clause 30, and Arcadian law makes it valid and covering Count 1 against Hexa, so Zorin broke it by suing in Utopia. Arcadia is not a Contracting State, so this is a common law clause, not a CCAA one. The injunction then ordinarily issues unless Zorin shows strong reasons (Per Sun Travels; Cooperative Muratori). Zorin's best point is fragmentation: as in Donohue, the same action also involves Mr Imran, not bound by clause 30, and Counts 2 and 3, outside it. This is arguable either way: if it is a strong reason, Count 1 stays in Utopia; if, per Asiana, fragmentation is not overstated, the injunction issues on Count 1.

  6. 6
    Mr Imran: outside clause 30 A9

    Mr Imran negotiated the Licence Agreement but is not a party to it. Per Asiana, a clause reaches claims against a non-party only with a quite clear indication, and the facts say only that clause 30 covers Count 1 against Hexa. Taking Arcadian law as the same as Singapore law, per VKC v VJZ he cannot use CRTPA s 2(1)(b) to enforce a jurisdiction clause, and clause 30 gives him no express right. Nor is this a bypass of clause 30, as Zorin sued Hexa too, not only him. So he must show vexation to himself: that Singapore is clearly the more appropriate forum for the claim against him, and that suing him in Utopia is vexatious or oppressive, which needs the clearest of circumstances (Per Kirkham). The timing and laboratory points go mainly to Count 2, so the facts give him little and his injunction is doubtful.

  7. 7
    Count 2: natural forum, then vexation G6G7

    Count 2 breaks no clause, and Hexa's Singapore action on the same agreement is pending, so Hexa must show Singapore is clearly the more appropriate forum (Per Lakshmi). It probably is: Singapore law governs, the expansion was built at Hexa's Singapore studio, the laboratory witnesses are here, and the General Division has already refused Zorin a stay. Per SNIA, that is never enough alone. Vexation needs the clearest of circumstances (Per Kirkham): as in Lakshmi, Zorin sued in Utopia the day after its stay failed instead of counterclaiming here, and the key laboratory witnesses cannot be compelled in Utopia, which per UBS v Telesto is vexatious; a parallel suit alone would not do. Zorin's lost disclosure counts for less as Utopia is not the natural forum (Per UBS v Telesto), and an undertaking by Hexa to give the same disclosure here answers it (Per SNIA). Result: with that undertaking, Count 2 is probably restrained.

  8. 8
    Count 3: a single forum claim G6

    Only a Utopian court can apply the Online Sales Act, so Singapore can never be the natural forum for Count 3. Per Airbus and BCS v Baker, the questions are whether Singapore still has a sufficient interest and whether pursuing the claim is unconscionable, and per C&Y an injunction is especially harsh, as it denies Zorin its only redress. As in British Airways v Laker, Hexa chose to sell to players in Utopia and so accepted Utopian law, and a claim unknown here is not vexatious for that reason alone. Sales to Utopian players are not dealings overwhelmingly centred in Singapore, as in Midland Bank v Laker. Result: Count 3 is not restrained.

  9. 9
    Delay, then the result G7

    Hexa waited seven months, from March to October 2026. Per Sun Travels, comity makes delay relevant even under a clause, and contesting jurisdiction in Utopia first is no excuse: Hexa should have objected there and applied here together. But progress abroad matters more than the length of delay, and the Utopian action has not gone beyond the jurisdiction ruling, so per ZHD v SQO the delay alone does not defeat the injunctions. Whether delay sits in strong reasons or in discretion is open and makes no difference here. Result: Count 1 for Hexa turns on sufficient interest and is probably refused; Mr Imran's application is doubtful; Count 2 is probably restrained if Hexa gives the disclosure undertaking; Count 3 is not.

Application questions · twist 1

⚡ Twist 1 · 1 of 3H10
What must Hexa show to restrain enforcement of the Utopian judgment?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Sun Travels, an anti-enforcement injunction needs exceptional circumstances tied to unconscionability, beyond the usual requirements. Neither breach of a jurisdiction clause nor vexatious conduct is enough alone, and party autonomy is not a separate basis.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Sun Travels and C&Y, an anti-enforcement injunction needs the usual anti-suit requirements and, on top, exceptional circumstances tied to unconscionability. Per Sun Travels, neither breach of the clause nor vexatious conduct is enough alone, and party autonomy is no separate basis (Arkhangelsky creates no “agreement” category). The recognised examples are fraud in obtaining the judgment and a debtor who did not know the judgment was being sought.

⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Sun Travels, such injunctions should generally be refused. They waste the foreign court's time and they stop other courts deciding recognition for themselves. The recognised exceptional cases are fraud and a judgment the applicant did not know was being sought. Neither is here: Hexa had notice of every step, and it first came to the Singapore court seven months after the Utopian action began. Delay coupled with knowledge counts against Hexa, and simply limiting the relief to reflect the delay is not the answer.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Sun Travels, anti-enforcement injunctions should generally be refused: they imply that the debtor delayed in not seeking an anti-suit injunction earlier, waste the foreign court's time and costs, stop other courts deciding recognition for themselves, and are akin to nullifying the judgment. The recognised exceptional cases are fraud and a judgment the debtor did not know was being sought. Neither is here: nothing suggests Zorin misled the Utopian court, and Hexa had notice of every step. Mere passage of time is not enough, but delay coupled with knowledge counts against the debtor, and Hexa first came to the Singapore court seven months after the Utopian action began. Simply limiting the relief to reflect the delay, for example to Elbonia, is not the answer.

The order acts on Zorin personally, not on the Utopian court. Per Chong (seminar), a foreign claim and a foreign anti-suit application are analysed separately, so this application needs its own basis, apart from the three counts.
