5Scorecards: weigh the factors

Prof Chong rewards applying facts to factor tests. Sort each fact, then answer the verdict question. These use the base facts unless a line says “Suppose”.

G7 Sort the factors: Vexation and injustice on Counts 2 and 3

Each line is a fact or argument about an injunction against Counts 2 and 3. Which way does it point? Lines marked “Suppose” are extra facts for this card only.

Zorin sued in Utopia the day after its stay application failed in Singapore, instead of counterclaiming here.
Points to an injunction. As in Lakshmi, a foreign suit begun just after a step in the Singapore action, which should have been a counterclaim, points to bad faith. J6.3.2 :: Bad Faith or No Good Reason
Hexa: the same Co-development dispute is now before two courts, with a risk of conflicting judgments.
Not enough on its own. Parallel proceedings and the risk of conflicting judgments do not alone justify an injunction. Something more is needed. J6.3.2 :: Parallel Proceedings Alone Not Enough
The independent laboratory staff who tested the expansion cannot be compelled to give evidence in Utopia.
Points to an injunction. It is vexatious where a key non-party witness cannot be compelled to attend the foreign trial and the evidence is central. J6.3.2 :: Key Witness Not Compellable
Zorin: an injunction would cost us the wide pre-trial disclosure that Utopian courts order.
Points against. This is injustice to the respondent, weighed against the injustice to Hexa. It counts for less where the foreign court is not the natural forum. J6.4 :: Factors
Suppose: Hexa undertakes to give in Singapore the same disclosure that a Utopian court would order.
Points to an injunction. As in SNIA, an undertaking that preserves the respondent's advantage removes the injustice of an injunction. J6.4 :: Undertakings Neutralise
Suppose: Hexa says that Count 2 is hopeless because no delivery date was ever agreed.
Not enough on its own. Weakness of the foreign claim is only a factor, to be put together with weightier ones. The court is prudent about judging the merits. J6.3.2 :: Bound to Fail
Hexa: Count 3 is vexatious because Singapore law has no such claim.
Not enough on its own. Respect for foreign substantive law is part of comity. A claim unknown here is not vexatious for that reason alone. J6.3.2 :: Claim Unknown Here Is Not Vexation
Suppose: the Utopian trial is fixed to start in three weeks.
Points against. How far the foreign action has gone matters more than the length of delay. An injunction on the eve of trial wastes the foreign court's resources. J6.3.1.5 :: Comity Re-Enters With Delay
Suppose: Hexa has a contribution claim against its Singapore subcontractor, who can be sued here but not in Utopia.
Points to an injunction. As in SNIA, a foreign action that costs the applicant a claim available only here is oppressive, if the respondent's legitimate advantages are protected. J6.3.2 :: Lost Remedy Available Only Here
⚡ Scorecard 1 · the verdictG7
On the base facts, with Hexa's disclosure undertaking, what is the likely result on Counts 2 and 3?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

An injunction issues only in the clearest of circumstances, so the result is probable, not certain, and Hexa's seven month wait counts against it. But Singapore is clearly the more appropriate forum for Count 2, the timing and the witness point show vexation, the undertaking answers the lost disclosure, and the Utopian action is at an early stage. Count 3 is a single forum claim about sales Hexa chose to make in Utopia, so it is tested separately and survives.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Kirkham and UBS v Telesto, an injunction issues only in the clearest of circumstances, so the result is probable, not certain, and Hexa's seven month wait counts against it. For Count 2, Singapore is clearly the more appropriate forum. As in Lakshmi, Zorin sued abroad just after a step in the Singapore action instead of counterclaiming there, and per UBS v Telesto it is vexatious where a key witness cannot be compelled to attend the foreign trial. Zorin's lost disclosure is weighed as injustice to it, counts for less as Utopia is not the natural forum (Per UBS v Telesto), and is answered by Hexa's undertaking (Per SNIA). The Utopian action is also at an early stage. Count 3 is a single forum claim about sales Hexa chose to make in Utopia, so as in British Airways v Laker it is not unconscionable, and it survives.

6Remember

🧠 FOR THE EXAM
  • Split the injunction by count and by applicant, and name each basis (Cooperative Muratori): one count can be restrained while another is not.
  • A clause for a foreign court leaves sufficient interest live: per Akai, go to the chosen court; reasons to come here are arguable but usually fail.
  • A non-party sued abroad usually cannot use the clause without a quite clear indication or an express right (Asiana; VKC v VJZ), so must show vexation to himself; one party's submission abroad does not bind another.
  • With no clause and both actions pending, Singapore must be the natural forum, but that is never enough alone (SNIA); a single forum claim about a market the applicant chose to trade in is not restrained (British Airways v Laker).
  • A foreign forum ruling raises no estoppel against an injunction (Lakshmi); fighting jurisdiction abroad does not excuse delay, but delay alone does not defeat the injunction while the foreign action is at an early stage (ZHD v SQO).
  • After judgment, an anti-enforcement injunction needs exceptional circumstances such as fraud or no notice (Sun Travels); otherwise resist recognition, though a merits defence abroad gives up the jurisdiction answer and probably the clause objection.

LAW302 · META GAME · QUESTION 1 · HYPO q1-08 · GEMINI PROMPT V1 · 16 QUESTIONS

Northcliff v Seah Ceramics and Ms Seah

Written by Claude for the drill and law reviewed. Gemini (prompt v1) wrote a guide to it; the guide was checked (1 corrections) and feeds the walkthrough. Gemini's file: northcliff_v_seah_ceramics_ms_seah_law302_study_.

Answers:

1Base facts

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Northcliff v Seah Ceramics and Ms Seah

Northcliff Kilns Ltd, a company incorporated in Utopia, makes industrial kilns. By a Sale Contract signed in Utopia on 6 February 2024, it sold two kilns to Seah Ceramics Pte Ltd, a Singapore incorporated company. Clause 19 reads:

“The courts of Utopia have exclusive jurisdiction over any claim by the Buyer. The Seller may sue the Buyer in Utopia or in any other court, and the Buyer submits to the jurisdiction of each such court.”

Ms Seah, who owns Seah Ceramics and lives in Singapore, guaranteed the price by a separate letter. She signed the letter in Utopia. It is governed by Utopian law and has no jurisdiction clause.

Seah Ceramics did not pay the last US$3 million. It says that the kilns crack. In May 2025 Northcliff sued both in Utopia. Seah Ceramics had run a stand at the Utopia Ceramics Fair for ten days in March 2025. The claim was delivered by courier to both defendants in Singapore in May 2025.

Seah Ceramics took no step. Ms Seah's lawyer applied to set aside service on her for want of jurisdiction. In the alternative he asked for a stay, on the ground that Singapore was the more convenient forum. The Utopian court dismissed the application. It ruled that Ms Seah had submitted by making it. She took no further part.

In March 2026 the Utopian court gave judgment in default against both. It ordered them (i) to pay US$3 million; (ii) to pay Northcliff's costs, “in an amount to be assessed”; and (iii) it declared that the kilns were free of defects. Northcliff now sues both in the General Division on the Utopian judgment.

Advise Seah Ceramics and Ms Seah.

ℹ ASSUME
  1. The Hague Convention on Choice of Court Agreements has been in force for Utopia since 1 January 2020. No other treaty or statute on foreign judgments applies between Singapore and Utopia.
  2. Under Utopian law a default judgment may be set aside on application within one year. Until then it is treated as final and may be enforced. No application has been made.
  3. The Utopian court took jurisdiction under a Utopian rule that allows a claim on any contract signed in Utopia.
  4. Apart from that stand, Seah Ceramics has never had an office or staff in Utopia.
  5. Seah Ceramics says that Singapore was the natural forum, because the kilns were installed and inspected here.
✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • H1
    Which regime. The first question is the regime. Utopia is a Contracting State, but clause 19 is one sided, and the guarantee has no clause. So say why Part 3 of the CCAA is out and go to the common law.
  • H2
    Common law: the four requirements; on the merits. A judgment outside the CCAA needs the four requirements. The first is a judgment on the merits, and this one was given by default.
  • H3
    International jurisdiction: presence. Presence is the first ground of international jurisdiction. The trade fair stand and the date of service are planted for it. The Utopian court's own ground is not the test.
  • H4
    International jurisdiction: submission. Submission is the second ground. Seah Ceramics agreed in clause 19 to submit. Ms Seah signed no clause, so her two applications in Utopia must each be tested.
  • H5
    Final and conclusive. A default judgment that the Utopian court can still set aside raises the final and conclusive requirement.
  • H6
    Money judgment, or a declaration?. The three orders are different in kind: a fixed sum, costs not yet assessed, and a declaration. Only a definite sum can be enforced as a debt.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • H9
    CCAA Part 3: judgment of the chosen court. Tempting because Utopia is a Contracting State and clause 19 uses the word “exclusive”. Wrong because the clause is asymmetric: the Seller may sue anywhere. Per CHLOE V it is not an exclusive agreement under the CCAA, so Part 3 does not apply.
  • E4
    SCORECARD · Spiliada stage 1: connecting factors. The natural forum facts look like Spiliada stage 1. But the question is whether a foreign judgment is enforced, and that turns on presence or submission. Whether Utopia was the natural forum is irrelevant.
  • D4
    Defendant abroad: service out and the three requirements. D4 is about a Singapore court serving a defendant abroad. Both defendants are in Singapore and are served here as of right. The Utopian court's service abroad is not tested by Singapore's own service out rules: there is no mirror image.
  • D3
    Defendant has taken a step in the Singapore action. D3 is about a step taken in a Singapore action. Ms Seah's steps were taken in Utopia. Whether they are a submission to the Utopian court is the H4 question.

Fair to tick but not needed: B1 CCAA gate: five conditions, B4 Outside the CCAA: say why, then the common law, A7 Asymmetric clause: one side may sue anywhere, H7 Defences to recognition and enforcement, H8 Issue estoppel from the foreign ruling

Application questions · base facts

⚡ Base facts · 1 of 7H1
Which regime governs the enforcement of the Utopian judgment?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per CHLOE V, a clause that ties one party to one court and lets the other sue anywhere is not exclusive under the CCAA. The words “or in any other court” are also an express provision against s 3(2) deeming. The guarantee has no clause at all. So Northcliff sues on the judgment debt at common law.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J1.2.1 :: Asymmetric Clause (−)

Presently, [clause X] gives [State B] exclusive jurisdiction but lets [the lender] sue [the borrower] [anywhere]. Per CHLOE V, following the Hartley–Dogauchi Report (VCLT art 32), such a clause is not exclusive under the CCAA, so s 12 cannot be engaged even on [the court's own motion], and even though [defendant] conceded the point.

  • Support: Per Etihad (EWCA) (obiter), the Convention probably excludes [asymmetric clauses] like [clause X], the Diplomatic Session having rejected a Swiss proposal to cover clauses exclusive "for some or all of the parties".
  • Counter (+): Earlier first-instance dicta (Commerzbank v Liquimar; Etihad (EWHC)) read the Convention's wording as wide enough for [clause X], but [the lender]'s reliance on them is weak after CHLOE V.
  • Consequence: At common law [clause X] stays exclusive against [the restricted party] (per C&Y), so J1.1 applies.
⚡ Base facts · 2 of 7H3
Northcliff says that Seah Ceramics was present in Utopia because of its stand at the Ceramics Fair. Is that right?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Dunlop v Cudell a nine day trade fair stand was a fixed place of business. But per Adams v Cape the debtor must be present at the time of suit, meaning when the process was served. The Utopian court's own ground does not count: Singapore's conflict rules decide, and they are narrower.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J7.1.2.1 :: Time of Presence

Per Adams v Cape, [debtor] must be present in [X] at the time of suit, meaning when [the X process] was served ([date]), not issued ([date]).

⚡ Base facts · 3 of 7H4
Seah Ceramics took no step in Utopia. Did the Utopian court have international jurisdiction over it?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per United Malayan Banking, a debtor submits in advance by agreeing to the jurisdiction of the foreign court. The CCAA point goes only to the regime. Per Vizcaya Partners, making a contract in the foreign country is not an agreement to submit.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J7.1.2.5 :: Express Agreement (+)

Per United Malayan Banking, [debtor] submitted in advance by agreeing in [clause] to the jurisdiction of [the X court / the courts of [X]].

⚡ Base facts · 4 of 7H4
Did Ms Seah submit by applying to set aside service for want of jurisdiction? The Utopian court ruled that she did.
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

As in Nimbus, objecting to jurisdiction, losing and then taking no part is not a submission. Whether a debtor submitted is for Singapore's conflict rules, so the foreign court's own finding raises no estoppel. Per Vizcaya Partners, choosing Utopian law and signing in Utopia are not enough for an implied agreement.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J7.1.2.4 :: Jurisdictional Objection (−)

As in Nimbus (objecting in Colombo under the Sri Lankan Arbitration Act, losing and then taking no part, was not submission), [debtor]'s [objection under [clause] / challenge to [service / nexus]] in [the X court] was not submission.

⚡ Base facts · 5 of 7H4
What about her alternative request for a stay, on the ground that Singapore was the more convenient forum?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Run both sides. On Henry's logic a stay application asks the court to decline a jurisdiction that it has. Per IGCF that line is unrealistic, and a stay on forum grounds is a protest unless the debtor sought more, such as relief on the merits. She sought nothing more. So there is probably no international jurisdiction over her. If Henry is followed, she submitted and the judgment can be enforced against her.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J7.1.2.4 :: Stay Application (±)

(+) On Henry's logic, [debtor]'s stay application accepted [the X court]'s jurisdiction. (−) Per IGCF, a stay [for arbitration / on FNC grounds] is a protest, unless [debtor] sought more, e.g., [consequential relief on the merits].

⚡ Base facts · 6 of 7H5
The time for setting aside the default judgment in Utopia has not run out. Is the judgment final and conclusive?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Finality is tested by Utopian law, and the Assume list says the judgment is treated as final and may be enforced. Per Humpuss and Eleven v Boxsentry that is enough for a default judgment. A default judgment is also on the merits: not taking part goes only to fraud or natural justice.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J7.1.3 :: Default Judgment (+)

Per Humpuss and Eleven v Boxsentry, [the default judgment] is final if given final effect until set aside, although [debtor] may still apply to [the X court] to set it aside.

⚡ Base facts · 7 of 7H6
Which of the three orders can Northcliff enforce as a debt against Seah Ceramics?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

The sum must be fixed or arithmetically ascertainable. A costs order is enforceable once it is final and definite, and this one is still to be assessed. A declaration is not a money order, but it can be pleaded as res judicata. A money order made among other orders still founds an action in debt.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J7.1.4 :: Definite Sum (+)

Per C&Y, [the sum] must be fixed or arithmetically ascertainable, and [a costs order] is enforceable if final and definite, even where [the merits judgment] has no money order.

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
⚡ BIG IDEA

Two debtors, one Utopian default judgment, and the common law, because clause 19 is asymmetric and so, per CHLOE V, outside the CCAA. The move that decides it is international jurisdiction, tested for each debtor under Singapore's rules: presence fails for both, because the fair stand had ended before service and Ms Seah was served in Singapore; Seah Ceramics submitted in advance in clause 19; Ms Seah's objection was a protest, and her stay application is open (Henry v Geoprosco against IGCF), so probably no submission. Then only order (i) is a definite sum. The twists test each defence on its own standard, then a judgment on a judgment, a part payment, and res judicata as sword and shield.

  1. 1
    Regime: clause 19 is asymmetric, so the common law H1

    Utopia has been a Contracting State since 1 January 2020 and the Sale Contract was signed in February 2024, so the date row passes. But clause 19 ties only the Buyer to the Utopian courts, while the Seller may sue “in any other court”. Per CHLOE V (following the Hartley–Dogauchi Report), such an asymmetric clause is not an exclusive agreement under the CCAA, and those words also displace s 3(2) deeming. Ms Seah's guarantee has no clause at all. So Part 3 does not apply to either defendant, and Northcliff sues each in the General Division on the debt that the Utopian judgment creates. Both are in Singapore, so they are served here as of right.

  2. 2
    The four requirements; a default judgment is on the merits H2

    Per C&Y, Northcliff must show, against each defendant, that the judgment is (a) on the merits, (b) given by a court with international jurisdiction over that defendant, (c) final and conclusive, and (d) for a definite sum that is not a tax, fine or penalty. The burden is on Northcliff. A default judgment is on the merits although the debtors did not appear and the Utopian court may not have looked at the evidence (Per C&Y). Not taking part goes only to fraud or natural justice. So (a) is met against both.

  3. 3
    Presence: neither defendant was in Utopia at service H3

    Per Adams v Cape, the debtor must be present in Utopia at the time of suit, meaning when the Utopian process was served: May 2025. Per Dunlop v Cudell a nine day trade fair stand was a fixed place of business, so Seah Ceramics' stand could count while it ran in March 2025. But the fair had ended by May 2025, and apart from it Seah Ceramics never had an office or staff in Utopia. Ms Seah lives in Singapore and was served there. The Utopian rule for contracts signed in Utopia does not count, because Singapore's conflict rules decide and there is no mirror image (Per C&Y). So presence fails for both.

  4. 4
    Submission: Seah Ceramics agreed in advance H4

    Per United Malayan Banking, a debtor submits in advance by agreeing to the jurisdiction of the foreign court. In clause 19 the Buyer “submits to the jurisdiction of each such court”, and the Utopian courts are one of them. Being outside the CCAA decides only the regime; at common law the clause still counts. So the Utopian court had international jurisdiction over Seah Ceramics, although it took no step. Its own ground, a contract signed in Utopia, adds nothing: per Vizcaya Partners, making a contract in the foreign country is not an agreement to submit.

  5. 5
    Ms Seah's objection: a protest, and no estoppel H4

    Ms Seah signed no clause, and per Vizcaya Partners choosing Utopian law and signing in Utopia are not enough for an implied agreement (whether Singapore accepts implied agreements at all is open). So each of her two steps must be tested. Per Nimbus, a step is a submission only if it necessarily waived her objection, judged practically, as business people would. As in Nimbus, objecting to jurisdiction, losing and then taking no further part is a protest. The Utopian ruling that she submitted raises no estoppel: submission is for Singapore's conflict rules, and per Roch LJ in Desert Sun an estoppel would “sub-contract” that question.

  6. 6
    Ms Seah's stay application: an open point H4

    Route 1, for Northcliff: on Henry v Geoprosco's logic, a stay asks the Utopian court to decline a jurisdiction it has, so the application accepted that jurisdiction; she submitted and the judgment can be enforced against her. Route 2, for Ms Seah: per IGCF, Henry's line is “unrealistic and irrational” and no common law jurisdiction follows it, so a stay on forum grounds is a protest unless the debtor sought more, such as relief on the merits. She sought nothing more, and Nimbus only assumed Henry without deciding. She may add that under the Rules of Court, challenging the exercise of Singapore's jurisdiction is not submission, although per C&Y that may not carry over, as there is no mirror image. Result: probably no submission, so probably no international jurisdiction over Ms Seah.

  7. 7
    Final and conclusive: the open set-aside window H5

    Per Sang Cheol Woo, a judgment is final and conclusive if the court that gave it cannot vary or set it aside and treats it as res judicata, and per Humpuss this is tested by Utopian law. A default judgment is final if it is given final effect until set aside, although the debtor may still apply to set it aside (Per Humpuss and Eleven v Boxsentry). The Assume list says the Utopian default judgment is treated as final and may be enforced until set aside, and no application has been made. So (c) is met.

  8. 8
    Definite sum: only order (i) can be enforced H6

    Per C&Y, only a fixed or arithmetically ascertainable sum is enforced as a debt. Order (i), US$3 million, qualifies, and per Giant Light Metal a money order made among other orders still founds an action in debt. Order (ii), costs “in an amount to be assessed”, is not yet definite, and a costs order is enforceable only once final and definite. Order (iii), the declaration, is not a money order, so it cannot be enforced, but it can be recognised, for example as res judicata.

  9. 9
    Advice

    Seah Ceramics: order (i) meets all four requirements and no defence appears on these facts, so Northcliff can enforce US$3 million against it. The costs cannot be enforced until they are assessed, and the declaration can only be recognised. Ms Seah: presence fails and, on the better view, she did not submit, so the judgment probably cannot be enforced against her; if Henry v Geoprosco is followed, it can be enforced against her too. Seah Ceramics' point that Singapore was the natural forum helps neither of them: enforcement turns on presence or submission, not on Spiliada.

2Twist 1

🧩 TWIST 1

Now add these facts.

The Utopian judgment made two more orders against both defendants: (iv) to pay US$6 million as “double damages for wilful non-payment” under the Utopian Prompt Payment Act, payable to Northcliff; and (v) to pay US$300,000 in Utopian sales tax on the kilns, to Northcliff “for the account of the Utopian Revenue”.

Seah Ceramics explains why it took no step. In June 2025 Northcliff's sales director emailed it: “The claim is a formality for our insurers. Do not file anything. We will not enter judgment.” It also says that Northcliff's engineer swore a false affidavit that the kilns had passed their firing tests. Seah Ceramics has held its own failed test report since 2024. Finally, it says that the Utopian court wrongly applied Utopian law to a contract governed by Singapore law.

✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • H7
    Defences to recognition and enforcement. Every new fact is offered as a defence: two kinds of fraud, a mistake of law, multiple damages and a tax. Each has its own standard on the defences card.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • H9
    CCAA Part 3: judgment of the chosen court. Section 16 of the CCAA lets a court refuse damages above actual loss, so order (iv) tempts this box. But the judgment is outside the CCAA. Section 16 can be cited only as a pointer for the common law.
  • H10
    Anti-enforcement injunction: the judgment already exists. Fraud is an exceptional circumstance for an anti-enforcement injunction. But no one is enforcing abroad. Northcliff is suing in Singapore, so the fraud is pleaded as a defence here.
  • G7
    SCORECARD · Vexation or oppression, and injustice to the respondent. The email looks like unconscionable conduct, which is the language of vexation. But vexation is the test for stopping a foreign action that is still running. This one has ended in judgment.

Fair to tick but not needed: H11 Limitation, penalties, reciprocity, REFJA

Application questions · twist 1

⚡ Twist 1 · 1 of 4H7
How is the sales director's email classified, and what must Seah Ceramics show?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Hong Pian Tee the test depends on the type of fraud. Extrinsic fraud is fraud that the debtor had no chance to examine and challenge, and it includes a creditor inducing the debtor to let judgment go by default. Abouloff then applies: no new evidence is needed, and the fraud may be raised here for the first time. Per Ong Han Nam the fraud must have produced the judgment. It is not natural justice, because Seah Ceramics had notice.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J7.2.2 :: Extrinsic Fraud (−)

Presently, [witnesses were bribed / [debtor] was never served / [creditor] induced [debtor] to let judgment go by default]. Per Hong Pian Tee, Abouloff applies: no new evidence is needed, and [debtor] may raise the fraud though [it was rejected in [X] / it is raised here for the first time].

⚡ Twist 1 · 2 of 4H7
And the engineer's false affidavit?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

False evidence goes to the merits, so it is intrinsic. Per Hong Pian Tee the debtor needs fresh evidence that reasonable diligence would not have uncovered and that would probably have changed the result. Per Eleven v Boxsentry the same test applies to a default judgment although the debtor took no part. The report was in its hands before the Utopian action began.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J7.2.2 :: Default and Summary Judgments (+)

Per Eleven v Boxsentry, the intrinsic test applies to [a default judgment] though [debtor] took no part. Per Ee Hoong Liang, [a summary judgment] that [debtor] knew of is not akin to a default judgment.

⚡ Twist 1 · 3 of 4H7
Can order (iv), the double damages, be enforced?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Run both sides. For Northcliff: penal means payable to the State (Raulin v Fischer; Sang Cheol Woo), and Singapore itself awards punitive damages in tort. For Seah Ceramics: Licea left multiple damages open, the statutes limit damages that do not compensate, and per Schnabel a punitive sum with a public purpose is penal even when the creditor receives it. If it is refused, it is severed and the US$3 million stands.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J7.2.5 :: Punitive Damages to a Private Party (±)

(+) Per C&Y, refusing [the X punitive award] would be anomalous when Singapore awards punitive damages in tort (ACB v Thomson Medical). (−) But the point is uncertain, Licea leaving open [US RICO treble damages]; s 4(5) REFJA and s 16 CCAA limit [non-compensatory damages], and courts may take their cue from them.

⚡ Twist 1 · 4 of 4H7
Order (v) is payable to Northcliff, a private company. Can it be enforced?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Maler Foundation a judgment is not recognised so far as it directly or indirectly enforces a foreign revenue law. The forum characterises it, and the form or label is not conclusive. Northcliff collects this sum for the Utopian Revenue, not in its own interest. Per Licea the creditor enforces the part that is unobjectionable if it is clearly identifiable and separable.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J7.2.5 :: Severance (+)

Per Licea, where [the X judgment] awards [compensatory sum] and [punitive sum], [creditor] enforces the unobjectionable part if clearly identifiable and separable; compare s 4(5) REFJA (J7.4.1) and ss 16, 19 CCAA (J7.5.4).

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes, and what stays

    The requirements stay as in the base: the judgment is enforceable in principle against Seah Ceramics, and probably not against Ms Seah. What is new is five defences, each with its own standard, and the burden of proving each is on the debtor (Per Eleven v Boxsentry). Northcliff will usually apply for summary judgment, so Seah Ceramics needs a fair or reasonable probability of a real defence, never a dispute on the merits (Per C&Y). A defence to one order leaves the others standing, unless it is fraud that produced the whole judgment.

  2. 2
    The email: extrinsic fraud H7

    Per Hong Pian Tee, the test depends on the type of fraud. By the email Northcliff induced Seah Ceramics to let judgment go by default, which is extrinsic fraud: fraud the debtor had no opportunity to examine and challenge. So Abouloff applies: no fresh evidence is needed, and the fraud may be raised here for the first time. Per Ong Han Nam, the fraud must have produced the judgment, so Seah Ceramics must show that the email caused its default. It is not a natural justice point, because Seah Ceramics was served and had notice. If the email caused the default, the whole judgment falls.

  3. 3
    The affidavit, the mistake of law and “never heard” H7

    The false affidavit goes to the merits, so it is intrinsic fraud. Per Hong Pian Tee, Seah Ceramics needs fresh evidence that reasonable diligence would not have uncovered and that would likely have changed the result, and per Eleven v Boxsentry that test applies to a default judgment too; it has held its failed test report since 2024, so this defence fails. The choice of law complaint fails as well: per Godard v Gray, Singapore does not sit on appeal from the Utopian court on fact or law. Per Merck it is open whether misapplying Singapore law is different, but this court did not apply Singapore law at all; its error, if any, was in its own choice of law. The plea that it was never heard fails too, because Seah Ceramics was served and chose not to appear (Per Sang Cheol Woo).

  4. 4
    Orders (iv) and (v): sever what fails H7

    The double damages are open. For Northcliff: they are paid to a private creditor in its own interest, so they are not penal (Per Raulin v Fischer; as in Sang Cheol Woo), and refusing them would be anomalous when Singapore awards punitive damages in tort; result, enforced. For Seah Ceramics: Licea left multiple damages open, s 16 of the CCAA (only a pointer here, as the judgment is outside the CCAA) and s 4(5) of the REFJA limit damages that do not compensate, and per Schnabel v Lui a punitive sum with a public purpose is penal though the creditor receives it; result, refused. The tax is refused: per Maler Foundation a judgment that indirectly enforces a foreign revenue law is not recognised, whatever its civil form, and Northcliff collects it “for the account of the Utopian Revenue”. Per Licea the creditor enforces the unobjectionable part if it is clearly identifiable and separable; each refused order is a separate order, so it is severed. Result: nothing if the email caused the default; otherwise US$3 million, plus US$6 million if the double damages are enforced, with the tax severed and the costs not yet a definite sum.

Northcliff took the Utopian judgment to Arcadia, where Seah Ceramics owned a warehouse. In August 2026 the Arcadian court declared the judgment enforceable in Arcadia. The warehouse was sold for US$1 million, which Northcliff received. The Arcadian order states that both defendants “shall pay the balance of US$2 million”.

In Singapore, Northcliff now relies on the Arcadian order as well. In the alternative it sues Ms Seah on her guarantee. Seah Ceramics has started its own claim in the General Division against Northcliff, for damages for the cracked kilns.

  1. Under Arcadian law the order is a judgment for US$2 million. The Arcadian court did not look at the merits of the kiln dispute.

Write from these boxes

Application questions · twist 2

⚡ Twist 2 · 1 of 4H2
Can Northcliff enforce the Arcadian order for US$2 million in Singapore?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Sang Cheol Woo, not following Morgan Stanley v Pilot Lead, a judgment on a judgment cannot be enforced at common law. It never examined the issues, it decides only its effect in Arcadia, and it would launder the Utopian judgment: Singapore would test the Arcadian court in place of the Utopian court, and Ms Seah would be reached by the back door. The words “shall pay the balance” restate the old liability, as in Poh Soon Kiat. Desert Palace saw no difficulty, but it did not deal with the theory.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J7.1.1 :: Judgment on a Judgment (−)

[The X judgment] merely declares [the Y judgment] enforceable in [X]. Per Sang Cheol Woo (not following Morgan Stanley v Pilot Lead (HK)), it is unenforceable at common law, and per REFJA s 3(4)(c) not registrable. [Creditor] must enforce [the Y judgment] directly.

⚡ Twist 2 · 2 of 4H11
If the Utopian judgment is enforced against Seah Ceramics, for how much?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

A judgment that has been satisfied cannot be enforced again, so the creditor may enforce only the balance. Enforcing in one country does not bar enforcement of the unpaid part elsewhere.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J7.2.8 :: Satisfaction (−)

Per C&Y, [debtor] has paid [amount] of [total], so [creditor] may enforce only [the balance]; a satisfied judgment cannot be enforced again (cf REFJA s 4(3), (9)).

⚡ Twist 2 · 3 of 4H8
Can Northcliff sue Ms Seah afresh on the guarantee, and does the Utopian judgment help it?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Ocean Tankers (a preliminary view), the original claim does not merge in a foreign judgment. But an estoppel needs a judgment capable of recognition, and on the better view the Utopian court had no international jurisdiction over Ms Seah. So Northcliff must prove the guarantee claim, and she may defend it. If Henry v Geoprosco is followed and she submitted, the judgment would bind her.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J7.3.1 :: No Merger (+)

Per Ocean Tankers (SGCA, preliminary view), [the original claim] does not merge into [the X judgment], unlike a Singapore judgment, so [the X loser] could re-sue on it here; whether [registration under REFJA or the CCAA] merges it is "arguable".

⚡ Twist 2 · 4 of 4H8
What is the effect of order (iii), the declaration, on Seah Ceramics' Singapore claim for the cracked kilns?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

For recognition the judgment must be on the merits, from a court with international jurisdiction, and final. There is no money requirement. All three are met against Seah Ceramics, which agreed to submit in clause 19. Its damages claim is the mirror image of the declaration that the kilns were free of defects, between the same parties. On the base facts no defence appears. Seah Ceramics may cite the Merck caution for a foreign defendant that had good reasons not to contest. That reply is weak, because clause 19 named the Utopian court. Its Singapore claim also breaks clause 19, so Northcliff could ask for a stay as well.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J7.3.1 :: Shield (+)

[The unsuccessful X claimant] re-sues [defendant] in Singapore on [the same cause], so [defendant] pleads [the X judgment] as res judicata, e.g., [a German declaration of non-liability under [contract]] against [a Singapore breach claim] (slides).

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes, and what stays

    Leave Twist 1 aside. The Utopian judgment is still enforceable against Seah Ceramics, and probably not against Ms Seah. What is new: an Arcadian order built on the Utopian judgment, US$1 million already received from the Arcadian sale, and two fresh claims in Singapore on the original contracts. The Arcadian order adds nothing except that credit, and the fresh claims bring in res judicata.

  2. 2
    The Arcadian order and the part payment H2H11

    The Arcadian order only declares the Utopian judgment enforceable in Arcadia, and the Arcadian court did not look at the merits. Per Sang Cheol Woo (not following Morgan Stanley v Pilot Lead), such a judgment on a judgment cannot be enforced at common law, even though Arcadian law treats it as a judgment for US$2 million. Per C&Y, it never examined the issues, it decides only its effect in Arcadia, and it would launder the Utopian judgment, Singapore testing the Arcadian court instead of the Utopian court; here that would reach Ms Seah by the back door. Desert Palace saw no difficulty, but per C&Y it did not grapple with the theory. So Northcliff must enforce the Utopian judgment itself. A satisfied judgment cannot be enforced again (Per C&Y), so after the US$1 million Northcliff may enforce only the balance of US$2 million against Seah Ceramics, and enforcing in Arcadia does not bar enforcing that unpaid part here.

  3. 3
    Northcliff's guarantee claim against Ms Seah H8

    Per Ocean Tankers (a preliminary view of the Court of Appeal), a claim does not merge in a foreign judgment, unlike a Singapore one, so Northcliff may sue Ms Seah afresh on the guarantee. The Utopian judgment helps it only if it can be recognised against her. On the better view (IGCF) the Utopian court had no international jurisdiction over her, so there is no estoppel: Northcliff must prove the guarantee claim, and she may defend it. If Henry v Geoprosco is followed, she submitted, and the judgment binds her.

  4. 4
    Seah Ceramics' kiln claim: the declaration as a shield H8

    Recognition needs a judgment on the merits, from a court with international jurisdiction, and final, with no defence, but no money order. All are met against Seah Ceramics, which agreed to submit in clause 19, and on the base facts no defence appears. Its damages claim says the kilns crack, while order (iii) declared between the same parties that they were free of defects, so Northcliff pleads the declaration as res judicata, a shield. Seah Ceramics may cite the Merck caution for a foreign defendant with good reasons not to contest, but that is weak, because clause 19 named the Utopian court. Result: the claim is barred unless Seah Ceramics shows a defence. The claim also breaks clause 19, which stays exclusive against the Buyer at common law (per C&Y), so Northcliff could ask for a stay as well, and per Vinmar Seah Ceramics would have to show strong cause.

4Scorecards: weigh the factors

Prof Chong rewards applying facts to factor tests. Sort each fact, then answer the verdict question. These use the base facts unless a line says “Suppose”.

H7 Sort the factors: Defences to the Utopian judgment

Each line is offered by Seah Ceramics as a defence to recognition or enforcement. Does it work? Lines marked “Suppose” are extra facts for this card only.

Northcliff's sales director told Seah Ceramics not to file anything, because no judgment would be entered.
Defence works. Inducing the debtor to let judgment go by default is extrinsic fraud. Abouloff applies: no fresh evidence is needed. The email must still have caused the default. J7.2.2 :: Extrinsic Fraud
Northcliff's engineer swore falsely that the kilns passed their tests. Seah Ceramics has held its own failed report since 2024.
Fails. False evidence goes to the merits, so it is intrinsic. That needs fresh evidence that reasonable diligence would not have found. The report is not fresh. The same test applies to a default judgment. J7.2.2 :: Intrinsic Fraud
The Utopian court applied Utopian law to a contract governed by Singapore law.
Fails. A mistake of fact or law by the foreign court is irrelevant. Singapore does not sit on appeal from the Utopian court. Per Merck it is open whether a clear misapplication of Singapore law is different. But this court did not apply Singapore law at all. Its mistake, if any, was in its own choice of law. J7.2.1 :: General Rule
Seah Ceramics: “We were never heard in Utopia.”
Fails. Natural justice needs notice and a chance to present a case. Seah Ceramics was served and chose not to appear, so there is no breach. Students miss this: its real complaint is the email, and that is fraud, not natural justice. J7.2.3 :: Default After Proper Service
Order (v): Utopian sales tax, payable to Northcliff for the account of the Utopian Revenue.
Defence works. It indirectly enforces a foreign revenue law. The civil form and the private payee are not conclusive. The defence removes this order only; the rest is severed and survives. J7.2.5 :: Label Not Conclusive
Order (iv): double damages for wilful non-payment, payable to Northcliff.
Open. A sum paid to a private creditor is not penal on the Raulin test. But the point is uncertain: Licea left multiple damages open, and courts may take their cue from s 16 of the CCAA. Run both and sever if refused. J7.2.5 :: Punitive Damages to a Private Party
Suppose: the US$3 million was credit for bets that Ms Seah placed at a licensed Utopian racecourse.
Open. Northcliff relies on Burswood, followed in Star v Yong Khong Yoong: s 5(2) of the Civil Law Act is only domestic policy. Per Venetian Macau, statutory policy prevails, s 5(2) draws no line between a direct claim and an action on a foreign judgment, and Burswood turned on a repealed statute. Give both; the newer case points to refusal. J7.2.4 :: Gambling: Creditor's Reply
Suppose: the courier never delivered the claim, and Seah Ceramics first heard of the case after judgment.
Defence works. The foreign court must give the debtor notice and then a chance to present its case. A debtor that learned of the claim only after judgment had neither. J7.2.3 :: §
Suppose: the General Division had ordered Northcliff to stop the Utopian action, and Northcliff went on to judgment all the same.
Defence works. A foreign judgment obtained in breach of a Singapore anti-suit injunction is contrary to public policy. J7.2.4 :: Breach of a Singapore ASI
⚡ Scorecard 1 · the verdictH7
Take the base facts with Twist 1. What can Northcliff recover from Seah Ceramics on the Utopian judgment?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Extrinsic fraud that produced the judgment defeats all of it, and needs no fresh evidence. If that defence fails on the facts, the false affidavit, the mistake of law and the natural justice plea do not help. The tax order is severed. The double damages are arguable both ways. The costs are not yet a definite sum.

5Remember

🧠 FOR THE EXAM
  • An asymmetric clause is outside the CCAA (per CHLOE V), but at common law its submission words still count as an agreement to submit (per United Malayan Banking).
  • Presence is tested when the foreign process was served (per Adams v Cape): a trade fair stand counts only while it runs.
  • Objecting to jurisdiction is a protest (per Nimbus), a forum stay is open (Henry v Geoprosco against IGCF), and the foreign court's own ruling on submission raises no estoppel.
  • A default judgment is on the merits, and final if it has final effect until set aside; only a definite sum is enforced, and a declaration is only recognised.
  • Classify the fraud first: inducing a default is extrinsic and needs no fresh evidence; false evidence is intrinsic and needs fresh evidence, even against a default judgment.
  • Sever rather than refuse the whole: a tax order is cut out, double damages are open, and part payment leaves only the balance; a judgment on a judgment is not enforced (per Sang Cheol Woo).

LAW302 · META GAME · QUESTION 1 · HYPO q1-02 · GEMINI PROMPT V1 · 14 QUESTIONS

Cascade v Kavala and Mr Varga

Written by Claude for the drill and law reviewed. Gemini (prompt v1) rebalanced the option lengths and wrote a note on each question; both were checked (4 corrections) and feed the notes here.

Answers:

1Base facts

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Cascade v Kavala and Mr Varga

Cascade Pictures Pte Ltd, a Singapore incorporated company, makes feature films. In 2024 it engaged Kavala Studios Ltd, a company incorporated in Elbonia, to edit and store the footage of a new film at Kavala's studio in Elbonia. Kavala is registered in Singapore as a foreign company. It runs a sales office at its registered office at Tanjong Pagar. The contract was signed there. Clause 9 reads:

“This contract is governed by Elbonian law. The parties submit to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of Elbonia.”

In June 2025 Mr Varga, Kavala's technical director, who lives in Elbonia, wiped the studio's servers during an upgrade. All the footage was lost. Cascade says that he ignored the backup procedure. Kavala says that the backup drives, supplied by an independent Elbonian company, were faulty.

In May 2026 Cascade sued Kavala in Elbonia. In early June 2026 it sued Kavala and Mr Varga in the General Division for breach of contract and negligence. It served Kavala at Tanjong Pagar. A process server handed the papers to Mr Varga at a Singapore hotel, where he was staying for three days for his niece's wedding. Two months earlier Cascade had invited him to Singapore “to talk things over”, and he had refused.

Each defendant has applied for a stay in favour of Elbonia. Both also say that Cascade must choose between its two actions.

Advise Cascade whether the General Division has jurisdiction over each defendant, and whether it will hear the claims. Do not advise on the merits.

ℹ ASSUME
  1. The Elbonian limitation period for all these claims expired on 30 June 2026. Cascade has never sued Mr Varga in Elbonia. The Singapore period has not expired.
  2. The Elbonian action against Kavala has not moved beyond filing.
  3. The engineers of the backup drive supplier refuse to travel to Singapore or to give evidence by video link.
  4. Apart from limitation, Elbonian law on these claims is the same as Singapore law in every material way.
  5. A civil trial takes about seven years in Elbonia and about 18 months in Singapore. Elbonian courts hear evidence in writing only and award no costs to the winner.
  6. Cascade says that the General Division can transfer the case to the Singapore International Commercial Court, where foreign law may be decided on submissions.
  7. Cascade paid Kavala's fees from its Singapore bank account. Its own editors, who checked the footage before it was sent, live in Singapore.
✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • D1
    Defendant can be served in Singapore. Both defendants were served in Singapore: a registered foreign company at its registered office, and an individual on a short visit. Each needs its own founding provision and mode of service.
  • A5
    Says "non-exclusive": a foreign court. Clause 9 names the Elbonian courts non-exclusively. Say what it promises: nobody breaks it by suing here, so it does not change the test. It is only a light stage 1 factor.
  • E2
    Stay after service in Singapore: Spiliada starter. Each defendant was served here as of right and asks for a stay. That is the Spiliada stay: stage 1 on each defendant, stage 2 on Cascade.
  • E4
    SCORECARD · Spiliada stage 1: connecting factors. The witness, governing law and Singapore contact facts are there to be marked on the stage 1 scorecard. Most of the Singapore contacts are neutral.
  • E5
    SCORECARD · Spiliada stage 2: substantial justice. The limitation dates, the seven year delay and the Elbonian procedure are Cascade's stage 2 points. Each needs its own block and its own result.
  • E9
    The SICC as a Spiliada factor. Cascade points to a possible transfer to the SICC to resist the stay. That is a stage 1 factor with its own limits.
  • E10
    Parallel foreign proceedings, and time bars. Cascade itself has an action in Elbonia on the same dispute. The defendants use it as a forum factor and to demand that Cascade elect.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • D2
    Foreign company never registered here, with an office or agent here. Tempting because Kavala is a foreign company and one of its directors was handed papers here. Wrong because Kavala is registered, so the Companies Act route needs no presence, and Mr Varga was served as a defendant in his own right.
  • E3
    Forum conveniens on service out: burden on the claimant. Tempting because both defendants are Elbonian. But both were served in Singapore as of right, so nobody served out. The stage 1 burden is on the defendants, not on Cascade.
  • E6
    Second bite: claimant fails stage 1 on service out. The second bite debate is about a claimant who served out and lost stage 1. Here service was in Singapore, so Cascade runs stage 2 in the ordinary way under E5.
  • E7
    Strong cause: starter and nature of the test. Tempting because clause 9 names the Elbonian courts and Cascade sued elsewhere. Wrong because the clause is non-exclusive, so no promise is broken. Strong cause needs a breach.

Fair to tick but not needed: E1 Which test, and who bears the burden, B1 CCAA gate: five conditions, B4 Outside the CCAA: say why, then the common law, D3 Defendant has taken a step in the Singapore action, F1 International and commercial, F6 SCORECARD · Transfer from the General Division: is the SICC "more appropriate"?

⚡ Base facts · 1 of 7D1
Mr Varga says that service on him should be set aside, because he was in Singapore only for a family wedding. Is he right?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Maharanee, temporary presence founds jurisdiction as of right under s 16(1)(a)(i) with O 7 r 2(1)(a). Service is set aside as an abuse only where the claimant lured the defendant here by a sham (Watkins). Mr Varga refused the invitation and came later for his own reasons. The fortuity of his visit goes to exercise.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per s 16(1)(a)(i) SCJA, Mr Varga, present at his hotel, was personally served as of right under O 7 r 2(1)(a). Per Maharanee of Baroda v Wildenstein and Colt Industries v Sarlie, presence on a short visit is enough without any other link, even though the events he is sued for happened wholly in Elbonia. Per Watkins v North American Land, service may be set aside as an abuse only where the claimant lured the defendant here, for example by a sham meeting, not where he came on business or holiday. Mr Varga refused Cascade's invitation and came two months later for his niece's wedding, so nobody lured him. Per C&Y, his weak connection is irrelevant to existence but supports a stay at the exercise stage.

1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

A foreign company that is registered and trading here is served under s 376(a) or (b), and that service founds jurisdiction through ss 16(2) and 17(1)(c). Adams v Cape is only for s 16(1)(a)(i). Maharanee is about a natural person, and Mr Varga is a separate defendant.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per ss 16(2) and 17(1)(c) SCJA, jurisdiction may rest on other written law, here s 376 of the Companies Act. A foreign company that is registered and trading here is served under s 376(a), at its Singapore registered office, or s 376(b), at its authorised representative's address, without Adams v Cape. Only s 16(1)(a)(i) needs Adams v Cape presence for a foreign company. The papers handed to Mr Varga were served on him as a defendant in his own right, and Maharanee is about a natural person defendant, so it says nothing about Kavala.

So Cascade's suit here is no breach, and the defendants' objection is none either, as Singapore is not named. Plain Spiliada applies. Both defendants were served here as of right, so they bear the stage 1 legal burden and Cascade bears stage 2 (Spiliada; JIO). Related proceedings are weighed by progress, parties and issues, not by who sued first (Lakshmi). Parallelism that the claimant itself created by suing in both places is disregarded (IM Skaugen (CA)), and an undertaking to discontinue neutralises it. Singapore has no first-seised rule.

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
⚡ BIG IDEA

Two defendants are served in Singapore in two different ways, and clause 9 names Elbonia only non-exclusively, so nobody is in breach and both stays run on plain Spiliada with stage 1 on the defendants. The deciding move is to weigh quality, not number: the tort and the uncompellable third party witnesses are in Elbonia, the Elbonian action that Cascade itself started is disregarded, and Cascade's own points (the SICC, delay, procedure and the time bar) each fail for a reason the blocks give. The twists change only Kavala's position: after deregistration s 376(c) is open, so the counterclaim (probably a submission) and service out with the forum burden on Cascade come in, and a never-registered company must itself be present before service on its officer is good.

  1. 1
    Mr Varga: present when served D1

    Mr Varga was handed the papers at a Singapore hotel, so jurisdiction rests on s 16(1)(a)(i) SCJA, with personal service under O 7 r 2(1)(a). Per Maharanee of Baroda v Wildenstein and Colt Industries v Sarlie, presence on a short visit is enough without any other link. Per Watkins v North American Land, service is set aside only where the claimant lured the defendant here, for example by a sham meeting. Mr Varga refused Cascade's invitation and came two months later for his niece's wedding, so there is no abuse. Per C&Y, his weak link with Singapore goes to the stay, not to existence.

  2. 2
    Kavala: served at its registered office D1

    Kavala is registered here as a foreign company and trades from its registered office at Tanjong Pagar. Cascade served it there under s 376(a) of the Companies Act, and per ss 16(2) and 17(1)(c) SCJA that founds jurisdiction. No Adams v Cape presence is needed, as that test is only for s 16(1)(a)(i). The papers handed to Mr Varga were served on him as a defendant in his own right.

  3. 3
    Clause 9 and the test A5E2

    Clause 9 says “non-exclusive”, so the CCAA does not apply and s 3(2) deeming is not engaged. Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), a clause naming a foreign court non-exclusively holds no promise not to sue elsewhere, so Cascade broke nothing by suing here and strong cause does not arise. Plain Spiliada applies to both stays, and Mr Varga is not a party to clause 9 in any case. Both defendants were served here as of right, so each must show that Elbonia, an available forum where both are based, is clearly or distinctly more appropriate (stage 1). Cascade bears stage 2.

  4. 4
    Stage 1: weigh quality, not number E4

    Per Rappo and JIO, there is no “balance sheet” of contacts: only links that bear on the dispute count, and the dispute is why the footage was lost. The careless act and the loss were both at Kavala's studio in Elbonia, so the tort is there, and the place of the tort is prima facie the natural forum (JIO; The Albaforth); the contract was also to be performed there, and as performance is disputed, that place counts too (C&Y; Rotary). The drive supplier's engineers are third parties who will not come here or give evidence by video, and their evidence is at least arguably relevant to Kavala's defence, so they point to Elbonia (JIO). Cascade's editors are its own staff, the bank account is tenuous, the place of signing is neutral, and the parties' bases cancel out. Elbonian law weighs little because it matches Singapore law and the dispute is about facts, and clause 9 carries little weight. Both claims against both defendants arise from the same facts, so they tilt to one forum (C&Y): probably Elbonia.

  5. 5
    Stage 1: Cascade's Elbonian action and the SICC E10E9

    Related proceedings are weighed by progress, parties and issues, not by who sued first (Lakshmi), and there is no first-seised rule. Cascade created this overlap itself, so it is disregarded (IM Skaugen (CA)); the action is only at filing and against Kavala only, and Cascade can undertake to discontinue it (C&Y). Per Rappo, the court must not shut its eyes to the SICC, but Cascade must name the feature that suits this dispute. Per IM Skaugen, the SICC factor is never decisive and at most discounts the weight of the foreign law. Elbonian law matches Singapore law and the dispute is factual, so there is little to discount, and stage 1 still points to Elbonia.

  6. 6
    Stage 2: Cascade's injustice points E5

    Per Rotary, once Elbonia is clearly more appropriate, refusing a stay is unusual, and Cascade needs cogent evidence of a real risk of injustice there. Per C&Y, delay counts only if egregious, and even alleged delays of over 10 years have failed (Grains and Industrial); written evidence only and no costs are ordinary differences in procedure, which are disregarded (C&Y) and do not defeat a stay where substantial justice is available (Spiliada; Trendtex). The claim against Kavala is not time-barred: Cascade sued it in Elbonia in May 2026, before the period expired. Against Mr Varga the bar is real: per Spiliada, if Cascade reasonably sued here and did not unreasonably let time run, the stay is conditional on his waiving the bar; if it did let time run, the stay is unconditional. Cascade was already suing in Elbonia and chose not to add him, so the unconditional route is more likely. The Singapore claims were filed in early June 2026, before the period expired, so they are in time here even if the FLPA applies the Elbonian period.

  7. 7
    Election comes after the stays E10

    Per Rappo, the stays are decided first, and election follows only if Elbonia is not clearly more appropriate. Election needs the same claimant suing the same defendant on the same issues in two places (Koh Kay Yew; Virsagi), so it can reach only Kavala, as Mr Varga is not sued in Elbonia. It is case management only: if Cascade elects Singapore, Kavala may still seek a stay (Rappo). As the stays will probably be granted, election should not arise.

  8. 8
    Result

    The General Division has jurisdiction over both defendants as of right. It will probably stay both claims in favour of Elbonia. A condition that Mr Varga waive the Elbonian time bar is possible but unlikely, because Cascade let time run.

Application questions · twist 1

⚡ Twist 1 · 1 of 3D1
Is posting the papers to Kavala's registered office in Elbonia good service now?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Tao Commodity, registration supplied the nexus, so s 376 is unavailable after deregistration and the claimant must serve out. Per the textbook, the plain words of s 376(c) cover a company that has ceased business, and the purpose is that companies that traded here cannot escape local creditors. Tao is a Registry decision. Give both routes and a result under each.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Tao Commodity, s 376 is unavailable after deregistration, registration having supplied the nexus, so Cascade must serve Kavala out with approval. But per C&Y, the plain words of s 376(c), which reach a company that “has ceased to maintain a place of business in Singapore”, cover a deregistered company too, ceasing business being the precursor to deregistration, and the purpose is that companies that traded here cannot escape local creditors. Tao is a Registry decision unreviewed by the Court of Appeal. Behind this lies a further split: per C&Y, s 376 itself confers jurisdiction through ss 16(2) and 17(1)(c), while per Tao registration is only “a statutory parallel to or substitute for” presence, a view that cannot survive deregistration. Route 1 (C&Y): the posting is good service and Kavala may only seek a stay. Route 2 (Tao): the posting founds nothing, and Cascade needs submission or approval to serve out.

The set-aside with a fall-back stay was not a submission. Submission under s 16(1)(b) cures irregular service.

Per Zoom (adopting Williams), submission is a step “only necessary or only useful” if the objection had been waived. Per Lakshmi Anil Salgaocar (HC), filing a counterclaim here is premised on jurisdiction. The earlier set-aside application with a fall-back stay was not submission (Zoom; Williams), even in the same summons. Per C&Y, submission under s 16(1)(b) cures irregular service, so the unapproved posting no longer matters, and Kavala can then only seek a stay.

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes

    Mr Varga's position and the Spiliada factors stay as they were. What changes is Kavala: it closed its Tanjong Pagar office in 2024, came off the register in January 2026, and was served by post in Elbonia without approval. It applied to set aside service, with a stay in the alternative, and a month later counterclaimed here with a reservation. So jurisdiction over Kavala now runs on three routes: s 376(c), submission, and, as the fallback, service out with the forum burden on Cascade.

  2. 2
    Section 376(c) after deregistration (open) D1

    Per Tao Commodity, s 376 is unavailable after deregistration because registration supplied the nexus, so the posting is not good service. Per C&Y, the plain words of s 376(c) cover a deregistered company too, ceasing business being the precursor to deregistration, and its purpose is that companies that traded here cannot escape local creditors; Tao is a Registry decision unreviewed by the Court of Appeal. Route 1 (C&Y): the posting is good service, jurisdiction exists through ss 16(2) and 17(1)(c), and Kavala can only seek a stay, bearing stage 1 as in the base. Route 2 (Tao): the posting founds nothing, so Cascade must rely on submission or serve out.

  3. 3
    Submission by the counterclaim D3

    The set-aside with a fall-back stay was not submission, even in one summons (Zoom). The counterclaim is different: per Zoom, submission is a step only necessary or useful if the objection had been waived, and a counterclaim here is premised on jurisdiction (Lakshmi Anil Salgaocar (HC)). Per Shanghai Turbo (SGCA), a reservation is “not a silver bullet” against conduct that contradicts it. So Kavala probably submitted under s 16(1)(b), which cures the irregular posting whatever the answer on s 376(c). It can then only seek a stay, bearing stage 1 as in the base, and on the same factors the stay probably still goes.

  4. 4
    Fallback: service out, burden on Cascade D4E3

    If Tao is right and Kavala has not submitted, Kavala is an absent defendant, so Cascade needs approval to serve out under O 8 on three requirements: a good arguable case on a gateway for each claim, forum conveniens, and a serious question to be tried. Per Zoom, forum conveniens is the Spiliada test with the burden reversed, and per Spiliada, Oriental Insurance and Zoom, Cascade keeps that burden on Kavala's set-aside, so Kavala should argue forum inside its set-aside rather than by a separate stay. Cascade must show that Singapore is clearly more appropriate (per Oro Negro “on balance” is enough; flag both), and on the base factors it probably fails on either standard. Whether it may then argue injustice is open (Oro Negro; IM Skaugen (CA)): against, failing stage 1 ends the matter (Konamaneni); for, per Spiliada itself and Shen Sophie, it may try, but delay and procedure fail and the claim against Kavala is in time in Elbonia. Either way, service on Kavala is probably set aside.

⚡ Twist 2 · 1 of 2D2
Can Cascade rely on s 376 of the Companies Act?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Division 2 applies to a registrable but unregistered company, but s 376(a) and (b) need a Singapore registered office or an authorised representative, and (c), read as a whole, is not meant for a company that still trades here. So the founding provision is s 16(1)(a)(i), and Adams v Cape must be written. Service out is needed only if presence fails.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Division 2 applies to a registrable but unregistered company (s 365), and Kavala, with a showroom here since 2022, is registrable. But per C&Y, s 376(a) and (b) fail with no Singapore registered office or representative, and s 376(c), read holistically, is not meant for a company still trading here. So the founding provision is s 16(1)(a)(i), and Cascade must prove presence under Adams v Cape. Service out is needed only if presence fails.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J2.1.5 :: s 376 Unavailable (must write)

although Division 2 applies to [a registrable but unregistered company] (s 365), per C&Y s 376(a)–(b) fail with [no Singapore office or representative] and (c), read holistically, is not meant for [a company still trading here]. So [claimant] relies on s 16(1)(a)(i) and must prove presence.

⚡ Twist 2 · 2 of 2D2
Is service on Ms Dragan good service on Kavala?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Adams v Cape, a company is present if it carries on its own business from a reasonably permanent fixed place for more than a minimal period. The showroom has run since 2022 and is staffed by Kavala's own employee. Power to contract is neither exclusive nor conclusive. If Kavala is present, leaving the papers with an officer under O 7 r 2(1)(b) is as of right. Her two day visit founds nothing by itself: Maharanee is for a natural person defendant.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Adams v Cape, a company is present if it carries on its own business at or from a reasonably permanent fixed place for more than a minimal period. The Tanjong Pagar showroom has been rented since 2022 and is staffed by Kavala's own employee, so the business is Kavala's, not hers (Okura). Kavala's best point is that she cannot sign contracts: Adams v Cape treats power to bind the company as the key question, but per C&Y that power is neither exclusive nor conclusive. If Kavala is present, leaving the papers with an officer under O 7 r 2(1)(b) is as of right. If Kavala is not present, the point is doubtful: per Yeo and Beranek it is the company's own presence that counts, so service on an officer who is only visiting founds nothing and Cascade must serve out; per COSCO it may still stand.

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes

    Mr Varga's position and the Spiliada analysis stay as they were. Kavala was never registered, so the Companies Act route is gone, but it has run a staffed showroom at Tanjong Pagar since 2022. This time the contract was signed in Elbonia, which changes nothing at stage 1, as the place of signing was neutral anyway. Cascade served its managing director, Ms Dragan, while she was at a two day film market here.

  2. 2
    Section 376 is unavailable D2

    Kavala is registrable, as it has a place of business here (s 365), but it never registered. Per C&Y, s 376(a) and (b) fail with no Singapore registered office or authorised representative, and s 376(c), read as a whole, is not for a company still trading here. So the founding provision is s 16(1)(a)(i), and Cascade must prove that Kavala itself is present (Adams v Cape). Service out is needed only if that fails.

  3. 3
    Presence first, then Ms Dragan as the mode D2

    Per Adams v Cape, Kavala is present if it carries on its own business at or from a reasonably permanent fixed place for more than a minimal period. For: it has rented the showroom since 2022 and staffs it with its own employee, so the business is Kavala's (Okura). Against: she cannot sign contracts, and Adams v Cape treats power to bind the company as the key question, though per C&Y it is neither exclusive nor conclusive. Result: Kavala is probably present, so leaving the papers with Ms Dragan under O 7 r 2(1)(b) is good service as of right, and the stays then run as in the base. If Kavala is not present, service on a visiting officer is doubtful: per COSCO it may still stand, but per Yeo, Beranek and Chong (mid-term feedback) only the company's own presence counts, and on that view Cascade must serve out, with the forum burden on it. Her remark that “our lawyers will deal with this” is not a step in the action, and nobody instructed Singapore solicitors to accept service, so there is no submission.

4Scorecards: weigh the factors

Prof Chong rewards applying facts to factor tests. Sort each fact, then answer the verdict question. These use the base facts unless a line says “Suppose”.

E4 Sort the factors: Spiliada stage 1 on the base facts

Each line is a connection that a party relies on. Where does it point? The line marked “Suppose” is an extra fact for this card only.

Cascade is based in Singapore. Kavala and Mr Varga are based in Elbonia.
Neutral or little weight. A claimant in one forum and a defendant in the other cancel out. J4.1.2 :: Parties: Neutral or Counterbalancing
The servers were wiped at Kavala's studio in Elbonia.
Points to Elbonia. The careless act and the damage were both in Elbonia. The place of the tort is prima facie the natural forum, and nothing makes it fortuitous. J4.1.2 :: Events: Tort
The backup drive supplier's engineers will not come to Singapore or give evidence by video link.
Points to Elbonia. They are third parties who cannot be compelled here, and their evidence is at least arguably relevant to Kavala's defence that the drives were faulty. J4.1.2 :: Witness Compellability
Cascade's own editors, who checked the footage, live in Singapore.
Neutral or little weight. They are Cascade's employees, not third parties, so there is no compellability problem. Mere convenience carries little weight. J4.1.2 :: Compellability Reduced
Elbonian law governs the contract and also applies to the tort claims.
Neutral or little weight. Students give this to Elbonia. But Elbonian law is the same as Singapore law, and the dispute is about what happened, not about law. The weight falls away. J4.1.2 :: Governing Law: Less Weight
The contract was signed at Kavala's office in Singapore.
Neutral or little weight. The place of contracting is neutral unless formation is in dispute. Nobody denies the contract. J4.1.2 :: Events: Contract
Cascade paid the fees from its Singapore bank account.
Neutral or little weight. The court draws no balance sheet of tenuous contacts. A bank account has nothing to do with why the footage was lost. J4.1.2 :: Quality over Quantity
Clause 9 names the Elbonian courts non-exclusively.
Neutral or little weight. It shows only that Elbonia is an appropriate forum, not that it is clearly more appropriate. It carries little weight. J4.1.2 :: Foreign NEJC (No Breach)
Suppose: an independent Singapore laboratory tried to recover the data, and its staff will not give evidence in Elbonia in any form.
Points to Singapore. These would be third party witnesses whom only Singapore can compel. They go to what could be recovered, so they have some weight, though less than the witnesses on why the footage was lost. J4.1.2 :: Witness Compellability
⚡ Scorecard 1 · the verdictE4
Leave out the “Suppose” line. Have the defendants shown that Elbonia is clearly the more appropriate forum?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Stage 1 is about quality, not numbers. The dispute is about why the footage was lost, and the events and the third party evidence on that are in Elbonia. The Singapore contacts do not bear on that question. The governing law and clause 9 are the wrong reasons: both carry little weight here.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Rappo and JIO, stage 1 weighs the quality of the links that bear on the dispute, not their number. The careless act and the loss of the footage were both at Kavala's studio in Elbonia, and per JIO and The Albaforth the place of the tort is prima facie the natural forum. The supplier's engineers are non-party witnesses who refuse to come or to testify by video, and their evidence is at least arguably relevant to Kavala's defence that the drives were faulty, so they point to Elbonia (JIO). Cascade's editors are its own employees, so they raise no compellability problem; the bank account is a tenuous contact; the place of signing is neutral because formation is not disputed; and the parties' bases cancel out. Elbonian law weighs little because it matches Singapore law and the dispute is about facts, and clause 9 shows only that Elbonia is an appropriate forum.

E5 Sort the factors: Spiliada stage 2 on the base facts

Stage 1 points to Elbonia. Each line is a reason Cascade gives for saying that a stay would deny it substantial justice. Does it work? Lines marked “Suppose” are extra facts for this card only.

A trial takes seven years in Elbonia and 18 months in Singapore.
Fails. Delay is disregarded unless it is egregious. Even alleged delays of more than ten years have failed. J4.1.3 :: Delay
Elbonian courts hear evidence in writing only and award no costs to the winner.
Fails. These are ordinary differences in procedure. They do not defeat a stay if substantial justice is available in Elbonia. J4.1.3 :: Ordinary Differences
The claim against Kavala is time-barred in Elbonia.
Fails. The facts do not say so. Cascade filed against Kavala in May 2026, before the period expired. Do not assume a time bar. J4.1.3 :: Time Bar: Limits
The claim against Mr Varga is time-barred in Elbonia, and Cascade never sued him there.
Could go either way. A stay can be made conditional on a waiver of the bar, but only if Cascade acted reasonably and did not unreasonably let time run. It was already suing in Elbonia, so that is hard to show. J4.1.3 :: Time Bar (±)
Suppose: Kavala is partly owned by an Elbonian ministry, and Cascade's lawyers say that Elbonian judges “tend to favour” state companies.
Fails. The court is slow to impugn a foreign court. A general complaint with no cogent evidence fails. J4.1.3 :: Comity (must write)
Suppose: sworn evidence shows that the only judge who hears film disputes in Elbonia is the brother of Kavala's chairman, and that the court files in two earlier Kavala cases went missing.
Works. Specific, cogent evidence of irregularities in cases like this one shows a real risk that justice will not be done. Several irregularities may add up. J4.1.3 :: Unfair Trial or Danger
Suppose: Elbonia has been under a state of emergency since a disputed election, but its courts sit as normal.
Fails. Political unrest is not enough while the courts still function to try the dispute. J4.1.3 :: Instability
⚡ Scorecard 2 · the verdictE5
On the base facts alone, what is the likely order?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Once Elbonia is clearly more appropriate, refusing a stay is unusual, and Cascade bears stage 2 on cogent evidence (Rotary). Delay and ordinary procedural differences fail. A time bar never keeps a claim here by itself: at most it makes the stay conditional on a waiver, and only for a claimant who acted reasonably.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Rotary, once Elbonia is clearly more appropriate, refusing a stay is “at least unusual”, and Cascade needs cogent evidence of a real and material risk of injustice there. Per AK Investment, a real risk is enough; proof that justice “will not” be done is not required. Per C&Y, delay is disregarded unless egregious, and per Grains and Industrial even alleged delays of over 10 years failed, so seven years fails. Evidence in writing only and no costs for the winner are ordinary differences in procedure, which are disregarded (C&Y) and do not defeat a stay if substantial justice is available (Spiliada; Trendtex). The claim against Kavala is in time in Elbonia. Against Mr Varga, per Spiliada, a waiver condition needs a claimant who reasonably sued here and did not unreasonably let time run; Cascade was already suing in Elbonia and did not add him, so an unconditional stay of both claims is likely, though a waiver condition for Mr Varga remains possible.

5Remember

🧠 FOR THE EXAM
  • Pair each defendant with its own founding provision and mode: a visitor under s 16(1)(a)(i) with O 7 r 2(1)(a); a registered company under ss 16(2) and 17(1)(c) with s 376.
  • A foreign non-exclusive clause holds no promise not to sue elsewhere: plain Spiliada, never strong cause, and the clause weighs little.
  • Stage 1 counts quality, not number: the place of the tort and uncompellable third party witnesses beat a bank account, the place of signing and the claimant's own staff.
  • Parallel proceedings the claimant started itself are disregarded; decide the stays before election, and election needs the same defendant sued in both places.
  • Check the dates before calling a claim time-barred abroad; a real bar gives at most a conditional stay, and only to a claimant who sued here reasonably and did not unreasonably let time run.
  • After deregistration s 376(c) is open (Tao against C&Y); a never-registered company must itself be present (Adams v Cape), and its officer is only the mode of service.
