LAW302 · META GAME · QUESTION 1 · HYPO q1-04 · GEMINI PROMPT V1 · 15 QUESTIONS

Camden v Klavier and Lark

Written by Claude for the drill and law reviewed. Gemini (prompt v1) rebalanced the option lengths and wrote a note on each question; both were checked (7 corrections) and feed the notes here.

Answers:

1Base facts

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Camden v Klavier and Lark

Camden Music Pte Ltd, a Singapore incorporated company, runs piano showrooms in Singapore. Klavier AG is incorporated in Arcadia. It is registered in Singapore as a foreign company and has a sales office at Orchard Road. In March 2024, at that office, Klavier's sales manager told Camden that Klavier's grand pianos were “built for the tropics”. Camden then signed a two page Order for 40 pianos. The Order states:

“This Order is governed by Arcadian law. The Klavier Export Terms 2021 apply (www.klavier.example/terms).”

Camden never opened the web page. Term 14 reads:

“The courts of Arcadia shall have exclusive jurisdiction over all disputes arising under this contract.”

The Order named Lark Movers Pte Ltd, a Singapore company, as “the Seller's delivery agent in Singapore”. Lark is not a party to the Order. Lark stored the pianos in its warehouse before delivery in July 2024. Within a year the soundboards cracked. Klavier blames damp in Lark's warehouse. Lark blames Klavier's wood.

In May 2026 Camden sued in the General Division. It claims against Klavier for breach of contract and for misrepresentation at the Orchard Road meeting, and against Lark in negligence. Camden says that it has rescinded the Order for misrepresentation, “term 14 and all”. Klavier has applied for a stay of the claims against it. It says that Camden must also pay its Singapore legal costs as damages.

Advise Camden whether the General Division will hear its claims against Klavier, and whether Klavier can recover its costs as damages.

ℹ ASSUME
  1. Arcadia is not a party to the Hague Convention on Choice of Court Agreements.
  2. Under Arcadian law, terms referred to in a signed order bind the signer even if it never read them. Under Singapore law, assume that they would not bind on these facts.
  3. Under Arcadian law all Camden's claims against Klavier had to be brought within two years of delivery. That period expired in July 2026. Camden has not filed a claim in Arcadia.
  4. An Arcadian court awards a buyer the cost of repair only, not lost profits. Camden's lost profits are four times the cost of repair.
  5. Lark refuses to submit to the Arcadian courts. The technicians who examined the soundboards all live in Singapore.
  6. Klavier uses the same Order form for every export sale. Camden signed it without asking for changes.
✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • A3
    Says "exclusive": a foreign court. Term 14 gives the Arcadian courts exclusive jurisdiction, yet Camden sued Klavier here. If the term binds and covers the claims, Camden is the party in breach.
  • A10
    The clause, or the contract holding it, is attacked. The clause is attacked twice: Camden never saw the Export Terms, and it says that rescission has swept term 14 away. Each attack needs its governing law and the infection test.
  • A9
    Is this claim, or this party, inside the clause?. A tort claim sits beside the contract claim, and one defendant is a stranger to the Order. Ask whether each claim and each party is inside term 14.
  • E7
    Strong cause: starter and nature of the test. If term 14 binds and covers the claims, Camden sued in breach. The test for the stay is strong cause, with the burden on Camden, although Klavier applies.
  • E8
    SCORECARD · Strong cause: the Eleftheria factors. The time bar, the smaller remedy, the split with Lark and the standard form are the facts to mark on the strong cause scorecard.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • B3
    CCAA applies and a foreign court is chosen (s 12). Tempting because term 14 is an exclusive clause for a foreign court. But Arcadia is not a Contracting State, so s 12 of the CCAA is never reached and the common law decides.
  • D2
    Foreign company never registered here, with an office or agent here. Tempting because Klavier is a foreign company with a sales office and a sales manager here. But it is registered, so it is served under the Companies Act and no presence need be proved.
  • D10
    Foreign clause, defendant abroad. Tempting because Klavier is an Arcadian company with an Arcadian clause. But it is registered here and was served here, so there is no service out to justify.
  • D3
    Defendant has taken a step in the Singapore action. Tempting because Klavier has applied for a stay and asks for its costs. But Klavier was validly served as of right, so jurisdiction already exists and submission adds nothing.

Fair to tick but not needed: A1 Any jurisdiction clause: what it promises, B1 CCAA gate: five conditions, B4 Outside the CCAA: say why, then the common law, D1 Defendant can be served in Singapore, E1 Which test, and who bears the burden, E2 Stay after service in Singapore: Spiliada starter

Application questions · base facts

⚡ Base facts · 1 of 7A10
Camden never opened the web page. Which law decides whether term 14 is part of the contract, and with what result?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Whether a clause was incorporated is for the proper law, and the law of the forum has no role in formation (Lew v Nargolwala). The choice of Arcadian law is in the Order that Camden signed, so that choice does not depend on the Terms that Camden never saw. Per Vinmar, the party relying on the clause needs only a good arguable case, the better of the argument, that it exists and applies.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per C&Y, whether a clause was incorporated is for the proper law. Per Lew v Nargolwala, the law of the forum has no role in formation, not even a residual one. The choice of Arcadian law is in the two page Order that Camden signed, not in the Export Terms, so that choice stands whether or not Camden read the Terms. Under Arcadian law, terms referred to in a signed order bind the signer even if unread, so term 14 is incorporated, and Singapore's contrary rule does not matter. Per Vinmar, Klavier, as the party relying on term 14, needs only a good arguable case that it exists and applies: “the better of the argument”, more than prima facie but less than a balance of probabilities. Lew left open only a very small caveat for grave injustice, whose effect is no contract under any law rather than Singapore law, and terms named in an Order that Camden signed are no such case.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J1.6 :: Incorporation and Service Out

Per C&Y, whether [clause X] was incorporated, e.g., by [a course of dealing], is for [the proper law]. Where [clause X] founds service out, [claimant] keeps that burden inter partes (J3.2).

⚡ Base facts · 2 of 7A10
Camden says that it has rescinded the Order for misrepresentation, so term 14 has gone as well. Is that right?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per PT Selecta and CIMB, the question is whether the vitiating factor also infects the clause. It does only where there was clearly no concluded contract at all, or non est factum. A misrepresentation about the pianos does not touch consent to term 14. Otherwise a bare allegation would neutralise every clause. Separability is a matter for the clause's governing law, and Arcadian law is presumed the same as Singapore law on it.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per C&Y, separability is a matter of substantive contract law, so ask whether the clause's governing law recognises it: here Arcadian law, presumed the same as Singapore law. Per PT Selecta and CIMB, the question is whether the vitiating factor also infects term 14. It does only where there was clearly no concluded contract at all, or non est factum; fraud in procuring the contract does not touch consent to the clause. The statement that the pianos were “built for the tropics” goes to the goods, not to term 14. Per CIMB, where the parties dispute validity, the dispute is decided under the contract's clauses as if valid, since otherwise a mere allegation would neutralise every clause.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J1.6 :: Infection Test

Per PT Selecta and CIMB, the question is whether [the vitiating factor] also infects [clause X]. It does only where there was clearly [no concluded contract at all] or [non est factum]; [fraud / duress] in procuring the contract, or [a common mistake as to subject matter] (CIMB), does not touch consent to [clause X].

⚡ Base facts · 3 of 7A9
Term 14 covers disputes “arising under this contract”. Is the misrepresentation claim inside it?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Subject-matter scope is for the proper law of the clause. Per Fiona Trust, applied to jurisdiction clauses in Trisuryo and Bunge, rational businessmen are presumed to want all disputes from their relationship in one forum unless the words clearly exclude them. Per The Jian He, reframing in tort rarely escapes a clause. Camden's answer is COSCO (CA): there is no presumption at the outset, and it depends on the claims and the words. If the tort claim were outside, it alone would go to Spiliada.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per C&Y, subject-matter scope is for the proper law of the clause, here Arcadian law, presumed the same as Singapore law. Per Fiona Trust, applied to jurisdiction clauses in Trisuryo and Bunge, rational businessmen are presumed to want all disputes from their relationship decided in one forum unless the words clearly exclude them. Per The Jian He, reframing a contractual dispute in tort rarely escapes a widely drafted clause. Camden's answer is COSCO (CA): there is no presumption at the outset, and the result depends on the claims and the clause's words. So the claim is probably inside; if it were outside, the misrepresentation claim alone would go to plain Spiliada, with stage 1 on Klavier because it was served here.

[Claimant] argues [the tort / statutory claim] is outside [clause X]. Per Fiona Trust, applied to jurisdiction clauses in Trisuryo and Bunge, rational businessmen are presumed to want all disputes arising out of [their relationship] decided in one forum unless [the words] clearly exclude them.

Does term 14 reach Camden's claim against Lark?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Asiana, adopting Team Y&R, whether a clause covers claims against third parties is a matter of construction, and in keeping with privity it usually will not. Being named as a delivery agent is not such an indication, and Lark does not rely on the clause. So the negligence claim stays here whatever happens to Klavier, and that is what creates the fragmentation point.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Asiana, adopting Team Y&R, whether a clause covers claims against third parties is a matter of construction, and in keeping with privity it usually will not, absent “a quite clear indication otherwise”. Naming Lark as the Seller's delivery agent in Singapore is not such an indication, and Lark does not rely on term 14. So the negligence claim against Lark stays here whatever happens to the claims against Klavier, and that is what creates the fragmentation point at strong cause.

[The non-party] invokes, or is sued in the teeth of, [clause X] in [the A–B contract]. Per Asiana, adopting Team Y&R, whether [clause X] avails claims against [third parties] is construction, and, in keeping with privity, it usually will not absent "a quite clear indication otherwise".

⚡ Base facts · 5 of 7E7
Klavier was served in Singapore and is the applicant. Which test applies to its stay, and who bears the burden?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Camden breaches a foreign exclusive clause by suing here, so strong cause is on Camden, although the defendant brings the stay and was served in. Per Vinmar, it should take more to keep a case from the chosen court than under Spiliada. Never call Spiliada the strong cause test.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Arcadia is not a Contracting State, so the CCAA is not engaged and the common law decides. Camden sued here in breach of the exclusive Arcadian clause, so per Vinmar, restating The Eleftheria, the court holds Camden to its bargain unless it shows strong cause. Per C&Y and Shanghai Turbo, the burden lies on the party seeking release from its promise, whether on a stay or a set-aside. So Camden bears it, although Klavier was served here as of right and brings the stay. Per Vinmar, “it should take more” to keep the case from the chosen court than under Spiliada. Never call Spiliada the strong cause test.

[Claimant] breaches by suing here, so strong cause is on [claimant], though [defendant] brings the [stay / set-aside], served in or out.

⚡ Base facts · 6 of 7E8
Camden says that a stay will split the dispute: Klavier in Arcadia, Lark here, each blaming the other. Is that strong cause?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Vinmar, citing Donohue, where non-parties are involved, splitting the dispute risks duplication, inconsistent findings and a race to judgment, and may be strong cause, unless that was foreseeable at contracting. Give both sides. For Camden: the overlap is real, and Lark will not go to Arcadia. For Klavier: Lark's role was written into the Order, and a stay is not presumptive merely because multiplicity may follow (Hive Marketing).

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Vinmar, citing Donohue, where non-parties are involved, splitting the dispute risks duplication, inconsistent findings and a race to judgment, and may be strong cause, unless that was foreseeable at contracting. For Camden: the overlap is real, as Klavier and Lark each blame the other, and Lark will not go to Arcadia. For Klavier: Lark's role in Singapore was written into the Order, so the split was a foreseeable price of term 14, and per Hive Marketing a risk of multiplicity does not by itself decide whether a stay is granted. ⚡ Base facts · 7 of 7A3
Can Klavier recover its Singapore legal costs from Camden as damages for breach of term 14?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

An exclusive clause contains a promise not to sue elsewhere, so damages are possible. Per Tradewaves, damages can, not must, be awarded, costs should normally be sought in the action in which they were incurred, and the claimant must prove unusual features. Here the costs were incurred in Singapore, where the court can make its own costs order.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

An exclusive clause contains a promise not to sue elsewhere, so suing in breach can sound in damages. Per Tradewaves, applying Sunrock Aircraft, damages “can”, not “must”, be awarded. Costs should normally be sought in the action in which they were incurred, and the party claiming damages must prove “unusual features” of the kind in Union Discount v Zoller, such as rules that allow costs only exceptionally and no costs order. Klavier's costs were incurred in this Singapore action, where the court can make its own costs order, so Klavier shows no unusual feature and its claim will probably fail.

⚡ BIG IDEA

Camden sued here although term 14 gives Arcadia exclusive jurisdiction, and it attacks the clause twice: it never read the linked Terms, and it says that it rescinded the Order. So the hypo tests the steps before strong cause: incorporation, separability and scope, each for Arcadian law as the proper law. Once term 14 binds and covers the claims against Klavier, strong cause sits on Camden although Klavier applies, and Camden's points fail as foreseeable or self-induced, leaving only the split with Lark arguable. Twist 1 keeps Camden in breach through the proved Arcadian rule on two court clauses, Twist 2 moves the breach to Klavier by making Singapore law govern, and Twist 3 moves the fight to existence by taking away Klavier's registration.

  1. 1
    Term 14 and the regime A3

    Term 14 says that the Arcadian courts “shall have exclusive jurisdiction”, so it holds a promise not to sue anywhere else. Arcadia is not a Contracting State, so the CCAA is not engaged, s 12 is never reached, and the common law decides. If term 14 binds Camden and covers its claims, Camden broke that promise by suing Klavier here and is the party in breach. Camden attacks the clause first, so its existence, validity and scope come before the test.

  2. 2
    Existence: Klavier was served here as of right D1

    Klavier is registered here as a foreign company and has a sales office at Orchard Road, so it was served here under s 376 of the Companies Act, which founds jurisdiction through ss 16(2) and 17(1)(c) SCJA. Only s 16(1)(a)(i) needs Adams v Cape presence, so Camden need prove none, and there is no service out to justify. Jurisdiction exists as of right, so Klavier's stay goes to exercise only, and whether it has submitted adds nothing.

  3. 3
    Is term 14 part of the contract? A10

    Klavier relies on term 14, so per Vinmar it needs a good arguable case, “the better of the argument”, that the clause exists and applies. Per C&Y, incorporation is for the proper law, and per Lew v Nargolwala the law of the forum has no role in formation, not even a residual one. The choice of Arcadian law is in the two page Order that Camden signed, so it does not depend on the Terms that Camden never opened. Under Arcadian law, terms referred to in a signed order bind even if unread, so term 14 is incorporated, and Singapore's contrary rule is irrelevant. Lew left open only a very small caveat for grave injustice, whose effect is no contract under any law rather than Singapore law, and terms named in an Order that Camden signed are no such case.

  4. 4
    Rescission does not sweep term 14 away A10

    Per C&Y, separability is for the clause's governing law: Arcadian law, which on these facts is not proved, so Singapore law applies, either in its own right if Arcadian law is not pleaded or by a fair presumption of similarity (Brownlie). Per PT Selecta and CIMB, a vitiating factor reaches the clause only where there was clearly no concluded contract at all, or non est factum. The statement that the pianos were “built for the tropics” attacks the sale, not Camden's consent to term 14. Per CIMB, a dispute about validity is decided under the contract's clauses as if valid, or a mere allegation would neutralise every clause. So term 14 survives the claimed rescission.

  5. 5
    Scope: the misrepresentation claim and Lark A9

    Per C&Y, scope is for the clause's proper law, Arcadian law, presumed the same as Singapore law. For Klavier: per Fiona Trust, applied in Trisuryo and Bunge, rational businessmen are presumed to want all disputes from their relationship in one forum unless the words clearly exclude them, and per The Jian He reframing in tort rarely escapes a clause. For Camden: per COSCO (CA), there is no presumption at the outset; it depends on the claims and the words. Probably inside, so strong cause covers both claims against Klavier; if outside, the misrepresentation claim alone goes to plain Spiliada, with stage 1 on Klavier as it was served here. Lark is different: per Asiana, adopting Team Y&R, a clause rarely reaches a non-party without a quite clear indication, and being named delivery agent is not one, so the negligence claim stays here.

  6. 6
    The test: strong cause, on Camden E7

    Camden sued here in breach of term 14, so the test is strong cause, never Spiliada. Per Vinmar, restating The Eleftheria, the court holds the parties to their bargain unless the party in breach shows strong cause, and “it should take more” than under Spiliada. Per C&Y and Shanghai Turbo, the burden lies on the party seeking release from its promise, so Camden bears it, although Klavier was served here and brings the stay. Where only the parties are involved, strong cause is generally abuse of process or denial of justice; with a non-party such as Lark, fragmentation may suffice (Vinmar).

  7. 7
    Mark Camden's points on the scorecard E8

    The statement, the pianos and the technicians are here, but per Vinmar such connections were foreseeable when a Singapore buyer agreed to Arcadia, so they carry little weight. The Arcadian time bar counts only if Camden shows “very good reasons” for not filing a protective claim there (Vinmar); it sued here in May 2026, about two months before the period ran out, and filed nothing in Arcadia, so the bar is self-induced. An award of repair costs only is a smaller remedy, not no remedy at all, and Trisuryo, where the chosen court could give none, was exceptional. The Order was Klavier's standard form, but per Vinmar (tentatively) strong cause probably still applies between businesses, though autonomy is weaker. Nothing suggests that Klavier is acting abusively.

  8. 8
    Fragmentation, and the result E8

    Per Vinmar, citing Donohue, splitting a dispute with a non-party risks duplication, inconsistent findings and a race to judgment, and may be strong cause unless foreseeable at contracting. For Camden: Klavier and Lark each blame the other, and Lark will not go to Arcadia; if the court finds the split unforeseeable, the claims against Klavier stay here beside the claim against Lark. For Klavier: the Order named Lark as its delivery agent in Singapore, so the split was a foreseeable price of term 14, and per Hive Marketing a risk of multiplicity does not by itself decide a stay. Result: Klavier's answer is stronger, so Camden probably fails to show strong cause; the claims against Klavier are stayed in favour of Arcadia, and the negligence claim against Lark continues here.

  9. 9
    Klavier's costs as damages A3

    Term 14 contains a promise not to sue elsewhere, so in principle its breach can sound in damages. Per Tradewaves, applying Sunrock Aircraft, damages “can”, not “must”, be awarded; costs should normally be sought in the action where they were incurred, and Klavier must prove “unusual features” (Union Discount v Zoller). Klavier's costs arise in this Singapore action, where the court makes its own costs order, so without unusual features its claim for damages fails.

⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

The clause follows the proper law of the Order, now Singapore law, so the Arcadian rule drops out. So Klavier's stay in favour of Arcadia is a breach, and Klavier must show strong cause. Shanghai Turbo (CA) left open whether this applies to a non-exclusive clause in a standard form; by analogy with Vinmar probably yes, and the form here is Klavier's own. ⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Ask first about the right to serve, then about the mode. Per Consistel, where the defendant is abroad the claimant must first seek permission to serve out, and substituted service arises only if personal service is impracticable. That the email in fact reached Klavier does not validate it afterwards. The exceptions, a defendant who left to evade service or who moves constantly, do not apply.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Beranek, ask first about the right to serve Klavier, then about the mode. Klavier is abroad, so the right exists only through O 8, by approval or agreement. Per Consistel, where the defendant is abroad, the claimant must first seek permission to serve out, and substituted service arises only if personal service is impracticable: “a hierarchy of service which must be adhered to”. That the email in fact reached Klavier does not validate it after the event. The exceptions, a defendant who left to evade service or who moves constantly between countries, do not apply, so the service is liable to be set aside.

Fails. A smaller recovery is not the same as no remedy. Strong cause was found where the chosen court could give no remedy at all, and that was exceptional. J4.3.3 :: No Remedy at All
Lark will not go to Arcadia, and each defendant blames the other.
Could go either way. A split with a non-party may be strong cause, unless it was foreseeable at contracting. The Order itself named Lark as the delivery agent. J4.3.4 :: Fragmentation
The Order was Klavier's standard form, and Camden did not negotiate it.
Fails. Strong cause probably still applies to a standard form between businesses, for consistency, although the autonomy point is weaker. J4.3.4 :: Standard Form Contracts
Suppose: after the Order was signed, Arcadia passed a law that bars its courts from hearing any claim by a foreign buyer against an Arcadian exporter.
Works. The chosen court would no longer be available to Camden, for a reason that it could not foresee at contracting. That is a denial of justice. J4.3.3 :: Chosen Court Unavailable
Suppose: Klavier is running a press campaign in Arcadia that calls Camden's owners fraudsters, just before the judges are assigned.
Could go either way. A media campaign to taint the trial is the example of abusive conduct. But the threshold is very high, and Camden would need evidence of a real effect on the trial. J4.3.3 :: Abuse Reformulated
⚡ Scorecard 1 · the verdictE8
On the base facts alone, what is the likely result for the claims against Klavier?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

The court holds the parties to their bargain unless the party in breach shows strong cause, which generally means abuse or a denial of justice, or fragmentation with non-parties. Natural forum points belong to Spiliada. The time bar is self-induced, and the tort claim is probably inside the clause. The claim against Lark continues in Singapore.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Vinmar, the court holds the parties to their bargain unless the party in breach shows strong cause: generally abuse of process or denial of justice, or, with non-parties, possibly fragmentation. Camden's connection points were foreseeable, and its Arcadian time bar is self-induced: it sued here in May 2026, about two months before the period ran out, and filed nothing in Arcadia. A smaller remedy is not no remedy at all; Trisuryo, where the chosen court could give none, was exceptional. Lark's role was written into the Order, so the split was probably foreseeable; if the court found it unforeseeable, fragmentation could be strong cause and the claims against Klavier would stay here beside the claim against Lark. So Camden probably fails, the claims against Klavier are stayed, and the negligence claim against Lark continues in Singapore.

6Remember

🧠 FOR THE EXAM
  • Incorporation, separability and scope are each decided by the clause's proper law; the law of the forum has no role in formation (Lew v Nargolwala).
  • A misrepresentation about the goods does not infect the jurisdiction clause; only no concluded contract at all, or non est factum, does (PT Selecta; CIMB).
  • A claimant suing here in breach of a foreign exclusive clause bears strong cause, even when the defendant was served here and brings the stay.
  • On the strong cause scorecard, foreseeable connections, a smaller remedy and a self-induced time bar fail; a split with a non-party may work unless it was foreseeable.
  • A two court clause is read under its governing law: a proved foreign rule can put the claimant in breach, while Singapore's reading makes it non-exclusive for both and puts the objecting defendant in breach.
  • A defendant abroad needs approval to serve out before any substituted service (Consistel), and with a foreign exclusive clause the claimant needs another gateway and strong cause.

LAW302 · META GAME · ★ DO FIRST · QUESTION 2 · HYPO q2-07 · GEMINI PROMPT V1 · 14 QUESTIONS

Calder Grid v Mr Kadir and Dorset Bank

Written by Claude for the drill and law reviewed. Gemini (prompt v1) wrote a guide to it; the guide was checked (8 corrections) and feeds the walkthrough. Gemini's file: law302_q2_07_calder_grid_v_mr_kadir_dorset_bank_.

Answers:

1Base facts

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Calder Grid v Mr Kadir and Dorset Bank

Calder Grid Pte Ltd, a Singapore incorporated company, builds electrical substations. In January 2026 it wanted a grid connection permit from the Ruritanian Ministry of Public Works. At a meeting in Ruritania, Mr Kadir, a Ruritanian consultant, told Calder Grid's project manager that he was on the Ministry's approved panel of advisers and could secure the permit within two months. The manager reported this to Calder Grid's board in Singapore, which resolved to hire Mr Kadir.

On 10 February 2026, Calder Grid and Mr Kadir signed a Consultancy Agreement in Singapore. Under it, Mr Kadir agreed to use his personal influence with Ministry officials in Ruritania to obtain the permit. Calder Grid agreed to pay him S$1.5 million in Singapore dollars into his Singapore bank account by 30 April 2026, whether or not the permit was issued. The Agreement is in English and contains no choice of law or jurisdiction clause.

To fund the fee, Calder Grid borrowed S$1.5 million from Dorset Bank Ltd, an Elbonian bank, under a Loan Agreement expressly governed by Elbonian law. Dorset Bank knew the loan was for Mr Kadir's fee.

Mr Kadir was never on the Ministry's panel, and no permit was issued. Calder Grid refuses to pay him. In the General Division, Mr Kadir sues Calder Grid for his S$1.5 million fee, and Calder Grid counterclaims against him in the tort of misrepresentation. Separately, Dorset Bank sues Calder Grid for repayment of the loan. Assume that the Singapore court has jurisdiction over all parties.

Advise Calder Grid on the choice of law issues in all three claims.

ℹ ASSUME
  1. Under Ruritanian law, using personal influence with a ministry official for a fee is not a crime, but a contract to do so is contrary to Ruritanian public policy.
  2. Singapore public policy also condemns contracts to buy personal influence over public officials.
  3. There is a sufficient connection between the Consultancy Agreement and the Loan Agreement to bar Dorset Bank's claim under Singapore law, but not under Elbonian law.
  4. Mr Kadir's statement about the approved panel is an actionable misrepresentation under Singapore tort law, but not under Ruritanian tort law.
✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • K1
    Characterise the issue. Characterise each issue first: Mr Kadir's fee claim and Dorset Bank's loan claim are contractual, while Calder Grid's misrepresentation counterclaim is tortious.
  • L6
    SCORECARD · Objective proper law: closest and most real connection. With no express or implied choice, weigh the connecting factors for the Consultancy Agreement: performance in Ruritania against signing, payment and Calder Grid's home in Singapore.
  • M1
    Illegality: pick the route. Route the illegality plea against Mr Kadir's fee claim: label the proper law, forum and place of performance, and separate Lemenda from Foster and Ralli.
  • M2
    The law broken is the proper law itself. Ruritanian law may be the objective proper law. If it is, the contract is against the public policy of its own proper law and fails there, before Lemenda is reached.
  • M4
    Lemenda: against the public policy of the place of performance. If Singapore law is the proper law, Lemenda applies: Singapore and Ruritania, the place of performance, both condemn buying personal influence over officials. The Westacre debate does not bite here, because no candidate proper law validates the contract.
  • M6
    SCORECARD · Tainting: a relevant illegality, sufficiently connected. Dorset Bank's Loan Agreement is valid in itself, so test tainting: whether a Lemenda breach meets Step 1, and whether Singapore or Elbonian law governs Step 2.
  • N1
    Starter: double actionability. Calder Grid's misrepresentation counterclaim is a tort governed by double actionability and its flexible exception.
  • N3
    SCORECARD · Locate the tort: where in substance did it arise?. Receipt was in Ruritania and reliance in Singapore, so the directed-statement gloss does not decide and the substance test locates the tort.
  • N4
    Limb 2 applied: is there liability under the law of that place?. Apply Limb 2: the statement is actionable under Singapore law, not Ruritanian law, so locating the tort in Ruritania defeats the claim unless displaced.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • M3
    SCORECARD · Foster v Driscoll: intention to break a friendly state's law. Tempting because influence is to be exerted on a foreign ministry. Wrong because Foster requires an intention to break a friendly state's written law, whereas personal influence is not a crime in Ruritania.
  • M5
    Ralli Bros: performance becomes illegal where it must be done. Tempting because performance takes place in Ruritania. Wrong because Ralli needs a law of the place of performance that makes the required act unlawful. Ruritanian law makes nothing unlawful. The contract is only contrary to its public policy.
  • K8
    Forum public policy; renvoi. Tempting because Singapore public policy condemns influence-peddling. Wrong because Lemenda rests on domestic public policy coinciding with the place of performance, not fundamental international public policy.
  • N6
    Party autonomy: does the contract's chosen law govern the tort?. Tempting because the tort induced the Consultancy Agreement. Wrong because the Consultancy Agreement has no choice of law clause.

Fair to tick but not needed: L1 Starter: the proper law and its three stages, L2 Express choice of law clause, L5 No clause: implied choice, N2 Limb 1: a tort under Singapore law, N5 SCORECARD · The flexible exception

Application questions · base facts

⚡ Base facts · 1 of 7K1
How should the court characterise Calder Grid's counterclaim against Mr Kadir for his statement about the approved panel?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Macmillan and JIO Minerals, the court looks to the true issue. Pre-contractual misrepresentation is a tort claim governed by double actionability, even though it induced a contract.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C1.1.1 :: Issue, Not Cause of Action

Per Murakami Takako and JIO Minerals, the court looks "beyond the formulation of the claim" to the true issue, so [claimant]'s framing as [restitution / constructive trust] cannot steer [the governing law]. In Macmillan, [the restitution claim] was really about [priority over the shares], for [the lex situs].

⚡ Base facts · 2 of 7L6
How does the court weigh the connecting factors for the Consultancy Agreement's objective proper law?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Factors are weighed differentially, with place of performance carrying great weight and place of contracting carrying little on its own. English as the lingua franca carries little weight.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C2.4.3 :: Application

Per Prof Chong, the strongest argument is usually [the place where both parties perform, e.g., country X], supported by [place of contracting / currency / incorporation and head office / related transaction], so [law X] is the OPL.

⚡ Base facts · 3 of 7M4
If Singapore law is the objective proper law of the Consultancy Agreement, is Mr Kadir's fee claim barred under Lemenda?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Lemenda, a contract to exert personal influence is unenforceable where it offends both Singapore's domestic policy founded on general morality and the public policy of the place of performance.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C2.10.4 :: Double Policy Breach

Per Lemenda, [a commission for influencing Qatari officials] under [an English-law contract] is unenforced if contrary to both a forum policy founded on general morality and the same policy at [the place where influence is to be exerted].

  • Domestic tier: per Phillips J, [buying influence] offends only domestic forum policy (it bites if [performed here]), hence the LLS element; international policy would make [the LLS / proper law] immaterial.
⚡ Base facts · 4 of 7M2
What if the court instead finds Ruritanian law to be the objective proper law of the Consultancy Agreement?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Run the proper law first. If Ruritanian law governs, the contract is contrary to the public policy of its own proper law and fails there. Lemenda is then not needed, and the Westacre debate does not arise because no proper law validates the contract. Foster is still not engaged because no written law is broken.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C2.10.1 :: Route A: Proper Law

Per Kahler and Zivnostenka, illegality under [the proper law] bars enforcement, unless [that illegality rule] itself offends Singapore public policy (The Playa Larga; Re Helbert Wagg).

⚡ Base facts · 5 of 7M6

Per Ryder Industries, not every breach qualifies for Step 1. Per Prof Chong, it is open whether a Lemenda breach suffices or only a breach of forum fundamental public policy.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C2.10.6 :: Sufficiently Serious

Per Ryder Industries, not every breach counts: [a breach of forum international policy / a forum mandatory rule / an LLS prohibition] qualifies, per Magdeev after [a balancing exercise], while [a Lemenda breach] is unclear (Prof Chong).

1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Which law governs Step 2 is unresolved. If tainting is part of the lex fori, Singapore principles apply and bar the claim; if of the proper law of the contract sued on (Elbonian law), the claim is not barred.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C2.10.6 :: Which Law's Principles?

Unresolved, as [Teng / Baker v BCS / Surewin] all involved [Singapore-law contracts]; per Prof Chong, if tainting is part of [the lex fori], Singapore's principles decide, and if of [the proper law], that law's do.

  • Which proper law: per Chong (seminar), that of [Contract 2, the claim sued on], not of [Contract 1, the tainting transaction].
  • Submission (C&Y; Forsyth): apply [the proper law]'s principles unless [the lex fori's] rise to overriding mandatory rules or international policy, though this raises an incidental question on [the related transaction's legality].
⚡ Base facts · 7 of 7N3
Where is Mr Kadir's misrepresentation located as a tort?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per JIO Minerals, where receipt and reliance occur in different countries, the directed-statement rule does not apply and the court returns to the substance test to weigh all events. If the tort is located in Ruritania, limb 2 fails unless the flexible exception displaces Ruritanian law. If it is located in Singapore, both limbs point to Singapore law and the claim is actionable.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C3.3.2 :: Misrepresentation Directed at the Claimant: Receipt + Reliance

Per JIO Minerals (tentatively, citing Yeo) and Ong Ghee Soon, [a representation] directed at [claimant] and received and acted on in [Singapore] is a tort there, unless [that place] is fortuitous.

  • Where reliance crystallises: where [claimant] gave [instructions via the Singapore branch], not [administrative execution in Geneva] (Ong Ghee Soon).
  • Fortuitous receipt: receipt in [India] merely because [claimant] is based there is fortuitous (JIO).
  • Receipt and reliance split: the specific rule fails, so use [the substance test], as in JIO where [negotiations and drilling] made [Indonesia] the place.
  • Several countries of making, receipt and reliance: where [the core representations] were made, e.g. [Germany], may prevail, receipt being fortuitous for [global operators] (IM Skaugen v MAN Diesel).
  • Receipt unclear on the pleadings: unevidenced receipt in [Germany] is "speculative", so [Singapore law] applies (Rickshaw).
📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
⚡ BIG IDEA

Three claims, three tools: the proper law and illegality for Mr Kadir's fee, tainting for Dorset Bank's loan, and double actionability for Calder Grid's counterclaim. Buying influence is no crime in Ruritania, only against its public policy, so the home is Lemenda, not Foster or Ralli. But find the proper law first: if it is Ruritanian law, the deal fails under its own proper law, and if it is Singapore law, Lemenda bars it, so Mr Kadir fails either way. The loan and the counterclaim then turn on open points, each needing a result under both routes: whether a Lemenda breach can taint, whose principles judge the connection, and where a statement heard in Ruritania and relied on in Singapore is located.

  1. 1
    Characterise the three claims K1

    Per Macmillan, the court (1) characterises the issue, (2) selects the connecting factor and (3) applies the law it points to, and the dispute turns on stage 1. Mr Kadir's claim for his fee and Dorset Bank's claim for repayment are contractual, so each goes to its own contract's proper law. Calder Grid's counterclaim is in the tort of misrepresentation. Per Murakami Takako and JIO Minerals, the court looks beyond the framing to the true issue, and per Rickshaw, absent bad faith, a claim framed in tort stays a tort claim although a contract sits behind it. So the counterclaim goes to double actionability, not to the Consultancy Agreement's proper law.

  2. 2
    The Consultancy Agreement's proper law L6

    There is no choice of law or court clause, and nothing else implies a choice, so find the law of closest and most real connection (Per Bonython; Pacific Recreation). For Ruritania: Mr Kadir uses his influence there, and the place of performance carries great weight (Bonython; Enka); he is Ruritanian, and the permit is Ruritanian. For Singapore: signing, payment in Singapore dollars into a Singapore account, and Calder Grid's home; but signing counts little unless performance is also there (Pacific Recreation), and only Calder Grid's payment is performed here; English, the lingua franca, carries little weight. Per Prof Chong, the strongest factor is usually where both parties perform, and here they perform in different countries, so the balance is close. Per Lew the court must still choose: Ruritanian law is arguably stronger, as his services and the permit are the point of the deal, but run both, because Mr Kadir fails under each.

  3. 3
    Route the illegality plea M1

    Calder Grid pleads illegality against the fee claim, so list the routes: the proper law, forum international policy, Foster, Lemenda, Ralli, tainting and reliance as a defence. Label the three laws that can matter: the proper law (Ruritanian or Singapore law), the forum (Singapore) and the place of performance (Ruritania, where the influence is to be used). Per C&Y, a foreign written law goes to Foster if breaking it was intended at formation, or to Ralli if required performance breaks it, while foreign public policy alone goes to Lemenda. Using influence for a fee is no crime in Ruritania, only against its public policy, so Foster has no law to break and Ralli has no unlawful act. Nor is this forum international policy: per Phillips J in Lemenda, buying influence offends only domestic policy.

  4. 4
    Mr Kadir's fee fails under either proper law M2M4

    Run the proper law first. If Ruritanian law governs, the contract is against the public policy of its own proper law, and per Kahler and Zivnostenka illegality under the proper law bars enforcement; the exception for a rule that itself offends Singapore policy does not help, as Singapore shares the policy. If Singapore law governs, apply Lemenda: a contract to buy influence is not enforced if it offends both a forum policy founded on general morality and the same policy where the influence is to be used. Both are met here, so Shaikh Faisal (foreign policy alone is not enough) does not help Mr Kadir. The Westacre debate does not arise, because no candidate proper law validates the contract. Mr Kadir's fee claim fails either way.

  5. 5
    Dorset Bank's loan: tainting Step 1 M6

    The Loan Agreement is valid under its chosen Elbonian law, so Calder Grid argues that the Consultancy Agreement taints Dorset Bank's claim. Per Euro-Diam, ask (1) is there a relevant foreign illegality, and (2) is it sufficiently connected to the claim? Per Surewin, Step 1 can ask whether Singapore would enforce the Consultancy Agreement, so beating Mr Kadir also helps Calder Grid here. But per Ryder Industries not every breach counts: a breach of forum international policy, a forum mandatory rule or a prohibition at the place of performance qualifies (per Magdeev, after a balancing exercise), and here there is only public policy. Whether a Lemenda breach is serious enough is open (Prof Chong). If it is not, Step 1 fails and Dorset Bank recovers its loan; if it is, go on to Step 2.

  6. 6
    Tainting Step 2: whose principles? M6

    Which law's principles judge the connection is unresolved, as Teng, Baker v BCS and Surewin all involved Singapore law contracts. Per Prof Chong, if tainting is part of the lex fori, Singapore's principles decide. They give a sufficient connection on the facts, and refusal is proportionate (Per Ting Siew May), as Dorset Bank knew the loan was for the fee, unlike the unaware bank in Surewin: Dorset Bank is barred. If tainting is part of the proper law, the law that counts is that of the contract sued on (Per Chong (seminar)), Elbonian law, which finds no sufficient connection: Dorset Bank recovers. Dorset Bank will add C&Y's submission that the proper law's principles apply unless Singapore's rise to overriding mandatory rules or international policy, which a domestic policy against buying influence does not.

  7. 7
    The counterclaim: double actionability N1N2

    Per Rickshaw, the counterclaim is governed by double actionability subject to a flexible exception (Boys v Chaplin; Red Sea). The statement must be (a) a tort under Singapore law and (b) give civil liability between these parties under the law of the place of the tort. Per EFT Holdings, Calder Grid proves limb 1, and Mr Kadir must plead and prove that the law of that place gives no liability. Limb 1 is met: per IM Skaugen, had everything happened in Singapore, the statement would be an actionable misrepresentation, as the facts assume.

  8. 8
    Where is the misrepresentation? N3

    Per JIO Minerals (tentatively) and Ong Ghee Soon, a statement directed at the claimant is a tort where it is received and acted on. The project manager heard it at a meeting in Ruritania, but the board relied on it in Singapore, so receipt and reliance split and that rule fails, as in the sample final scheme. Per Distillers and Metall, the court then asks where in substance the cause of action arose. For Ruritania: the statement was made and received there, by a Ruritanian, about a Ruritanian ministry, much as negotiations and drilling made Indonesia the place in JIO. For Singapore: per Vibrant Group, the place of reliance counts more for misrepresentation than for negligence, the board decided and the Agreement was signed here, and per Metall the court need not ignore harm done to a Singapore company by acts abroad. Either is arguable, so give limb 2 under each place.

  9. 9
    Limb 2 under each place, and the exception N4N5

    Route 1, Ruritania: Ruritanian tort law gives no liability, so limb 2 fails and Mr Kadir escapes unless Calder Grid displaces Ruritanian law. The flexible exception is unlikely to help: per Rickshaw it is strictly applied and needs a purely fortuitous place, and Ruritania is where a Ruritanian made the statement about his own country's ministry. Route 2, Singapore: a local tort still runs both limbs (Per Rickshaw), both point to Singapore law, and the counterclaim is actionable. So Calder Grid's counterclaim probably succeeds only if the tort is located in Singapore.

2Twist 1

🧩 TWIST 1

Go back to the base facts and add one clause.

Suppose the Consultancy Agreement had contained an express choice of law clause:

“This Agreement is governed by Utopian law.”

Under Utopian law, a contract to use personal influence with a foreign ministry is valid and enforceable.

✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • L2
    Express choice of law clause. An express choice of Utopian law is virtually conclusive under Vita Food and Peh Teck Quee, even though Utopia has no connection to the deal.
  • L4
    Law chosen to dodge another country's rule. Test whether choosing Utopian law was not bona fide because its sole purpose was to evade Ruritanian public policy or Singapore law.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • M3
    SCORECARD · Foster v Driscoll: intention to break a friendly state's law. Wrong because there is still no breach of Ruritanian written law, only public policy.
  • M5
    Ralli Bros: performance becomes illegal where it must be done. Tempting because the influence is still to be used in Ruritania. Wrong because no Ruritanian law makes any act the contract requires unlawful there. The objection is still public policy only.

Fair to tick but not needed: M4 Lemenda: against the public policy of the place of performance, M6 SCORECARD · Tainting: a relevant illegality, sufficiently connected, L6 SCORECARD · Objective proper law: closest and most real connection, M2 The law broken is the proper law itself, N6 Party autonomy: does the contract's chosen law govern the tort?

Application questions · twist 1

⚡ Twist 1 · 1 of 3L4

⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Peh Teck Quee, an unrelated law is permitted and evasion defeats the clause only if it was the sole purpose. If struck out, the court skips Stage 2 and goes to the objective proper law.

Per Waller LJ in Westacre, Lemenda likely bites only where the proper law's domestic policy is also offended. Against that, Lemenda itself rests on the coincidence of forum and place-of-performance policy.

Per Waller LJ in Westacre, [the contract] is enforceable unless it offends the domestic policy of [the proper law / curial law], so per C&Y Lemenda likely bites only where [the lex fori] is [the proper law].

  • Advising enforcement: [Utopian law], the proper law, does not condemn [the commission], so per Westacre it is payable.
  • Advising unenforceability: Lemenda rests on the general morality of [the forum] and [the LLS], so breaching those two suffices.
  • Prof Chong's query: does validity under [the proper law] trump the coincidence of [forum] and [LLS] policy?
⚡ Twist 1 · 3 of 3M6
How does the express choice of Utopian law affect Dorset Bank's loan claim?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Step 1 of tainting asks whether there is a relevant foreign illegality. If the Consultancy Agreement is enforceable under Utopian law and not barred by Lemenda, Step 1 fails.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C2.10.6 :: Act or Transaction

Anuva excluded illegal acts, but per C&Y a transaction is made of acts (cf Howard v Shirlstar), so per Surewin ask whether [the act] breached [foreign law], or whether Singapore would enforce [Contract 1] (C2.10.3 to C2.10.5).

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes, and what stays

    The Consultancy Agreement now chooses Utopian law, which has no link to the deal and holds a contract to use influence with a foreign ministry valid. Singapore and Ruritania still condemn such contracts, and using influence is still no crime in Ruritania. The Loan Agreement keeps its Elbonian law, but whether it is tainted may now change. The tort counterclaim is unchanged.

  2. 2
    Does the Utopian clause stand? L2L4

    Per Peh Teck Quee, applying Vita Food, the choice is virtually conclusive unless it is not bona fide, legal or consistent with public policy, and the chosen law needs no connection, as parties may want a neutral law (Amin Rasheed). Calder Grid argues that the choice is not bona fide, which succeeds only if evading Ruritanian or Singapore policy was the sole purpose (Per Peh Teck Quee). For Calder Grid: Utopia has no link at all, and its only visible attraction is that it validates a deal that both other laws condemn. For Mr Kadir: an unrelated law is permitted, and nothing in the facts shows that evasion was the only reason. If the clause falls, it falls completely, and the court goes straight to the objective proper law (Per Shanghai Turbo; The Iran Vojdan), so the base answer returns and Mr Kadir fails either way.

  3. 3
    If the clause stands: the Westacre debate M4

    Utopian law validates the contract, so there is no proper law illegality, and Foster and Ralli stay out, as there is still no breach of Ruritanian written law, only public policy. Singapore's and Ruritania's policies still coincide, but the proper law does not share them. Per Waller LJ in Westacre, the contract is enforceable unless it offends the domestic policy of the proper law, so per C&Y Lemenda likely bites only where the forum is the proper law: Mr Kadir recovers his fee. Against that, Lemenda rests on the general morality of the forum and the place of performance, and both are offended: the claim is barred. Prof Chong's query is whether validity under the proper law trumps that coincidence, so give both results. Forum international policy is no fallback, as buying influence offends only domestic policy (per Phillips J).

  4. 4
    The knock-on effect on the loan M6

    If the clause stands and the Westacre view wins, Singapore would enforce the Consultancy Agreement and no Ruritanian law is broken, so there is no relevant illegality: Step 1 fails and Dorset Bank recovers. If Lemenda still bars the contract, or the clause is struck out, Step 1 is open as in the base. Step 2 then runs as before: Singapore principles bar Dorset Bank, Elbonian principles do not. The Loan Agreement keeps its own Elbonian law, and the tort analysis is unchanged.

    SCORECARD · Foster v Driscoll: intention to break a friendly state's law. Tempting because paying the official is now a crime in a friendly foreign state. Wrong because Ruritanian law is the proper law itself, so proper law illegality decides and Foster is irrelevant.
  • M4

  • M5

Application questions · twist 2

⚡ Twist 2 · 1 of 2M2
How does the court analyse Mr Kadir's fee claim now that paying him is a crime under Ruritanian law and Ruritanian law governs?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Kahler and Zivnostenka, illegality under the proper law bars enforcement unless that rule offends Singapore public policy. Foster and the parties' intentions are then irrelevant.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C2.10.1 :: Route A: Proper Law

Per Kahler and Zivnostenka, illegality under [the proper law] bars enforcement, unless [that illegality rule] itself offends Singapore public policy (The Playa Larga; Re Helbert Wagg).

⚡ Twist 2 · 2 of 2M6
How does this change affect Step 1 of tainting on Dorset Bank's loan claim?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

A criminal offence under the proper law and place of performance is sufficiently serious for Step 1 under Ryder Industries, removing the Lemenda threshold doubt. Step 2 still turns on lex fori vs Elbonian proper law.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C2.10.6 :: Sufficiently Serious

Per Ryder Industries, not every breach counts: [a breach of forum international policy / a forum mandatory rule / an LLS prohibition] qualifies, per Magdeev after [a balancing exercise], while [a Lemenda breach] is unclear (Prof Chong).

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes, and what stays

    Two facts change: paying for personal influence with an official is now a crime under the Ruritanian Anti-Corruption Code, and the Consultancy Agreement is governed by Ruritanian law. So there is no proper law to find, and the deal now breaks a written law that is part of its own proper law. Step 2 of tainting and the tort counterclaim stay as in the base.

  2. 2
    Proper law illegality decides M2

    Ruritanian law is both the proper law and the law broken. Per Kahler and Zivnostenka, illegality under the proper law bars enforcement, unless that rule itself offends Singapore public policy (The Playa Larga; Re Helbert Wagg); an anti-corruption law does not, as Singapore shares the policy. Per the sample final answer scheme, Foster and the parties' intentions are then irrelevant. Lemenda drops out, as there is now a written law and it is the proper law. Ralli is not the route either: the ban is part of the proper law, and the payment it forbids is due in Singapore. Mr Kadir's fee claim fails.

  3. 3
    Tainting: Step 1 is now met M6

    Per Ryder Industries, a prohibition at the place of performance can qualify for Step 1, per Magdeev after a balancing exercise. A serious corruption offence under the proper law, in the country where the influence is to be used, plainly passes, unlike the minor customs breach in Ryder Industries. So the Lemenda doubt drops out and Step 1 is met. Step 2 is unchanged: Singapore principles bar Dorset Bank, while Elbonian principles, as the law of the loan sued on, let it recover.

Application questions · twist 3

⚡ Twist 3 · 1 of 2M7
What test decides whether Mr Kadir can rely on the Consultancy Agreement to resist Calder Grid's claim to recover the S$1.5 million?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Esben Finance, a defendant may rely on the illegal arrangement as a defence to an unjust enrichment claim unless the outcome would stultify the policy. Esben concerned a Foster and Ralli arrangement and comity, so its use for a Lemenda contract is by analogy.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C2.10.7 :: Stultification

Per Esben Finance, [Defendant] may rely on [the Foster / Ralli arrangement] against [an unjust enrichment claim] unless the outcome would stultify comity, which it [does / does not] as [reliance merely explains the payments / gives effect to the illegal performance].

⚡ Twist 3 · 2 of 2M7
Which statement about illegality and Mr Kadir's defence matches Esben Finance?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Esben Finance (a provisional view), illegality is a shield, not a sword, and rejecting the defence restores the status quo ante, because the money goes back. So the court asks whether the outcome would stultify the policy.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C2.10.7 :: Supporting Points (provisional)

Per Esben, ex dolo malo bars [causes of action], not defences; illegality is a shield, not a sword (cf [promissory estoppel]); and rejecting [the defence] restores the status quo ante.

  • Contract vs unjust enrichment: per Esben, in [contract] the illegality argument almost always is [the defence], so the two may differ.
📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes, and what stays

    Calder Grid has already paid the S$1.5 million and now sues Mr Kadir to get it back. His fee claim falls away, and the question becomes whether he may rely on the Consultancy Agreement to keep the money. Dorset Bank's loan claim and the tort counterclaim stay as in the base.

  2. 2
    Reliance as a defence: the Esben test M7

    Mr Kadir relies on the Consultancy Agreement to explain why he was paid. Per Esben Finance, a defendant may rely on the illegal arrangement against an unjust enrichment claim unless the outcome would stultify the policy. Esben concerned Foster and Ralli arrangements and comity, so for this Lemenda contract the test runs by analogy, against the policy that Singapore and Ruritania share. It is not Ralli, as no Ruritanian law makes any required act unlawful, and not a question of an unknown foreign remedy.

  3. 3
    Stultification: both sides M7

    On Esben's provisional points, ex dolo malo bars causes of action, not defences; illegality is a shield, not a sword; and rejecting the defence restores the status quo ante. Calder Grid argues that letting Mr Kadir keep S$1.5 million paid for influence gives effect to the very bargain both laws condemn, so the defence stultifies the policy and the money goes back. Mr Kadir answers that his reliance merely explains why he was paid, so the defence stands and he keeps the fee. Give both, with the result under each.

5Remember

🧠 FOR THE EXAM
  • Foreign public policy with no statute behind it goes to Lemenda, not Foster or Ralli; but find the proper law first, since a deal that offends its own proper law fails there.
  • Lemenda needs Singapore's domestic policy and the same policy where the influence is used; if a foreign proper law validates the deal, the Westacre debate is open, so give both results.
  • Where the law broken is the proper law itself, proper law illegality decides, and Foster and the parties' intentions are irrelevant.
  • Tainting has two open points: is a Lemenda breach serious enough at Step 1, and do Singapore principles or the proper law of the contract sued on judge the connection at Step 2?
  • Receipt and reliance in different countries: the directed statement rule fails and the substance test decides, so give limb 2's result under each location.
  • A chosen law needs no connection; a bona fides attack succeeds only if evasion was the sole purpose, and then the court goes straight to the objective proper law.

LAW302 · META GAME · ★ DO FIRST · QUESTION 2 · HYPO q2-08 · GEMINI PROMPT V2 · LAW REVIEWED 17 NOV · 10 QUESTIONS

Tidewell v Veldon, Cairn and Harbourline

Gemini wrote this hypo with prompt v2. Claude reviewed it in three passes and made 61 changes before it went into the drill. Gemini's file: bramwell_v_veldon_cairn_and_harbourline_q2_08.ht.

Answers:

1Base facts

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Tidewell v Veldon, Cairn and Harbourline

Tidewell Cranes Pte Ltd, a Singapore company, refurbishes port cranes. Veldon Logistics SA, incorporated in Ruritania, runs a terminal at Port Ruri. By a Sale Agreement signed in Singapore on 10 March 2026 and written in English, Tidewell sold Veldon two cranes for S$8 million. Delivery, installation and payment in Ruritanian dollars were all due at Port Ruri. Clause 14 reads:

“14. This Agreement shall be governed by Singapore law or Ruritanian law, as the Seller may elect by written notice to the Buyer.”

Veldon paid half the price on delivery, but withheld the S$4 million balance after installation. In June 2026 Tidewell gave Veldon written notice under clause 14 electing Singapore law. Veldon relies on two Ruritanian statutes. The Port Language Act provides: “No action shall be brought to enforce a contract for the sale of port infrastructure unless it is in the Ruritanian language.” The Port Equipment Act makes any contract to supply port cranes for Ruritania illegal and void unless the seller holds a Ministry licence. Neither party knew of this Act or obtained a licence.

Before signing, Veldon asked Cairn Appraisals LLP, a Ruritanian firm, to value two old cranes Tidewell was taking in part-exchange. Cairn inspected them in Ruritania, wrote its report there, and emailed it directly to Tidewell in Singapore. Tidewell’s board read and relied on it in Singapore. The valuation was carelessly inflated by S$600,000.

In April 2026 Tidewell emailed Harbourline Pte Ltd, a Singapore haulage company, a draft Haulage Agreement for moving parts in Singapore. It stated: “Governed by Ruritanian law” and “Accepted unless you object within seven days.” Harbourline did not reply or perform.

Advise Tidewell on its claims against Veldon for S$4 million, Cairn for negligent misstatement, and Harbourline for breach of contract. Assume Singapore jurisdiction over all parties.

ℹ ASSUME
  1. Floating choice of law clauses are valid under Ruritanian conflict of laws rules, not Singapore’s.
  2. Singapore law has no language or licence rule for crane sales.
  3. Under Ruritanian law, delivering, installing or paying for cranes when the seller has no licence is lawful and not an offence, though the sale contract is void.
  4. Under Singapore tort law, Cairn owed and breached a duty of care. Under Ruritanian law, a valuer owes a duty only to its client, Veldon.
  5. Under Ruritanian contract law, commercial silence is acceptance. Under Singapore law, it is not.
✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • L3
    Floating or one-sided choice of law clause. Clause 14 leaves the governing law to Tidewell’s later election, so it is a floating clause. Which law tests its validity is open between the lex fori and the objective proper law.
  • L6
    SCORECARD · Objective proper law: closest and most real connection. The objective proper law is needed on both views: it tests clause 14 under The Iran Vojdan, and it governs if clause 14 fails under Singapore law (Stage 2 is skipped). Both parties perform at Port Ruri, which points strongly to Ruritanian law.
  • K2
    Substance or procedure. The Ruritanian Port Language Act uses the words “no action shall be brought”, raising the Star City divide between substance and procedure.
  • L8
    Formal validity. Language is a formal requirement. A contract is formally valid if it meets the rules of either the proper law or the place of contracting, here Singapore.
  • M2
    The law broken is the proper law itself. If Ruritanian law is the proper law, the missing licence is illegality under the proper law itself, making Foster and the parties’ innocence irrelevant.
  • N1
    Starter: double actionability. Tidewell’s claim against Cairn is in tort, governed by double actionability and the flexible exception.
  • N3
    SCORECARD · Locate the tort: where in substance did it arise?. Cairn prepared the report in Ruritania while Tidewell received and relied on it in Singapore, so locating the tort decides whether Ruritanian law applies under Limb 2.
  • N4
    Limb 2 applied: is there liability under the law of that place?. Apply limb 2: under Ruritanian law a valuer owes a duty only to its client, so if the tort is located in Ruritania there is no liability between Cairn and Tidewell, and the claim fails unless Ruritanian law is displaced.
  • L7
    Was a contract formed at all?. Whether Harbourline is bound by silence is a formation dispute, governed by the putative proper law and subject to the Lew grave-injustice caveat.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • L5
    No clause: implied choice. When an express choice of law clause fails, Singapore skips Stage 2 and goes straight to the objective proper law because inferring a choice is artificial.
  • L4
    Law chosen to dodge another country's rule. Tempting because electing Singapore law lets Tidewell escape the Ruritanian Act. Wrong because a choice fails only if evasion is its sole purpose (Peh Teck Quee): Singapore is Tidewell’s home and the place of signing, and clause 14 was agreed when neither party knew of the Act.
  • M3
    SCORECARD · Foster v Driscoll: intention to break a friendly state's law. Foster requires an intention at formation to break a friendly foreign state’s law. Here neither party knew of the licence rule.
  • M5
    Ralli Bros: performance becomes illegal where it must be done. Tempting because delivery, installation and payment are all due at Port Ruri. Wrong because Ralli needs an act the contract requires to be unlawful there, and under Ruritanian law delivering, installing and paying are lawful without a licence; only the contract is void.
  • N6
    Party autonomy: does the contract's chosen law govern the tort?. Cairn is a third party and not a party to the Sale Agreement, so clause 14 cannot govern the tort claim against Cairn.

Fair to tick but not needed: K1 Characterise the issue, L1 Starter: the proper law and its three stages, M1 Illegality: pick the route, N2 Limb 1: a tort under Singapore law, N5 SCORECARD · The flexible exception

Application questions · base facts

Which law tests a floating clause is open between the lex fori (Shanghai Turbo HC) and the OPL (The Iran Vojdan). Under Singapore law it fails even with an election mechanism (per Prof Chong), and Ruritania is the OPL; under Ruritanian law it stands and Tidewell’s notice selects Singapore law.

  • Lex fori (−): per Prof Chong, under Singapore law [cl X] is invalid even with [an election mechanism], so [the OPL] governs.
  • OPL (+): per Prof Chong, if [the OPL, e.g., law Z] permits floating clauses, [cl X] is valid and [law A] governs once [party] [elects / sues first].

Does the Ruritanian Port Language Act bar Tidewell’s claim in Singapore?

Per Star City, “no action shall be brought” bars only enforcement, not the right, so it is procedural and ignored here. On the functional view (Goh Suan Hee) it would be substantive form, and Singapore law, the law of the place of contracting, has no language rule, so the contract still stands.

If the language rule is treated as substantive, is the Sale Agreement formally valid?

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
⚡ BIG IDEA

Three claims, three tools: the Sale Agreement’s proper law for the S$4 million, double actionability for Cairn’s valuation, and the putative proper law for Harbourline’s silence. The deciding move is to settle the floating clause before the licence. If Singapore law tests clause 14, it is void, Ruritanian law governs as the objective proper law and its licence rule voids the sale whatever the parties knew; if Ruritanian law tests it, Tidewell’s election makes Singapore law govern, and the licence rule falls away: it is not part of the proper law, and Ralli fails as no act of performance is unlawful in Ruritania. The “no action” language rule fails on every route, while Cairn’s tort and Harbourline’s silence are open points, each needing a result under both routes.

  1. 1
    Clause 14 floats: argue both tests L3

    The price claim is contractual, so the Sale Agreement’s proper law governs it. Clause 14 leaves the law to Tidewell’s later election, so no law was fixed at signing; under Singapore law, per Shanghai Turbo, such a clause is “meaningless”, as a contract cannot exist in a legal vacuum (Amin Rasheed). Which law tests its validity is open, so argue both: per C&Y, the Shanghai Turbo High Court on balance used the lex fori, and The Iran Vojdan the objective proper law. Lex fori route: per Prof Chong, Singapore law voids the clause even with an election mechanism, so the court skips implied choice, which would be “artificial”, and applies the objective proper law (Per Shanghai Turbo; The Iran Vojdan). Objective proper law route: per Prof Chong, if that law permits floating clauses, the clause is valid and the elected law governs.

  2. 2
    The objective proper law is Ruritanian law L6

    Per Bonython, the objective proper law is the law with the closest and most real connection, and per Prof Chong the strongest argument is usually where both parties perform. Here delivery, installation and payment are all due at Port Ruri. Signing in Singapore matters little unless performance is also there (Per Pacific Recreation), English as the lingua franca carries little weight, and the Singapore dollar price is offset by payment in Ruritanian dollars, so Ruritanian law is the objective proper law. Lex fori route: Ruritanian law governs the Sale Agreement. Objective proper law route: Ruritanian law upholds floating clauses, so Tidewell’s June notice makes Singapore law govern. Veldon cannot strike out that election as evasion: per Peh Teck Quee evasion must be the sole purpose, and Singapore is Tidewell’s home and the place of signing.

  3. 3
    The language rule: procedure, or else form K2L8

    Per CIFG v Polimet, substance follows the lex causae and procedure the lex fori. Per Star City, a rule that bars only an “action” regulates enforcement, not the existence of the right, so the Port Language Act is procedural, and a Singapore court applies only its own procedure, which has no language rule. Star City remains law because Goh Suan Hee left the point open (Per CIFG v Polimet), so give Veldon the functional view in the alternative: the rule is then substantive form. Per AQCEL, form is satisfied under either the proper law or the law of the place of contracting. The Sale Agreement was signed in Singapore, whose law has no language rule, so it is formally valid even if Ruritanian law is the proper law. The language defence fails on every route.

  4. 4
    The missing licence: proper law illegality M2

    Per Kahler and Zivnostenka, illegality under the proper law bars enforcement, unless that rule itself offends Singapore public policy (The Playa Larga; Re Helbert Wagg), and nothing suggests a licensing rule does. Lex fori route: the Port Equipment Act is part of the proper law, so the Sale Agreement is void and the price claim fails; per the sample final answer scheme, Foster and the parties’ innocence are then irrelevant. Objective proper law route: Singapore law governs and has no licence rule, so proper law illegality does not arise. Foster cannot fill the gap, because it needs an intention at formation to break Ruritanian law, and neither party knew of the Act. Ralli fails too: it needs an act the contract requires to be unlawful where it must be done, and under Ruritanian law delivering, installing and paying are lawful; only the contract is void. So the price claim succeeds only on this route.

  5. 5
    Cairn: double actionability N1N2

    Tidewell sues Cairn in tort, so per Rickshaw the rule is double actionability subject to a flexible exception (Boys v Chaplin; Red Sea). The valuation must be (a) a tort under Singapore law and (b) give civil liability between Tidewell and Cairn under the law of the place of the tort (Per Lord Wilberforce in Boys v Chaplin). Per EFT Holdings, Tidewell proves limb (a), and Cairn must plead and prove that the law of that place gives no liability. Limb (a) is met: per IM Skaugen, had everything happened in Singapore, Cairn would have owed and breached a duty of care, as assumed. Clause 14 cannot govern this claim, because Cairn is not a party to the Sale Agreement.

  6. 6
    Where was Cairn’s tort? Argue both N3

    Per Distillers and Metall, the court asks where in substance the cause of action arose. Singapore: per JIO Minerals (tentatively) and Ong Ghee Soon, a statement directed at the claimant and received and acted on in Singapore is a tort there, and Cairn emailed its report straight to Tidewell, whose board relied on it here. Ruritania: per Vibrant Group, in negligence the place of the careless act prevails despite reliance and loss in Singapore, and Cairn inspected the cranes and wrote the report in Ruritania. Cairn will add that receipt here is fortuitous, being only where Tidewell is based (JIO); Tidewell answers that the report was aimed at it, and per Metall the court need not “turn a blind eye” to damage caused to persons here by acts abroad. A negligent misstatement sits between the two rules, so give limb 2 under each place.

  7. 7
    Limb 2 under each place N4N5

    Singapore route: per Rickshaw a local tort still runs both limbs, both pointing to Singapore law, under which Cairn owed and breached a duty. Cairn may invoke the exception only if Singapore is purely fortuitous, and it is not, as Cairn emailed its report to Tidewell here and Tidewell relied on it here, so Cairn is liable. Ruritania route: Ruritanian law gives a valuer a duty only to its client, Veldon, so there is no liability between Cairn and Tidewell and limb 2 fails (Per Lord Wilberforce in Boys v Chaplin). Tidewell can escape that only through the flexible exception, which per Rickshaw is strictly applied and needs the displaced law to be purely fortuitous. Ruritania is not fortuitous: Cairn is a Ruritanian firm, and it inspected the cranes and wrote its report there for a Ruritanian client. So the claim against Cairn succeeds only if the tort is located in Singapore.

  8. 8
    Harbourline: was a contract formed? L7

    Harbourline never replied, so the issue is whether a contract exists at all: formation, not validity. Per Lew v Nargolwala, formation is for the putative proper law, not the lex fori, which Lew calls “illogical” and gives no role even residually. The draft’s own clause points to Ruritanian law, and per Prof Chong’s double bootstraps that law decides first whether the clause was incorporated and then whether a contract was formed. Under Ruritanian law commercial silence is acceptance, so on both questions Harbourline accepted by not objecting within seven days, and it broke the contract by not performing.

  9. 9
    The grave-injustice caveat: both results L7

    Where the putative law binds a party by silence, Lew left open “a very small caveat, very rarely applicable”, whose effect is no contract under any law, not the lex fori; per C&Y, forum public policy is the better tool. Harbourline’s route: it is a Singapore company, the job is in Singapore, and the only Ruritanian link is a clause in Tidewell’s own draft that it never agreed to, so holding it to Ruritanian silence would be gravely unjust and there is no contract. Tidewell’s route: the caveat very rarely applies, so Harbourline is bound and liable for breach. Harbourline may add Prof Chong’s critique that the lex fori should decide agreement on a putative clause, but Lew gives the lex fori no role.

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes, and what stays

    Clause 14 now fixes both laws at signing: Ruritanian law for delivery and installation, Singapore law for payment and everything else. Nothing is left to a later election, so it is not a floating clause, and the base’s two tests fall away. The language defence still fails: the rule is procedural, and as form Singapore law, the law of the place of contracting, saves the contract. The claims against Cairn and Harbourline do not change.

  2. 2
    Is the split valid? L2L9L6

    Per Peh Teck Quee, applying Vita Food, an express choice is virtually conclusive. Per Libyan Arab Foreign Bank, one law may govern one part of a contract and another law the rest. The split must be internally coherent, and per Kahler it is not inferred readily, as parties expect one law (Enka), but this one is express. Each obligation has one law, so the split is coherent on its face. Veldon may argue that a split leaving supply void but payment due is incoherent; if so, the clause fails, the objective proper law, Ruritanian law, governs as in the base, and the licence rule voids the contract.

  3. 3
    Which law carries the licence rule? L9M2

    Which part of a split contract carries its validity is not settled, so argue both. Veldon’s route: the licence rule attaches to supply and installation, governed by Ruritanian law, under which the Act voids the contract (Route A), so no price is payable. Tidewell’s route: its claim is for payment, governed by Singapore law, which has no licence rule, and Ralli fails because no act of performance is unlawful in Ruritania, so the S$4 million is payable. Neither route turns on intention. Foster stays out because neither party knew of the Act, so neither intended to break it, and for the same reason the split cannot have been made to evade it.
