4Remember

🧠 FOR THE EXAM
  • A floating clause: argue both tests; under Singapore law it is void even with an election mechanism, while an objective proper law that permits it lets the elected law govern.
  • Find the proper law before illegality: where the law broken is the proper law itself, the contract fails whatever the parties knew, and Foster is irrelevant.
  • Ralli needs an act the contract requires to be unlawful where it must be done; a foreign law that voids the contract but leaves delivery and payment lawful does not engage it.
  • “No action shall be brought” is procedural under Star City; read as form, the contract still stands if either the proper law or the law of the place of contracting is met (AQCEL).
  • A careless valuation sent abroad: receipt and reliance (JIO Minerals; Ong Ghee Soon) against the place of the careless act (Vibrant Group); give limb 2’s result under each place.
  • Silence as acceptance: the putative proper law decides (Lew v Nargolwala), the lex fori has no role, and the grave-injustice caveat, if it applies, leaves no contract under any law.

LAW302 · META GAME · ★ DO FIRST · QUESTION 2 · HYPO q2-06 · GEMINI PROMPT V1 · 15 QUESTIONS

Yarrow v Dr Orrin

Written by Claude for the drill and law reviewed. Gemini (prompt v1) rebalanced the option lengths and wrote a note on each question; both were checked (8 corrections) and feed the notes here.

Answers:

1Base facts

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Yarrow v Dr Orrin

Yarrow Biotech Pte Ltd, a Singapore incorporated company, engaged Dr Orrin, a scientist who lives in Utopia, to lead a research project at its laboratory in Singapore. The terms were agreed orally at a meeting in Utopia. Nothing was signed. It is common ground that the parties agreed that Utopian law would govern the engagement. Dr Orrin had asked for Utopian law because it was the law he knew. He was paid in Singapore dollars into a Singapore bank account.

In 2024 Dr Orrin copied the project data at the laboratory in Singapore and sold it to a rival of Yarrow for US$2 million. The sale was a crime under Utopian law. Dr Orrin says that Yarrow's research head, who has since died, told him that he was free to sell the data. No document records this.

Yarrow sues Dr Orrin in the General Division. It claims (a) damages of US$900,000 for breach of contract, and (b) an account of his US$2 million profit for breach of an equitable duty of confidence. Yarrow says that claim (b) is governed by Singapore law, because equity acts on the conscience of any defendant who is before the court. Assume that the court has jurisdiction.

Advise Yarrow on the law that governs each issue, and on what it is likely to recover.

ℹ ASSUME
  1. A Utopian statute provides: “No action shall be brought on a contract for research services unless the contract is in writing.” Singapore law has no such rule.
  2. Under Utopian law, a consultant who discloses project data must prove that he was authorised. Under Singapore law, the client must prove that he was not.
  3. Under Utopian law, damages against an individual consultant are capped at US$100,000. Where the breach was deliberate, the court must then double the capped sum.
  4. Utopian law has no remedy that strips a wrongdoer of his profit. It awards compensation for loss only.
  5. Both sides have filed expert reports on Utopian law.
✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • K1
    Characterise the issue. Claim (b) is framed in equity, and Yarrow uses the label to reach Singapore law. Characterise first: look past the label to the legal foundation of the duty.
  • L2
    Express choice of law clause. The lex causae must be fixed before anything is called substance. The parties expressly chose Utopian law for the engagement, and that is virtually conclusive.
  • K2
    Substance or procedure. Two Utopian rules may be procedure and so not applied here: a statute worded “no action shall be brought”, and a rule on who bears the burden of proof.
  • L8
    Formal validity. An oral contract and a writing rule. If the writing rule is substance, it is a rule of form, and form has two validating laws: the proper law and the law of the place of contracting.
  • K3
    Damages: head or quantum. A cap and a doubling rule under the lex causae. Head of loss or quantum? The traditional split and the Goh Suan Hee dicta give different figures.
  • K4
    A remedy the other law does not know. Yarrow wants an account of profits. Utopian law has no such remedy. Is a remedy procedure for Singapore law, or a function of the law that governs the relationship?

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • N1
    Starter: double actionability. Copying done in Singapore tempts you into double actionability. No tort is pleaded. Yarrow sues in contract and on an equitable duty founded on the engagement, so the place of the copying does not choose the law.
  • L6
    SCORECARD · Objective proper law: closest and most real connection. Currency and place of payment are objective proper law factors. The parties made an express choice, so the third stage is never reached.
  • M1
    Illegality: pick the route. A crime under a foreign law looks like illegality. The illegality rules stop a party enforcing a contract. No one is enforcing the sale to the rival, and the engagement itself is lawful.
  • L4
    Law chosen to dodge another country's rule. Utopian law has a cap that suits Dr Orrin, so the choice may look like a dodge. A choice fails only if evasion was its sole purpose. He chose the law of his own home because he knew it.
  • K6
    Foreign law not pleaded, or not proved. K6 is for foreign law that is not pleaded or not proved. Here Utopian law is pleaded and both sides have proved it by experts.

Fair to tick but not needed: L1 Starter: the proper law and its three stages, K8 Forum public policy; renvoi

Application questions · base facts

⚡ Base facts · 1 of 6K1
Yarrow says claim (b) is governed by Singapore law because it is equitable. Is that right?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Rickshaw, which rejected the Australian lex fori approach, an equitable claim follows its legal foundation, found from its nature and origins. A duty of confidence that arises from a contract is contractual for this purpose (Rappo; Perry). Rickshaw left open a separate equitable category for novel claims, but this is not one. The label a claimant chooses does not steer the governing law.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Macmillan, the court first characterises the issue, and per Murakami Takako and JIO Minerals it looks beyond the formulation of the claim to the true issue, so Yarrow's equitable label cannot steer the governing law. Per Rickshaw, rejecting the Australian lex fori approach, an equitable claim is characterised by its legal foundation, found from its nature and origins; Rickshaw applied the German law of the employment contract to the equitable claims there. Per Rappo and Perry, fiduciary and trust claims founded on an agreement are contractual. Dr Orrin's duty of confidence springs from his engagement, so claim (b) follows the engagement's chosen law, Utopian law. Rickshaw left open a separate equitable category for novel claims, but a duty that arises from the engagement is not novel.

⚡ Base facts · 2 of 6K2
Dr Orrin relies on the Utopian statute: “No action shall be brought ... unless the contract is in writing.” Does it bar claim (a) in Singapore?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Star City, a rule on the existence of a right is substantive, and a rule that only regulates proceedings to enforce it is procedural. “No action shall be brought” bars enforcement only. Prof Chong's scheme treats a provision in these words as procedural, with Goh Suan Hee as the counter. Star City remains the law (CIFG v Polimet), so apply it first and run the functional view in the alternative. Section 6 covers guarantees and land, not research contracts.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per CIFG v Polimet, substance follows the lex causae and procedure the lex fori. Per Star City, judged by its effect and purpose, a rule on the existence of a right is substantive, and one that only regulates proceedings to enforce it is procedural. “No action shall be brought” leaves the right in place and bars only the action, so it is procedural; the sample final scheme reads a provision in these words the same way, with Goh Suan Hee as the counter. Per CIFG v Polimet, Star City remains law because Goh Suan Hee left the point open, so apply Star City first. In the alternative, Dr Orrin argues the functional view: procedure covers only the mode or conduct of court proceedings (Goh Suan Hee), so the writing rule is substantive and becomes a rule of form.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C1.2.2 :: Scenario B: Procedural (−)

⚡ Base facts · 3 of 6L8
Suppose the court takes the functional view and treats the Utopian writing rule as substance. What then?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per AQCEL, meeting the formal requirements of either the proper law or the lex loci contractus is enough. The terms were agreed at a meeting in Utopia, so both laws are Utopian and nothing saves the oral contract. Had the meeting been in Singapore, Singapore law would have saved it, which is how the sample final scheme deals with form. So the result on claim (a) depends on the substance or procedure point.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per the Giuliano-Lagarde Report, form is every external manifestation required of a person expressing the will to be bound, so a writing requirement is form. Per AQCEL (adopting the obiter in PT Jaya Putra), meeting the form rules of either the proper law or the lex loci contractus is enough. Per Transniko, the place of contracting is where acceptance is received, and the terms were agreed at a meeting in Utopia. So both validating laws are Utopian, both require writing, and the oral contract is formally invalid on this route. Had the meeting been in Singapore, Singapore law would have saved it, which is how the sample final scheme deals with form.

⚡ Base facts · 4 of 6K2
Whether Dr Orrin was authorised to sell is disputed, and the only other witness is dead. Who bears the burden of proof?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

What must be proved is substance. How it is proved is procedure. Per Re Fuld's Estate (No 3), the burden of proof is generally procedural, so Singapore's allocation applies whatever the lex causae says. Applying a foreign presumption because foreign law governs the claim is a common error. Yarrow's counter is Re Cohn: a presumption that goes to the existence of the right is substantive.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per C&Y, what must be proved is substance and how it is proved is procedure. Per Re Fuld's Estate (No 3), the burden of proof is generally procedural, so Singapore's allocation applies whatever the lex causae says, and Yarrow must prove that Dr Orrin was not authorised. Applying the Utopian allocation because Utopian law governs the claim is a common error. Yarrow's counter is Re Cohn: a rule that goes to the existence of the right is substantive. If the Utopian rule were substantive but Singapore's stayed procedural, both would apply and clash (cumulation), so Yarrow would also argue, as in Re Cohn, that Singapore's rule is substantive too, leaving only the Utopian rule.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C1.6.1 :: Burden of Proof

Per Re Fuld's Estate (No 3), generally procedural, so [Singapore's allocation] applies despite [lex causae].

⚡ Base facts · 5 of 6K3
Yarrow's loss is US$900,000. What do the Utopian cap and doubling rule do to claim (a)?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Boys v Chaplin and Harding v Wealands, heads of loss are substantive and quantum is procedural, and a cap goes to quantum. The Court of Appeal in Goh Suan Hee called the split wholly artificial, but obiter, and left it open. If quantum is substantive, the foreign rules of law on assessment, such as a statutory cap, apply. The doubling rule is a multiplier on the amount, so on the traditional view it is quantum too and Singapore ignores it. A sum that punishes a deliberate breach also has a penal flavour. Give both routes and a figure under each.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Boys v Chaplin and Harding v Wealands, heads of loss are substantive and quantum is procedural. A cap limits the amount and the doubling multiplies it, so both go to quantum, and on this view Singapore assesses damages at Yarrow's loss of US$900,000. Per Goh Suan Hee (obiter), the split is “wholly artificial”; if quantum is substantive, the lex causae's rules of law on assessment, such as a statutory cap, apply, while pure questions of fact stay with the forum. If Dr Orrin is liable, he copied and sold the data on purpose, so the breach was deliberate and the figure is US$100,000 doubled to US$200,000. The Court of Appeal left the point open, so give both figures.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C1.4 :: Critique

Per Goh Suan Hee (obiter), the split is "wholly artificial", so if quantum is substantive [claimant] recovers [the amount under lex causae] (cf The "Reecon Wolf").

  • Reasons: it encourages forum shopping for [a higher award], making outcomes a matter of chance, and he who travels to [country X] accepts its law, including quantum.
  • Support: [claimant / defendant] cites Art 15(c) Rome II and Pfeiffer v Rogerson (HCA), which apply [the lex loci delicti] to quantum.
  • C&Y: [the foreign legislature] links liability to quantum, e.g., [a cap tied to insurance costs], so severing them distorts [lex causae], and quantifying [a head unknown here] is hard.
  • Status: left open, the CA cautioning [claimants] against suing here for a larger award; in Goh Suan Hee [the damages gap] was a neutral FNC factor (J4).
⚡ Base facts · 6 of 6K4
Can Yarrow have an account of the US$2 million profit under claim (b)?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Traditional view: the court grants only its own remedies (Phrantzes v Argenti; Shanghai Electric), so the account is available. Modern view: it is untenable to separate remedy from rights (Goh Suan Hee). In Rappo a constructive trust was unavailable even in Singapore because Swiss law governed: remedies are a function of the law that governs the relationship. The textbook's synthesis: the lex causae decides entitlement, and the court grants only remedies known to the lex fori. On that view Yarrow gets compensation only.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Traditional view: per Phrantzes v Argenti and Shanghai Electric, the court grants only its own remedies, and Singapore law knows an account of profits, so it is available. Modern view: per Goh Suan Hee it is “untenable in principle to separate remedy from rights”, so the lex causae decides whether, and what kind of, remedy lies. Per Rappo, a constructive trust was unavailable even in Singapore because Swiss law governed, remedies being “a function of the law that governs the relevant relationship”, and per Perry a trust claim failed as Swiss law does not recognise trusts. C&Y's synthesis: the lex causae decides entitlement, and the court grants only remedies known to the lex fori. Utopian law governs claim (b) and awards compensation for loss only, so on the modern view and the synthesis Yarrow gets compensation, not the US$2 million profit.

  • FNC link: per Rappo, [the remedy's absence in country X] is then no substantial injustice at [Spiliada stage 2] (J4).
📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
⚡ BIG IDEA

This is the Week 1 toolkit in one hypo: characterise, fix the lex causae, then ask of each Utopian rule whether it is substance or procedure, because Singapore applies only the substantive ones. Claim (b) follows its foundation, the engagement, so Utopian law governs both claims and the equity label cannot pull it to Singapore. The deciding moves are that “no action shall be brought” is probably procedure (with form as the alternative), the burden of proof is generally procedure, and the cap and the account of profits are open, so give a figure or a result under each route. The twists test time under the FLPA, pleading and proof of foreign law, and framing a claim in tort.

  1. 1
    Characterise claim (b): look past the label K1

    Per Macmillan the court first characterises the issue, and per Murakami Takako and JIO Minerals it looks beyond the formulation of the claim to the true issue. Yarrow says equity acts on the conscience of any defendant here, but Rickshaw rejected that Australian lex fori approach: an equitable claim follows its legal foundation, found from its nature and origins. Dr Orrin's duty of confidence springs from his engagement, so claim (b) is contractual for choice of law (Rickshaw; Rappo) and follows the engagement's proper law, like claim (a). Rickshaw left open a separate equitable category for novel claims, but a duty that springs from the engagement is not novel. No tort is pleaded, so the place of the copying does not choose the law.

  2. 2
    The proper law: Utopian law by express choice L2

    Per Peh Teck Quee, applying Vita Food, an express choice is virtually conclusive unless it is not bona fide, not legal or against public policy. It is common ground that the parties agreed on Utopian law for the engagement. Dr Orrin asked for it because it was the law he knew, so evasion was not its sole purpose and the choice is bona fide. With an express choice the objective factors, such as payment in Singapore dollars, are never reached. So Utopian law is the lex causae of both claims, and both sides have proved it by experts.

  3. 3
    The writing statute: procedure on its wording K2

    Per CIFG v Polimet, substance follows the lex causae and procedure the lex fori. Per Star City, a rule on the existence of a right is substantive, and a rule that only regulates proceedings to enforce it is procedural. “No action shall be brought” leaves the contract in place and bars only the action, so it is procedural and Singapore, which has no writing rule, does not apply it; the sample final scheme reads these words the same way. Star City remains law because Goh Suan Hee left the point open (CIFG v Polimet), so this is the main route, and Dr Orrin runs the functional view in the alternative.

  4. 4
    Alternative: the writing rule as form L8

    On the functional view, procedure covers only the mode or conduct of court proceedings (Goh Suan Hee), so the writing rule is substantive and is a rule of form. Per AQCEL, a contract is formally valid if it meets the form rules of either the proper law or the law of the place of contracting. The terms were agreed at a meeting in Utopia, so both laws are Utopian and nothing saves the oral contract. Result on this route: claim (a) fails. Had the meeting been in Singapore, Singapore law would have saved it, as in the sample final scheme.

  5. 5
    Burden of proof: generally procedure K2

    Whether Dr Orrin was authorised is the key disputed fact, and with the research head dead, whoever bears the burden may well lose. Per C&Y, what must be proved is substance and how it is proved is procedure. Per Re Fuld's Estate (No 3), the burden of proof is generally procedural, so Singapore's allocation applies and Yarrow must prove that Dr Orrin was not authorised. Yarrow's counter is Re Cohn: a rule that goes to the existence of the right is substantive, which would put the burden on Dr Orrin. If Singapore's rule stayed procedural, both rules would apply and clash (cumulation), so Yarrow must also argue, as in Re Cohn, that Singapore's rule is substantive, leaving only the Utopian rule. Result: probably Yarrow bears the burden.

  6. 6
    The cap and the doubling: quantum (open) K3

    Per Boys v Chaplin and Harding v Wealands, heads of loss are substantive and quantum is procedural, and a cap and a multiplier both go to quantum. Route 1 (traditional): Singapore ignores both, so Yarrow recovers its loss of US$900,000. Route 2: per Goh Suan Hee (obiter) the split is “wholly artificial”, and if quantum is substantive, Utopia's rules of law on assessment apply, so US$100,000, doubled for a deliberate breach to US$200,000. The Court of Appeal left the point open, so give both figures.

  7. 7
    Account of profits: remedy (open) K4

    Route 1 (traditional): per Phrantzes v Argenti and Shanghai Electric, the court grants only its own remedies, and Singapore law knows an account of profits, so Yarrow can have an account of the US$2 million. Route 2 (modern): per Goh Suan Hee it is untenable to separate remedy from rights, and per Rappo remedies are a function of the law that governs the relationship, so Utopian law decides and gives compensation for loss only. C&Y's synthesis agrees that the lex causae decides entitlement. So the account is doubtful, and Yarrow should expect compensation only.

  8. 8
    Result

    Utopian law governs both claims. Claim (a) probably survives the writing statute (it fails on the functional view), Yarrow probably bears the burden of proving that the sale was unauthorised, and if it succeeds it recovers US$900,000 on the traditional split or US$200,000 on the Goh Suan Hee dicta. On claim (b) an account of the US$2 million is doubtful, and on the modern view Yarrow gets compensation only. The Utopian crime raises no illegality point, as no one sues on the sale and the engagement itself is lawful.

  2. Under Singapore law the period is six years. Utopian law has no rule that stops time while a defendant promises to pay.

Application questions · twist 1

⚡ Twist 1 · 1 of 3K5
Which limitation period applies to claim (a)?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per s 3(1) FLPA, only the limitation law of the lex causae applies, not Singapore's. Per s 6(2), its procedural or substantive label is irrelevant. The old common law split between barring the remedy and extinguishing the right is gone. Only the domestic Utopian period applies. The claim was issued almost 22 months after 10 January 2025.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per s 3(1) FLPA, only the limitation law of the lex causae applies, not Singapore's, and per s 6(2) its procedural or substantive label is irrelevant, so the common law split between barring the remedy and extinguishing the right (BBA v BAZ) no longer matters. Renvoi is excluded (ss 3(5), 6(2)), so only the domestic Utopian period applies. Utopian law has no rule that stops time while a defendant promises to pay, so the year ran from 10 January 2025 and ended in January 2026. Yarrow issued on 2 November 2026, almost 22 months after it learned of the sale, so claim (a) is barred unless s 4(2) undue hardship saves it.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C1.5.2 :: s 3(1) + s 6(2)

Per s 3(1) FLPA, only [lex causae]'s limitation law applies, not Singapore's, and per s 6(2) its [procedural / substantive] label is irrelevant, so [the claim] [is / is not] barred.

  • Renvoi: excluded (ss 3(5), 6(2)), so only [lex causae]'s domestic period applies, not [its COL rules].
⚡ Twist 1 · 2 of 3K5
Does the equitable claim (b) escape the Utopian time bar?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

The FLPA applies equally to equitable claims. Unlike the English Act, it has no laches carve out, which is consistent with characterising an equitable claim by its foundation. So the time bar of the lex causae applies to claim (b).

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Rickshaw, claim (b) follows its foundation, the engagement, so Utopian law is its lex causae. The FLPA applies equally to equitable claims, and unlike s 4(3) of the UK FLPA 1984 it has no laches carve-out, which fits characterising an equitable claim by its foundation. So the Utopian year bars claim (b) as it bars claim (a), unless s 4(2) undue hardship applies. C&Y's backstop runs the other way: where delay is unacceptably long though within the foreign period, the foreign statute may be disapplied on public policy, which does not arise here.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C1.5.5 :: No Laches Carve-Out

Unlike s 4(3) UK FLPA 1984, the FLPA has no laches carve-out, consistent with COL for equity (Rickshaw), so [lex causae]'s time bar applies to [the equitable claim].

  • Backstop: per C&Y, if [claimant]'s delay is unacceptably long though within [the foreign period], [the foreign statute] may be disapplied on Singapore public policy.
⚡ Twist 1 · 3 of 3K5
Yarrow pleads undue hardship under s 4(2). How strong is the plea?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Recovery Vehicle 1, undue hardship is greater hardship than the circumstances warrant, and it can exist even for a claimant at fault where the consequences are out of proportion to the fault. The court looks at the objective reasonableness of the foreign bar (being shorter is not enough), the complexity of the claim and the claimant's justification for letting time run. The hardship must flow from the foreign period itself and must not be self-induced. Dr Orrin will say Yarrow knew everything in January 2025 and chose to wait.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per s 4(2) FLPA, a foreign period is contrary to public policy if it causes a party undue hardship. Per Recovery Vehicle 1 (adopting The Pegasus), that is greater hardship than the circumstances warrant, and it can exist even for a claimant at fault where the consequences are disproportionate to its fault. The factors are the objective reasonableness of the foreign bar (being shorter than Singapore's is not enough), the complexity of the claim and the claimant's justification for letting time run. For Yarrow: Dr Orrin wrote every few months promising to pay “as soon as my funds are released”, which explains the wait. Against: the hardship must flow from the Utopian period itself and must not be self-induced, and Yarrow knew everything in January 2025, so complexity does not explain the delay. If the plea succeeds, the Utopian year is set aside and both claims go on; if it fails, both claims are barred.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C1.5.4 :: Undue Hardship

Per s 4(2) FLPA, [the foreign period] is contrary to public policy if it causes [a party / potential party] undue hardship. Per Recovery Vehicle 1 (adopting The Pegasus), that is "greater hardship than the circumstances warrant", even for [a claimant at fault] where the consequences are disproportionate to its fault.

  • Factors: per Recovery Vehicle 1, the objective reasonableness of [the foreign bar] (being shorter than Singapore's is not enough), the complexity of [the claim], and [claimant]'s justification for letting time run.

    The FLPA: only the Utopian year, whatever its label K5

    Per s 3(1) FLPA, only the limitation law of the lex causae applies, not Singapore's, and per s 6(2) its procedural or substantive label is irrelevant, so “may not be heard” does not call for a Star City analysis. Renvoi is excluded, so the domestic Utopian year applies. The FLPA applies equally to equitable claims and, unlike s 4(3) of the UK FLPA 1984, has no laches carve-out, so claim (b) is caught too.     Undue hardship under s 4(2) (arguable) K5

Application questions · twist 2

⚡ Twist 2 · 1 of 3K6
Dr Orrin pleads the Utopian cap but leads no evidence of Utopian law. What happens to the cap?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

A party relying on foreign law must plead and prove it, and there is no judicial notice. Once it is pleaded the court must apply it, so a party who fails to prove its case under it may simply lose that point (Brownlie; EFT Holdings). The presumption would only make Utopian law the same as Singapore law, which has no cap. A party cannot improve its position by pleading foreign law and then resting on the presumption.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Brownlie and The “Chem Orchid”, a party relying on foreign law must plead and prove it, and there is no judicial notice, so Dr Orrin's request that the court “take notice” of a Utopian cap fails. Per Pacific Recreation, proof is by official statute books and law reports or by expert opinion, and he led neither. Per Brownlie, once foreign law is pleaded the court must apply it, so a party who fails to prove its case under it may simply lose (EFT Holdings), unless the foreign law is presumed similar to Singapore law (The “Chem Orchid”). Both routes end the same way: Dr Orrin loses the cap, or Utopian law is presumed to match Singapore law, which has no cap. A party cannot improve its position by pleading foreign law and resting on the presumption (Tamil Nadu).

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C1.6.3 :: Pleaded but Unproved

Per Brownlie, once [law X] is pleaded the court must apply it, so [party] failing to prove its case under it may simply lose (EFT Holdings), unless [law X] is presumed similar to Singapore law (The "Chem Orchid").

⚡ Twist 2 · 2 of 3K6
Neither side pleads Utopian law on the burden of proof or on remedies. Which law applies to those points?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Brownlie, if neither party pleads foreign law, Singapore law applies in its own right, not by presumption. Per EFT Holdings, no conflicts issue arises. Pleading foreign law is voluntary, so each side pleads it only where it helps. Keep the two cases apart: not pleaded (the default rule) and pleaded but not proved (lose, or the presumption).

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Goh Chok Tong v Tang Liang Hong, pleading foreign law is not obligatory, so each side pleads it only where it helps. Per Brownlie, if neither party pleads it, Singapore law applies in its own right (adversarial procedure, arguably tacit agreement), not by presumption, and per EFT Holdings no conflicts issue arises. Keep the two cases apart: not pleaded (the default rule) and pleaded but not proved (lose the point, or the presumption). On the burden of proof Yarrow bears it as in the base, and as it has not pleaded the Utopian rule it gives up its Re Cohn counter. On remedies the result changes: in the base the modern view would let Utopian law refuse an account, but with Utopian law unpleaded on remedies Singapore law applies, and it grants one.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C1.6.3 :: Not Pleaded: Default Rule

Per Brownlie, if neither party pleads [law X], Singapore law applies in its own right (adversarial procedure, arguably tacit agreement), not by presumption. Per EFT Holdings, no conflicts issue arises, so [the claim] is decided under [Singapore law].

⚡ Twist 2 · 3 of 3K6
Suppose Dr Orrin had instead pleaded, without proof, that Utopian law gives no account of profits, and Yarrow asked the court to presume that Utopian law is the same as Singapore law. Would the court presume it?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Brownlie, the presumption is a rule of evidence that is applied only where it is fair and reasonable to expect the foreign law to be materially similar. It suits a common law system and great and broad principles. The textbook says it is not apt for a civil law system where no universal principle is in play. Here Dr Orrin bears the burden and has proved nothing, so he may simply lose the point in any case.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Brownlie, the presumption of similarity is a rule of evidence about the content of foreign law, applied only where it is fair and reasonable to expect the foreign law to be materially similar. It suits a common law system, “great and broad” principles and interlocutory stages more than a trial, and it is less apt for a statutory rule. Per C&Y it does not suit a civil law system lacking universal principles, so if Utopia is a civil law system, as Dr Orrin says, the presumption is doubtful for a specific rule on profit-stripping. For Yarrow, the limit on intrusive relief does not bite: per C&Y, for damages or an account the presumption presumably applies. Either way, Dr Orrin bears the burden on the Utopian law he pleaded and proved nothing, so he may simply lose the point (EFT Holdings).

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C1.6.3 :: Nature of the Presumption

Per Brownlie, a rule of evidence on content, applied only where fair and reasonable to expect [law X] to be materially similar. Per D'Oz, a "rule of convenience", refused where holding [defendant] liable under [unproved law X] is unjust.

    What changes

    The characterisation of the claims and the choice of Utopian law stay. What changes is proof: no expert reports are filed, Dr Orrin pleads only the Utopian cap and leads no evidence, and he asks the court to “take notice” that Utopia is a civil law country with a cap. Neither side pleads Utopian law on the burden of proof or on remedies. So ask, rule by rule, whether Utopian law was pleaded at all, and if so whether it was proved.

  2. 2
    The cap: pleaded but not proved K6

    Per Brownlie and The “Chem Orchid”, a party relying on foreign law must plead and prove it, and there is no judicial notice, so “take notice” fails. Per Brownlie, once it is pleaded the court must apply it, so Dr Orrin, who proved nothing, may simply lose the point (EFT Holdings). If Utopian law is instead presumed similar, it matches Singapore law, which has no cap, and a party cannot improve its position by pleading foreign law and resting on the presumption (Tamil Nadu). Either way there is no cap, so the head or quantum question never arises.

  3. 3
    The unpleaded points: Singapore law in its own right K6

    Per Brownlie, where neither party pleads foreign law, Singapore law applies in its own right, not by presumption, and per EFT Holdings no conflicts issue arises. So Yarrow bears the burden of proof under Singapore's rule, and an account of profits is available under Singapore law. Dr Orrin's defence pleads only the cap, so the Utopian writing statute is not pleaded either, and on the same rule it does not bar claim (a).

  4. 4
    If he had pleaded “no account” without proof K6

    Per Brownlie, the presumption of similarity applies only where it is fair and reasonable to expect Utopian law to be materially similar. It suits a common law system and great and broad principles, and per C&Y not a civil law system without universal principles, which is what Dr Orrin says Utopia is. So the court may presume it, but that is less likely here. If it does, Utopian law is taken to match Singapore law, which grants an account. If it does not, Dr Orrin bears the burden on the Utopian rule he pleaded and proved nothing, so he may simply lose the point (EFT Holdings). Either way the account is likely to stay available.

  2. Under Utopian law the taking is also a civil wrong, but the cap on damages against a consultant applies to it.

Application questions · twist 3

⚡ Twist 3 · 1 of 2N1
Can Yarrow add a tort claim in order to get away from Utopian law?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Rickshaw, absent bad faith a claimant may frame its claim in the most advantageous way, and a tort claim is characterised as tort despite the contract and its chosen law. Choosing the better cause of action is not bad faith. The equitable claim is different: it follows its foundation, the contract. Rickshaw itself treated conversion as tort and the equitable claims as contractual.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Rickshaw, absent bad faith a claimant may frame its claim in the way most advantageous to it, tort liability being concurrent with contract (Henderson v Merrett), so a tort claim is characterised as tort despite the contract and its chosen law. Choosing the better cause of action is not bad faith. The limit is equity: per Rickshaw an equitable claim rooted in the contract is usually characterised as contractual, and per Macmillan the court looks to the true issues. Rickshaw itself treated conversion as a tort and the equitable claims as contractual, so claim (c) is a tort while claim (b) stays with Utopian law.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C3.1.1 :: Framing / Concurrent Liability

Per Rickshaw, absent bad faith [claimant] may frame in tort despite [the law Y clause], the claim being characterised as tort though it arises from [the contract].

  • Contrast: [equitable claims] rooted in [the contract] follow contract COL (C1.1.5), and [a "parasitic" tort] may follow [the contract's law] (C3.6.5).
⚡ Twist 3 · 2 of 2N6
Dr Orrin says the agreed choice of Utopian law governs claim (c) as well, so that the cap applies. Is that right?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Rickshaw, whether a choice covers non-contractual claims is a matter of construction under its proper law, and the clause there was conceded to be non-exclusive. Whether a wide clause then governs the tort is open (Ong Ghee Soon). The route is the flexible exception, which is strictly applied: the laboratory, the taking and the claimant are all in Singapore. Rickshaw declined to apply the contract's law on similar facts, though it has been criticised for that.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Rickshaw, whether a choice of law covers non-contractual claims is construction under its proper law, here Utopian law, and the clause in Rickshaw was conceded to be non-exclusive. Even if the agreed choice is wide enough, whether it can govern a tort is an open question (Ong Ghee Soon), though per C&Y “just a small step away”. The route is the flexible exception: the chosen law applies as the law of the relationship at the centre of the dispute (C&Y, citing Chen v BHNV as an analogy only). Dr Orrin's best factor is the agreed choice, and Briggs criticises Rickshaw for keeping Singapore law where the torts arose from a contract. But per Rickshaw the exception is strictly applied and needs the displaced law to be purely fortuitous; the laboratory, the taking and Yarrow are all in Singapore, as on similar facts in Rickshaw, so Singapore law probably governs claim (c) and the cap does not apply. If Dr Orrin's route did succeed, Utopian law would govern claim (c), and its cap would apply only if quantum is substantive (the Goh Suan Hee dicta), as in the base.

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes

    Claims (a) and (b) stay under Utopian law. Yarrow adds claim (c), conversion of its hard drive, which Dr Orrin carried out of the laboratory; it is about a physical drive, so no intellectual property point arises. Dr Orrin says Yarrow is dressing up its contract claim, and that the agreed choice of Utopian law governs “everything between us”, which would bring in the cap.

  2. 2
    Framing: claim (c) is a tort N1

    Per Rickshaw, absent bad faith a claimant may frame its claim in the way that suits it best, tort liability being concurrent with contract (Henderson v Merrett), so claim (c) is characterised as tort despite the engagement and its chosen law. Choosing the better cause of action is not bad faith, and evasion (Peh Teck Quee) is the wrong test, as it is about choosing a law, not framing a claim. Claim (b) cannot move the same way: an equitable claim rooted in the engagement follows the engagement's law, as in Rickshaw itself.

  3. 3
    A local tort: both limbs are Singapore law N1N9

    Per Rickshaw, the rule is double actionability subject to a flexible exception: the wrong must be a tort under Singapore law and give civil liability between the parties under the law of the place of the tort (Boys v Chaplin). Rickshaw runs both limbs for a tort committed in Singapore too, rejecting Metall's English-law-only rule, and both limbs then point to Singapore law. Every act of taking was done here, and Dr Orrin is liable for conversion under Singapore law, so both limbs are met. Utopian law, and with it the cap, can come in only through the exception.

  4. 4
    Party autonomy through the exception (open) N6

    Whether the agreed choice reaches claims outside the contract is construction under its proper law (Rickshaw), and even then whether a contract's chosen law can govern a tort is open (Ong Ghee Soon). Dr Orrin's route: the tort arose from the engagement, so its agreed law should displace both limbs through the flexible exception (C&Y; Briggs' critique of Rickshaw), and Utopian law would then govern claim (c). Yarrow's route: per Rickshaw the exception is strictly applied and needs Singapore to be purely fortuitous, and the laboratory, the taking and Yarrow are all here, as on similar facts in Rickshaw. Result: Singapore law probably governs claim (c) and the cap does not apply; even on Dr Orrin's route, the cap would apply only if quantum is substantive, the same open point as in the base.

5Scorecards: weigh the factors

Prof Chong rewards applying facts to factor tests. Sort each fact, then answer the verdict question. These use the base facts unless a line says “Suppose”.

K2 Sort the factors: Substance or procedure: which rules does the Singapore court apply?

Each line is a rule that a party wants applied in Yarrow's action. Utopian law is the lex causae. Is the rule substance (the lex causae applies), procedure (Singapore law applies), or an open point where you must give both routes? Lines marked “Suppose” are extra facts for this card only.

Utopian statute: “No action shall be brought on a contract for research services unless the contract is in writing.”
Procedure: Singapore law. The words bar only enforcement of the right, so under Star City the rule is procedural and a Singapore court does not apply it. Prof Chong's scheme treats these words the same way. Run the functional view in the alternative. C1.2.2 :: Scenario B: Procedural
Suppose: the Utopian statute said “A contract for research services is void unless it is in writing.”
Substance: the lex causae. This negates the right itself, so it is substantive and the lex causae applies. It is then a rule of form, with two validating laws. C1.2.2 :: Scenario A: Substantive
Utopian law: the consultant must prove that he was authorised to disclose the data.
Procedure: Singapore law. The burden of proof is generally procedural, so Singapore's allocation applies whatever the lex causae says. C1.6.1 :: Burden of Proof
Utopian law: damages against an individual consultant may not exceed US$100,000.
Open. A cap is quantum, which is procedural on the traditional split. But the Goh Suan Hee dicta call the split wholly artificial and the point was left open. State both, with a figure under each. C1.4 :: Critique
Suppose: Utopian law does not allow damages for lost profits against a consultant at all.
Substance: the lex causae. Whether a head of loss exists is substantive on every view, so the head must exist under the lex causae. C1.4 :: Traditional Split
Suppose: under Utopian law a loss is too remote unless the consultant actually foresaw it.
Substance: the lex causae. Remoteness is substantive although it affects the amount (D'Almeida Araujo v Becker). C1.4 :: Remoteness and Mitigation
Suppose: Utopian law would not admit Dr Orrin's oral evidence of what the research head told him.
Procedure: Singapore law. What must be proved is substance, but how it is proved is procedure. The admissibility of evidence is for the lex fori. C1.6.1 :: What / How Divide
Suppose: Yarrow also sues on an oral guarantee governed by Utopian law. Section 6 of the Civil Law Act bars any “action” on a guarantee without signed writing.
Procedure: Singapore law. The same words as the Utopian statute, so the same answer. On its wording s 6 is procedural and binds a foreign law contract sued on here (Leroux v Brown), so the guarantee claim is barred. Run the functional view in the alternative: s 6 would then be a rule of form for the proper law or the place of contracting, and the claim could survive. C1.6.1 :: Writing Requirements
Utopian law: a claim against a consultant must be brought within one year, and a late claim “may not be heard”.
Substance: the lex causae. The trap. The wording looks procedural, but for limitation the label is irrelevant: by statute the limitation law of the lex causae applies in place of Singapore's. C1.5.2 :: s 3(1) + s 6(2)
⚡ Scorecard 1 · the verdictK2
Putting the card together on the base facts, where does Yarrow stand on claim (a)?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

The writing statute is procedural on its wording, so it is not applied here. The burden of proof is procedural, so Yarrow bears it under Singapore's allocation. The cap and the doubling are quantum on the traditional split, which gives US$900,000, but the Goh Suan Hee dicta would give US$200,000. Liability itself, and any head of loss, stay with Utopian law.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Put the card together. The writing statute is procedural on its wording under Star City, so it is not applied; on the functional view it is a rule of form and claim (a) fails, as both validating laws are Utopian (AQCEL). The burden of proof is generally procedural (Re Fuld's Estate (No 3)), so Yarrow bears it, with Re Cohn as its counter. The cap and the doubling are quantum: US$900,000 on the traditional split, US$200,000 on the Goh Suan Hee dicta. Liability itself, any head of loss and remoteness (D'Almeida Araujo v Becker) stay with Utopian law.

6Remember

🧠 FOR THE EXAM
  • Characterise first: an equitable claim follows its legal foundation (Rickshaw), so a duty of confidence from an engagement takes the engagement's law, while a real tort beside a contract may be framed as tort absent bad faith.
  • Fix the lex causae, then sort each foreign rule: substance applies and procedure does not (CIFG v Polimet); “no action shall be brought” is procedure on Star City, with form and its two validating laws (AQCEL) as the alternative.
  • The burden of proof is generally procedure (Re Fuld's Estate (No 3)); a cap, a multiplier and a missing foreign remedy are open points, so give a figure or a result under each route (Goh Suan Hee).
  • Under the FLPA only the lex causae's limitation law applies, whatever its label and to equitable claims too; the claimant's way out is undue hardship under s 4(2).
  • Ask first whether foreign law was pleaded: if not, Singapore law applies in its own right; if pleaded but not proved, the party relying on it may simply lose, or the presumption of similarity may apply where fair (Brownlie; EFT Holdings).
  • A tort committed in Singapore still runs double actionability, with both limbs Singapore law; a contract's chosen law can reach it, if at all, only through the strictly applied flexible exception (an open point).

LAW302 · META GAME · QUESTION 2 · HYPO q2-04 · GEMINI PROMPT V1 · 16 QUESTIONS

Wexford v Kessel

Written by Claude for the drill and law reviewed. Gemini (prompt v1) rebalanced the option lengths and wrote a note on each question; both were checked (11 corrections) and feed the notes here.

Answers:

1Base facts

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Wexford v Kessel

Wexford Aqua Pte Ltd is a Singapore incorporated company. Its head office is in Singapore, but its only business is a prawn farm in Ruritania. Its two executive directors live at the farm. Kessel Hydro Ltd is incorporated in Elbonia, where it makes water treatment units.

In 2025 Wexford asked Kessel about its K9 unit. Kessel's engineers visited the farm twice to measure the ponds. Kessel's technical director then emailed a test report from his office in Elbonia. He sent it to Wexford's general address, and it was opened at the head office in Singapore. The report said that the K9 kills 99% of a common prawn virus. Head office forwarded the report to the farm. The two directors met there, decided to buy 30 units and signed the Supply Agreement at the farm. The units were delivered to the farm. The price was paid in US dollars into Kessel's bank account in Utopia.

The Agreement provides:

“19. This Agreement, and any dispute arising out of or in connection with it, is governed by Elbonian law.”

The report was wrong, because the test had been run on a different model. The units did not stop the virus, and Wexford lost its whole stock at the farm.

Wexford sues Kessel in the General Division for damages for negligent misrepresentation at common law. Kessel says that Elbonian law governs the claim, and that under Elbonian law it owes nothing. Assume that the court has jurisdiction.

Advise Wexford on the law that governs its claim, and on whether the claim will succeed.

ℹ ASSUME
  1. The report is an actionable misrepresentation under Singapore tort law.
  2. It is also actionable under Ruritanian tort law. It is not actionable under Elbonian tort law, which gives no claim for a careless statement made before a contract.
  3. Both sides have filed expert reports on Elbonian and Ruritanian law.
  4. Under every relevant law, a claim of this kind must be brought within six years. Wexford sued within one year.
✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • N1
    Starter: double actionability. A tort claim, although a contract sits behind it. Absent bad faith Wexford may frame its claim in tort, so the rule is double actionability with the flexible exception. Kessel bears the burden on limb 2.
  • N2
    Limb 1: a tort under Singapore law. Limb 1 in one line: had everything happened in Singapore, the report would be a tort. The first Assume item gives you that.
  • N3
    SCORECARD · Locate the tort: where in substance did it arise?. The statement was sent from Elbonia, received in Singapore and acted on in Ruritania. The tort must be given one place before limb 2 can be applied. This is the scorecard.
  • N4
    Limb 2 applied: is there liability under the law of that place?. The laws differ: liability under Ruritanian law, none under Elbonian law. So the result of limb 2 depends on where the tort is located.
  • N5
    SCORECARD · The flexible exception. If the tort is in Ruritania, Kessel's only way to reach Elbonian law is the exception. It must show that Singapore and Ruritania are both there by accident.
  • N6
    Party autonomy: does the contract's chosen law govern the tort?. Clause 19 covers “any dispute arising out of or in connection with” the Agreement. Kessel will say that this makes Elbonian law govern the tort.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • N9
    Tort committed in Singapore. Tempting because the email was opened in Singapore. But N9 is for a tort whose every element happened here. Only receipt was here, and only because the head office is. Reliance and loss were in Ruritania.
  • L6
    SCORECARD · Objective proper law: closest and most real connection. Delivery, currency and the place of payment are objective proper law factors. But the contract has an express choice in clause 19, and no contract claim is made. These facts are not elements of the tort either.
  • K6
    Foreign law not pleaded, or not proved. K6 is for foreign law that is not pleaded or not proved. Both foreign laws are pleaded and proved by experts, so there is no default rule and no presumption to discuss.
  • K5
    Limitation periods. A limitation point needs a claim that is in time under one law and out of time under another. Here the claim is in time under every law, so nothing turns on which period applies.
  • N10
    Statutory misrepresentation; defamation; damages and limitation in tort. Tempting because the word is “misrepresentation”. But Wexford pleads the common law tort only. No claim is made under the Misrepresentation Act, and no limitation or damages point is planted.

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
⚡ BIG IDEA

a misrepresentation sent from Elbonia, opened in Singapore and acted on in Ruritania must be given one place before limb 2 can run. Receipt and reliance split, so the substance test decides: receipt at head office is fortuitous, the tort is arguably in Ruritania, where limb 2 gives liability, and Kessel's routes to Elbonian law fail or stay open: the place of making is the weaker argument, the flexible exception fails on fortuity, and applying clause 19 to the tort is an open point. The twists add a no reliance clause, split on the preferred approach into admissibility for both limbs and validity for Elbonian law, which upholds it, and then flip the Ruritanian rule so that the parties swap arguments.

  1. 1
    A tort claim: the rule and the burden N1

    Wexford sues for negligent misrepresentation at common law. Per Rickshaw, absent bad faith it may frame the claim in tort although the Supply Agreement sits behind it, and the claim stays a tort claim. The rule is double actionability subject to the flexible exception (Rickshaw; Boys v Chaplin; Red Sea). Per EFT Holdings, Wexford proves limb 1, and Kessel must plead and prove that the law of the place of the tort gives no liability. Both foreign laws are proved by experts and the claim is in time under every law, so neither the default rule nor limitation arises.

  2. 2
    Limb 1 in one line N2

    Per IM Skaugen, ask whether the acts, if all done in Singapore, would be a tort. The first Assume item says the report is an actionable misrepresentation under Singapore tort law, so limb 1 is met. No claim is made under the Misrepresentation Act, so nothing more is needed here.

  3. 3
    Locating the tort: the directed statement rule fails N3

    Kessel's case turns on where the tort was committed, so locate it before applying limb 2. Per JIO Minerals (tentatively) and Ong Ghee Soon, a statement directed at the claimant and received and acted on in one country is a tort there, unless that place is fortuitous. The report was emailed from Elbonia, opened at head office in Singapore and acted on at the farm in Ruritania, so receipt and reliance split and the rule fails, as the sample final scheme also says. Per Distillers and Metall, the court then finds the one single place where in substance the cause of action arose.

  4. 4
    The substance test: arguably Ruritania N3

    Per Vibrant Group, reliance weighs more for misrepresentation than for negligence. The engineers visited the farm twice, the directors read the report, decided to buy and signed there, and the stock died there, so the dealings centre on the farm, much as the negotiations and the drilling made Indonesia the place in JIO. Receipt in Singapore merely because the head office is there is fortuitous (JIO), and the Utopian bank account is not an element of the tort. Kessel's fair argument is Elbonia: where making, receipt and reliance are in several countries, the place where the core representations were made may prevail (IM Skaugen v MAN Diesel). So the tort is arguably in Ruritania, and the answer gives the result each way.

  5. 5
    Limb 2 under each route N4

    Limb 2 looks only at the law of the place of the tort, which must give civil liability between these parties (Boys v Chaplin). Route 1, Ruritania: Ruritanian law gives liability, so both limbs are met and the Elbonian rule does nothing by itself. Route 2, Elbonia: Elbonian law gives no claim for a careless statement made before a contract, so limb 2 fails and Kessel escapes unless Wexford displaces Elbonian law. That is unlikely, because Kessel is based in Elbonia and wrote the report there, so Elbonia is not purely fortuitous.

  6. 6
    Kessel's flexible exception fails N5

    If the tort is in Ruritania, Kessel needs the exception to reach Elbonian law. A defendant may invoke it (Ang Ming Chuang, obiter), but Elbonian law is a third law, so per Rickshaw and IM Skaugen both Singapore and Ruritania must be purely fortuitous, which per C&Y will rarely succeed. Singapore may be fortuitous, as Wexford has only its incorporation and head office here, but Ruritania holds Wexford's only business and both directors, and the visits, the reliance and the loss. Displacing Singapore law alone leaves Ruritanian law, under which Kessel is liable, and closest connection alone is not the test, so the plea fails.

  7. 7
    Clause 19 and the tort (open) N6

    Whether clause 19 reaches a tort is construction under its proper law (Rickshaw), and “any dispute arising out of or in connection with” the Agreement is wide enough. Whether a contract's chosen law can then govern a tort is an open question (Ong Ghee Soon), though C&Y call it “just a small step away”. If a court took that step, Elbonian law would govern and the claim would fail. If it does not, Kessel can argue the chosen law only through the flexible exception, as the law of the relationship (C&Y; Chen v BHNV is only an analogy), and Rickshaw's fortuity threshold blocks it because Ruritania is not fortuitous. A claim framed in tort stays a tort claim (Rickshaw).

  8. 8
    Advice to Wexford

    The claim is governed by double actionability with the flexible exception. Wexford has the better argument that the tort is in Ruritania, where both limbs give liability; Kessel's flexible exception fails, and so does clause 19 argued through it, so the claim probably succeeds. If the court accepts Kessel's argument for Elbonia, or takes the open step of applying clause 19 to the tort directly, Elbonian law gives no claim and Wexford loses.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Limb 2 fails where the law of the place of the tort imposes no liability between these parties (Boys v Chaplin), and absent displacement Wexford recovers only what both laws allow. So the parties swap arguments. Wexford will locate the tort in Singapore by receipt, which is weak because receipt at head office merely because it is based there is fortuitous (JIO Minerals), or in Elbonia, where the report was made (IM Skaugen v MAN Diesel); or it will invoke the flexible exception or clause 19. The burden on limb 2 stays on Kessel.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C3.3.3 :: Limb 2 Fails Where

[law X] [bars the head / provides a defence] or imposes no liability between [these parties] (Lord Wilberforce, Boys v Chaplin), so [defendant] escapes unless [law X] is displaced (C3.6.3).

⚡ Twist 2 · 2 of 4N5
Wexford invokes the flexible exception to displace Ruritanian law. It says that losing under that law is unjust. Will it succeed?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Rickshaw, the court must not be quick to apply the exception unless the displaced law is purely fortuitous. Wexford's only business and both its directors are in Ruritania, and the visits, the reliance and the loss were there. The interest argument from Boys v Chaplin worked for British servicemen who were only stationed in Malta for a time. It does not fit a company that farms in Ruritania.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Rickshaw, courts “must not be quick” to apply the exception unless the displaced law is purely fortuitous, and per C&Y applying a fortuitous law is itself the injustice, so fortuity is the real test. A law cannot be displaced merely because it is less favourable (Rickshaw). Lord Wilberforce's interest analysis in Boys v Chaplin helped servicemen who were stationed in Malta for a time, but Wexford's whole business and both its executive directors are in Ruritania. As the party invoking the exception, Wexford must also prove the connecting factors.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C3.6.1 :: Threshold

Per Rickshaw, courts "must not be quick" to apply it unless [the displaced law] is purely fortuitous and applying it causes [injustice], on "clear and satisfying grounds" (Lord Wilberforce), lest it become [a proper law of the tort].

⚡ Twist 2 · 3 of 4N6
Wexford now relies on clause 19 to say that Elbonian law governs the tort. Suppose that argument succeeded. Would Wexford win?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

The chosen law can reach the tort, if at all, as the law of the relationship under the flexible exception, and Rickshaw's fortuity threshold stands in the way. Chen v BHNV is an analogy only. And the clause cuts both ways: Elbonian law is also the law under which clause 24 is valid.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Wexford's clause 19 argument faces two hurdles. First, whether a contract's chosen law can govern a tort is open (Ong Ghee Soon); the arguable route is the flexible exception, with the chosen law as the law of the relationship (C&Y), and Rickshaw's fortuity threshold stands in the way, as Ruritania is not fortuitous (Chen v BHNV is only an analogy). Second, Elbonian law cuts both ways: clause 24 is valid under it, and the Assume list lets it be raised, so it bars the misrepresentation claim.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C3.6.5 :: Route Through the Exception (C&Y)

[the chosen / proper law] applies via the flexible exception as the law of [the centred relationship], as in Chen v BHNV ([a conspiracy] "so intimately connected" to [the Belize-law contract]), Oro Negro and Trafigura.

  • Caution: Chen was an FNC ruling not running [Rickshaw's fortuity test], and Trafigura applied [s 12 PIL(MP)A], so they are analogies only.
  • Obstacle: Rickshaw's [fortuity threshold] and [non-exclusive concession] blocked it (C3.4), so [the opponent] argues [the separate tort] stays.
  • Application (+): [the platform / mandate] was the conduit, so [the proper law] displaces [both limbs].
⚡ Twist 2 · 4 of 4N10
Can Wexford use the Misrepresentation Act?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per JIO Minerals, the Act only supplements common law remedies, so it applies only if Singapore law governs the issue, and to a misrepresentation abroad only if the contract has a Singapore proper law. Here Singapore law does not govern on either view of the issue: as contract, Elbonian law governs, and as tort, the tort is located abroad. Wexford's one argument is that the email was opened here, so the statement was made here. JIO does not decide that case, but receipt at head office is fortuitous and the proper law is still Elbonian. So there is probably no claim under s 2, and s 3 probably cannot strike down clause 24.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per JIO Minerals, the Act, including ss 2 and 3, applies only where Singapore law governs the issue, and to a misrepresentation abroad only where the contract has a Singapore proper law. Here Elbonian law governs the contract, and the tort is probably located abroad, arguably in Ruritania. Wexford's one argument is that the email was opened in Singapore, so the statement was made here. JIO does not decide that case, but receipt at head office is fortuitous and the proper law is still Elbonian, so there is probably no claim under s 2, and s 3 probably cannot strike down clause 24.

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes

    Clause 24 and the Assume items on it stay. Now the report is actionable under Singapore and Elbonian tort law but not under Ruritanian tort law, and Wexford adds a claim under the Misrepresentation Act and a plea of injustice. The place of the tort does not move: it is still arguably Ruritania. But limb 2 now fails there, so the parties swap arguments.

  2. 2
    Limb 2 fails in Ruritania N4N3

    If the tort is in Ruritania, limb 2 fails once Kessel pleads and proves Ruritanian law, and the burden stays on Kessel (EFT Holdings). Absent displacement Wexford recovers only what both laws allow, so it now argues for another place. Singapore is weak, because receipt at head office merely because Wexford is based there is fortuitous (JIO Minerals). Elbonia, where the report was made, is the argument Kessel ran in the base (IM Skaugen v MAN Diesel). Even if Wexford won on location, clause 24 is valid under Elbonian law and may be raised, so it still answers the claim; s 3 of the Act probably cannot strike it down (below).

  3. 3
    The exception and clause 19 do not help N5N6

    Per Rickshaw, the exception needs the displaced law to be purely fortuitous, and a law is not displaced merely because it is less favourable. Ruritania holds Wexford's only business and both directors, and the visits, the reliance and the loss, so it is not there by accident. Boys v Chaplin does not help: Lord Wilberforce's interest analysis concerned servicemen only stationed in Malta for a time, and Rickshaw's fortuity test is stricter. A rule that merely differs from Singapore law is not against fundamental public policy (C&Y), and public policy is not a ground for the exception. Whether clause 19 can make Elbonian law govern the tort is open, and through the exception it meets the same fortuity threshold. Even if Wexford won on either point, clause 24 is valid under Elbonian law and may be raised, so it still answers the claim.

  4. 4
    The Misrepresentation Act N10

    Per JIO Minerals, the Act only supplements common law remedies, so it applies only if Singapore law governs the issue, and to a misrepresentation abroad only under a Singapore law contract. As contract the issue is for Elbonian law, and as tort the tort is probably abroad. Wexford's one argument is that the email was opened here, so the statement was made here; JIO does not decide that case, but receipt at head office is fortuitous and the proper law is still Elbonian. So there is probably no claim under s 2, s 3 probably cannot strike down clause 24, and the claim probably fails on every route.

4Scorecards: weigh the factors

Prof Chong rewards applying facts to factor tests. Sort each fact, then answer the verdict question. These use the base facts unless a line says “Suppose”.

N3 Sort the factors: Locating the misrepresentation on the base facts

Kessel says the tort was committed in Elbonia. Wexford says Ruritania. For each line, decide whom it helps in finding the one place where the tort in substance arose. Lines marked “Suppose” are extra facts for this card only.

The two directors read the report at the farm, decided to buy there and signed there.
Helps Wexford: Ruritania. Reliance is at the heart of misrepresentation. Prof Chong's scheme counts both the place of the decision and the place of signing as places of reliance. C3.3.2 :: Misrepresentation Directed at the Claimant
Kessel's engineers visited the farm twice before the report was sent.
Helps Wexford: Ruritania. In JIO Minerals, with receipt and reliance split, the negotiations and the drilling made Indonesia the place. The dealings here were centred on the farm. C3.3.2 :: Misrepresentation Directed at the Claimant
The email was opened at Wexford's head office in Singapore.
Little or no weight. Receipt in a country merely because the claimant is based there is fortuitous (JIO Minerals). Nothing else happened in Singapore. C3.3.2 :: Misrepresentation Directed at the Claimant
The technical director wrote and sent the report from his office in Elbonia.
Helps Kessel: Elbonia. Kessel's best fact. Where making, receipt and reliance are in several countries, the place where the core representations were made may prevail (IM Skaugen v MAN Diesel). But a directed statement is normally located by receipt and reliance, not by making. C3.3.2 :: Misrepresentation Directed at the Claimant
Wexford pleads negligent misrepresentation, not negligence in running the test.
Helps Wexford: Ruritania. The weight of each element depends on the tort pleaded. Reliance counts for more in misrepresentation than in negligence, where the place of the careless act prevails. C3.3.1 :: As Pleaded
The price was paid into Kessel's bank account in Utopia.
Little or no weight. A connecting factor for the proper law of a contract. It is not an element of the tort, and the test looks only at the elements of the tort. C3.3.1 :: The Test
Elbonian tort law gives no claim for a careless statement made before a contract.
Little or no weight. What a law says does not help to locate the tort. Locate first, then ask what the law of that place provides. C3.3.1 :: §
Suppose: Wexford's accounts, kept in Singapore, record the loss.
Little or no weight. The place of damage may be quite fortuitous. Loss felt at the claimant's home base does not by itself locate the tort. C3.3.1 :: Damage Not Determinative
Suppose: the report had been posted on Kessel's website for all prawn farmers to read.
Helps Kessel: Elbonia. A statement made to the world at large is a tort where it is made, unlike one directed at the claimant. C3.3.2 :: Representation Made at Large

1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Receipt and reliance split, so the gloss does not decide and the substance test does. The visits, the reliance, the signing and the loss point to Ruritania. Receipt in Singapore is fortuitous. Kessel's argument for Elbonia is fair but weaker, so write “arguably” and state the result each way.

With receipt and reliance split, the directed statement rule does not decide and the substance test does (Distillers; Metall; JIO Minerals). The visits, the reliance, the signing and the loss point to Ruritania, under whose law the report is actionable, so both limbs are met. Kessel is left to argue Elbonia as the place, where the core representation was made (IM Skaugen v MAN Diesel), or the flexible exception.

On the base facts Kessel asks the court to apply Elbonian law alone. Does each line help Kessel, hurt Kessel, or carry no weight? Lines marked “Suppose” are extra facts for this card only.

Clause 19 chooses Elbonian law for any dispute “in connection with” the Agreement.
Helps Kessel. The chosen law may apply through the exception as the law of the relationship between the parties. This is the only route for party autonomy in tort. C3.6.5 :: Route Through the Exception (C&Y)
Kessel is incorporated in Elbonia and wrote the report there.
Helps Kessel. The place of conduct and a party's place of incorporation are both factors that the court weighs. C3.6.1 :: Factors to Weigh

Wexford's only business and both its executive directors are in Ruritania.

⚡ Scorecard 2 · the verdictN5
What is the likely result of Kessel's plea?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

A third law needs both the forum and the place of the tort to be purely fortuitous. Ruritania is the centre of the events. Displacing Singapore law alone would leave Ruritanian law, under which Kessel is liable. The exception is strictly applied so that it does not become a proper law of the tort.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Displacing both limbs in favour of a third law, Elbonian law, needs both Singapore and Ruritania to be purely fortuitous (Rickshaw; IM Skaugen). Ruritania is the centre of the transaction and the loss, so it cannot be displaced, and displacing Singapore alone leaves Ruritanian law, under which Kessel is liable. The exception is strictly applied so that it does not become a proper law of the tort (Rickshaw).

5Remember

🧠 FOR THE EXAM
  • Receipt and reliance in different countries: the directed statement rule fails, so run the substance test, where receipt at a head office merely because the claimant is based there is fortuitous.
  • Limb 2 looks at one foreign law only, the law of the place of the tort, and the defendant pleads and proves it (EFT Holdings).
  • A third law needs both the forum and the place of the tort to be purely fortuitous; displacing Singapore law alone does not help a defendant.
  • Whether a contract's chosen law can govern a tort is open (Ong Ghee Soon): give the result if a court applied it directly, and through the flexible exception, where fortuity usually blocks it.
  • A contract clause against a tort: on the preferred approach, admissibility for both limbs and validity for the proper law; UCTA reaches a foreign law contract only through s 27(2).
  • The Misrepresentation Act applies only where Singapore law governs the issue, and abroad only under a Singapore law contract (JIO Minerals).

LAW302 · META GAME · QUESTION 2 · HYPO q2-12 · GEMINI PROMPT V2 · LAW REVIEWED 17 NOV · 14 QUESTIONS

Crestwood v Valmont; Crownline v Valmont

Gemini wrote this hypo with prompt v2. Claude reviewed it in three passes and made 49 changes before it went into the drill. Gemini's file: q2_12_crestwood_v_valmont_crownline_v_valmont.ht.

Answers:

1Base facts

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Crestwood v Valmont; Crownline v Valmont

Crestwood Machinery Pte Ltd (“Crestwood”), a Singapore incorporated company, manufactures industrial packaging machines at its factory in Jurong. Valmont Packaging SA (“Valmont”) is incorporated in Ruritania, where it runs a bottling plant. Crownline Finance Ltd (“Crownline”) is a lender incorporated in Utopia.

On 10 February 2025 Crestwood and Valmont signed a Supply Contract in Singapore. It is in English and contains no choice of law clause and no jurisdiction clause. Crestwood agreed to manufacture two machines in Singapore, deliver them FOB Singapore port, and arrange Ruritanian customs clearance. The price of US$1.5 million is payable in US dollars into Crestwood's Singapore bank account, with a US$200,000 deposit paid on signing.

The Supply Contract is lawful on its face. However, after signing, Crestwood decided to save import duty when clearing the machines through Ruritanian customs, and deliberately declared their value at 40% of the contract price on the customs entry. Valmont knew of Crestwood's plan before shipment and raised no objection. Valmont paid the deposit, received the machines, and now refuses to pay the US$1.3 million balance. Crestwood sues Valmont in the General Division for the balance.

To fund the purchase, Valmont borrowed US$1 million from Crownline under a Facility Agreement signed in Utopia and expressly governed by Utopian law. Clause 9 sets default interest at 24% per annum. Crownline knew nothing of Crestwood's customs plan. Valmont defaulted, and Crownline sues Valmont in the General Division for repayment and default interest. Valmont argues that the Facility Agreement is tainted by the Ruritanian customs offence, and that a Singapore statute caps default interest at 12% per annum. Assume the court has jurisdiction over all parties.

Advise Valmont on both claims.

ℹ ASSUME
  1. Singapore has friendly relations with Ruritania and Utopia.
  2. Under Ruritanian customs law, deliberately underdeclaring the value of imported goods is a serious criminal offence punishable by fine and imprisonment.
  3. Under Utopian law, the Facility Agreement is sufficiently connected to the Ruritanian customs offence to be tainted and unenforceable. Under Singapore law, it is not sufficiently connected.
  4. The Singapore statute capping default interest at 12% per annum says nothing about loans governed by foreign law.
  5. The Supply Contract is valid and enforceable under Singapore contract law apart from any illegality.
✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • K1
    Characterise the issue. Characterise both claims as contractual issues governed by their proper laws before applying contract choice of law rules.
  • L1
    Starter: the proper law and its three stages. The Supply Contract has no choice of law clause, so open with the three-stage proper law framework.
  • L6
    SCORECARD · Objective proper law: closest and most real connection. Weigh the connecting factors at Stage 3: manufacture, FOB delivery, payment, and signing all point to Singapore law as the objective proper law.
  • M1
    Illegality: pick the route. Label the proper laws (Singapore for the Supply Contract, Utopia for the Facility Agreement), the forum (Singapore) and the place of the illegal act (Ruritania), then route to Foster and tainting while ruling out M2, M4 and M5.
  • M3
    SCORECARD · Foster v Driscoll: intention to break a friendly state's law. Crestwood broke Ruritanian customs law in performing a facially lawful contract and now sues for the price; test Foster outside the paradigm against the guilty claimant.
  • M6
    SCORECARD · Tainting: a relevant illegality, sufficiently connected. Run both steps of tainting on the Facility Agreement, where Utopian and Singapore law disagree on sufficient connection. If Foster is confined to intention at signing, tainting is also the fallback against Crestwood's own claim.
  • K7
    A Singapore statute said to override the chosen law. Test whether the silent Singapore interest cap overrides Utopian law under JIO Minerals.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • M2
    The law broken is the proper law itself. Tempting because Ruritanian customs law was broken. Wrong because Singapore law is the objective proper law of the Supply Contract and Utopian law governs the Facility Agreement.
  • M5
    Ralli Bros: performance becomes illegal where it must be done. Tempting because the customs breach happened in Ruritania. Wrong because the Supply Contract required only customs clearance there, not a false declaration, so no act it requires is illegal in Ruritania.
  • M4
    Lemenda: against the public policy of the place of performance. Tempting because foreign state interests are harmed. Wrong because Ruritanian customs law is a written statute, not mere foreign public policy.
  • K8
    Forum public policy; renvoi. Tempting because 24% default interest looks high. Wrong because a commercial interest rate offends at most domestic policy, not Singapore's fundamental international public policy.
  • L4
    Law chosen to dodge another country's rule. Tempting because Utopian law avoids the Singapore interest cap. Wrong because Crownline is incorporated in Utopia and the loan was signed there, so evasion was not the sole purpose.

Fair to tick but not needed: L2 Express choice of law clause, K2 Substance or procedure, L5 No clause: implied choice

Application questions · base facts

⚡ Base facts · 1 of 6L6
Which law is the objective proper law of the Supply Contract?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

At Stage 3 the place where both parties perform carries the greatest weight. Manufacture, FOB delivery, payment, and contracting all point to Singapore. USD and English carry little weight. A related contract can carry its law even between different parties (JIO Minerals), but the Facility Agreement only funds Valmont's side and the sale does not depend on it.
