⚡ BIG IDEA

One buyer faces two claims, and the same customs crime attacks each in a different way. Against Crestwood's price claim the live route is Foster, which is open because the plan came after signing: barred if Foster reaches illegal performance, otherwise a tainting question for Singapore proportionality. Against Crownline's loan the route is tainting, where Step 2 splits: no taint on Singapore principles, taint on Utopian principles. The move that shapes the answer: find each contract's proper law and what the Supply Contract required, so Route A and Ralli drop out in two lines and your words go to the open points, with a result under each.

  1. 1
    Characterise both claims K1

    Per Macmillan, the court characterises the issue, picks the connecting factor and applies the law it points to. Crestwood claims the price under the Supply Contract, and Crownline claims repayment and default interest under the Facility Agreement: both are contractual issues. So each claim is governed by its own contract's proper law (Per Amin Rasheed), and per C&Y that law also governs illegality under it. Valmont's illegality and interest cap points are defences inside those claims.

  2. 2
    The two proper laws L1L6

    The Supply Contract has no choice of law clause and no jurisdiction clause, and nothing implies a choice, so go to Stage 3: the closest and most real connection (Per Bonython; Pacific Recreation). Per Prof Chong, the strongest argument is usually where both parties perform: Crestwood makes the machines in Singapore and delivers them FOB Singapore port, and Valmont pays into a Singapore account. Signing in Singapore supports this; Valmont's Ruritanian home and the customs clearance there point away; English and US dollars carry little weight. A related contract can carry its law (Per JIO Minerals), but the Utopian-law loan only funds Valmont's side and the sale does not depend on it, so Singapore law is the objective proper law. The Facility Agreement's express choice of Utopian law stands: Crownline is Utopian and the loan was signed in Utopia, so evading the Singapore cap was not the sole purpose (Per Peh Teck Quee).

  3. 3
    Label the laws and pick the routes M1

    Valmont pleads illegality, so list the routes: the proper law, forum international public policy, Foster, Lemenda, Ralli, tainting and reliance as a defence. Label the laws: the proper laws are Singapore law (Supply Contract) and Utopian law (Facility Agreement), the forum is Singapore, and the illegal act happened in Ruritania. Route A is out, as Ruritanian law is the proper law of neither contract; Ralli is out, as the contract required customs clearance, which is lawful, not a false declaration; Lemenda is out, as a written statute was broken. Per OUB v Chua, Ruritania's customs law is recognised as a fact, not enforced, so it still counts. That leaves Foster against Crestwood's claim and tainting against both claims.

  4. 4
    Crestwood's price claim: Foster in performance (open) M3M6

    Per Foster v Driscoll and Regazzoni, a contract whose real object is to evade a friendly State's customs is unenforceable, and Ruritania is a friendly State. But intention at formation is the crux (Per Magdeev), and Crestwood planned the underdeclaration only after signing, so the point is open. Route 1: per Prof Chong (mid-term feedback), Foster may also reach illegal performance, the thrust being the guilty party's wicked intention; Crestwood, the guilty claimant, is then barred, though it can argue that cheating customs was only a side feature of a real sale, not the dominant object (Per Magdeev), and if that succeeds Foster fails. Route 2: if Foster is confined to intention at signing, the illegal performance goes to tainting (Howard v Shirlstar); Step 1 is met, and with Singapore as both forum and proper law, Singapore proportionality decides Step 2. No Assume line fixes the weighing, so give a view: if the deliberate crime and Crestwood's intent weigh most, refusal is proportionate and the claim fails; if the lawful sale and Valmont keeping US$1.5 million of machines for US$200,000 weigh most, refusal is disproportionate and Crestwood recovers. On either route, Valmont's knowledge does not cure Crestwood's illegality.

  5. 5
    Crownline's claim: does the crime taint the loan? M6

    Valmont argues tainting, asking per Euro-Diam (1) is there a relevant foreign illegality, and (2) is it sufficiently connected to the claim. Step 1, a lex fori question, is met: Anuva excluded illegal acts, but per C&Y and Surewin an act can count, and this one breaks a prohibition of Ruritania, where Crestwood had to clear the machines, and is a deliberate crime punishable by imprisonment (Per Ryder Industries). Step 2: which law's principles decide is unresolved, as Teng, Baker v BCS and Surewin all involved Singapore-law contracts; per Prof Chong, Singapore's decide if tainting is part of the lex fori, and the proper law's if it is part of the proper law, so run both. Per Chong (seminar), the proper law that counts is that of the contract sued on, the Facility Agreement: under Utopian principles the loan is tainted and Crownline's claim fails. Under Singapore principles there is no sufficient connection, so the claim is not barred. Valmont can add the C&Y submission (with Forsyth) that the proper law's principles apply unless Singapore's rise to overriding mandatory rules or international policy.

  6. 6
    Step 2 on Singapore principles: proportionality M6

    Per Ting Siew May (applied in Surewin), refusing the claim must be proportionate, weighing the rule's purpose, gravity, centrality, the parties' object, intent and conduct, and the consequences of refusal. Apply it with care to a foreign breach, as the forum poorly gauges a foreign State's view of gravity (Per Ryder Industries). Crownline knew nothing of the customs plan and only lent money, so, as in Surewin, where the bank was unaware, refusing its claim would be disproportionate. That matches the Assume list: no sufficient connection under Singapore law.

  7. 7
    The 12% interest cap K7

    Per JIO Minerals, a Singapore statute overrides the proper law only if Parliament clearly intended so; Parliament may legislate extraterritorially, and conflicts rules are tools to find a statute's reach. This statute is silent on foreign-law loans, so the presumption applies in both its aspects: it reaches only issues governed by Singapore law, and only conduct within Singapore. Utopian law governs, and the loan was signed in Utopia, so the cap probably does not apply. Valmont's reply is that the cap is protective, and protective statutes apply abroad more readily (Per JIO Minerals). Forum public policy does not help either: a 24% commercial rate offends at most domestic policy, not Singapore's fundamental policy.

  8. 8
    Advice to Valmont

    Price claim: if Foster reaches illegal performance, Crestwood is barred and Valmont need not pay the US$1.3 million balance, though Crestwood will argue the fraud was not the dominant object. If Foster does not reach it, tainting turns on Singapore proportionality: Valmont wins if Crestwood's deliberate crime weighs most, and must pay if the lawful sale and its own windfall weigh most. Loan: Valmont escapes repayment only if Utopian principles decide Step 2 of tainting; on Singapore principles it must repay. If it must repay, the silent 12% cap probably does not cut the 24% default rate.

5Remember

🧠 FOR THE EXAM
  • Find each contract's proper law first: Route A needs the law broken to be the proper law, and Ralli needs a required act to be illegal where it must be done, so Crestwood's false declaration engages neither, whenever it was planned.
  • Foster in performance is open: if, per Prof Chong (mid-term feedback), it reaches illegal performance, the guilty claimant is barred; if not, the illegal performance goes to tainting, and where Singapore is both forum and proper law, proportionality decides.
  • Tainting: Step 1 is a lex fori threshold that minor or administrative breaches fail (Per Ryder Industries); at Step 2 run Singapore principles and the proper law of the contract sued on, with a result under each.
  • A silent Singapore statute is presumed to reach only Singapore-law contracts and conduct in Singapore (Per JIO Minerals), so it probably does not touch a Utopian-law loan signed in Utopia.
  • Pleaded but unproved foreign law may sink the party whose case needs it, and presumed similarity cannot save that party where Singapore law gives it no better answer; “no action shall be brought” is procedural under Star City, with the functional view run for the losing party.
  • Per Esben (a provisional view), a guilty party may still rely on the contract as a defence unless the outcome stultifies comity; keeping a deposit for goods the buyer kept probably does not.

    Before: “Go back to the base facts and change these details.”
    Now: Go back to the base facts and change or add these details.

LAW302 · META GAME · QUESTION 2 · HYPO q2-01 · GEMINI PROMPT V1 · 17 QUESTIONS

Quillon v Dorval

Written by Claude for the drill and law reviewed. Gemini (prompt v1) wrote a guide to it; the guide was checked (5 corrections) and feeds the walkthrough. Gemini's file: law302_question_2_review_plain_english_study_gui.

Answers:

1Base facts

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Quillon v Dorval

Quillon Pte Ltd is a Singapore incorporated company. It builds weather radar units at its workshop in Singapore. Dorval SA is incorporated in Ruritania, where it runs three private airfields.

In March 2025 the parties negotiated the sale of two radar units by email. Quillon emailed its “Supply Terms” to Dorval. Under them, Quillon is to deliver and install the units at Dorval's airfields in Ruritania and to train Dorval's staff there for 12 months. The price is US$6 million. Half is payable to Quillon's bank in Singapore before shipment, and half in Ruritania when the units are commissioned. The Supply Terms are in English. They say nothing about the governing law or about any court.

Dorval's operations manager replied by email from Ruritania: “Terms noted. Please proceed with the build.” Quillon's sales team read the reply in Singapore, and work began. Neither party signed anything.

In 2026 new owners took over Dorval. It refuses to take the units or to pay. It says that there was never a contract, that an unsigned contract cannot be enforced, that it had no power to buy the units, and that it would be unjust to hold it to a hurried email. Quillon waited 14 months before suing. It now sues Dorval in the General Division for the price. Assume that the court has jurisdiction.

Advise Quillon.

ℹ ASSUME
  1. Under Ruritanian contract law, the reply “Please proceed with the build” is an acceptance and a contract was made. Under Singapore contract law, assume that the reply is not an acceptance and that there is no contract.
  2. The Ruritanian Commercial Code provides: “No action shall be brought on a contract for the sale of aviation equipment unless it is in writing and signed by both parties.” Singapore law has no such rule.
  3. As Ruritanian company law requires, Dorval's constitution states that it “has no power” to buy equipment costing more than US$5 million without a resolution of its shareholders. None was passed. Under Ruritanian law such a contract still binds the company unless the other party knew of the limit. Quillon did not know.
  4. Dorval's staff who dealt with Quillon all live in Ruritania.
  5. If a valid contract exists, Dorval is liable for the price under both laws.
✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • K1
    Characterise the issue. Dorval runs three separate points: no contract, no signature and no power. Formation, form and capacity each have their own choice of law rule, so split them in two lines before naming any law.
  • L1
    Starter: the proper law and its three stages. A contract claim with no governing law clause. Run the three stages aloud: no express choice, nothing clear enough for an implied choice, then the closest connection.
  • L6
    SCORECARD · Objective proper law: closest and most real connection. With no clause, the objective proper law does the work. The facts give performance, payment and places of business in two countries, so they are there to be weighed.
  • L7
    Was a contract formed at all?. Dorval denies that any contract was made, and the two laws disagree on whether the reply was an acceptance. That is a formation dispute for the putative proper law.
  • L8
    Formal validity. A signature rule that only Ruritanian law has. Form is satisfied under either the proper law or the law of the place of contracting, and the reply was read in Singapore.
  • K2
    Substance or procedure. The Code is worded “No action shall be brought”. That wording bars enforcement, not the right, so ask whether the rule is procedural.
  • L9
    Other attacks on the clause; capacity. “Has no power” is a limit on what the company can do. That is capacity: two laws must both give capacity, and the proper law then fixes the consequences.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • M1
    Illegality: pick the route. Tempting because a Ruritanian statute stands in the way of the claim. Wrong because the Code does not forbid the sale. It says how such a contract must be made or sued on, which is form or procedure.
  • M2
    The law broken is the proper law itself. Tempting because Ruritanian law may be the proper law and a Ruritanian rule was not followed. Wrong because a limit on what a company can do is capacity, with its own rule. Nothing makes the sale unlawful.
  • K5
    Limitation periods. Tempting because of the 14 month delay. Wrong because no limitation period is given under either law, so nothing turns on the delay.
  • K8
    Forum public policy; renvoi. Tempting because Dorval pleads unfairness. Wrong because Dorval is a Ruritanian company held to Ruritania's own rule on its own written reply. Fundamental public policy is narrower than a sense of unfairness.

Fair to tick but not needed: L2 Express choice of law clause, L5 No clause: implied choice

Application questions · base facts

⚡ Base facts · 1 of 7L6
The Supply Terms have no governing law clause. How should the answer reach the governing law?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

The proper law is found in three stages, and the answer should say why stages 1 and 2 fail before weighing. At stage 3 the strongest argument is usually the place where both parties perform. There is no default to the lex fori and no burden on Dorval.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C2.4.3 :: Application

Per Prof Chong, the strongest argument is usually [the place where both parties perform, e.g., country X], supported by [place of contracting / currency / incorporation and head office / related transaction], so [law X] is the OPL.

⚡ Base facts · 2 of 7L7
Dorval says that there was never a contract. Which law decides that?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Lew v Nargolwala, a formation dispute is governed by the putative proper law. With no law agreed in negotiations, the three-stage test is applied to the transaction. Under Ruritanian law the reply is an acceptance, so a contract was made. The place of contracting is not the test for the governing law.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C2.6 :: Putative Proper Law

As [the dispute] concerns existence, per Lew v Nargolwala a law agreed during negotiations governs (rare), failing which a JIO-style three-stage test applied to [the negotiations / transaction] finds the putative proper law, matching The Parouth and CIMB.

⚡ Base facts · 3 of 7L7
Dorval argues that the emails give too few connecting facts, so Singapore law should decide whether its manager's short reply was an agreement at all. Is that open to it?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Lew calls the lex fori “illogical” for formation and rejects it even residually. The critique of Prof Chong and Teo is that negotiations alone give too few factors, so the lex fori should decide agreement on a putative law clause and break battle of the forms ties. Here there is no clause and the Supply Terms give plenty to weigh, so Dorval is stretching the critique. Run the putative proper law first, then put this as Dorval's argument and give the result under it.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C2.6 :: Critique: Lex Fori in a Subsidiary Role

Per Prof Chong (and Teo), [the negotiations alone] give too few factors, and [non est factum / a voiding mistake] favours one side, so [the lex fori] should decide agreement on [the putative clause] and break [battle of forms] ties.

⚡ Base facts · 4 of 7L8
Dorval says that the contract fails because no one signed it. Suppose Ruritanian law is the proper law. Is the contract formally valid?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per AQCEL, compliance with either the proper law or the lex loci contractus is enough. Per Transniko, the lex fori places the contract where the acceptance is received. That is Singapore, and Singapore law has no signature rule for this sale.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C2.7 :: Alternative Reference Rule

Per AQCEL (adopting PT Jaya Putra's obiter), meeting [requirement X] under either [the proper law] or [the lex loci contractus] suffices, parties rarely thinking about [formalities].

  • Not form: per PT Jaya Putra, [a government approval requirement] goes to validity under [the proper law].
⚡ Base facts · 5 of 7K2
The Code says “No action shall be brought ...”. What does that wording add to the answer?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Procedure is for the lex fori, so a foreign procedural rule is not applied here. A rule that only bars an “action” regulates enforcement and is procedural on the Star City test. Star City remains the law, but the functional view is argued in the alternative, and on that view the rule may be substantive form.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C1.2.2 :: Scenario B: Procedural (−)

Per Star City, [provision, e.g., "no action shall be brought"] bars only enforcement of [the right], so Singapore law applies.

⚡ Base facts · 6 of 7L9
Dorval's constitution says that it “has no power” to make this purchase without a shareholders' resolution. What kind of rule is that, and which law applies to it?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

A rule of “real substance” about what the company may do is capacity, not form. A corporation needs capacity under both the law of its incorporation and the proper law. Ruritanian law is the law of incorporation whatever the proper law turns out to be.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C2.8.2 :: Dual Test

Per C&Y (Dicey r 162), [Corporation] needs capacity under both [the law of incorporation] and [the proper law], a subjective proper law being acceptable as [companies] are less exploitable.

⚡ Base facts · 7 of 7L9
Dorval lacked capacity under Ruritanian law. Is that the end of Quillon's claim?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

There are two questions. The law of incorporation says whether the company had capacity. The proper law then decides what follows from the lack of it. Students stop at the first. Here the second question saves the contract under Ruritanian law itself.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C2.8.2 :: Consequences: The Proper Law

Per Haugesund, once [the law of incorporation] denies capacity, [the proper law, English law] decides the consequences, so [the contract] is void, but [the lender] recovers [the sums advanced] in unjust enrichment, [change of position] failing.

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
⚡ BIG IDEA

Dorval runs three defences (no contract, no signature, no power), and they go to formation, form and capacity, each with its own choice of law rule, so split them before naming any law. The move that decides the base is the objective proper law: with no clause, the main performance on both sides is in Ruritania, so Ruritanian law is the putative proper law and a contract was made. Form is saved because the acceptance was received in Singapore (and the “no action” rule is procedural anyway), and the capacity defect does not undo the contract under Ruritanian law. The twists test the governing law with a court clause (which may move it to Singapore law) and with clashing forms (Ruritanian law on either route), then turn Ruritanian law against Quillon on its own silence.

  1. 1
    Characterise: three defences, three rules K1

    Per Macmillan, the court characterises the issue before it picks a law. Dorval runs three separate points: “never a contract” is formation, “unsigned” is form (and the “no action” wording also raises procedure), and “no power” is capacity. Per C&Y these sit outside the proper law's ordinary scope, and each has its own choice of law rule, so say so in two lines before naming any law. If a valid contract exists, Dorval owes the price under both laws, so the answer turns only on which law governs each point.

  2. 2
    Stages 1 and 2: no choice L1

    Per Amin Rasheed the proper law governs the contract, and per Pacific Recreation it is found by express choice, implied choice or, failing both, the closest and most real connection (Bonython). Stage 1: the Supply Terms have no governing law clause. Stage 2: there is no court clause, related contract or term of art, and English and US dollars carry little weight, so nothing is clear enough for an implied choice. Quillon cannot imply Ruritanian law just because it upholds the contract: per C&Y the principle of validation does not apply where formation is disputed. Say this in a line each, then weigh; there is no default to Singapore law as the lex fori.

  3. 3
    Stage 3: Ruritanian law L6

    Per Bonython, the contract is governed by the law with which it has its closest and most real connection, and per Prof Chong the strongest argument is usually where both parties perform: Quillon delivers, installs and trains staff in Ruritania for 12 months, and Dorval pays the second half there on commissioning. Per C&Y, Pacific Recreation's “equal weight” dictum is puzzling, because the place of performance carries great weight (Bonython; Enka). Singapore has real links: Quillon's business and workshop, and the first half of the price paid to its bank. Per Las Vegas Hilton each party's place of business counts, and Dorval's, in Ruritania, balances Quillon's. English and US dollars carry little weight, and per Prof Chong witness convenience (Dorval's staff live in Ruritania) is a Spiliada factor, irrelevant unless tied to the contract. Courts do not declare ties (Lew) and the forum's law gets no preference, so Ruritanian law is the objective proper law.

  4. 4
    Formation: Ruritanian law, so a contract L7

    Per Lew v Nargolwala, whether a contract exists is decided by a law agreed in negotiations (there is none), or else by the three stages applied to the transaction: the putative proper law. That is Ruritanian law, and under it “Please proceed with the build” is an acceptance, so a contract was made. Not Singapore law as the lex fori: Lew calls that “illogical” and gives it no role, even residually. Not the place of contracting either: it matters for form, not formation. Dorval's plea that a hurried email should not bind it fails too: Lew's grave injustice caveat is “a very small caveat, very rarely applicable”, framed for a party bound by its silence, and Dorval sent a written reply; holding a Ruritanian company to Ruritania's own rule on that reply offends no fundamental public policy.

  5. 5
    Dorval's lex fori argument: argument only L7

    Dorval may say the emails give too few connecting facts, so Singapore law should decide whether the reply was an agreement at all. Prof Chong (and Teo) do criticise Lew: negotiations alone can give too few factors, so the lex fori should decide agreement on a putative law clause and break battle of the forms ties. But Lew rejects the lex fori even as a fallback, and also rejected Yeo's fallback where the whole contract is disputed, which is Dorval's case. Here there is no clause and the Supply Terms give plenty to weigh, so Dorval is stretching the critique. Put it as Dorval's argument with its result (Singapore law: no contract), then conclude under Lew: Ruritanian law and a contract.

  6. 6
    Form: the signature rule does not bite L8

    A rule requiring writing signed by both parties is form: per the Giuliano-Lagarde Report, form is “every external manifestation required” of one expressing the will to be bound. Per AQCEL, meeting the form rules of either the proper law or the lex loci contractus is enough. Per Transniko, the lex fori places the contract where the acceptance is received: the reply was read in Singapore, so Singapore is the place of contracting (the wider Rome I list is not Singapore law). Singapore law has no signature rule. So even with Ruritanian law as the proper law, the contract is formally valid.

  7. 7
    “No action shall be brought”: procedure K2

    Per CIFG v Polimet, substance follows the lex causae and procedure the lex fori. Per Star City, a rule that bars only an “action” regulates enforcement, not the existence of the right, so it is procedural, as s 6 CLA is (per Leroux v Brown). A Ruritanian procedural rule is not applied by a Singapore court, and Singapore has no such rule, so Dorval loses here. Star City remains the law because Goh Suan Hee left the point open, so give Dorval the functional view in the alternative: the rule may then be substantive form. On that view the either-law rule still saves the contract, because it was made in Singapore.

  8. 8
    Capacity: two laws, then the consequences L9

    “Has no power” limits what Dorval can do, so it is capacity, not form or illegality: per Integral Petroleum a requirement of “real substance”, like a missing joint signature, is capacity. Per C&Y (Dicey r 162), a company needs capacity under both its law of incorporation and the proper law, so Ruritanian law applies whatever the proper law, and under it Dorval lacked capacity because no resolution was passed. Do not stop there. Per Haugesund Kommune, the proper law then decides the consequences, and under Ruritanian law the contract still binds because Quillon did not know of the limit. If Singapore law were the proper law, Quillon would already have lost at formation, so on these facts the capacity defence adds nothing for Dorval.

  9. 9
    Advice, and what not to write

    Quillon should recover the price. A contract was made under Ruritanian law, the putative proper law; it is formally valid under Singapore law as the place of contracting, and the “no action” rule is procedural anyway; and Dorval's lack of capacity does not undo it under Ruritanian law. Do not run illegality: the Code says how such a contract is made or sued on and does not forbid the sale, and the constitution's limit is capacity. Nothing turns on the 14 month delay, because no limitation period is given under either law. Dorval's sense of unfairness is not Singapore's fundamental public policy, which is narrower than domestic policy.

2Twist 1

🧩 TWIST 1

Now add one clause to the Supply Terms.

Suppose that the Supply Terms also contained clause 14:

“The courts of Singapore shall have jurisdiction over any dispute arising out of these terms.”

Dorval relies on clause 14 to say that Singapore law governs, so that no contract was ever made. How does your advice change?

✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • L5
    No clause: implied choice. There is still no governing law clause, but there is now a court clause. A chosen court is presumed to apply its own law, so this is a heavy pointer to an implied choice of Singapore law.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • N6
    Party autonomy: does the contract's chosen law govern the tort?. Tempting because of the words “any dispute arising out of”. Wrong because N6 is about a governing law clause reaching a tort claim. Clause 14 picks a court, and no tort is claimed.
  • L4
    Law chosen to dodge another country's rule. Tempting because Dorval uses Singapore law to escape a contract that Ruritanian law would enforce. Wrong because nothing suggests that clause 14 was put in to dodge any country's rule. It is in Quillon's own draft.

Fair to tick but not needed: L2 Express choice of law clause, L6 SCORECARD · Objective proper law: closest and most real connection, L7 Was a contract formed at all?

Application questions · twist 1

⚡ Twist 1 · 1 of 3L5
What does clause 14 do to the search for the proper law?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Pacific Recreation, submitting to the courts of a country implies a choice of that country's law. The contrast is the Hague Principles, under which such a clause is not in itself equivalent to a choice of law, so the opposing party urges stage 3. It is not an express choice of law.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C2.3.2 :: Jurisdiction / Arbitration Clause (heavy)

Per Pacific Recreation, submitting to [the courts of / arbitration in] [country Y] implies [law Y], the chosen forum being presumed to apply its own law.

  • Contrast: per Art 4 Hague Principles, [such a clause] is "not in itself equivalent to a choice of law", so [the opposing party] urges [Stage 3].
⚡ Twist 1 · 2 of 3L7
Clause 14 sits inside Supply Terms that Dorval says it never accepted. Can clause 14 still be used to find the law that governs formation?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

The putative proper law is found by applying the three-stage test to the negotiations and the transaction. The lex fori answer reaches Singapore law too, but for a reason Lew rejects: the lex fori has no role in formation.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C2.6 :: Putative Proper Law

As [the dispute] concerns existence, per Lew v Nargolwala a law agreed during negotiations governs (rare), failing which a JIO-style three-stage test applied to [the negotiations / transaction] finds the putative proper law, matching The Parouth and CIMB.

⚡ Twist 1 · 3 of 3L5
If the court finds an implied choice of Singapore law, what is the result, and what does Quillon say against it?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

An implied choice is as effective as an express one. So if Singapore law is implied, it is the putative proper law and formation fails. Quillon's route is to deny the inference and move to stage 3, where delivery, installation, training and the final payment point to Ruritania.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C2.3.1 :: Starter

Per Pacific Recreation, absent cl [X], a choice of [law Y] may be inferred from [the terms] and [the circumstances], weighing Las Vegas Hilton factors of differing weight. Per Enka v Chubb, an implied choice is as effective as an express one, and the Vita Food limits apply (C2.2.1).

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes, and what stays

    Clause 14 picks a court, not a law, so stage 1 still finds no express choice. What changes is stage 2: it now has a heavy pointer to Singapore law, and Dorval uses it to make Singapore law the putative proper law, under which the reply is not an acceptance. The form point stays answered for Quillon under either law, and the capacity analysis matters only if a contract survives. Clause 14 is not a governing law clause reaching a tort (no tort is claimed), and nothing shows it was put in to dodge any law: it is in Quillon's own draft.

  2. 2
    Clause 14 counts in the putative proper law L7

    Per Lew, formation is tested by the law that would govern if the contract existed, so the three stages run on the putative contract, clause 14 included. The alleged clause counts whichever party relies on it, and the lex fori gets no role in its place. So the question is whether clause 14 implies a choice of Singapore law.

  3. 3
    Implied choice: both routes L5

    Per Pacific Recreation, submitting to the courts of a country implies a choice of its law, because the chosen court is presumed to apply its own law; this is the weightiest stage 2 factor. Per Enka v Chubb, an implied choice is as effective as an express one. Dorval's route: Singapore law is the implied putative proper law, the reply is not an acceptance, and there is no contract. Quillon's route: per Art 4 of the Hague Principles a court clause is “not in itself equivalent to a choice of law”, so stage 3 decides; the clause still weighs for Singapore there, but performance on both sides is in Ruritania, so Ruritanian law governs and a contract was made. Pacific Recreation is on Dorval's side and Quillon's reply rests on the Hague contrast, so Quillon is now at real risk of losing at formation.

3Twist 2

🧩 TWIST 2

Go back to the base facts and change how the deal was made.

Suppose instead that Quillon's Supply Terms state: “Governed by Singapore law.” Dorval replied with its own purchase order, which states: “Governed by Ruritanian law.” Quillon began work without replying. The price, the units and the dates are the same in both documents.

ℹ ASSUME
  1. Under Singapore contract law, assume that where two forms conflict, neither form's choice of law clause becomes part of the contract. Under Ruritanian contract law, the last form sent prevails.
  2. Under both laws, a contract on the agreed price, units and dates was made when Quillon began work.
✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • L7
    Was a contract formed at all?. Two forms, two law clauses, and each law has its own rule on which form wins. Which clause was incorporated is a formation question with clashing putative laws.
  • L2
    Express choice of law clause. There are now express clauses, so the answer starts at stage 1. If one clause is held to be part of the contract, it is an express choice and is virtually conclusive.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • L3
    Floating or one-sided choice of law clause. Tempting because two laws are in play. Wrong because neither form has a floating clause. Each fixes one law. The question is which form's clause was incorporated.
  • L5
    No clause: implied choice. Tempting if neither clause survives. Wrong because nothing in the facts points to an implied choice, and parties who turned their minds to the governing law and failed do not get an inferred one. The answer goes straight to stage 3.

Fair to tick but not needed: L6 SCORECARD · Objective proper law: closest and most real connection, L9 Other attacks on the clause; capacity

Application questions · twist 2

⚡ Twist 2 · 1 of 3L7
Which choice of law clause, if either, is part of the contract?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Each clause may validate itself, and it makes no sense to choose between them by either putative law (Dornoch). On Yeo's mapping, the Ruritanian clause prevails under Ruritanian law (last form) while the Singapore clause fails under Singapore law, so only one clause validates itself. Under Art 6(1)(b) of the Hague Principles a clause applies only if its terms prevail under both laws, so there is no choice. Give the result under each route. Here Ruritanian law governs either way: by express choice on the mapping, and as the objective proper law on the Hague test.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C2.6 :: Battle of Forms: Clashing Putative Laws

[A]'s [law X clause] and [B]'s [law Y clause] may each validate themselves, and "it makes no sense to decide which one to choose by any putative law" (Dornoch).

  • Lex fori: The Heidberg and Dornoch applied [the lex fori], but Lew now bars [that fallback].
  • Putative OPL: per Prof Chong, rejected in The Heidberg as no more correct than [arbitrarily preferring one clause], so [party] needs [another tiebreak].
  • Yeo (deadlock overstated): map each law's [first shot / last shot / knock-out] rule; both clauses apply only where each validates itself; where neither survives, use [the putative OPL], then [the lex fori].
  • Art 6(1)(b) Hague Principles: [the law X clause] applies only if [its standard terms] prevail under both laws, else no choice.
⚡ Twist 2 · 2 of 3L7
Quillon argues that a Singapore court should simply apply Singapore's own rule on clashing forms to pick the clause. What is the answer?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

The lex fori was used in The Heidberg and Dornoch, but Lew now bars that fallback. Prof Chong and Teo argue that the lex fori should break battle of the forms ties. So the route has to get past Lew: say so before using it.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C2.6 :: Counter: Lex Fori

Per Lew, applying [the lex fori] regardless of [any connection to the forum] is "illogical" and defeats uniformity, so it has no role, even residually.

⚡ Twist 2 · 3 of 3L2
Suppose the court holds that the Ruritanian clause was incorporated. What follows?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Once a clause is incorporated it is an express choice. Per Peh Teck Quee it is virtually conclusive, subject only to the Vita Food limits, which the lex fori tests. The connecting facts are weighed only if no clause survives.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C2.2.1 :: Starter

Per Peh Teck Quee, applying Vita Food, cl [X]'s choice of [law X] is virtually conclusive unless not (a) bona fide, (b) legal, or (c) consistent with public policy, each tested by the lex fori on objective intention, so [D]'s claim not to have [seen the standard terms] is irrelevant.

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes, and what stays

    Each form now names a law, so the answer starts at stage 1, not stage 3. Formation of the contract itself is no longer in dispute: under both laws a contract on the agreed price, units and dates was made when Quillon began work. The question is which choice of law clause, if either, was incorporated, and the laws answer it differently: Singapore law knocks out both clauses, while Ruritanian law takes the last form sent, Dorval's purchase order. This is not a floating clause, because each form fixes one law. The capacity analysis is unchanged.

  2. 2
    Which clause? An open point L7

    Each clause may validate itself, and per Dornoch “it makes no sense to decide which one to choose by any putative law”. Route 1, Yeo's mapping: the Ruritanian clause wins under Ruritanian law, but the Singapore clause fails under Singapore law, so only the Ruritanian clause validates itself and Ruritanian law governs by express choice. Route 2, Art 6(1)(b) of the Hague Principles: a clause applies only if its terms prevail under both laws, and neither does, so there is no choice. The parties turned their minds to the law and failed, so no choice is inferred and the answer goes straight to stage 3, which gives Ruritanian law as in the base. So Ruritanian law governs on either route. Do not use the objective proper law to pick between two surviving clauses: per Prof Chong, The Heidberg rejected that tiebreak as no more correct than preferring one clause arbitrarily.

  3. 3
    The lex fori tiebreak must get past Lew L7

    Quillon may say a Singapore court should simply apply Singapore's own rule to pick the clause. The Heidberg and Dornoch did apply the lex fori, and Prof Chong and Teo argue that the forum should break battle of the forms ties. But Lew now bars the lex fori in formation, even as a fallback, so say so before using the route. Even on this route nothing changes: Singapore's rule knocks out both clauses, so the objective proper law, Ruritanian law, governs.

  4. 4
    If the Ruritanian clause is in L2

    An incorporated clause is an express choice. Per Peh Teck Quee, applying Vita Food, it is virtually conclusive unless it is not bona fide, not legal or against public policy, each tested by the lex fori. Ruritania is Dorval's home and the place where the units are installed, so nothing suggests evasion. Stage 3 is not reached, and the capacity analysis runs as in the base, with Ruritanian law as the proper law.

4Twist 3

🧩 TWIST 3

Go back to the base facts and add a later event.

In June 2025 Dorval emailed Quillon a “Change Notice”: “Add a third radar unit at the same unit price. This change forms part of our contract. It is agreed unless you object within seven days.” Quillon did not reply and built only two units.

Dorval now says, in the alternative, that if there is a contract Quillon broke it by not building the third unit. It counterclaims damages. Quillon answers that Singapore law protects a Singapore company from being bound by silence, whatever law governs.

ℹ ASSUME
  1. Under Ruritanian law, silence in reply to a written change between commercial parties is acceptance. Under Singapore law it is not.
✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • L7
    Was a contract formed at all?. A second formation question. Whether Quillon agreed to the third unit is for the putative proper law of the change, and the laws differ on silence. The grave injustice caveat is part of this box.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • K7
    A Singapore statute said to override the chosen law. Tempting because Quillon claims a Singapore rule that applies whatever law governs. Wrong because K7 needs a Singapore statute that Parliament meant to override the proper law. A common law rule on silence is not one.
  • K3
    Damages: head or quantum. Tempting because damages are claimed. Wrong because no law is said to deny or cap any head of loss. The only dispute is whether Quillon agreed to the third unit.

Fair to tick but not needed: K8 Forum public policy; renvoi, L6 SCORECARD · Objective proper law: closest and most real connection

Application questions · twist 3

⚡ Twist 3 · 1 of 3L7
Which law decides whether Quillon agreed to the third unit?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Formation is for the putative proper law, and the change is put forward as part of the main contract. The Hague Principles and Rome I rule on a party's own law is soft law for comparison only. The principle of validation is not used where formation itself is in dispute.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C2.6 :: Application

[The alleged express clause / prior dealings on law X terms / closest connection of the negotiations] identifies [law X], under which [the contract] [was / was not] formed because [silence constitutes acceptance / the offer was accepted].

  • Double bootstraps (Prof Chong): [law X] first decides whether [the law X clause] was incorporated, then whether [the contract] was formed.
⚡ Twist 3 · 2 of 3L7
Quillon says that it is gravely unjust to bind a Singapore company by its silence. How far does that take it?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

The caveat exists but is very narrow, and it does not bring in the lex fori. Quillon is also poorly placed to plead injustice: it chose to deal on terms whose closest connection is with Ruritania, and it relies on Ruritanian law itself for the main contract.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C2.6 :: Grave-Injustice Caveat

Where [law X] binds [D] by [silence], Lew left open "a very small caveat, very rarely applicable", whose effect is no contract under any law, not [the lex fori]; per C&Y, use [forum public policy] instead.

  • Cf soft law: Art 10(2) Rome I and Art 6(2) Hague Principles let [a party] rely on [its habitual residence / establishment law] to deny consent.
⚡ Twist 3 · 3 of 3L7
What is awkward about Quillon's position across the two formation questions?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

The party's preferred law changes from issue to issue, and a good answer says so. Under Ruritanian law Quillon wins the price and loses on the third unit. Under Singapore law there is no main contract at all.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C2.6 :: Putative Proper Law

As [the dispute] concerns existence, per Lew v Nargolwala a law agreed during negotiations governs (rare), failing which a JIO-style three-stage test applied to [the negotiations / transaction] finds the putative proper law, matching The Parouth and CIMB.

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes, and what stays

    The main contract stays as in the base: Ruritanian law governs, a contract was made, it is formally valid and it binds Dorval despite the capacity defect. What is new is a second formation question: did Quillon agree to the third unit by staying silent? The roles reverse, because Ruritanian law, which Quillon needs for the main contract, treats silence in reply to a written change between commercial parties as acceptance. The counterclaim raises no point on heads of loss, and Quillon's Singapore rule on silence is common law, not a statute that Parliament meant to override the proper law.

  2. 2
    The change takes the main contract's law L7

    Per Lew, formation is for the putative proper law. The Change Notice says it “forms part of our contract”, so its putative proper law is the main contract's law, Ruritanian law, and under it Quillon's silence was acceptance. So, subject to the caveat below, Quillon agreed to build a third unit and broke the contract by building only two. Not the lex fori (Lew gives it no role), not Quillon's home law (Art 6(2) of the Hague Principles and Art 10(2) of Rome I are soft law, for comparison only), and not whichever law upholds the change (per C&Y, the principle of validation does not apply where formation is disputed).

  3. 3
    The grave injustice caveat: open, but weak here L7

    Where the putative law binds a party by silence, Lew left open “a very small caveat, very rarely applicable”. Its effect is no contract under any law, not the lex fori; per C&Y, forum public policy is the tool to use instead, and that needs a breach of Singapore's fundamental policy, narrower than domestic policy. Quillon's route: being bound by silence is gravely unjust, so there is no agreement on the third unit and the counterclaim fails. Dorval's route: the caveat very rarely applies, and Quillon chose to deal on terms whose closest connection is with Ruritania and relies on Ruritanian law for the main contract. Result: Quillon is probably bound, so the counterclaim probably succeeds on liability.

  4. 4
    No separate law for each question L7

    Quillon's preferred law changes from issue to issue, and a good answer says so. Under Ruritanian law it wins the price but is bound to the third unit. Under Singapore law there is no main contract at all, because the reply was not an acceptance. A change that forms part of the contract takes the contract's law, so Quillon cannot take Ruritanian law for one and Singapore law for the other.

5Scorecards: weigh the factors

Prof Chong rewards applying facts to factor tests. Sort each fact, then answer the verdict question. These use the base facts unless a line says “Suppose”.

L6 Sort the factors: The objective proper law on the base facts

Each line is a connecting fact. Does it point to Singapore law or Ruritanian law at stage 3, or does it carry little weight? Lines marked “Suppose” are extra facts for this card only.

Quillon must deliver and install the units at Dorval's airfields in Ruritania and train staff there for 12 months.
Ruritania. The place of performance carries great weight, and this is the main performance under the contract. C2.4.3 :: Critique of "Equal Weight"
Half the price is payable in Ruritania when the units are commissioned.
Ruritania. With delivery and installation, this makes Ruritania a place where both parties perform. That is usually the strongest argument. C2.4.3 :: Application
Half the price is payable to Quillon's bank in Singapore before shipment.
Singapore. Part of Dorval's performance is in Singapore. It is a real pointer, though only half of one obligation. C2.4.3 :: Application
Quillon has its place of business and its workshop in Singapore, where the units are built.
Singapore. A party's place of business counts, and the building work is done there. C2.3.2 :: Residence, Business, Purpose
The Supply Terms are in English and the price is in US dollars.
Little weight. English is the lingua franca and the US dollar is a common trading currency. Neither points to any one country. C2.3.2 :: Language and Currency (little)
Dorval's staff who dealt with Quillon all live in Ruritania and would be its witnesses.
Little weight. Where witnesses live is a Spiliada factor for the forum question. It is irrelevant to the proper law unless tied to the contract itself. C2.4.2 :: Wrong Factors
Suppose: the parties had signed the Supply Terms at a trade fair in Utopia.
Little weight. The place of contracting matters little unless performance is also there. Nothing is performed in Utopia. C2.3.2 :: Residence, Business, Purpose
Suppose: the warranty in the Supply Terms is the “Ruritanian Aviation Standard” warranty, a term of art known only to Ruritanian law.
Ruritania. Terms of art peculiar to one legal system are a strong pointer to that system. C2.3.2 :: Standard Form / Terms of Art (strong)
Suppose: a spare parts contract between the same parties, signed the same day and referred to in the Supply Terms, is governed by Singapore law.
Singapore. A closely related contract can be decisive. A contract that the Supply Terms refer to and that was made with them is closely related. C2.3.2 :: Related Contract (can be decisive)
⚡ Scorecard 1 · the verdictL6
On the base facts alone (no “Suppose” lines), which law is the objective proper law?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Singapore has real connections: Quillon's business, the building work and half the price. But the main performance on both sides is in Ruritania. Courts do not declare ties (Lew), and the forum's law gets no preference. Ruritanian law is then the putative proper law for formation, and under it a contract was made.

6Remember

🧠 FOR THE EXAM
  • Split formation, form and capacity before naming any law: each has its own choice of law rule.
  • Formation goes to the putative proper law (Lew), not the place of contracting, and the lex fori only as an argument against Lew; a change that forms part of the contract takes the same law.
  • Form is valid under either the proper law or the place of contracting, which is where the acceptance is received (AQCEL; Transniko); a “no action” rule is procedural on Star City, with the functional view in the alternative.
  • Company capacity needs both the law of incorporation and the proper law, and the proper law then decides the consequences (Haugesund): never stop at “no capacity”.
  • A court clause is a heavy pointer to an implied choice of that court's law, not an express choice (Pacific Recreation; contrast Art 4 Hague Principles).
  • Clashing law clauses are open: run Yeo's mapping and Art 6(1)(b) of the Hague Principles with a result under each, and say that a lex fori tiebreak must get past Lew.

LAW302 · META GAME · QUESTION 2 · HYPO q2-05 · GEMINI PROMPT V1 · 17 QUESTIONS

Xanthe v Norvik, Ibis and Mr Thorne

Written by Claude for the drill and law reviewed. Gemini (prompt v1) rebalanced the option lengths and wrote a note on each question; both were checked (1 corrections) and feed the notes here.

Answers:

1Base facts

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Xanthe v Norvik, Ibis and Mr Thorne

Xanthe Games Pte Ltd is a Singapore incorporated studio that runs an online game. It books all its revenue in Singapore, but most of its players are in Utopia. The game runs on servers in a data centre in Ruritania. Norvik Cloud Ltd, an Elbonian company, maintains those servers for the data centre's owner. Norvik has no contract with Xanthe.

In March 2026 Norvik's engineers, working at its office in Elbonia, wrote and sent out a faulty software update. It wiped the saved games on the servers in Ruritania. Thousands of players left the game.

Ibis Interactive Inc is a rival studio incorporated in Utopia. At a trade fair in Suburbia, Ibis agreed to pay Mr Thorne, a Norvik engineer who lives in Elbonia, to slow Xanthe's servers during its June launch. Taking the payment was a crime under Elbonian law. Mr Thorne slowed the servers from his desk in Elbonia. In the same week Ibis ran adverts in Utopia that invited Xanthe's players to switch. Many did.

Xanthe sues in the General Division. It claims damages from Norvik for negligence, and from Ibis and Mr Thorne for conspiracy. Xanthe's lawyers say that a law which lets a careless contractor walk away is unjust and should simply be ignored. Assume that the court has jurisdiction over all three defendants.

Advise Xanthe on the law that governs each claim, and on whether each claim will succeed.

ℹ ASSUME
  1. Under Singapore law Norvik owed Xanthe a duty of care and broke it, and Ibis and Mr Thorne are liable for conspiracy.
  2. Under Ruritanian law Norvik is also liable. Under Elbonian law a contractor owes no duty of care to a person with whom it has no contract.
  3. Conspiracy is a tort under Utopian and Elbonian law. Suburbian law has no such tort.
  4. Under every relevant law, a claim in tort must be brought within three years.
  5. Both sides have filed expert reports on all the foreign laws.
✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • N1
    Starter: double actionability. Two tort claims, so two runs of double actionability with the flexible exception. Each defendant bears the burden on limb 2 for the claim against it.
  • N2
    Limb 1: a tort under Singapore law. Limb 1 in one line for each claim. Nothing was done in Singapore, so use the test properly: would the acts be a tort if they had all been done here?
  • N3
    SCORECARD · Locate the tort: where in substance did it arise?. Both torts cross borders. Negligence: act in Elbonia, damage in Ruritania, loss booked in Singapore. Conspiracy: agreed in Suburbia, carried out from Elbonia and in Utopia. Each has its own locating rule.
  • N4
    Limb 2 applied: is there liability under the law of that place?. The laws differ. Elbonian law gives no duty of care, and Suburbian law has no tort of conspiracy. Whether limb 2 fails depends on where each tort is located.
  • N5
    SCORECARD · The flexible exception. Always finish with the exception. Xanthe needs it if the negligence is located in Elbonia, and must show that Elbonia is there by accident.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • N9
    Tort committed in Singapore. Tempting because Xanthe is a Singapore company and books its loss here. But N9 is for a tort whose every element happened in Singapore. Loss felt at the home base does not locate a tort.
  • M1
    Illegality: pick the route. A crime under a foreign law looks like illegality. The illegality boxes are about enforcing a contract. No one sues on the agreement between Ibis and Mr Thorne. The crime is only the unlawful means of the conspiracy.
  • K8
    Forum public policy; renvoi. This is the tempting wrong doctrine. A foreign rule that merely differs from Singapore law is not against fundamental public policy, and public policy is not a ground for the flexible exception. The argument must be put as fortuity under N5.
  • K5
    Limitation periods. A limitation point needs periods that differ. Every law gives three years and Xanthe sued within months, so nothing turns on which period applies.
  • K6
    Foreign law not pleaded, or not proved. K6 is for foreign law that is not pleaded or not proved. Here every foreign law is pleaded and proved by experts.

Fair to tick but not needed: K1 Characterise the issue

Application questions · base facts

⚡ Base facts · 1 of 7N1
How many times must the double actionability rule be run?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

The rule is applied to each tort claim. The issue is which law governs each claim arising from its own acts, so negligence and conspiracy are located separately and may end under different laws. Collapsing two claims into one answer is a common way to lose marks.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Rickshaw, a tort claim is governed by double actionability subject to a flexible exception (Boys v Chaplin; Red Sea). The rule is applied to each claim on its own. Each claim is located by the rule for that tort: the careless act for negligence (Vibrant Group), a weighing of factors for conspiracy (EFT Holdings). Per EFT Holdings, Xanthe proves limb 1 on each claim, and the defendants must plead and prove that the law of the place of their tort gives no liability. Collapsing the two claims into one answer is a common way to lose marks.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C3.1.1 :: Global Starter

The issue is which law governs [claimant]'s claim for [negligence / misrepresentation / conspiracy / defamation / conversion] arising from [acts] in [country X]. Per Rickshaw, it is double actionability subject to a flexible exception (Boys v Chaplin; Red Sea).

⚡ Base facts · 2 of 7N2
Mr Thorne says limb 1 fails, because nothing he did took place in Singapore. Is he right?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per IM Skaugen, limb 1 is a counterfactual test: suppose all the acts were done in Singapore, and ask whether they would be a tort. No real link with Singapore is needed. That is why the lex fori limb is called parochial.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per IM Skaugen, limb 1 asks whether the acts, if all done in Singapore, would be a tort under Singapore law. It tests Singapore's elements of the tort, not any real link with Singapore, which is why the lex fori limb is criticised as parochial. Where the acts really happened matters at limb 2, when the tort is located, and under the exception. The Assume list makes Ibis and Mr Thorne liable for conspiracy, and Norvik for negligence, under Singapore law, so limb 1 is met on both claims.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C3.2 :: Counterfactual Test

Per IM Skaugen, ask whether [the acts], if all done in Singapore, would be [a tort, e.g., Spandeck duty, breach, causation, damage], so limb 1 [is satisfied / fails].

⚡ Base facts · 3 of 7N3
The update was written and sent in Elbonia. It destroyed data in Ruritania. The loss shows in accounts in Singapore. Where was the negligence most likely committed?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Vibrant Group, for negligence the place of the negligent act prevails, and careless services are located where they were rendered. The place of damage may be quite fortuitous (Distillers), and loss at the home base does not locate a tort. The test finds one single place. Give the result each way: Elbonia, limb 2 fails; Ruritania, Norvik is liable.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Distillers and Metall, the court looks back over the events and asks where in substance the cause of action arose, finding one single place. Per Vibrant Group, the weight of each element depends on the tort pleaded, and for negligence the place of the negligent act prevails, so the place where the update was written and sent counts most. Per Distillers, the place of damage may be quite fortuitous, and the loss shown in Xanthe's Singapore accounts does not by itself locate the tort. Result each way: Elbonia, limb 2 fails because Elbonian law gives no duty; Ruritania, Norvik is liable under both limbs.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C3.3.2 :: Negligence: Focus on the Act

Per Vibrant Group, the place of [the negligent act] prevails, so [the audit / advice] performed in [country X] locates the tort there despite [reliance and loss] in Singapore.

  • Negligent services / advice: where [the services] were or ought to have been [rendered] (Voth).
  • Trading decisions: where [the decision to speculate] was made, e.g. [Moscow] (Base Metal Trading).
  • Product liability: where [the product] was [marketed without the warning], not where [it was made] or [the damage] occurred (Distillers; Castree v Squibb).
  • Reliance weighs less: in [negligence], reliance is only one route to [a duty] (NTUC Foodfare; Vibrant).
⚡ Base facts · 4 of 7N4
Suppose the negligence was committed in Elbonia. Norvik would be liable under Ruritanian law. What follows?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Limb 2 looks to one foreign law only: the law of the place where the tort was in substance committed. If that is Elbonia, there is no civil liability between Norvik and Xanthe, so Norvik escapes unless Elbonian law is displaced. The exception can displace the lex fori, the law of the place of the tort, or both.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Lord Wilberforce in Boys v Chaplin, limb 2 asks whether the law of the place of the tort gives civil liability between the actual parties, and it fails where that law imposes none between them. If the negligence was committed in Elbonia, Norvik escapes unless Elbonian law is displaced. Ruritanian law counts only if Ruritania is the place of the tort; otherwise Ruritania, where the damage was done, is at most a factor under the exception. Per Rickshaw, the exception may displace the lex fori, the law of the place of the tort, or both, so Xanthe's next step is to argue that Elbonia is fortuitous.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C3.3.3 :: Limb 2 Fails Where

[law X] [bars the head / provides a defence] or imposes no liability between [these parties] (Lord Wilberforce, Boys v Chaplin), so [defendant] escapes unless [law X] is displaced (C3.6.3).

⚡ Base facts · 5 of 7N5
Xanthe asks the court to displace Elbonian law under the flexible exception. Will it?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Rickshaw, the exception must be strictly applied. The party needs clear fortuity, not a more favourable law. Injustice means applying a law that is there by chance, not “my client loses”. Elbonia is where the defendant is based and where it acted.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Rickshaw, courts must not be quick to apply the exception: the displaced law must be purely fortuitous, on “clear and satisfying grounds” (Lord Wilberforce), and the exception must be strictly applied, so a party needs clear fortuity, not a more favourable law. Whether injustice is a separate requirement is unclear, but per C&Y applying a fortuitous law is itself the injustice, so fortuity is the real test. Elbonia is where Norvik is incorporated and where the careless work was done, so it is not there by accident. Xanthe's plea that the rule is unjust fails as well: public policy is not a ground for the exception, and a rule that merely differs from Singapore law does not offend fundamental public policy.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C3.6.1 :: Strictly Applied

per Rickshaw, it is "imperative" that [the exception] be strictly applied, favouring certainty over flexibility, so [party] needs [clear fortuity], not [a more favourable law].

⚡ Base facts · 6 of 7N3
Ibis and Mr Thorne say the conspiracy was committed in Suburbia, where they made their agreement. Is that right?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per EFT Holdings, conspiracy is located by weighing a list of factors, not by one element. Neither conspirator lives in Suburbia, nothing was done there and no loss arose there. A meeting at a trade fair is close to an accident. The Metall rule for inducing breach of contract is a different rule for a different tort.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per EFT Holdings, the court weighs the conspirators' identity and location, where they combined, the concerted acts, the claimant's location and where the losses arose; in EFT itself Taiwan prevailed. Here the conspirators are in Utopia (Ibis) and Elbonia (Mr Thorne), the concerted acts were the slowing from Elbonia and the adverts in Utopia, and the players were lost in Utopia. Suburbia has only an agreement made at a trade fair that neither conspirator lives near, which is close to an accident. Metall's rule, the place where a contract was broken, is for inducing breach of contract, not conspiracy.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C3.3.2 :: Conspiracy

Per EFT Holdings, weigh [the conspirators' identity and location], where [they combined], [the concerted acts], [claimant]'s location and [where losses arose], as in EFT where [Taiwan] prevailed.

  • Parasitic conspiracy: one "so intimately connected" to [a contract] may follow [its law] without being located (Chen v BHNV; C3.6.5).
⚡ Base facts · 7 of 7N4
On that weighing, the conspiracy was committed in Utopia or in Elbonia. Does it matter which?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Limb 2 is satisfied if the law of the place of the tort gives some civil remedy for the conduct. Utopian and Elbonian law both do. Where the result is the same under each candidate, say so and move on. Do not spend words choosing between them.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Limb 2 is satisfied if the law of the place of the tort gives some civil remedy for the conduct, and per EFT Holdings it is the defendants who must plead and prove that it does not. Utopian and Elbonian law both treat conspiracy as a tort, so the result is the same whichever place wins: say so in a line and move on. Mr Thorne's crime under Elbonian law does not change this: it is only the unlawful means of the conspiracy, Elbonian law still treats the conspiracy as a tort, and no one sues on the agreement to pay him.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C3.3.3 :: Applying Limb 2

Limb 2 is satisfied if [law X] gives [some civil remedy] for [the conduct].

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
⚡ BIG IDEA

Two cross-border torts, each run through double actionability on its own and each located by its own rule. The negligence is located by the careless act, so Elbonia is the likely place and limb 2 fails there (on Xanthe's Ruritania reply, Norvik is liable), and the flexible exception is unlikely to rescue Xanthe: Elbonia is Norvik's home, not an accident, and an “unjust” foreign rule is no ground for it. The conspiracy is located by weighing the EFT Holdings list, and since Utopia and Elbonia both treat it as a tort, it does not matter which wins. The move that decides it: locate first, then apply the law of that place, then ask whether that place is purely fortuitous.

  1. 1
    Two torts, two runs of the rule N1

    Both claims are tort claims. Per Rickshaw, each is governed by double actionability subject to a flexible exception (Boys v Chaplin; Red Sea): the wrong must be a tort under Singapore law and give civil liability between the actual parties under the law of the place of the tort. So run the rule twice, once for negligence against Norvik and once for conspiracy against Ibis and Mr Thorne, and locate each tort by its own rule. Per EFT Holdings, Xanthe proves limb 1, and each defendant must plead and prove that the law of the place of its tort gives no liability. Limitation does not matter, as every law gives the same three years, so nothing turns on which period applies, and every foreign law is proved by experts.

  2. 2
    Limb 1 for both claims N2

    Per IM Skaugen, limb 1 is counterfactual: if all the acts had been done in Singapore, would they be a tort? Nothing was done here, but no real link with Singapore is needed. The Assume list says that under Singapore law Norvik owed Xanthe a duty of care and broke it, and Ibis and Mr Thorne are liable for conspiracy. So limb 1 is met for both claims.

  3. 3
    Locate the negligence: the act prevails N3

    Per Distillers and Metall, ask where in substance the cause of action arose, and find one single place. The update was written and sent in Elbonia, the saved games were wiped in Ruritania, and the loss shows in Xanthe's accounts in Singapore. Per Vibrant Group, for negligence the place of the careless act prevails, so Elbonia is the likely place. Xanthe's best reply is Ruritania, where the damage was done. Singapore is not a candidate: per Distillers the place of damage may be quite fortuitous, and loss at the claimant's home base does not by itself locate a tort.

  4. 4
    Limb 2 for the negligence: both routes N4

    Limb 2 fails where the law of the place of the tort imposes no liability between these parties (Lord Wilberforce, Boys v Chaplin). Route 1, Elbonia: Elbonian law gives a contractor no duty to a person it has no contract with, so limb 2 fails and Norvik escapes unless Elbonian law is displaced; Ruritanian law is not a limb on this route. Route 2, Ruritania: Ruritanian law makes Norvik liable, so both limbs are met and the claim succeeds.

  5. 5
    The exception is unlikely to save the negligence claim N5

    Per Rickshaw, the exception may displace the lex fori, the law of the place of the tort, or both, but courts must not be quick to use it: the displaced law must be purely fortuitous and applying it must cause injustice, on “clear and satisfying grounds”, and the exception is strictly applied. Elbonia is where Norvik is incorporated and where its engineers did the careless work, so it is not there by accident, and a kinder law in Ruritania or Singapore is no ground. Xanthe's plea that the Elbonian rule is unjust and should be ignored fails too: public policy is not a ground for the exception, and a rule that merely differs from Singapore law does not offend fundamental public policy. Result: on route 1 the negligence claim probably fails; on route 2 it succeeds.

  6. 6
    Locate the conspiracy: weigh the list N3

    Per EFT Holdings, weigh the conspirators' identity and location, where they combined, the concerted acts, the claimant's location and where the losses arose. Ibis is based in Utopia and ran its adverts there, where the players were lost; Mr Thorne lives in Elbonia and slowed the servers from there. Suburbia has only the agreement, made at a trade fair neither lives near, which is close to an accident, and Xanthe's books in Singapore carry little weight. So the conspiracy was committed in Utopia, or else Elbonia. Metall's rule, the place where a contract was broken, is for inducing breach of contract, not conspiracy.

  7. 7
    Limb 2 for the conspiracy, and the result N4N5

    Limb 2 is satisfied if the law of the place of the tort gives some civil remedy for the conduct. Conspiracy is a tort under both Utopian and Elbonian law, so limb 2 is met whichever place wins: say so and move on, as only Suburbia would have defeated it. Mr Thorne's crime under Elbonian law is only the unlawful means of the conspiracy; no one sues on the agreement to pay him, so the illegality rules, which are about enforcing a contract, do not arise. Neither Utopia nor Elbonia is fortuitous, so the exception changes nothing, and Ibis and Mr Thorne are liable.

Application questions · twist 1

⚡ Twist 1 · 1 of 3N10
Where was the defamation committed?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Low Tuck Kwong, the tort is where the statement is published, and each publication is a separate tort. For internet material that is where it is downloaded and accessed (Dow Jones v Gutnick), not where it was uploaded or hosted. Result: Singapore readings, liable; Ruritanian readings, liable under both limbs; Utopian readings, limb 2 fails because a company cannot sue.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Low Tuck Kwong, double actionability applies to defamation, the tort is committed where the statement is published, and each publication is a separate tort. Per Dow Jones v Gutnick and Qingdao Bohai, internet material is published where it is downloaded and accessed; Gutnick rejected the publisher's argument for the law of the server's place. So typing the post in Singapore and hosting it in Suburbia locate nothing. Results: Singapore readings, a local tort, liable; Ruritanian readings, liable under both limbs; Utopian readings, limb 2 fails because under Utopian law a company cannot sue.

Can the court order the post to be taken down?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Traditional view: the court grants only its own remedies, so Singapore law decides (Phrantzes v Argenti; Shanghai Electric). Modern view: it is untenable to separate remedy from rights, so the lex causae decides whether and what kind of remedy lies (Goh Suan Hee). For the Singapore readings both views lead to Singapore law. For the Ruritanian readings they part, because Ruritanian law gives damages only. For the Utopian readings there is no right to protect at all.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

For the Singapore readings both views lead to Singapore law, which gives a take down order. For the Ruritanian readings they part, because Ruritanian law awards damages only; C&Y's synthesis, under which the lex causae decides entitlement, lands with the modern view here. The Utopian readings are not torts at all, so there is no right to protect.

⚡ Twist 2 · 1 of 3K3
Without the exception, can Xanthe recover its lost profits?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Boys v Chaplin and Harding v Wealands, heads of damage are substantive, so in tort the head must exist under both laws. Absent displacement the claimant recovers only the common ground, as in McElroy v McAllister. Whether loss of profits is recoverable is a head, not an amount.

🔎 More depth (Gemini's note, checked)

Per Boys v Chaplin and Harding v Wealands, heads of loss are substantive, while quantum is traditionally procedural (open after Goh Suan Hee). In tort a head must therefore exist under both Singapore law and the law of the place of the tort, and absent displacement the claimant recovers only what both laws allow, as the widow in McElroy v McAllister got only funeral expenses. Loss of profits is a head of its own, not a larger amount of the restoration cost, so Elbonian law's refusal of it bites unless the exception displaces Elbonian law on that issue.

In Boys v Chaplin, British servicemen collided in Malta, and per Lord Wilberforce Malta had no interest in applying its special-damages-only rule to non-residents, so it yielded on that head.
