1Base facts

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Pandan Coldchain v Valen Compressors

Pandan Coldchain Pte Ltd (“Pandan”), a Singapore company, runs cold-storage warehouses in Jurong. Valen Compressors SA (“Valen”) is incorporated in Ruritania, where it makes industrial chillers. Valen has never registered in Singapore under the Companies Act.

Valen leases an office in Ubi, Singapore, where Mr Quek, a Singapore resident paid a fixed monthly salary by Valen, manages Valen's Singapore sales and servicing, has authority to bind Valen to contracts, and negotiated Valen's contracts with Pandan.

Under a Supply Contract signed in April 2025, Valen agreed to build 40 chillers at its Ruritanian plant, ship them from Port Ruri, and install them at Pandan's Jurong warehouse, with Pandan paying S$800,000 in Singapore dollars into Valen's Singapore bank account. The contract has no governing law or jurisdiction clause.

In August 2025, Valen installed 10 chillers in Jurong. They leaked refrigerant owing to a design error made in Ruritania, ruining S$300,000 of Pandan's stored goods in Singapore.

In September 2025, the parties signed a Calibration Contract, expressly governed by Ruritanian law, for Valen to service Pandan's older chillers in Singapore for S$150,000.

In October 2025, Ruritania banned the export of industrial chillers from Ruritania. Valen refused to deliver the remaining 30 chillers or perform the Calibration Contract.

Pandan obtained permission and served the originating claim on Mr Quek at the Ubi office under O 7 r 4 ROC 2021, suing Valen for breach of both contracts and negligence. Valen applies to stay the Singapore action on forum non conveniens grounds. Valen's design engineers live in Ruritania.

Advise Pandan on whether the Singapore court has and will exercise jurisdiction, and on its prospects on the merits.

ℹ ASSUME
  1. Under Singapore contract law, Valen could fulfil the Supply Contract from its Malaysian plant; under Ruritanian law, the export ban discharges it.
  2. Under Ruritanian law, the export ban taints the Calibration Contract; under Singapore law, it does not.
  3. Under Ruritanian tort law, a manufacturer owes no duty of care to a commercial buyer for defective goods. Under Singapore law, Valen is liable in negligence.
  4. Ruritanian courts take six years to reach trial against 12 months in Singapore, and both courts have video-conferencing facilities.

⚡ BIG IDEA

Valen never registered but trades from an office in Ubi, so the first move is Adams v Cape presence, not s 376, and then a Spiliada stay with the burden on Valen. On the merits, the export ban, the tainting plea and the negligence claim each turn on an open point (the Ralli reading, which law tests tainting, and where a product tort happens), so the deciding skill is to run both routes and give a result under each. The twists add a Singapore non-exclusive clause, which puts strong cause on Valen for the stay but leaves Pandan only a vexation anti-suit injunction, and then a Ruritanian judgment whose effect hinges on whether a stay application abroad was submission.

  1. 1
    Existence: s 376 fails, so prove presence D2

    Valen never registered, so it has no registered office or authorised representative here (both are lodged on registration under s 368), and per C&Y s 376(a) and (b) fail, while s 376(c) is not meant for a company still trading here; so Pandan relies on s 16(1)(a)(i) SCJA and must prove Adams v Cape presence. Valen has traded from a fixed office it leases in Ubi since at least the April 2025 negotiations, and Mr Quek runs Valen's business there, not his own, on a fixed salary (Okura), and he can bind Valen to contracts (Adams v Cape), so Valen is present. Service on him under O 7 r 4 meets Rosenberg: he can contract for Valen, and the action relates to the contracts he negotiated and the servicing he manages. Which limb r 4 rests on is open: per Chong (mid-term feedback), in line with Beranek, limb (i), so Mr Quek is only the mode of service; per Yeo, limb (ii), with his control as the nexus. On either view jurisdiction exists, as Valen is present and Pandan had permission. Flag in one line Chong's unresolved query: if Valen is present, how is it “absent” under r 4(a)?

  2. 2
    The stay: Spiliada, stage 1 on Valen E2

    There is no jurisdiction clause, so no one breaks a promise and the test is Spiliada, not strong cause. Valen was served in Singapore, through Mr Quek under O 7 r 4 with permission, so jurisdiction exists and Valen may only seek a stay. Per Zoom, after service in the defendant bears the burden: per Spiliada and JIO, Valen bears the legal burden at stage 1 to show that Ruritania, its home and plainly available, is clearly or distinctly more appropriate, and Pandan bears stage 2. That Valen is foreign does not shift the burden, since the claimant bears it only on service out.

  3. 3
    Spiliada stages 1 and 2 E4E5

    Stage 1 weighs the quality of the links, not their number (JIO; Rappo). Valen's engineers are its own employees and both courts have video-link, so their location carries little weight (JIO; Chong's feedback), and Valen itself does business here through its Ubi office (JIO). The place of the tort is open (Ruritania for the design, Singapore for marketing and installation), and the governing law is split, the Supply Contract arguably under Singapore law and the Calibration Contract under Ruritanian law, so that factor is reduced or neutral (C&Y). On such mixed factors Valen will struggle to show that Ruritania is clearly more appropriate, and finely balanced factors mean no stay (JIO; C&Y). Even if it did, stage 2 would not save Pandan: refusing a stay is then “at least unusual” (Rotary), delay is disregarded unless egregious (alleged delays of over 10 years failed in Grains and Industrial), and no tort duty in Ruritania is a narrower remedy, which is not decisive (The Rainbow Joy).

    Proper law of the Supply Contract L6

    The Supply Contract has no governing law or jurisdiction clause and nothing shows an implied choice, so per Bonython the court asks which law has the closest and most real connection. Per Prof Chong, the strongest argument is usually where both parties perform: Valen installs the chillers in Jurong, and Pandan pays in Singapore dollars into Valen's Singapore account. Manufacture in Ruritania and shipment from Port Ruri pull the other way, while where witnesses live is a Spiliada factor, not a proper law factor (Prof Chong). The Calibration Contract's Ruritanian law clause came five months later, and the proper law is fixed at contracting (Las Vegas Hilton), so it does not count. Courts do not declare ties (Lew), so Singapore law is the likely, though arguable, objective proper law.

  5. 5
    The export ban: run all three Ralli readings M5

    Foster does not arise, as the ban came after the April 2025 signing and no one intended to break it at formation (Magdeev), and Lemenda is for foreign public policy, not written law. The contract requires shipment from Port Ruri, and the ban makes that act illegal there, so Ralli is engaged, but only “in so far as” performance is illegal: that points to the 30 chillers still to be shipped, not the 10 installed before the ban, though per C&Y Esben leaves unclear whether the whole contract or only part falls. On Esben's independent rule (start here; per Prof Chong arguably preferable as the later SGCA ruling), which catches a supervening ban, Valen's obligation is unenforceable. On the frustration reading (Peh Teck Quee), the proper law decides: under Singapore law, the likely proper law, Valen could supply from its Malaysian plant and is liable, while under Ruritanian law the ban discharges the contract. The third reading, comity abstention, rests only on dicta (Toprak; Magdeev), and per Peh Teck Quee Ralli has “nothing to do with” public policy. Pandan should press the frustration reading, citing Chong's point (seminar) that Esben's reading gives an odd result for a Singapore buyer.

  6. 6
    Calibration Contract: tainting M6

    Valen says the ban taints the Calibration Contract, which Ruritanian law expressly governs. Per Euro-Diam, Step 1 asks whether there is a relevant foreign illegality: no one exported in breach of the ban, so per Surewin the Supply Contract counts only if Singapore would refuse to enforce it. That holds on Esben's reading of Ralli, and on the frustration reading if Ruritanian law governs the Supply Contract (a prohibition at the place of performance can be serious enough: Ryder Industries), but not on the frustration reading if Singapore law governs it, which would end the plea at Step 1. Step 2 asks whether the illegality is sufficiently connected to the claim, and which law's principles decide is unresolved. Per Prof Chong, if tainting is part of the lex fori, Singapore's principles decide (proportionality, per Ting Siew May) and, per the Assume list, there is no taint; if it is part of the proper law, that law's principles decide, here Ruritanian law, and the claim is tainted. Per Chong (seminar), that is the proper law of the Calibration Contract sued on, not of the Supply Contract.

  7. 7
    Negligence: where is the tort? N3

    Per Rickshaw, the negligence claim needs double actionability, subject to the flexible exception, and limb 1 is met because Valen is liable in negligence under Singapore law. For limb 2 the tort must be located by the substance test (Distillers), and here that is open. Per Vibrant Group, negligence focuses on the act, and the design error was made in Ruritania, where a manufacturer owes a commercial buyer no duty, so on that route limb 2 fails. But for a defective product, Distillers and Castree v Squibb look to where it was marketed, not where it was made, and Valen sold through its Ubi office and installed the chillers in Jurong. On that route the tort is in Singapore, both limbs point to Singapore law (Rickshaw), and Pandan succeeds in tort.

  8. 8
    If the tort is in Ruritania: the exception N5

    On the act route, Pandan must displace Ruritanian law. Per Rickshaw, the exception is strictly applied and works only if the displaced law is purely fortuitous, on clear and satisfying grounds, and a less favourable law is no ground. Ruritania is where Valen is incorporated and designed the chillers, so it is not there by accident. Pandan's best argument is that the tort is intimately connected with the Supply Contract, arguably governed by Singapore law, so that law applies through the exception (C&Y, citing Chen v BHNV). But Chen was a forum non conveniens ruling that did not run Rickshaw's fortuity test, so it is an analogy only, and the exception probably fails, leaving Pandan with no tort claim on this route.

  9. 9
    Advice to Pandan

    Jurisdiction exists, as Valen is present through its Ubi office, and a stay is unlikely on these mixed factors. On the Supply Contract, if Singapore law is the proper law, as is likely, Pandan wins on the frustration reading of Ralli but loses its claim for the 30 undelivered chillers on Esben's reading; if Ruritanian law governs, that claim fails on both main readings. The Calibration Contract claim survives if Step 1 fails or tainting runs through the lex fori, but is tainted if it runs through Ruritanian law as the proper law. In negligence, Pandan wins if the tort is in Singapore and probably loses if it is in Ruritania, as the exception likely fails there.

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes and what stays

    Clause 18 gives the Supply Contract a Singapore non-exclusive clause, and Valen, after applying for a stay here, sues Pandan in Ruritania for S$200,000 for the first 10 chillers and a declaration of non-liability. Jurisdiction over Valen exists as before, and the merits run as before, though clause 18 now also points to Singapore law for the Supply Contract (per Pacific Recreation, submitting to a country's courts implies its law). What changes is the test for the stay, and there is a new question: can Pandan restrain the Ruritanian action? Clause 18 was agreed in April 2025, after the Convention entered into force for Singapore on 1 October 2016, but it expressly says “non-exclusive”, so s 3(2) deeming cannot apply, the CCAA is out and the common law governs.

  2. 2
    The stay: strong cause on Valen A4E7

    Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), Singapore takes the contractual approach, not the general approach under which a non-exclusive clause is only a Spiliada factor. Under Singapore law, the Supply Contract's likely proper law, “submits” means Valen consented to Singapore's jurisdiction and waived any objection to its exercise; if Ruritanian law governed, the presumption of similarity reads in the same waiver unless Ruritanian law is proved to imply none, in which case Spiliada applies. Valen's stay application tries to escape that promise, so per Vinmar it must show strong cause, which per Shanghai Turbo means the same for a non-exclusive clause. Foreseeable factors such as witnesses in Ruritania carry little weight, related foreign proceedings were not enough in Shanghai Turbo, and nothing shows abuse or a denial of justice, so Valen will likely fail. The negligence claim is likely within clause 18, as it arises “in connection with” the Supply Contract (Fiona Trust, applied in Trisuryo and Bunge). The Calibration Contract claim is arguably outside, being a later contract on other chillers with its own Ruritanian law clause and so probably not one package under Allianz, and if so Spiliada governs it as in the base facts.

  3. 3
    Anti-suit injunction: no breach, so vexation G1G4

    Per SNIA and Lakshmi, an anti-suit injunction issues only where the ends of justice require it, with caution, and Pandan bears the burden and must name its basis, contractual or vexation, as the elements differ (Cooperative Muratori). Per Shanghai Turbo and C&Y, suing abroad is not ordinarily a breach of a Singapore non-exclusive clause, the parties having accepted parallel proceedings; only a challenge to Singapore's jurisdiction, like Valen's stay application, breaks it. The arguable breach route needs a foreign order or declaration sought to stop the Singapore action, but Valen's declaration of non-liability is a claim on the merits and the Assume list says it has sought no restraining order. So Pandan cannot use the contractual basis and must run vexation. Valen is amenable, having been validly served here, and clause 18 arguably supplies Singapore's sufficient interest (Shanghai Turbo; C&Y); otherwise Pandan must show that Singapore is the natural forum.

  4. 4
    Vexation and injustice to Valen G7

    Per Kirkham and UBS v Telesto, a vexation injunction issues only in the clearest of circumstances, and parallel proceedings with the risk of conflicting judgments are not enough alone, especially under a non-exclusive clause. Pandan's best “something more” is timing: Valen sued in Ruritania two weeks after applying for a stay here, for a price claim that could have been a counterclaim in Singapore (Lakshmi). PT Sandipala helps less, as the Singapore action is not far advanced. Against that, per SNIA the court weighs Valen's loss of its Ruritanian advantages, such as the discharge defence, against the injustice to Pandan, and per UBS v Telesto such an advantage counts for less if Ruritania is not the natural forum. The Ruritanian action is only three weeks old with no defence filed, which points towards the injunction. So if the court sees Valen's suit as filed without good reason just after the Singapore action, instead of a counterclaim here (Lakshmi), the injunction likely issues; if it sees only the parallel proceedings that clause 18 accepted (UBS v Telesto), it is refused, and Pandan falls back on a stay application in Ruritania or on resisting recognition here later.

Application questions · twist 2

⚡ Twist 2 · 1 of 3H4
Did Pandan submit to the Ruritanian court by applying for a stay in favour of Singapore and then taking no part?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

On Henry v Geoprosco's logic, asking the Ruritanian court to decline a jurisdiction it has accepts that jurisdiction, so Pandan submitted. Per IGCF (PC), which calls Henry's line between existence and exercise “unrealistic and irrational”, a stay on forum non conveniens grounds is a protest unless more is sought; Pandan sought nothing more and took no further part, so it did not submit. The ROC 2021 rule governs Singapore proceedings and may not carry over by mirror image.

⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Merck (HC) and Chong (seminar), governing law is not so sensitive that Singapore must decide it itself, so a ruling on it can found an estoppel, but per First Laser only if decided at the final trial. Whether the estoppel arises here is open. Per First Laser, it is immaterial that Ruritania's choice of law rules differ from Singapore's, so the estoppel can arise. Per Gonzalo Gil White, there is no identity if the issue arose under different laws; on Chong's narrow reading (seminar), that bites only where Singapore's rules pick Singapore law, as they likely do here (installation and payment here, and clause 18), so there is no estoppel. Pandan, which took no part after its stay failed, may also invoke the Carl Zeiss caution.

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes and what stays

    No anti-suit injunction was granted. Pandan, which has no office, staff or assets in Ruritania, applied there for a stay in favour of Singapore, lost and took no further part, and the Ruritanian court then gave a final judgment for Valen on governing law, discharge and negligence, with an order for S$200,000. Valen now enforces the money order here and pleads the rulings as estoppels, so the question moves from which court hears the case to what effect the Ruritanian judgment has. Pandan's merits arguments on the Supply Contract and in negligence matter only if the judgment is not recognised or raises no estoppel; the judgment does not rule on the Calibration Contract, so it does not bar that claim.

  2. 2
    Common law, and was the stay application submission? H1H4

    Ruritania was not the chosen court under an exclusive choice of court agreement, so the CCAA does not apply and Valen sues on the judgment debt at common law. It must show that the judgment is on the merits, final and conclusive, for a definite sum, and given by a court with international jurisdiction over Pandan under Singapore's rules (C&Y). Pandan had no presence in Ruritania and clause 18 names only Singapore, so everything turns on submission by conduct, which is open. On Henry v Geoprosco's logic, asking the Ruritanian court to decline a jurisdiction it had accepted that jurisdiction, so Pandan submitted and, subject to the defences, the money order is likely enforceable (Nimbus assumed Henry without deciding). Per IGCF (PC), which calls Henry's line “unrealistic and irrational”, a stay on forum non conveniens grounds is a protest unless more is sought; Pandan sought nothing more, so it did not submit, and the judgment is neither enforced nor recognised. Pandan's reliance on the ROC 2021 rule that challenging exercise is not submission is weaker, as that rule governs Singapore proceedings and may not carry over (C&Y).

  3. 3
    Defences H7

    Pandan bears the burden of any defence (Eleven v Boxsentry). No anti-suit injunction was granted, so the public policy defence for a judgment obtained in breach of one (Nimbus) does not arise, and Pandan had notice, applied in the action and then chose to take no part, so natural justice does not help (Sang Cheol Woo). Breach of a jurisdiction clause is an undecided defence at common law, but per Prof Chong (March 2026 answer scheme) it needs a breach of a promissory clause, and suing in Ruritania broke nothing in clause 18 (Shanghai Turbo); had Pandan submitted, it would probably lose the objection anyway (C&Y). Any error by the Ruritanian court on governing law or the merits is no defence, as Singapore does not sit on appeal (Godard v Gray). One open point remains: per Merck it is undecided whether a judgment given while Singapore proceedings on the same subject were pending is recognised; Prof Yeo would recognise it, but by analogy with Art 7(2) of the Hague Judgments Convention it may be refused, as Singapore was seised first and the dispute is closely connected with Singapore.

  4. 4
    If recognised: the estoppels H8

    If the judgment is recognisable, Valen pleads it as res judicata, the parties being the same (Merck). The declarations that the ban discharged the Supply Contract and that Valen is not liable in negligence raise cause of action estoppel, as a foreign declaration of non-liability does against a breach claim here: per Arnold it needs the same cause between the same parties, and per C&Y it is an absolute bar absent fraud or collusion, so they may bar Pandan's Supply Contract and negligence claims. Pandan can reply, borrowing Gonzalo Gil White, that rulings made under Ruritanian law do not decide claims that Singapore's rules send to Singapore law (the Supply Contract, and the tort if located in Singapore); that case is about identity of issue, so the reply is untested here, but if it works those claims proceed as in the base facts. The ruling on governing law raises an issue estoppel, which is open: per Merck (HC) and Chong (seminar), governing law is not so sensitive that Singapore must decide it itself, so a ruling made at the final trial can found an estoppel, and per First Laser Ruritania's different choice of law rules do not matter. But on Chong's narrow reading of Gonzalo Gil White (seminar), identity fails where Singapore's rules pick Singapore law, as they likely do here (installation and payment in Singapore, and clause 18), so there is no estoppel. Pandan, which took no part after its stay failed, may also invoke the Carl Zeiss caution, and it is unclear whether a judgment given after it stopped taking part was decided at a final trial.

4Remember

🧠 FOR THE EXAM
  • A never-registered foreign company served through its Singapore agent: s 376 fails, so prove Adams v Cape presence, then run Spiliada with stage 1 on the defendant.
  • A later ban at the required place of performance: run all three Ralli readings; Esben refuses enforcement, while on frustration the proper law decides.
  • Tainting: Step 1 needs a relevant illegality; at Step 2 run both the lex fori and the proper law, which per Chong (seminar) is that of the contract sued on, not the tainting contract's.
  • Where a defective product tort happens is open: the act (Vibrant Group) or where it was marketed (Distillers; Castree v Squibb); the exception needs pure fortuity.
  • A Singapore non-exclusive clause puts strong cause on a defendant who objects here, but suing abroad is not ordinarily a breach, so an anti-suit injunction needs vexation.
  • A stay application abroad as submission is open (Henry v Geoprosco against IGCF), and so is an issue estoppel on a foreign ruling about governing law (Gonzalo Gil White).

LAW302 · META GAME · ★ DO FIRST · MIXED · HYPO mx-01 · GEMINI PROMPT V1 · 16 QUESTIONS

Mekar Seeds v Vantor Labs

Written by Claude for the drill and law reviewed. Gemini (prompt v1) wrote a guide to it; the guide was checked (7 corrections) and feeds the walkthrough. Gemini's file: mekar_seeds_v_vantor_labs_mx_01_plain_english_re.

Answers:

1Base facts

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Mekar Seeds v Vantor Labs

Mekar Seeds Pte Ltd is a Singapore incorporated seed trader. Vantor Labs SA is a Ruritanian seed breeder. By a contract signed in Singapore on 1 March 2022, Vantor sold Mekar 40 tonnes of modified rice seed. Vantor was to deliver at Port Ruri in Ruritania, and Mekar was to pay into Vantor's bank account there. The contract provides:

“12. This contract is governed by Singapore law.”
“25. The Buyer has not relied on any statement made before signing.”
“30. The Seller may, by written notice before any proceedings begin, elect the courts of Ruritania or of Singapore as the exclusive forum for any dispute arising out of or in connection with this contract.”

Clause 20 brings in Vantor's Standard Export Terms, one of which reads: “Every sale is governed by Ruritanian law.”

Before the contract, Vantor's sales director emailed Mekar's chief executive from Ruritania that the seed had a 95% germination rate. She read the email while changing planes in Arcadia. Mekar's board relied on it at a meeting in Singapore, where it resolved to buy. The statement was careless and wrong, and most of the seed failed.

When Mekar demanded damages, Vantor at once gave notice electing the courts of Ruritania and sued Mekar there for the unpaid price. Mekar then sued Vantor in the General Division for breach of contract and misrepresentation, and served it in Ruritania with the court's approval. Vantor has applied to set aside service.

Advise Mekar whether the General Division will hear its claims and, if so, whether they will succeed.

ℹ ASSUME
  1. Ruritania is not a party to the Hague Convention on Choice of Court Agreements.
  2. Under Singapore law an express term in the main contract prevails over an incorporated term. Under Ruritanian law the incorporated term prevails.
  3. Under all these laws a contract term may be pleaded against a tort claim. Clause 25 is effective under Ruritanian law but not under Singapore law.
  4. Under Singapore and Arcadian law the email is an actionable negligent misstatement. Under Ruritanian law a seller is not liable in tort for a pre-contract statement.
  5. Since 2019 the Utopian Biosafety Act has made importing modified seed into Utopia a crime. Mekar always planned to resell all the seed to a Utopian grower, labelled as ordinary seed. Vantor did not know.
  6. A trial takes about six years in Ruritania. Last month, after Mekar had sued here, its claims became time-barred in Ruritania. It filed nothing there.
✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • A8
    Floating clause, or two courts named. Clause 30 names two courts and lets one party pick. It is a floating court clause with an election mechanism, and Vantor used it before anyone sued.
  • E7
    Strong cause: starter and nature of the test. After the election Ruritania is the exclusive forum, so Mekar's Singapore action breaks the clause. The test is strong cause, and Mekar bears it.
  • E8
    SCORECARD · Strong cause: the Eleftheria factors. The six year wait and the time bar are there to be marked on the strong cause scorecard. Both fail, for different reasons.
  • L7
    Was a contract formed at all?. Two terms choose two laws, and each law prefers its own term. The battle of the forms block on clashing putative laws is the home for this.
  • L6
    SCORECARD · Objective proper law: closest and most real connection. If the clash leaves no choice, the objective proper law decides. The place where both parties perform is planted for it.
  • M3
    SCORECARD · Foster v Driscoll: intention to break a friendly state's law. A written law of a friendly State, in force at signing, and a plan from the start to break it. That is Foster. Here the party with the plan is the claimant.
  • N3
    SCORECARD · Locate the tort: where in substance did it arise?. The statement was sent from Ruritania, read in Arcadia and relied on in Singapore, and the three laws differ. The tort must be located.
  • N7
    A contract clause is raised against the tort claim. Clause 25 is a contract term raised against a tort claim. It is valid under one candidate proper law and not under the other.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • B3
    CCAA applies and a foreign court is chosen (s 12). An exclusive clause for a foreign court suggests s 12 of the CCAA. But Ruritania is not a party to the Convention on the base facts, so the common law decides.
  • L3
    Floating or one-sided choice of law clause. The court clause floats, and two laws are named, so a floating choice of law clause comes to mind. But each law term fixes one law from the start. They clash; they do not float. Do not confuse the court clause with the law clauses.
  • E5
    SCORECARD · Spiliada stage 2: substantial justice. A long wait and a time bar look like substantial justice at Spiliada stage 2. But a promise is broken, so the test is strong cause, where foreseeable delay and a self-induced time bar count for little.
  • M5
    Ralli Bros: performance becomes illegal where it must be done. A foreign ban suggests Ralli. But Ralli needs an act that the contract requires in the country whose law forbids it. This contract requires delivery and payment in Ruritania, and nothing in Utopia. The point is Mekar's plan at signing, which is Foster.
  • M2
    The law broken is the proper law itself. A statute is broken, which suggests illegality under the proper law. But Utopian law is not a candidate proper law. Only Singapore law and Ruritanian law are in play.
  • A7
    Asymmetric clause: one side may sue anywhere. Only Vantor may elect, so the clause looks one sided. But an asymmetric clause lets one party sue anywhere. After the election clause 30 ties both parties to the same court.

Fair to tick but not needed: B1 CCAA gate: five conditions, B4 Outside the CCAA: say why, then the common law, D4 Defendant abroad: service out and the three requirements, D5 Gateway: name the sub-limb of PD para 63(3), D10 Foreign clause, defendant abroad, E1 Which test, and who bears the burden, E10 Parallel foreign proceedings, and time bars, K1 Characterise the issue, K5 Limitation periods, L1 Starter: the proper law and its three stages, L2 Express choice of law clause, M1 Illegality: pick the route, N1 Starter: double actionability, N2 Limb 1: a tort under Singapore law, N4 Limb 2 applied: is there liability under the law of that place?, N5 SCORECARD · The flexible exception

Application questions · base facts

⚡ Base facts · 1 of 7A8
Clause 30 names two courts and lets only Vantor choose. What is its effect once Vantor has given notice?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), a floating jurisdiction clause is valid at common law if it is not too uncertain, unlike a floating choice of law clause. It needs an election mechanism, such as one party's option. Two named courts become non-exclusive for both only where there is no mechanism. The clause stands apart from the two law terms, so their clash does not touch it.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J1.1.3 :: Floating Jurisdiction Clause Valid

Per Shanghai Turbo (CA) and C&Y, a floating jurisdiction clause is valid at common law if not too uncertain, unlike [a floating choice of law clause], which is void (C2). It needs an election mechanism, e.g., [one party's option / a prescribed event].

⚡ Base facts · 2 of 7E7
Vantor applies to set aside service. What is the test on forum, and who bears the burden?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

The burden lies on the party seeking release from its promise. Mekar breaches by suing here, so strong cause is on Mekar, whether it was served in or out. For service out it also needs a nexus from another factor, such as a contract made in Singapore, and a serious question. Strong cause takes the place of forum conveniens.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J4.0.2 :: Foreign EJC

[Claimant] breaches by suing here, so strong cause is on [claimant], though [defendant] brings the [stay / set-aside], served in or out.

⚡ Base facts · 3 of 7L7
Clause 12 chooses Singapore law. The incorporated term chooses Ruritanian law. Which law governs the contract?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Each term validates itself under its own law, and it makes no sense to choose between them by either putative law (Dornoch). The Heidberg and Dornoch used the lex fori, but Lew v Nargolwala now rejects the lex fori for formation. The putative objective proper law was rejected in The Heidberg. Under the Hague Principles a term applies only if it prevails under both laws; otherwise there is no choice. Per Prof Chong's critique, the lex fori should still break a tie of this kind. So run both: no choice leads to the objective proper law, probably Ruritanian law; a lex fori tie-break leads to clause 12 and Singapore law.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C2.6 :: Battle of Forms: Clashing Putative Laws

[A]'s [law X clause] and [B]'s [law Y clause] may each validate themselves, and "it makes no sense to decide which one to choose by any putative law" (Dornoch).

  • Lex fori: The Heidberg and Dornoch applied [the lex fori], but Lew now bars [that fallback].
  • Putative OPL: per Prof Chong, rejected in The Heidberg as no more correct than [arbitrarily preferring one clause], so [party] needs [another tiebreak].
  • Yeo (deadlock overstated): map each law's [first shot / last shot / knock-out] rule; both clauses apply only where each validates itself; where neither survives, use [the putative OPL], then [the lex fori].
  • Art 6(1)(b) Hague Principles: [the law X clause] applies only if [its standard terms] prevail under both laws, else no choice.
⚡ Base facts · 4 of 7L6
If neither law term takes effect, what does the court do next, and with what result?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Where the parties turned their minds to the governing law and failed, inferring a choice is artificial, so the court goes to stage 3. There the strongest factor is usually the place where both parties perform. The place of contracting matters little unless performance is also there.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C2.4.3 :: Application

Per Prof Chong, the strongest argument is usually [the place where both parties perform, e.g., country X], supported by [place of contracting / currency / incorporation and head office / related transaction], so [law X] is the OPL.

⚡ Base facts · 5 of 7M3
Vantor pleads that Mekar's contract claim is barred by illegality. Is it?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

A contract whose real object and intention is to break the law of a friendly State is not enforced. Intention at formation is the crux. A unilateral intention bars only its holder, and here the holder is the claimant, so test Foster against Mekar. The forbidden act must be contemplated within Utopia, but Utopia need not be the stipulated place of performance. Foster is forum public policy, so the clash of law terms does not matter. Reselling all the seed makes the illegal object dominant. Vantor could have sued; Mekar cannot.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C2.10.3 :: Unilateral Intention

Per Royal Boskalis, unilateral intention bars only its holder, so [the innocent party] may sue (Ang v Lyu; Surewin), though not for [an order compelling the illegal performance].

  • Mental state: per Dimplex Gems, [mere knowledge] does not disqualify [the claimant]; active participation is needed (doubting Soetanto).
⚡ Base facts · 6 of 7N3
Where was the misrepresentation committed?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

A representation directed at the claimant and received and acted on in one country is a tort there, unless that place is fortuitous. Where receipt and reliance split, that rule fails and the court asks where in substance the cause of action arose. For misrepresentation the place of reliance counts for more, and the place of damage alone is not decisive. Vantor will argue for Ruritania, where the statement was made, and under Ruritanian law limb 2 would fail. So carry both: if the tort is in Singapore both limbs are met; if in Ruritania, Mekar needs the flexible exception.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C3.3.2 :: Misrepresentation Directed at the Claimant: Receipt + Reliance

Per JIO Minerals (tentatively, citing Yeo) and Ong Ghee Soon, [a representation] directed at [claimant] and received and acted on in [Singapore] is a tort there, unless [that place] is fortuitous.

  • Where reliance crystallises: where [claimant] gave [instructions via the Singapore branch], not [administrative execution in Geneva] (Ong Ghee Soon).
  • Fortuitous receipt: receipt in [India] merely because [claimant] is based there is fortuitous (JIO).
  • Receipt and reliance split: the specific rule fails, so use [the substance test], as in JIO where [negotiations and drilling] made [Indonesia] the place.
  • Several countries of making, receipt and reliance: where [the core representations] were made, e.g. [Germany], may prevail, receipt being fortuitous for [global operators] (IM Skaugen v MAN Diesel).
  • Receipt unclear on the pleadings: unevidenced receipt in [Germany] is "speculative", so [Singapore law] applies (Rickshaw).
⚡ Base facts · 7 of 7N7
Can Vantor rely on clause 25 against the misrepresentation claim?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

On the preferred approach, admissibility is a tort question for the laws of both limbs, and validity is a contract question for the proper law. The Assume list settles admissibility. Validity then follows the clash: if Ruritanian law governs the contract, clause 25 is effective and the claim fails; if Singapore law governs, it is not enforceable and the claim survives. The Sayers majority, which looks only to the proper law of the contract, ends in the same place here.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · C3.8.2 :: Preferred Approach (Kahn-Freund; North; cf Brodin v A/R Seljan)

(1) admissibility is a tort question for double actionability, and (2) validity a contract question for [its proper law], so cl [X], valid under [law Y], succeeds only if admissible under both [Singapore law] and [the lex loci delicti].

  • Incidental question: [the forum's] COL rules (simple, but [forum shopping]) or [the tort law's] (Harris: coherent, avoiding "the law of no one state") pick [the contract's law].
  • Which to choose: per C&Y, it may track Singapore's views on [renvoi] and [party autonomy] in tort.
  • Pre-existing contract: the exception may apply [law Y] to both questions (C3.6.5), though Rickshaw declined for [the employment contract].
  • OSRAA overlay: s 102 voids [the clause] as an admissibility rule (Yeo), or as [procedural / mandatory] even on [the Sayers view] (C3.3.4).
📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
⚡ BIG IDEA

This hypo turns on clause 30, a floating court clause that Vantor used before anyone sued. Once Ruritania is elected, Mekar is the party in breach and must show strong cause, which a foreseeable delay and a self-induced time bar cannot supply. On the merits, Foster probably bars Mekar's contract claim whatever law governs, and the tort claim turns on two open points: the clash of law terms and where the tort happened. The twists test whether an elected floating clause is inside the CCAA, and how an election for Singapore flips the burden and supports an anti-suit injunction.

  1. 1
    Regime and clause 30 A8

    Ruritania is not a party to the Convention, so the CCAA cannot apply and the common law decides. Clause 30 names two courts and lets Vantor elect one by written notice before proceedings begin. Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), a floating jurisdiction clause is valid at common law if it is not too uncertain, unlike a floating choice of law clause, and it needs an election mechanism such as one party's choice. Vantor elected Ruritania before anyone sued, so Ruritania is now the exclusive forum for both parties. This is not an asymmetric clause, because neither party may now sue elsewhere, and the clash of the law terms does not touch it.

  2. 2
    Scope and burden: strong cause on Mekar E7

    Clause 30 covers any dispute “arising out of or in connection with” the contract, so it reaches the misrepresentation claim as well as the contract claim (Per Fiona Trust, as applied in Trisuryo and Bunge). Mekar sued here after the election, so it is the party breaking its promise. Per C&Y and Shanghai Turbo, the burden lies on the party seeking release from its promise, so strong cause is on Mekar although Vantor brings the set-aside. Per Vinmar (restating The Eleftheria), the court holds the parties to their bargain unless the party in breach shows strong cause, a higher hurdle than Spiliada. On service out Mekar also needs, for each claim, a nexus through another factor (such as the contract being made in Singapore) and a serious question, with strong cause in place of forum conveniens.

  3. 3
    Strong cause scorecard: Mekar fails E8

    On the base facts every point fails. The six-year wait: per Vinmar, notorious delay in the chosen court is foreseeable and insufficient, unlike an unforeseeable closure of that court, for example through war. The time bar: per Vinmar, it counts only if the claimant shows very good reasons for not filing a protective claim, and Mekar knew of the election yet filed nothing in Ruritania, so the bar is self-induced. That Ruritanian law gives no tort claim is a worse result on the merits, not the exceptional case of no remedy at all (Per Trisuryo), as Mekar can still bring its contract claim there. Nothing amounts to abuse or a denial of justice, so service is set aside and the General Division will not hear either claim.

  4. 4
    If heard: two law terms clash L7

    The ask also covers the merits, so assume the court hears the case. Clause 12 picks Singapore law and the incorporated term picks Ruritanian law from signing, so they clash rather than float, and each law prefers its own term. Per Dornoch it makes no sense to choose between them by either putative law; The Heidberg and Dornoch used the lex fori, but Lew v Nargolwala now bars it in formation, and The Heidberg rejected the putative objective proper law. The point is open, so run both routes. Route 1, the Hague Principles test: a term applies only if it prevails under both laws, so there is no choice. Route 2, per Prof Chong's critique (with Teo): the lex fori breaks the tie, so clause 12 wins and Singapore law governs.

  5. 5
    Route 1: the objective proper law L6

    With no effective choice the court skips implied choice: the parties tried to choose and failed, so inferring a choice is artificial (Per Shanghai Turbo and The Iran Vojdan). Per Bonython, the test is the closest and most real connection. Per Prof Chong, the strongest argument is usually the place where both parties perform, and here Vantor delivers at Port Ruri and Mekar pays into Ruritania. Signing in Singapore matters little unless performance is also there (Per Pacific Recreation), and Mekar's base here is matched by Vantor's base in Ruritania. Courts do not declare ties (Per Lew), so Ruritanian law is the likely objective proper law on route 1, while Singapore law governs on route 2.

  6. 6
    Contract claim: Foster bars Mekar M3

    Per Foster v Driscoll and Regazzoni (in Singapore, Patriot v Lam Hong; Esben), a contract whose real object and intention is to break the law of a friendly State is not enforced. Intention at formation is the crux (Per Magdeev): from the start Mekar planned to resell all the seed to a Utopian grower, labelled as ordinary seed, so the import that the 2019 Act forbids is planned inside Utopia (Per Surewin) and is the dominant object. Foster is forum public policy, so it applies whichever law governs the contract (Per Ang v Lyu and Surewin). Per Royal Boskalis, a unilateral intention bars only its holder: Vantor could sue, but Mekar, the claimant, probably cannot. Ralli does not fit, because the contract requires nothing in Utopia, and proper law illegality does not fit, because Utopian law is not a candidate proper law.

  7. 7
    Tort: where was the misrepresentation? N3

    Per Rickshaw, the tort claim needs double actionability, subject to the flexible exception, and limb 1 is met because the email is an actionable negligent misstatement under Singapore law. Per JIO Minerals and Ong Ghee Soon, a statement directed at the claimant and received and acted on in one country is a tort there unless that place is fortuitous; here receipt (Arcadia) and reliance (Singapore) split, so the substance test decides. For misrepresentation the place of reliance counts more (Per Vibrant Group), and reading the email while changing planes was an accident, so the tort is probably in Singapore and both limbs are met. Vantor will argue for Ruritania, where the email was written, since the place of making may prevail when making, receipt and reliance are in different countries (Per IM Skaugen v MAN Diesel). On that route limb 2 fails under Ruritanian law, and Mekar needs the flexible exception, which is strictly applied and needs Ruritanian law to be purely fortuitous (Per Rickshaw), a hard case when Vantor wrote the email from its home.

  8. 8
    Clause 25 against the tort claim N7

    On the preferred approach (Kahn-Freund; North), admissibility of a contract term against a tort is a tort question for both limbs, and its validity is a contract question for the contract's proper law. The Assume list settles admissibility: every law here lets a contract term be pleaded against a tort claim. Validity then follows the clash of law terms. On route 1 (Ruritanian law) clause 25 is effective and the tort claim fails; on route 2 (Singapore law) it is not enforceable and the claim survives, provided the tort is in Singapore. The Sayers majority, which looks only to the proper law of the contract, ends in the same place.

  9. 9
    Advice to Mekar

    The General Division will probably not hear the claims: Mekar shows no strong cause, so service is set aside. If the claims were heard, the contract claim is probably barred by Foster whichever law governs. The tort claim needs both open points to go Mekar's way: the tort located in Singapore, and Singapore law governing the contract through a lex fori tie-break so that clause 25 falls. On the objective proper law route clause 25 defeats it, and if the tort is in Ruritania limb 2 defeats it unless the flexible exception applies.

2Twist 1

🧩 TWIST 1

How would your advice differ on these further facts?

Suppose that the Hague Convention has been in force for Ruritania since 1 January 2020. Mekar was served in the Ruritanian action in good time but did not appear. The Ruritanian court has given judgment in default. It ruled that clause 30 is an exclusive choice of court agreement under the Convention. It declared that Vantor is not liable to Mekar for breach of contract or for misrepresentation, and it ordered Mekar to pay the balance of the price. It decided the misrepresentation point under Ruritanian law.

ℹ ASSUME
  1. The judgment has effect and can be enforced in Ruritania.
✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • B1
    CCAA gate: five conditions. Ruritania is now a Contracting State, so run the gate. The hard row is the floating clause: it had no chosen court until Vantor alone elected.
  • B5
    The foreign court has already ruled that the HCCCA applies. The Ruritanian court has ruled that the Convention applies. Ask whether that ruling binds, and note that the judgment was by default.
  • B3
    CCAA applies and a foreign court is chosen (s 12). If the CCAA applies, a foreign court is chosen and Mekar has sued here. Section 12 replaces strong cause.
  • H9
    CCAA Part 3: judgment of the chosen court. If the CCAA applies, the judgment is that of the chosen court. Part 3 decides its effect, and its declarations answer Mekar's claims.
  • H4
    International jurisdiction: submission. If the CCAA does not apply, the common law does. Mekar did not appear, so international jurisdiction rests on clause 30 as an agreement to submit.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • B2
    CCAA applies and Singapore is the chosen court (s 11). Clause 30 names Singapore too, which suggests s 11. But after the election only Ruritania is designated. Singapore is not the chosen court.
  • H10
    Anti-enforcement injunction: the judgment already exists. A foreign judgment exists, which suggests an anti-enforcement injunction. But Mekar is not trying to stop enforcement abroad. The judgment is raised against it here.

Fair to tick but not needed: B4 Outside the CCAA: say why, then the common law, E8 SCORECARD · Strong cause: the Eleftheria factors, H1 Which regime, H2 Common law: the four requirements; on the merits, H5 Final and conclusive, H6 Money judgment, or a declaration?, H7 Defences to recognition and enforcement, H8 Issue estoppel from the foreign ruling

Application questions · twist 1

⚡ Twist 1 · 1 of 4B1
Is clause 30 inside the CCAA, and does the Ruritanian ruling settle that?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Coverage of a floating clause is unclear. Before election there is no chosen court. Once notice was served the clause crystallised into a choice of one court for both parties, probably inside the CCAA. Section 3 needs an agreement, but an election arguably suffices where both parties agreed that one of them could elect. The contract is later than Ruritania's Convention date. Per Prof Chong's answer scheme the debtor may argue that a foreign ruling on the Convention raises no estoppel. Section 13(3)(b) does not apply to a default judgment and never covers legal evaluation.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J1.2.1 :: Floating Clause (±)

Presently, [clause X] lets [party] choose between [Court A] and [Court B]; per C&Y, CCAA coverage is unclear. (−) Before election there is no chosen court, so arguably no s 3(1) agreement. (+) Once [notice of election] was served on [date], [clause X] crystallised into a mutually exclusive choice of [Court A], probably within the CCAA.

  • Unilateral election (±): s 3 requires agreement between the parties, but arguably [party]'s election suffices where [all parties agreed it could elect / [other party] received written notice and did not object].
⚡ Twist 1 · 2 of 4B3
If the CCAA applies, what happens to Mekar's Singapore action? Mekar points to the six year wait and the time bar.
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Section 12(1) applies despite any other rule of law. The exceptions are read narrowly, for the most exceptional circumstances. Manifest injustice must be clear, extremely serious and highly probable, and mere delay or expense does not show that the agreement cannot reasonably be performed. The Ruritanian court has in fact heard the case.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J1.4 :: Must Stay or Dismiss (must write)

[Claimant] sued here, and [defendant] seeks a stay because [clause X] designates [the courts of State B]. Per s 12(1), "despite any other written law or rule of law", [Singapore] must stay or dismiss unless exception (a)–(e) applies; per s 12(2), a stay on other grounds remains possible.

⚡ Twist 1 · 3 of 4H9
If the CCAA applies, must the Ruritanian judgment be recognised? It was given by default and is partly a declaration.
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

The court must recognise a judgment of the chosen court unless a listed ground applies, and the list is exhaustive. A “judgment” includes a default judgment and a non-money judgment. The merits are not reviewed. The natural ground against a default judgment is lack of notice in time, but Mekar was served in good time and stayed away. Once recognised, the declarations answer the claims that Mekar brings here.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J7.5.1 :: Judgment (+)

Per s 2(1), [the X judgment] is a "judgment" as it is [a final decision on the merits / a consent order or judgment / a default judgment], or [a costs determination] relating to one, including [non-money judgments]. Per s 10, [interim relief] is excluded (Motacus), though Singapore may grant [interim relief in support] (s 10(2)).

⚡ Twist 1 · 4 of 4H4
If clause 30 is outside the CCAA, can the judgment still be recognised at common law? Mekar never appeared in Ruritania.
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per United Malayan Banking a debtor submits in advance by agreeing to the jurisdiction of the foreign court. Recognition, unlike enforcement, has no money requirement, so the declarations can be pleaded as a shield and the price order enforced as a debt. Mekar's one reply is on the misrepresentation ruling: it was decided under Ruritanian law, and per Gonzalo Gil White there is no identity of issue where the issue arose under different laws in the two courts. That is strongest where Singapore's own rules would apply Singapore law to the tort. The argument does not reach the contract ruling.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J7.1.2.5 :: Express Agreement (+)

Per United Malayan Banking, [debtor] submitted in advance by agreeing in [clause] to the jurisdiction of [the X court / the courts of [X]].

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes and what stays

    Ruritania has been a Contracting State since 1 January 2020, before the 2022 contract, and its court has given a default judgment after Mekar was served in good time and stayed away. That court ruled clause 30 inside the Convention, declared Vantor not liable in contract or for misrepresentation (the latter under Ruritanian law), and ordered Mekar to pay the price. The merits analysis (the clash of law terms, Foster, the tort) stays the same, but Mekar may never reach it. Whether the CCAA applies is open, so run both regimes.

  2. 2
    Is clause 30 inside the CCAA? B1B5

    The contract postdates Ruritania's Convention date, the parties are in different States and the sale is commercial, so the hard row is exclusivity. Per C&Y, coverage of a floating clause is unclear: before the election there was no chosen court, but once Vantor served notice the clause crystallised into a choice of one court for both parties, probably inside the CCAA. Section 3 needs an agreement, but one party's election arguably suffices where both parties agreed that it could elect. The Ruritanian ruling does not settle the point: per Prof Chong's answer scheme, Mekar may argue that it raises no estoppel, each Contracting State court deciding for itself whether the Convention applies, while if an estoppel does arise the judgment is a Convention judgment. Section 13(3)(b) does not close it either, because it does not apply to a default judgment and never binds on legal evaluation.

  3. 3
    If the CCAA applies: s 12 and Part 3 B3H9

    Singapore is not the chosen court, so per s 12(1) it must stay or dismiss Mekar's action “despite any other written law or rule of law” unless an exception applies; strong cause plays no part unless one does. Exceptions (c) and (d) apply only in the most exceptional circumstances: delay is not enough, the time bar is Mekar's own doing, and the Ruritanian court has heard the case. Per s 13(4), the judgment must be recognised unless a ground in ss 14 to 16 applies; a default judgment and a declaration both count, and the merits are not reviewed. Lack of notice under s 14(a) fails, because Mekar was served in good time and chose not to appear. The judgment has effect and is enforceable in Ruritania, so its declarations answer Mekar's claims here and Vantor can enforce the price order.

  4. 4
    If the CCAA does not apply: the common law H4

    Mekar's Singapore action still fails for want of strong cause, as on the base facts. Nothing shows that Mekar was present in Ruritania, and it did not appear, but per United Malayan Banking a party submits in advance by agreeing to the foreign court's jurisdiction, and in clause 30 Mekar agreed to the court Vantor would elect, so the judgment is probably recognised. A default judgment can be on the merits and final, and recognition has no money requirement, so the declarations work as a shield and the price order is enforceable as a debt. Mekar's one reply is that the misrepresentation ruling was decided under Ruritanian law: per Gonzalo Gil White there is no identity of issue where the issue arose under different laws, and on Chong's narrow reading (seminar) that holds only where Singapore's own rules would pick Singapore law. So if the tort is in Singapore, Singapore law alone governs it and the reply probably defeats an issue estoppel on misrepresentation; if the tort is in Ruritania, Singapore also applies Ruritanian law at limb 2, so the reply gains Mekar nothing unless the flexible exception applies. The facts give a different law only for the misrepresentation ruling, so the reply does not reach the contract ruling.

3Twist 2

🧩 TWIST 2

Go back to the base facts and change one thing.

How would your advice differ if Vantor's notice had elected the courts of Singapore, and Vantor had then sued Mekar in Ruritania all the same? The Ruritanian action is a month old, and Mekar has taken no step in it.

✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • B2
    CCAA applies and Singapore is the chosen court (s 11). After the election Singapore is the exclusive forum. Singapore is a Contracting State and the contract dates from 2022, so ask whether s 11 applies.
  • D8
    Singapore clause, defendant abroad. Vantor is still abroad, but the clause now points to Singapore. The clause itself carries service out.
  • G3
    Contractual ASI: a Singapore clause is breached. Vantor is suing in Ruritania in breach of what is now an exclusive Singapore clause. That is the contractual basis for an anti-suit injunction.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • E3
    Forum conveniens on service out: burden on the claimant. Vantor is served abroad, which suggests that Mekar must show the proper forum. But the clause now names Singapore. Under s 11 there is no forum inquiry, and at common law the burden is on Vantor.
  • G6
    Vexation ASI: sufficient interest. G6 is for an injunction where no clause is breached and Singapore must be the natural forum. Here Vantor is in breach, so the basis is contractual.
  • H10
    Anti-enforcement injunction: the judgment already exists. An anti-enforcement injunction needs a foreign judgment. The Ruritanian action is a month old.

Fair to tick but not needed: B1 CCAA gate: five conditions, E1 Which test, and who bears the burden, E7 Strong cause: starter and nature of the test, G1 ASI starter, and the basis, G2 Amenability, G9 ASI in a CCAA case

Application questions · twist 2

⚡ Twist 2 · 1 of 3B2
Will the General Division hear Mekar's claims now? Vantor still points to Ruritania.
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Whether an elected floating clause is inside the CCAA is unclear, but probably yes after election. If so, s 11 applies: the court must not decline unless the clause is null and void under Singapore law, and it cannot decline in favour of another State, so neither Spiliada nor a pending foreign action matters. If not, the clause is still an exclusive Singapore clause at common law, and Vantor's objection needs strong cause.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J1.3 :: Must Hear (must write)

[Clause X] designates [the Singapore High Court / the SICC] and the CCAA applies (J1.2). Per s 11(1), [Singapore] must not decline unless [clause X] is null and void under Singapore law, including its choice of law rules.

⚡ Twist 2 · 2 of 3D8
How does Mekar now serve Vantor in Ruritania?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Where Singapore is the chosen court under the CCAA, the claimant seeks approval on the ground that the court has the jurisdiction, so no nexus and no forum conveniens inquiry arises. Outside the CCAA, the Singapore clause supplies the nexus, and if Vantor contests the forum it bears strong cause. Approval is still needed, because the contract says nothing about service.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J1.3 :: Serving Abroad: General Division (+)

[Claimant] seeks approval on the "has the jurisdiction" ground (O 8 r 1(1) ROC 2021), created partly for CCAA cases, so [no nexus] and [no forum conveniens] inquiry arises (per C&Y; J3.1.1). If [contract] permits service out, no approval is needed (O 8 r 1(3); J3.1.5).

  • Open (±): whether [defendant] may still argue [the claim] is outside the CCAA, and so resist "has the jurisdiction", should be raised inter partes (J3.1.1).
⚡ Twist 2 · 3 of 3G3
Can Mekar stop the Ruritanian action?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Breach of an exclusive clause is a separate basis for an injunction: no vexation is needed, and it ordinarily issues unless the respondent shows strong reasons. The clause is exclusive by its own words, so this is not the open point about a clause that is exclusive only by deeming. The foreign action is at an early stage and Mekar has not submitted to it. Vantor must also be amenable, which valid service out supplies.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J6.3.1.1 :: Exclusive Clause Breached (+)

Per C&Y, breach is a question of interpretation under [proper law]. Presently, [respondent] breached [clause X], an exclusive [Singapore / SICC / arbitration] clause, by suing in [foreign court]. Per Sun Travels, breach is a separate basis: no unconscionability is needed, and the ASI ordinarily issues absent strong reasons (J6.3.1.4).

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes and what stays

    Vantor's notice now elects Singapore, yet Vantor sues Mekar in Ruritania; that action is a month old and Mekar has taken no step in it. Jurisdiction flips: Mekar is in the agreed court and Vantor is the party in breach, so strong cause on Mekar falls away. Ruritania is still not a Contracting State. The merits (the clash of law terms, Foster, the tort and clause 25) are answered as before, and Mekar now reaches them, so Foster becomes its real problem.

  2. 2
    Singapore must hear the case B2

    Singapore has been a Contracting State since 1 October 2016 and the contract dates from 2022, and after the election clause 30 is probably an exclusive choice of Singapore inside the CCAA. If so, per s 11(1) the court must not decline unless the clause is null and void under Singapore law, and per s 11(2) it cannot decline in favour of Ruritania. Spiliada, strong cause and the pending Ruritanian action are then all irrelevant. If the CCAA does not apply, clause 30 is still an exclusive Singapore clause at common law, so Vantor's objection is itself a breach and Vantor must show strong cause.

  3. 3
    Serving Vantor in Ruritania D8

    Inside the CCAA, Mekar seeks approval on the “has the jurisdiction” ground, so there is no nexus and no forum conveniens inquiry. Outside it, Mekar uses the “appropriate court” ground with the clause itself as the nexus (para 63(3)(r) or (d)(iv)), and in practice it need only show that the clause is valid, binds Vantor and covers the dispute, plus a serious question (Per Chong's answer scheme and C&Y). The forum need not be proved: if Vantor contests it, that is a breach, and per Shanghai Turbo (CA) Vantor bears strong cause. Approval is still needed, because clause 30 says nothing about service, so O 8 r 1(3) does not help.

  4. 4
    Anti-suit injunction G3

    Vantor sued in Ruritania in breach of what is now an exclusive Singapore clause. Per Sun Travels, breach is a separate basis: no vexation is needed, natural forum drops out (Per Cooperative Muratori), and the injunction ordinarily issues unless Vantor shows strong reasons. The clause is exclusive by its own words, so this is not the open point about a clause that is exclusive only by s 3(2) deeming. Ruritania is not a Contracting State, so even if the CCAA applies this is an ordinary contractual injunction, which per C&Y upholds the agreement. Vantor is amenable through valid service out, and the Ruritanian action is at an early stage with no step by Mekar, so Mekar should apply promptly and take no step on the merits there. An injunction will probably issue.

4Scorecards: weigh the factors

Prof Chong rewards applying facts to factor tests. Sort each fact, then answer the verdict question. These use the base facts unless a line says “Suppose”.

E8 Sort the factors: Strong cause: can Mekar keep its claims in Singapore?

On the base facts Mekar must show strong cause to escape clause 30. Each line is a fact it offers. Does it work? Lines marked “Suppose” are extra facts for this card only.

A civil trial takes about six years in Ruritania.
Fails. Parties are taken to know the chosen court's delays. Notorious delay is foreseeable and is not a denial of justice. J4.3.3 :: Chosen Court Unavailable
Mekar's claims became time-barred in Ruritania last month, and Mekar filed nothing there.
Fails. A time bar counts only if the claimant shows very good reasons for not filing a protective claim. Mekar knew of the election from the start, so the bar is self-induced. Students often mark this as prejudice that works. J4.3.3 :: Time Bar
Ruritanian law gives no claim in tort for a statement made before the contract.
Fails. A worse result under the chosen court's law goes to the merits. The exceptional case is a claimant with no remedy at all there, and Mekar still has its contract claim. J4.3.3 :: No Remedy at All
Suppose: Mekar's agronomists, who tested the failed seed, all live in Singapore.
Fails. Where the witnesses live was foreseeable when the clause was agreed, so it carries little weight. J4.3.1 :: Foreseeable Factors
Suppose: Mekar says that Vantor has no real defence to the claim for bad seed.
Fails. The merits are not entertained. Parties choose a forum to win or lose there. J4.3.3 :: Merits Irrelevant
Suppose: Vantor has admitted in writing that it owes the full sum claimed, and says only that it cannot pay yet.
Could go either way. Admitting liability and quantum while stalling is the example of abusive conduct, but the threshold is very high. J4.3.3 :: Abuse Reformulated
Suppose: Ruritania's commercial courts have been closed by a civil war that began after the contract was signed.
Works. A chosen court that is unavailable through war, where that was not foreseeable, is strong cause. J4.3.3 :: Chosen Court Unavailable
Suppose: in the same Singapore action Mekar also sues a Singapore laboratory, a stranger to the contract, that certified the seed for Vantor.
Could go either way. With a non-party involved, splitting the dispute between two courts may be strong cause, unless that was foreseeable when the clause was agreed. J4.3.4 :: Fragmentation
⚡ Scorecard 1 · the verdictE8
On the base facts alone, what is the likely result of Vantor's application?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Strong cause is a higher hurdle than Spiliada, and the burden is on Mekar. Nothing on the base facts amounts to abuse or a denial of justice. Clause 30 covers any dispute “arising out of or in connection with” the contract, so the misrepresentation claim goes with the contract claim.

L6 Sort the factors: The objective proper law of the seed contract

Suppose the clash of law terms leaves no choice. Sort each fact by where it points. Lines marked “Suppose” are extra facts for this card only.

Vantor delivers the seed at Port Ruri.
Points to Ruritania. The place of performance carries great weight. One half of the performance is in Ruritania. C2.4.3 :: Application
Mekar pays the price into Vantor's bank account in Ruritania.
Points to Ruritania. The other half of the performance is there too. The place where both parties perform is usually the strongest argument. C2.4.3 :: Application
The contract was signed in Singapore.
Little or no weight. The place of contracting matters little unless performance is also there. Students often give it full weight. C2.3.2 :: Residence, Business, Purpose
Mekar is a Singapore company and trades from Singapore.
Points to Singapore. A party's residence and place of business count as a connecting factor. C2.3.2 :: Residence, Business, Purpose
Vantor is a Ruritanian company and breeds the seed in Ruritania.
Points to Ruritania. The other party's residence and place of business count as well, and they point the same way as the performance. C2.3.2 :: Residence, Business, Purpose
Suppose: the price is stated in US dollars and the contract is written in English.
Little or no weight. English and the US dollar are used everywhere, so they carry little weight. C2.3.2 :: Language and Currency
Suppose: Mekar's agronomists, who tested the failed seed, all live in Singapore.
Little or no weight. Witness convenience is a Spiliada factor. It says nothing about the law the contract is most closely connected with. C2.4.2 :: Wrong Factors
Suppose: the contract uses the standard form of the Ruritanian Seed Exchange, with terms of art from Ruritanian sales law.
Points to Ruritania. A standard form or terms of art tied to one legal system point strongly to that system's law. C2.3.2 :: Standard Form
⚡ Scorecard 2 · the verdictL6
If there is no effective choice, which law is the objective proper law?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

The test is the closest and most real connection. The place where both parties perform is the strongest factor, and courts do not declare ties. On that result clause 25 is effective, so the misrepresentation claim fails. If the lex fori breaks the tie instead, Singapore law governs and clause 25 falls.

5Remember

🧠 FOR THE EXAM
  • A floating court clause with an election mechanism is valid (Shanghai Turbo (CA)); once elected it binds both parties, so it is not asymmetric.
  • The party that sues in breach bears strong cause even when the other side applies; foreseeable delay and a self-induced time bar fail (Vinmar).
  • Two law terms that each win under their own law: the point is open, so run no choice (objective proper law) and a lex fori tie-break.
  • Foster bars only the holder of the illegal intention, whatever the proper law, so check whether that holder is the claimant.
  • Receipt and reliance in different countries: use the substance test; reliance weighs more for misrepresentation, and receipt while merely in transit is likely fortuitous.
  • After one party's election a floating clause is probably inside the CCAA, and the foreign court's ruling on that arguably raises no estoppel, so run both regimes.

LAW302 · META GAME · ADDITIONAL PRACTICE · QUESTION 1 · HYPO q1-27 · GEMINI PROMPT V1 · LAW REVIEWED 17 NOV · 15 QUESTIONS

Larchfield v Nordhaven

Gemini (prompt v1) sent only a guide for this hypo, with no usable file. Claude rebuilt the full hypo from it (26 gaps filled or errors fixed), then reviewed it in three passes (14 changes). Gemini called it q1-10 “Bramwell v Nordhaven”. Gemini's file: bramwell_v_nordhaven_q1_10_plain_english_guide_d.

ADDITIONAL PRACTICE

This hypo closely repeats q1-10. Same sample-final pattern as q1-10: an SICC-only clause inside the CCAA, a contractual anti-suit injunction, then common law enforcement of the foreign judgment (79% of its Menu boxes are the same). Do q1-10 first and come here for a second run at the same moves on new facts.

Answers:

1Base facts

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Larchfield v Nordhaven

Larchfield Valves Pte Ltd, a Singapore incorporated company, makes industrial valves at its plant in Loyang. Nordhaven Gas SA is incorporated in Ruritania, where it runs a gas processing plant. Nordhaven has no office, staff or assets in Singapore. The two companies have made three contracts.

Under the Frame Agreement, signed on 15 June 2016 and governed by Singapore law, Larchfield supplies valves to Nordhaven's plant on call-off orders. Clause 14 reads:

“The High Court of Singapore shall have exclusive jurisdiction over all disputes arising out of or in connection with this Agreement.”

Under the Commissioning Agreement, signed on 10 March 2019 and governed by Ruritanian law, Larchfield's engineers installed and tested a new valve system at the plant. Clause 19 reads:

“All disputes arising out of or in connection with this Agreement shall be submitted exclusively to the courts of Ruritania.”

Under the Maintenance Agreement, signed on 12 August 2023 and governed by Singapore law, Larchfield services the valves. Clause 25 reads:

“Any dispute arising out of or in connection with this Agreement shall be heard exclusively by the Singapore International Commercial Court.”

Nordhaven has not paid US$4 million for valves delivered under the Frame Agreement, the final US$1.2 million due under the Commissioning Agreement, or US$600,000 in maintenance fees. It says that the valves leak. Larchfield wants all three claims heard in Singapore, in the Singapore International Commercial Court if possible. Nordhaven says that it will contest any Singapore proceedings.

Advise Larchfield whether a Singapore court will hear each claim, and in which court it should sue.

ℹ ASSUME
  1. Ruritania is a Contracting State to the Hague Convention on Choice of Court Agreements. The Convention entered into force for Ruritania on 1 January 2018.
  2. None of the three contracts says how legal process may be served.
  3. Nordhaven's engineers, who will give evidence about the leaks, all live in Ruritania. They can give evidence by video link.
  4. A civil trial takes about five years in Ruritania and about 18 months in Singapore.
  5. Each clause is valid under every relevant law and covers the claim under its contract.
✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • B1
    CCAA gate: five conditions. Run the gate for each clause against the date for the chosen court's State. Clause 14 fails, as it predates 1 October 2016. Clause 19 passes on Ruritania's date, and clause 25 on Singapore's.
  • B2
    CCAA applies and Singapore is the chosen court (s 11). Clause 25 names the SICC and is inside the CCAA, so Singapore is the chosen court. Under s 11 the court must hear the Maintenance claim: no Spiliada and no strong cause.
  • B3
    CCAA applies and a foreign court is chosen (s 12). Clause 19 is inside the CCAA and chooses Ruritania, so s 12 governs the Commissioning claim. Larchfield's delay point must be tested against the listed exceptions, and none applies.
  • D8
    Singapore clause, defendant abroad. Nordhaven is abroad and clause 14 is a Singapore clause outside the CCAA. Larchfield serves out with approval, using the clause as the nexus and showing a serious question.
  • E7
    Strong cause: starter and nature of the test. If Nordhaven contests the Frame claim, it breaks its promise in clause 14. So the test is strong cause, with the burden on Nordhaven.
  • E8
    SCORECARD · Strong cause: the Eleftheria factors. The Ruritanian witnesses are the fact Nordhaven would offer as strong cause on the Frame claim. Mark it as failing: it was foreseeable at signing, and video link is available.
  • F2
    Primary jurisdiction under a written jurisdiction agreement. Clause 25 is a written agreement to submit to the SICC, and the action is international and commercial. The SICC has primary jurisdiction over the Maintenance claim.
  • F3
    "Singapore High Court" clause: check the date. Larchfield wants the SICC. Clause 14 names the High Court and predates 1 October 2016, so it does not of itself reach the SICC. Clause 25 names only the SICC, so it does not of itself reach the General Division.
  • F6
    SCORECARD · Transfer from the General Division: is the SICC "more appropriate"?. With no primary jurisdiction over the Frame claim, the SICC is reached only by transfer from the General Division, on the “more appropriate” test.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • E3
    Forum conveniens on service out: burden on the claimant. Forum conveniens with the burden on the claimant is the service out test where no one breaks a promise. If Nordhaven contests the Frame claim, it breaks clause 14, so strong cause is on Nordhaven.
  • E4
    SCORECARD · Spiliada stage 1: connecting factors. Witnesses in Ruritania look like a Spiliada stage 1 fact. But no claim here runs Spiliada: the Frame claim uses strong cause, the Commissioning claim s 12, and the Maintenance claim s 11.
  • E5
    SCORECARD · Spiliada stage 2: substantial justice. The five year wait looks like a Spiliada stage 2 point. But s 12 leaves no Spiliada, and mere delay opens no exception under s 12(1)(c) or (d).
  • D10
    Foreign clause, defendant abroad. D10 is the common law route for a claimant who sues here despite a foreign clause, with strong cause in place of forum conveniens. Clause 19 is inside the CCAA, so s 12 displaces that test.
  • F7
    Transfer in a CCAA case. F7 is a transfer in a CCAA case, which needs every party's consent. The Frame Agreement is outside the CCAA, so Nordhaven's objection is no veto. The test is whether the SICC is more appropriate (F6).

Fair to tick but not needed: A1 Any jurisdiction clause: what it promises, A2 Says "exclusive": Singapore courts, A3 Says "exclusive": a foreign court, B4 Outside the CCAA: say why, then the common law, D4 Defendant abroad: service out and the three requirements, D5 Gateway: name the sub-limb of PD para 63(3), D7 Serious question to be tried, E1 Which test, and who bears the burden, F1 International and commercial, F4 Serving the defendant abroad from the SICC, F5 Exercise in the SICC: O 2 r 3, no Spiliada

Application questions · base facts

⚡ Base facts · 1 of 7B1
Which Convention date decides whether the CCAA applies to each clause?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

The test date is when the Convention entered into force for the State of the chosen court. Clause 14 (15 June 2016) is earlier than Singapore's date, so the Frame Agreement is outside the CCAA and the common law decides. Clause 19 (10 March 2019) is later than Ruritania's date of 1 January 2018, and clause 25 (12 August 2023) is later than Singapore's, so both are inside. Section 12 covers a clause that chooses a foreign Contracting State's court.

  • UK clauses (±): the HCCCA applied to the UK via the EU from 1 October 2015 and in its own right from 1 January 2021; continuity across Brexit is contested, so [an English clause] concluded on [a date between them] is arguable either way.

⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Nordhaven is not in Singapore and the contract says nothing on service, so approval is needed under O 8 r 1(1). The Frame Agreement is outside the CCAA, so s 11 does not apply. “Has the jurisdiction” is arguably reserved for CCAA cases; outside them the ground is “appropriate court”. Clause 14 supplies the nexus (para 63(3)(d)(iv) and (r)). Those limbs are neutral on the merits, so the serious question is shown separately. Forum need not be proved: if Nordhaven contests it, Nordhaven bears strong cause.

Per Week 9 slides, [claimant] relies on [the Singapore clause] against [defendant]:

  • Nexus: [the clause] itself, under para 63(3)(r) ([defendant] "agreed to submit") or (d)(iv) (Shanghai Turbo (CA); J3.1.2).

The burden lies on the party seeking release from its promise. By contesting Singapore, Nordhaven breaks clause 14, so it must show strong cause, whether it attacks existence or exercise (Shanghai Turbo). Per Vinmar, witnesses abroad that were foreseeable at contracting carry little weight, and these witnesses can give evidence by video link.
