Larchfield wants the Frame claim heard in the SICC. How can it get the claim there?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per O 2 r 2(2), a High Court clause concluded before 1 October 2016 does not of itself submit to the SICC, so there is no primary jurisdiction (Prof Chong's sample-final answer scheme). Larchfield sues in the General Division and asks for a transfer under O 2 r 4(1)(c). Outside the CCAA the General Division may transfer without every party's consent, though per C&Y the parties' level of consent is a factor, and Nordhaven objects. Per Chong (seminar), the test turns on how international and commercial the dispute is, not its complexity. It could go either way: the buyer, its plant and its witnesses are in Ruritania, but Singapore law governs and the claim needs no special SICC feature.

Per Chong (sample-final answer scheme; AY23-24 mid-term feedback), where [clause X] [predates 1 October 2016 / does not cover [the claim against C]], the SICC has no primary jurisdiction, so [claimant] reaches it only by transfer under the O 2 r 4(1)(c) "more appropriate" test.

⚡ Base facts · 5 of 7B3

⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

The CCAA applies to clause 19 on Ruritania's date. Per s 12(1), which applies “despite any other written law or rule of law”, the court must stay or dismiss unless an exception in (a) to (e) applies. Per 6DM the court asks two things: is there an exclusive agreement that does not designate a Singapore court, and does an exception apply. Per C&Y the CCAA overrides Spiliada and strong cause. The common law returns only if an exception applies.

Per O 2 r 2(3), a clause naming the SICC alone is not “of itself” a submission to the General Division, so Larchfield suing there cannot rely on it alone (C&Y). In the SICC, clause 25 is a written jurisdiction agreement and the action is international and commercial, so the SICC has primary jurisdiction (O 2 r 1(1) and s 18D(1)). Transfer matters only where there is no primary jurisdiction.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J5.2.3 :: SICC-Only Clause (−)

⚡ Base facts · 7 of 7B2

1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per s 11(1), the chosen court must not decline unless clause 25 is null and void under Singapore law, including its choice of law rules, and it is valid. Per s 11(2), it cannot decline in favour of Ruritania, so neither Spiliada nor strong cause applies. O 2 r 3(3) points the same way: the SICC must not decline solely because the action is connected with another country. Service was proper: a party to the written jurisdiction agreement may be served out without permission (O 5 r 6(2)(a)), whether or not the clause mentions service.

Per s 11(2), [Singapore] cannot decline in favour of [State B], so neither Spiliada nor strong cause applies, and per C&Y no other s 11(3) ground has been prescribed. [Defendant]'s points that [witnesses / governing law] point to [State B], or that proceedings are pending there, are irrelevant.

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
⚡ BIG IDEA

Three contracts with three exclusive clauses go to three different regimes, so run the CCAA gate clause by clause, using the date for each chosen court's State, before any forum question. The Frame Agreement (15 June 2016) is outside the CCAA: Larchfield serves out on clause 14, Nordhaven bears strong cause, and the pre-2016 “High Court” clause reaches the SICC only by transfer. Inside the CCAA, s 12 sends the Commissioning claim to Ruritania, and s 11 makes the SICC, which clause 25 alone names, hear the Maintenance claim. The twists add a contractual anti-suit injunction that delay probably defeats, then a common law action on an Elbonian default judgment that fails because Larchfield was never present there and only protested.

  1. 1
    The CCAA gate, clause by clause B1

    Run the gate for each clause, testing its date against the date the Convention entered into force for the chosen court's State. Clause 14 chooses Singapore and says “exclusive”, but it was concluded on 15 June 2016, before Singapore's date of 1 October 2016, so the Frame Agreement is outside the CCAA and the common law decides. Clause 19 chooses Ruritania and was concluded on 10 March 2019, after Ruritania's date of 1 January 2018; clause 25 chooses the SICC and was concluded on 12 August 2023, after Singapore's date. Both say “exclusively”, so they are exclusive under s 3(1); the parties reside in different States, so the cases are international (s 4(1)); and claims for unpaid fees under business contracts are commercial (C&Y). So s 12 governs the Commissioning claim and s 11 the Maintenance claim.

  2. 2
    Frame claim: serving Nordhaven out on clause 14 D8

    Nordhaven has no office, staff or assets in Singapore, so it must be served out. None of the contracts says how process may be served, so O 8 r 1(3) does not apply, and Larchfield needs approval under O 8 r 1(1). The ground is “appropriate court”, as “has the jurisdiction” is arguably reserved for CCAA cases. In principle Larchfield must meet all three requirements; in practice it shows a good arguable case that clause 14 is valid, binds Nordhaven and covers the claim, which supplies the nexus under para 63(3)(d)(iv) or (r), plus a serious question on the unpaid US$4 million, shown separately because those factors say nothing about the merits. Forum need not be proved: if Nordhaven contests it, it breaks clause 14 and must show strong cause. On the assumed facts each point is met, so approval should be granted.

  3. 3
    Frame claim: strong cause on Nordhaven E7E8

    If Nordhaven applies to set aside service or for a stay on forum grounds, it breaks its promise in clause 14 not to object to Singapore. Per Vinmar (restating The Eleftheria), the court then holds it to its bargain unless it shows strong cause, on a set-aside as on a stay (Shanghai Turbo). This is not Spiliada: the hurdle is higher, because the court is asked to sanction a breach. Nordhaven's engineers live in Ruritania, but per Vinmar witnesses that were foreseeable when the clause was signed carry little weight, and they can give evidence by video link. Singapore law governs the Frame Agreement, and nothing suggests abuse by Larchfield or real prejudice to Nordhaven in defending here, so there is no strong cause and the General Division will hear the Frame claim.

  4. 4
    Frame claim: the SICC only by transfer F3F6

    Clause 14 names the High Court and predates 1 October 2016, so per O 2 r 2(2) it does not of itself submit to the SICC, and per Chong (sample-final answer scheme) the SICC has no primary jurisdiction. Larchfield sues in the General Division and seeks a transfer under O 2 r 4(1): the action is international and commercial and seeks no prerogative relief, so the question is whether the SICC is more appropriate. Outside the CCAA Nordhaven's consent is not needed, but per C&Y the parties' level of consent is a factor, and Nordhaven objects. Per Chong (seminar), the test turns on how international and commercial the dispute is, not its complexity. If the court stresses that the buyer, its plant and its witnesses are in Ruritania, it transfers; if it stresses that Singapore law governs, no SICC feature is needed and Nordhaven objects, the claim stays in the General Division.

  5. 5
    Commissioning claim: s 12 sends it to Ruritania B3

    Clause 19 is inside the CCAA and chooses Ruritania, so per s 12(1), “despite any other written law or rule of law”, Singapore must stay or dismiss the Commissioning claim unless an exception applies. Per 6DM the court asks whether there is an exclusive agreement not designating a Singapore court, which clause 19 plainly is, and then whether an exception in s 12(1)(a) to (e) applies. Clause 19 is valid, so (a) fails, and per the Hartley–Dogauchi Report (c) and (d) apply only in the most exceptional circumstances. A five year trial in Ruritania is mere delay: not enough under (d), and far from the clear, extremely serious and highly probable injustice that (c) needs (Brand & Herrup, in 6DM). Splitting the claims fails too, as in 6DM even the risk that a related party could not be joined abroad failed (c). So the claim is stayed or dismissed and Larchfield must sue in Ruritania; Spiliada and strong cause play no part (C&Y).

  6. 6
    Maintenance claim: file in the SICC F2F3

    Clause 25 is a written jurisdiction agreement naming the SICC (O 2 r 1(7)). The action is international, as Nordhaven's place of business is in Ruritania, and commercial, and it seeks no prerogative relief, so per O 2 r 1(1) and s 18D(1) the SICC has primary jurisdiction and no transfer is needed. Nordhaven, a party to clause 25, may be served in Ruritania without permission (O 5 r 6(2)(a)). But per O 2 r 2(3), a clause naming only the SICC is not of itself submission to the General Division (C&Y), so Larchfield should not file the Maintenance claim there.

  7. 7
    Maintenance claim: the SICC must hear it B2

    Clause 25 is inside the CCAA and chooses a Singapore court, so per s 11(1) the SICC must not decline unless clause 25 is null and void under Singapore law, including its choice of law rules, and it is valid. Per s 11(2) it cannot decline in favour of Ruritania, so neither Spiliada nor strong cause applies, and Nordhaven's Ruritanian witnesses are irrelevant. The SICC's own rule points the same way: it must not decline solely because the action is connected with Ruritania (O 2 r 3(3)). So the SICC will hear the Maintenance claim.

  8. 8
    Advice to Larchfield

    Larchfield cannot have all three claims heard together in Singapore. Frame: sue in the General Division, serving Nordhaven out with approval on clause 14; Nordhaven cannot show strong cause, and the SICC is reachable only by a transfer that could go either way. Commissioning: Singapore must stay or dismiss under s 12, so Larchfield must sue in Ruritania. Maintenance: file in the SICC, which has primary jurisdiction under clause 25 and must hear the claim under s 11.

2Twist 1

🧩 TWIST 1

Now add these facts.

Larchfield sues Nordhaven on the Frame Agreement in the General Division and, with the court's approval, serves it in Ruritania. A month later, Nordhaven sues Larchfield in Elbonia for damages for the leaking valves under the Frame Agreement.

Larchfield applies to the Elbonian court to set aside the claim for want of jurisdiction, relying only on clause 14. It files no defence on the merits and makes no other application. The Elbonian court dismisses the application, holding that it has jurisdiction because the valves were shipped through an Elbonian port.

Eleven months after the Elbonian action began, Larchfield asks the General Division for an anti-suit injunction. The Elbonian trial starts next month.

ℹ ASSUME
  1. Elbonia is not a Contracting State to the Hague Convention on Choice of Court Agreements.
✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • G1
    ASI starter, and the basis. Larchfield wants to stop the Elbonian action. Start with the caution, the burden on the applicant and the basis it relies on: breach of clause 14.
  • G2
    Amenability. Nordhaven must be within the court's personal jurisdiction. It was validly served out, but it has no presence or assets here, so Akai is the counter.
  • G3
    Contractual ASI: a Singapore clause is breached. Suing in Elbonia breaks clause 14, so the injunction is contractual. But eleven months of delay, with trial next month, brings comity back.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • G9
    ASI in a CCAA case. G9 is for a contract inside the CCAA. The Frame Agreement was signed on 15 June 2016, before 1 October 2016, so it is outside. That Elbonia is not a Contracting State is not the reason: G9 also covers a suit in a non-Contracting State when the contract is inside the CCAA.
  • G6
    Vexation ASI: sufficient interest. Sufficient interest through the natural forum is needed only where no clause is breached. Here clause 14 itself supplies the connection.
  • G7
    SCORECARD · Vexation or oppression, and injustice to the respondent. Vexation is the basis when no clause is broken. Nordhaven breaks clause 14, so Larchfield need not show vexation. The delay is weighed under the contractual basis (G3).
  • H10
    Anti-enforcement injunction: the judgment already exists. An anti-enforcement injunction needs a foreign judgment. The Elbonian trial has not even started.

Fair to tick but not needed: G11 Relitigation after a Singapore judgment; third parties; if the ASI is ignored

Application questions · twist 1

⚡ Twist 1 · 1 of 3G2
Is Nordhaven amenable to the General Division for the injunction?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Amenability is needed whatever the basis. Valid service out brings Nordhaven within the court's in personam jurisdiction (Cooperative Muratori). Akai is the counter: a respondent served out, with no presence or assets here, was held not amenable. The settled view (C&Y; Cooperative Muratori) is that valid service or submission is enough, and a lack of assets goes only to whether the order would be effective.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J6.1 :: Submission or Valid Service (+)

Presently, [respondent] is amenable, having [submitted by [appearing / defending / counterclaiming] in [Suit X]] or been validly served [in / out of] Singapore (Koh Kay Yew; Westbridge v Mittal; C&Y). Per Cooperative Muratori, being within the court's in personam jurisdiction is what amenability requires.

⚡ Twist 1 · 2 of 3G3
Must Larchfield show that Singapore is the natural forum, or that the Elbonian action is vexatious?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Westbridge v Mittal and C&Y, a Singapore exclusive clause itself supplies the connection, and per Cooperative Muratori the applicant need not show that Singapore is more appropriate. Per Sun Travels, breach is a separate basis: no unconscionability is needed, and the injunction ordinarily issues unless Nordhaven shows strong reasons. The CCAA plays no part: the Frame Agreement predates 1 October 2016, but clause 14 is still an exclusive clause at common law.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J6.3.1.1 :: Exclusive Clause Breached (+)

Per C&Y, breach is a question of interpretation under [proper law]. Presently, [respondent] breached [clause X], an exclusive [Singapore / SICC / arbitration] clause, by suing in [foreign court]. Per Sun Travels, breach is a separate basis: no unconscionability is needed, and the ASI ordinarily issues absent strong reasons (J6.3.1.4).

⚡ Twist 1 · 3 of 3G3
Larchfield says it waited because it was first contesting jurisdiction in Elbonia. Will the injunction be granted?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Sun Travels, comity is relevant to delay even in contractual cases, and how far the foreign action has progressed matters more than the length of the delay: an injunction on the eve of trial would waste more of the Elbonian court's resources. Per Sun Travels, contesting jurisdiction abroad does not excuse delay (no “two bites at the cherry”); Larchfield should have objected in Elbonia and applied here together. Whether delay sits within strong reasons or the court's discretion is open, but either way it probably defeats the injunction here. The challenge in Elbonia was a protest, not a submission.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J6.3.1.5 :: Contesting Jurisdiction Is No Excuse (−)

[Applicant] says it first objected to [foreign court]'s jurisdiction. Per Sun Travels (citing The Angelic Grace, Toepfer and Ecobank), that does not excuse delay: no "two bites at the cherry". Similar to ADM v PT Budi, refused on "general discretionary considerations and the needs of comity", [applicant] should have [objected abroad and applied here] together.

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes: an anti-suit injunction against the Elbonian action G1

    The three base answers stay the same. What is new: Larchfield sued on the Frame Agreement in the General Division and served Nordhaven out, Nordhaven then sued in Elbonia on the same agreement, and eleven months later Larchfield seeks an anti-suit injunction, with the Elbonian trial next month. Per SNIA and Lakshmi, an injunction interferes indirectly with the foreign court, so it issues only where the ends of justice require; Larchfield bears the burden (Kirkham; C&Y) and must name its basis (Cooperative Muratori). The basis is contractual: amenability, breach of clause 14 and no strong reasons, with natural forum and vexation dropping out. The Frame Agreement is outside the CCAA, so this is an ordinary contractual injunction, not a CCAA one.

  2. 2
    Amenability: valid service out, with Akai against it G2

    Amenability is always required: Nordhaven must be within the court's personal jurisdiction (Cooperative Muratori). Per Chong (answer scheme), Larchfield should seek the injunction as ancillary relief in the Frame action, so amenability comes from the valid service out with approval there. Nordhaven will cite Akai, where a respondent that was served out, had no presence or assets here and only opposed the injunction was held not amenable. But the settled view (C&Y; Cooperative Muratori) is that valid service is enough, and a lack of assets goes only to whether the order would be effective. So Nordhaven is amenable on the settled view; only if Akai were followed would no injunction issue.

  3. 3
    Breach of clause 14, and no strong reasons G3

    Breach is a question of interpretation under the clause's proper law (C&Y): clause 14 is an express exclusive clause in a Singapore-law contract, and Nordhaven's claim for the leaking valves arises out of the Frame Agreement, so suing in Elbonia breaks it. Per Westbridge v Mittal and C&Y, clause 14 itself supplies Singapore's connection, and per Cooperative Muratori Larchfield need not show Singapore is more appropriate. Per Sun Travels, breach is a separate basis needing no unconscionability, and the injunction ordinarily issues unless Nordhaven shows strong reasons, in practice the strong cause test (C&Y). Apart from Larchfield's delay, weighed in the next step, Nordhaven shows none on these facts: there are no third parties and no claim outside clause 14. Larchfield's challenge in Elbonia was a protest, not a submission (Nimbus; IGCF), so it did not give up clause 14.

  4. 4
    Delay and comity: the injunction is probably refused G3

    Per Sun Travels, comity is relevant to delay even in contractual cases, and how far the foreign action has progressed matters more than the length of the delay, as a late injunction wastes more of the foreign court's resources (C&Y). Larchfield waited eleven months and the Elbonian trial starts next month; similar to Hilton, where the Maldivian proceedings were too far advanced, an injunction now would waste the Elbonian court's work. Contesting jurisdiction in Elbonia first is no excuse: per Sun Travels there are no “two bites at the cherry”, and Larchfield should have objected there and applied here together. Whether delay sits within strong reasons or the court's discretion is open (C&Y), but either way the injunction is probably refused.

Application questions · twist 2

⚡ Twist 2 · 1 of 4H1
Which regime governs Nordhaven's claim on the Elbonian judgment?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per s 2(1), Part 3 covers only a judgment of the court of a Contracting State chosen in an exclusive agreement within the Convention, or of a court it transferred the case to. Elbonia is not a Contracting State, and its court was neither chosen (clause 14 chose Singapore) nor a transferee. So Nordhaven sues on the debt the judgment creates, usually by summary judgment. Larchfield gets leave to defend only by showing a real defence, never by reopening the merits.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J7.0.2 :: Common Law Residual

Otherwise [creditor] sues [debtor] on the debt [the X judgment] creates, usually by [summary judgment]. Per C&Y, [debtor] gets leave to defend only by showing a fair or reasonable probability of [a real defence] under J7.2, never [the merits] (J7.2.1).

⚡ Twist 2 · 2 of 4H2
Larchfield says that a default judgment is not a judgment on the merits. Is it right?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per C&Y, a default judgment is on the merits although the debtor did not appear and the foreign court may not have considered the evidence; non-participation goes only to fraud or natural justice. It is also final: per Humpuss and Eleven v Boxsentry, a default judgment given final effect until set aside is final although it may still be set aside. US$2 million is a definite sum.

Per C&Y, [the default judgment] is on the merits although [debtor] did not appear and [the X court] may not have considered [the evidence]; non-participation goes only to fraud (J7.2.2) or natural justice (J7.2.3).

⚡ Twist 2 · 3 of 4H4
Did the Elbonian court have international jurisdiction over Larchfield?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Singapore tests international jurisdiction by its own rules: presence or submission (Republic of India v Deutsche Telekom). The Elbonian court's own ground does not count, its finding on jurisdiction creates no estoppel, and the grounds are closed (Schibsby v Westenholz). Larchfield had no office, staff or assets in Elbonia. As in Nimbus, objecting to jurisdiction, losing and then taking no part is not submission. Clause 14 is an agreement to submit to Singapore, not Elbonia. So enforcement fails. Had Larchfield asked for a stay on forum non conveniens grounds instead, submission would be arguable (Henry v Geoprosco against IGCF).

⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per C&Y, no case decides the defence. For it: Larchfield could recover damages for the breach here anyway (Union Discount), REFJA s 5(4)(b) gives an analogue favouring convergence (Merck), and it fits party autonomy. Against it: no Singapore authority recognises it. Per Prof Chong (March 2026 answer scheme), the defence needs a breach, so the clause must be promissory; clause 14 is an express exclusive clause under Singapore law. The objection is probably lost by submitting (C&Y), but here jurisdiction rests on presence, and the challenge in Elbonia was not a submission. The public policy rule in Nimbus needs a breach of a Singapore anti-suit injunction, and none was granted.

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes: Nordhaven sues on the Elbonian default judgment H1

    The base answers and the refused injunction stay as they were. What is new: Larchfield took no further part in Elbonia, the Elbonian court gave a default judgment for US$2 million, and Nordhaven sues on it in Singapore. Per s 2(1), CCAA Part 3 covers only a judgment of the chosen court of a Contracting State, or of a court it transferred the case to; Elbonia is not a Contracting State, and clause 14 chose Singapore, so the common law decides. Nordhaven sues on the debt the judgment creates, usually by summary judgment, and per C&Y Larchfield gets leave to defend only by showing a real defence, never by reopening the merits.

  2. 2
    On the merits, final and for a definite sum H2

    Per C&Y, Nordhaven must show that the judgment is on the merits, given by a court with international jurisdiction over Larchfield, final and conclusive, and for a definite sum that is not a tax, fine or penalty. A default judgment is on the merits although Larchfield did not defend (C&Y); not taking part goes only to fraud or natural justice, and Larchfield knew of the action and chose not to defend. Per Humpuss and Eleven v Boxsentry, a default judgment given final effect until set aside is final, and Elbonian law treats this one so, although Larchfield may still apply to set it aside. US$2 million is a definite sum, so everything turns on international jurisdiction.

  3. 3
    International jurisdiction: no presence and no submission H3H4

    Per C&Y, Singapore tests international jurisdiction by its own rules, so the Elbonian court's port ground does not count, and its ruling on its own jurisdiction creates no estoppel. Per Republic of India v Deutsche Telekom, Larchfield must have been present in Elbonia, or have claimed there, voluntarily appeared or agreed in advance to submit, and per Schibsby v Westenholz the grounds are closed. Larchfield never had an office, staff or assets in Elbonia, so it was not present (Adams v Cape), and clause 14 is an agreement to submit to Singapore, not Elbonia. As in Nimbus, objecting to jurisdiction, losing and then taking no part is not submission. So the Elbonian court had no international jurisdiction, and the judgment is not enforced. Had Larchfield asked for a stay on forum grounds instead, submission would be open: on Henry v Geoprosco's logic it would have submitted, giving Elbonia jurisdiction, but per IGCF a stay is a protest, so the judgment would still fail.

  4. 4
    In the alternative: breach of clause 14 as a defence H7

    Suppose instead that the Elbonian court had international jurisdiction, say because Larchfield had a sales office there when served. Larchfield could then argue that the judgment was obtained in breach of clause 14. Per Prof Chong's March 2026 answer scheme the defence needs a breach, so the clause must be promissory: clause 14 is an express exclusive clause under Singapore law, and Nordhaven broke it; the objection is probably lost by submitting (C&Y), but Larchfield only protested. Per C&Y no case decides the defence: for it, Larchfield could recover damages for the breach anyway (Union Discount), REFJA s 5(4)(b) gives an analogue (Merck) and it fits party autonomy; against it, no Singapore authority recognises it. So if the defence is recognised, enforcement is refused; if not, the judgment is enforced. The public policy bar in Nimbus needs a breach of a Singapore anti-suit injunction, and none was granted.

4Scorecards: weigh the factors

Prof Chong rewards applying facts to factor tests. Sort each fact, then answer the verdict question. These use the base facts unless a line says “Suppose”.

B3 Sort the factors: The s 12 exceptions on the Commissioning claim

Each line is a point Larchfield might use to keep the Commissioning claim in Singapore despite clause 19. Does it open an exception in s 12(1)? Lines marked “Suppose” are extra facts for this card only.

Larchfield: a trial takes about five years in Ruritania, against 18 months here.
No exception. Mere delay is not enough under s 12(1)(d), and it is nowhere near the clear, extremely serious and highly probable injustice that s 12(1)(c) needs. J1.4.2 :: (d) Cannot Reasonably Be Performed
Larchfield: the leaks will also be tried here under the Frame Agreement, so one dispute is split between two countries.
No exception. As in 6DM, where the risk that a related party could not be joined abroad failed s 12(1)(c), splitting a dispute is no manifest injustice: that test is far higher than fragmentation as strong cause at common law. The split also follows from the parties' own choice of a different court for each contract. J1.4.2 :: (c) Fragmentation
Suppose: Larchfield says Singapore has a strong policy that suppliers are paid promptly, which a five year wait in Ruritania defeats.
No exception. As in Motacus (cited in 6DM), a forum policy of quick payment does not justify ignoring a foreign exclusive clause. Parliament could have made an art 21 declaration. J1.4.2 :: (c) Domestic Policy
Suppose: Larchfield says Ruritanian judges favour local companies. Its only evidence is one newspaper article.
No exception. No fair trial for bias is the classic example, but per Brand & Herrup (in 6DM) the injustice must be clear, extremely serious and highly probable, not speculative. One article is not cogent evidence. J1.4.2 :: (c) Manifest Injustice: Rule
Suppose: Nordhaven's own engineers signed the commissioning test reports, so it has no real defence.
No exception. The merits are not one of the exceptions in s 12(1)(a) to (e). The court must stay or dismiss however strong the claim is. J1.4 :: Must Stay or Dismiss
Suppose: civil war has broken out in Ruritania, and its courts have stopped sitting.
Opens an exception. Exceptional reasons beyond the parties' control mean clause 19 cannot reasonably be performed (s 12(1)(d)). The stay is then decided at common law. J1.4.2 :: (d) Cannot Reasonably Be Performed
Suppose: Ruritania has issued arrest warrants for Larchfield's directors on charges brought to stop the company suing there, and there is cogent evidence of this.
Opens an exception. Reasons special to a party that stop it suing in the chosen State are the kind of case the Hartley–Dogauchi Report has in mind for s 12(1)(c), if proved by cogent evidence. J1.4.2 :: (c) Exceptional Case
Suppose: Larchfield first sued in Ruritania, and the Ruritanian court declined jurisdiction over the claim.
Opens an exception. The chosen court has declined (s 12(1)(e)), so Singapore may hear the case under its own rules without breaching the Convention. J1.4.2 :: (e) Chosen Court Declined

1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

No exception in s 12(1)(a) to (e) is made out on the base facts. Exceptions (c) and (d) apply only in the most exceptional circumstances, and delay, expense and fragmentation fall far short. So the court must stay or dismiss, and Larchfield must sue in Ruritania. Even at common law the delay would fail: notorious delay in the chosen court is foreseeable (Vinmar).

5Remember

🧠 FOR THE EXAM
  • Run the CCAA gate clause by clause, testing each clause's date against the date the Convention entered into force for the chosen court's State (Singapore: 1 October 2016).
  • A Singapore exclusive clause outside the CCAA, with no term on service: serve out with approval on the “appropriate court” ground (valid, binds, covers, plus a separate serious question); a forum objection by the defendant needs strong cause, never Spiliada.
  • A pre-1 October 2016 “High Court” clause gives the SICC no primary jurisdiction, only a transfer on “more appropriate” (no all-party consent outside the CCAA); an SICC-only clause is not of itself submission to the General Division.
  • Inside the CCAA, s 11 makes the chosen Singapore court hear the claim and s 12 makes Singapore stay for a chosen foreign court; mere delay and a split dispute open no s 12 exception.
  • A contractual anti-suit injunction needs no natural forum or vexation, but comity returns with delay: contesting jurisdiction abroad first is no excuse, and on the eve of trial relief is probably refused.
  • At common law a foreign default judgment is on the merits and can be final, but objecting to jurisdiction, losing and taking no further part is a protest, not submission (Nimbus), so without presence enforcement fails.

LAW302 · META GAME · ADDITIONAL PRACTICE · MIXED · HYPO mx-09 · GEMINI PROMPT V1 · LAW REVIEWED 17 NOV · 17 QUESTIONS

Rimbun Joinery v Korsak Forestry

Gemini (prompt v1) sent only a guide for this hypo, with no usable file. Claude rebuilt the full hypo from it (72 gaps filled or errors fixed), then reviewed it in three passes (12 changes). Gemini called it mx-02 “Banyan Timber v Korsak Forestry”. Gemini's file: banyan_timber_v_korsak_forestry_law302_walkthrou.

ADDITIONAL PRACTICE

This hypo closely repeats mx-02. Same mid-term pattern as mx-02, with identical base boxes: an unregistered foreign company served through its agent here, Spiliada, Ralli, tainting and a defective product tort, then a Singapore non-exclusive clause and a foreign judgment (85% of its Menu boxes are the same). Do mx-02 first and come here for a second run at the same moves on new facts.

Answers:

1Base facts

🧩 HYPOTHETICAL
Rimbun Joinery v Korsak Forestry

Rimbun Joinery Pte Ltd, a Singapore company, makes hardwood furniture. Korsak Forestry Ltd is incorporated in Elbonia, where it runs sawmills. Korsak has never registered in Singapore, but since 2023 it has leased a sales office in Jurong, where its salaried agent, Mr Seet, signs contracts for it without prior approval.

In January 2025 Mr Seet signed a Supply Contract with Rimbun at the Jurong office. Korsak was to mill 5,000 cubic metres of hardwood in Elbonia and load it on board at an Elbonian port for carriage to Singapore. Rimbun was to pay in Singapore dollars into Korsak's Elbonian bank account. The contract has no governing law clause.

In February 2025 Korsak shipped the first 1,000 cubic metres. Rimbun says that Korsak's mill workers carelessly failed to kiln-dry and treat it, so beetles spread from it into Rimbun's Jurong warehouse and destroyed S$600,000 of other stock. That month Mr Seet also signed an Equipment Agreement, expressly governed by Elbonian law: Rimbun lent Korsak S$400,000 to buy kilns to dry the rest of the order. Neither contract has a jurisdiction clause.

In March 2025 Elbonia made it a crime to export hardwood. Korsak has shipped nothing since. It also refuses to repay the loan, which is now due.

With the court's permission, Rimbun served its claim on Mr Seet at the Jurong office under O 7 r 4. It claims damages for the undelivered timber, repayment of the loan, and damages in negligence for the destroyed stock. Korsak applies for a stay in favour of Elbonia.

Advise Rimbun on jurisdiction and on the merits of its three claims.

ℹ ASSUME
  1. Under Elbonian law the ban does not discharge the Supply Contract, so Korsak is liable in damages for the unshipped timber. Under Singapore law the ban would frustrate it.
  2. Under Elbonian law the Equipment Agreement is so closely connected with the banned exports that the loan cannot be recovered. Under Singapore law the connection is not close enough.
  3. Under Singapore law Korsak is liable in negligence for the beetle damage. Under Elbonian law it has no civil liability of any kind for that damage.
  4. Korsak's mill workers live in Elbonia, as do the Elbonian state inspectors who passed the first shipment. The inspectors cannot be made to testify in Singapore. Both courts have video link.
  5. A civil trial takes about six years in Elbonia and 12 months in Singapore.
✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • D2
    Foreign company never registered here, with an office or agent here. Korsak never registered here, so s 376 is unavailable. It trades from a fixed office in Jurong through a salaried agent who can bind it, so Rimbun must show Adams v Cape presence, and service on Mr Seet must meet O 7 r 4.
  • E2
    Stay after service in Singapore: Spiliada starter. Korsak was served here, no clause is broken, and it asks for a stay, so Spiliada applies. It bears stage 1, and Rimbun bears stage 2.
  • E4
    SCORECARD · Spiliada stage 1: connecting factors. The inspectors, the mill workers, Elbonian law and the place of the tort are stage 1 factors. Mark which way each points and weigh their quality, not their number.
  • E5
    SCORECARD · Spiliada stage 2: substantial justice. The six-year wait is Rimbun's stage 2 point. Delay in the foreign court is disregarded unless it is egregious.
  • L6
    SCORECARD · Objective proper law: closest and most real connection. No law clause, and nothing clear enough for an implied choice. Both parties perform in Elbonia, against signing in Jurong and a Singapore dollar price, so weigh the connections.
  • M5
    Ralli Bros: performance becomes illegal where it must be done. After signing, Elbonia made a crime of the very act the contract requires there: loading hardwood for export. Elbonian law is also the proper law, so Route A comes first, but it does not discharge the contract. The readings of Ralli then give different results.
  • M6
    SCORECARD · Tainting: a relevant illegality, sufficiently connected. Korsak says the illegality taints the loan. The Assume list answers Step 2 differently under each law, and Step 1 turns on the Ralli reading, so it is arguable, not settled.
  • N3
    SCORECARD · Locate the tort: where in substance did it arise?. The drying was skipped in Elbonia, the timber was sold through Jurong and the stock was destroyed here, and the two laws differ. Locate the tort before limb 2, and carry both answers.
  • N5
    SCORECARD · The flexible exception. If the tort is in Elbonia, limb 2 fails and Rimbun can only argue the flexible exception. Elbonia is Korsak's home and the place of the careless act.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • D4
    Defendant abroad: service out and the three requirements. Tempting because Korsak is an Elbonian company that never registered here. Wrong because Rimbun served Mr Seet in Singapore under O 7 r 4, so the O 8 requirements for service out do not arise. Service out is a fallback only if that service fails.
  • E3
    Forum conveniens on service out: burden on the claimant. Tempting because Korsak is a foreign company. Wrong because it was served here and asks for a stay, so it bears stage 1. The burden falls on the claimant only on a set-aside after service out.
  • E7
    Strong cause: starter and nature of the test. Tempting because Korsak wants to leave Singapore. Wrong because neither contract has a jurisdiction clause, so no promise is broken and the test is Spiliada.
  • M3
    SCORECARD · Foster v Driscoll: intention to break a friendly state's law. Tempting because exporting hardwood is now an Elbonian crime. Per Rickshaw, courts must not be quick to apply the exception: the displaced law must be purely fortuitous, on clear and satisfying grounds, and the exception is strictly applied. 📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
⚡ BIG IDEA

This is the mid-term build in one long question. Korsak never registered but trades from a Jurong office, so service turns on Adams v Cape presence, and with no clause Korsak bears Spiliada stage 1, where Elbonian law and the non-compellable inspectors probably earn it a stay. On the merits each claim turns on an open point (the Ralli reading, which law decides tainting, and where negligence over a defective product is located), so the deciding move is to run both routes with a result under each. The twists add a Singapore non-exclusive clause (strong cause for the stay, but only vexation for an injunction, and a pointer to Singapore law), then an Elbonian declaration that Rimbun submitted to, whose ruling on governing law may or may not bind.

  1. 1
    Service on Korsak through Mr Seet D2

    Korsak never registered, so per C&Y s 376(a) and (b) fail for want of a registered office or authorised representative, and s 376(c) is not meant for a company still trading here. So Rimbun relies on s 16(1)(a)(i) SCJA and must prove Adams v Cape presence: a fixed place (the Jurong office Korsak leases), for more than a minimal period (since 2023), carrying on Korsak's business, not Mr Seet's own, as he is salaried and binds Korsak without prior approval. Order 7 r 4 needs permission, which Rimbun had, and per Rosenberg an agent with power to contract who controls the business the action relates to. Mr Seet signed both contracts, and the negligence claim arises from timber he sold, though Korsak will say it concerns its Elbonian milling. Per Chong (mid-term feedback), in line with Beranek, r 4 arguably rests on presence, so Mr Seet is only the mode of service; per Yeo it fits the service out limb. On either view service probably stands; flag in one line the puzzle of how a present company is “absent” under r 4.

  2. 2
    The stay: Spiliada, stage 1 on Korsak E2

    Neither contract has a jurisdiction clause, so no one breaks a promise and the test is Spiliada, not strong cause. Korsak was served here and asks for a stay, not to set the service aside. Per Spiliada and JIO, it bears the legal burden at stage 1 to show that Elbonia, its home and an available forum, is clearly or distinctly more appropriate, and Rimbun bears stage 2. Even if r 4 counted as service out, a defendant who applies for a stay bears stage 1 (Per Zoom), and Singapore rejects the Australian “clearly inappropriate forum” test (Per JIO).

  3. 3
    Spiliada stages 1 and 2: probably a stay E4E5

    Stage 1 weighs the quality of the links, not their number (Per Rappo and JIO). Residence cancels out, and Korsak's mill workers count for little: they are its own employees (Chong's feedback), and both courts have video link (Per JIO). The Elbonian inspectors are non-parties who cannot be compelled here, and their evidence is at least arguably relevant because they passed the shipment, so they point to Elbonia (Per JIO). Elbonian law governs both contracts, the loan expressly, and matters to the ban and the taint, so it weighs (Per Rickshaw, JIO and Rappo), while signing in Jurong is neutral, as formation is not disputed. The place of the tort points to Elbonia if the negligence is located there (Per JIO); if it is located in Singapore the balance is closer, and finely balanced factors mean no stay. At stage 2, delay is disregarded unless egregious (Per C&Y), and in Grains and Industrial even alleged delays of over 10 years failed, so the six-year wait fails and a stay is probable.

  4. 4
    If heard: the proper law of the Supply Contract L6

    The ask covers the merits, so assume the Singapore court hears the claims. The Supply Contract has no law clause, and with no court clause or standard form nothing implies a choice; the Equipment Agreement's choice of Elbonian law came a month later and, if it counts at all, points the same way. Per Bonython, the test is the closest and most real connection, and per Prof Chong the strongest argument is usually where both parties perform: Korsak mills the timber and loads it at an Elbonian port, and Rimbun pays into Korsak's Elbonian account. The Singapore dollar price, Rimbun's base and Korsak's Jurong office point to Singapore but are outweighed, signing in Jurong counts little (Per Pacific Recreation), and where witnesses live is a Spiliada factor only. Courts do not declare ties (Per Lew), so Elbonian law is the objective proper law.

  5. 5
    The export ban: Route A, then Ralli M5

    Elbonian law is both the proper law and the law broken, so start with Route A (Per Kahler and Zivnostenka): Elbonian law decides what its ban does, and it leaves Korsak liable in damages, so Route A gives Korsak nothing. Foster is out, as the ban came after both contracts and the proper law is the law broken. Ralli applies, because loading hardwood for export at an Elbonian port is the very act the contract requires there, and it is now a crime there. On Esben's independent rule (start here; per Prof Chong arguably preferable as the later Court of Appeal ruling), the claim for the undelivered timber fails in so far as performance is unlawful there, an odd result for a Singapore buyer (per Chong (seminar)). On the frustration reading, which Peh Teck Quee leaned to, Elbonian law decides and Korsak stays liable. Mention comity abstention (dicta in Toprak and Magdeev) in one line; per Ryder Industries the readings differ only because the proper law is not Singapore law.

  6. 6
    The loan: does the ban taint it? M6

    Korsak says the illegality taints the Equipment Agreement, so per Euro-Diam ask (1) whether there is a relevant foreign illegality and (2) whether it is sufficiently connected to the claim. Step 1 asks whether Singapore would enforce the Supply Contract: on Esben's reading it would not, and a prohibition at the place of performance can be serious enough (Per Ryder Industries; Per Magdeev, after a balancing exercise). On the frustration reading the contract stays binding, so Step 1 is weaker (if it fails, the taint argument fails with it): flag it and assume it met. Step 2 is unresolved, as the cases so far all involved Singapore-law contracts. Per Prof Chong, if tainting is part of the lex fori, Singapore principles decide and, per the Assume list, find no taint, so the loan is recoverable. If it is part of the proper law, per Chong (seminar) that of the Equipment Agreement sued on, Elbonian law decides and the loan is lost.

  7. 7
    Negligence: double actionability, and where the tort happened N3

    Per Rickshaw, the negligence claim needs double actionability, subject to the flexible exception. Limb 1 is met, as Singapore law makes Korsak liable. Limb 2 needs civil liability between the parties under the law of the place of the tort, of any kind (Per Ong Ghee Soon), and Elbonian law gives none, so the tort must be located. Per Distillers and Metall, find the one place where in substance the cause of action arose; the stock destroyed in Jurong does not decide it alone. Per Vibrant Group, for negligence the careless act prevails, so Korsak says Elbonia, where the drying was skipped; Rimbun replies that for a product the tort is where it was marketed without a warning, not where it was made (Per Distillers and Castree v Squibb), and Korsak sold the timber through its Jurong office. If the tort is in Singapore, both limbs point to Singapore law (Per Rickshaw) and Rimbun succeeds; if it is in Elbonia, limb 2 fails.

  8. 8
    If the tort is in Elbonia: the exception fails N5

    On the Elbonia route, Rimbun must displace Elbonian law. Per Rickshaw, courts must not be quick to apply the exception: it is strictly applied, the displaced law must be purely fortuitous on clear and satisfying grounds, and a less favourable law is not enough. Elbonia is where Korsak is incorporated, runs its mill and did the careless act, so it is not there by accident, and the negligence claim fails on this route. If the tort is in Singapore the exception is not needed, and Korsak cannot call Singapore fortuitous either.

  9. 9
    Advice to Rimbun

    Service on Mr Seet probably stands, but Korsak will probably obtain a stay in favour of Elbonia. If Singapore hears the claims, Elbonian law governs the Supply Contract, and the timber claim fails on Esben's reading of Ralli but succeeds on the frustration reading, which Rimbun should press. If tainting Step 1 is met, the loan is recoverable if Singapore principles decide Step 2, and lost if Elbonian law does. The negligence claim succeeds only if the tort is located in Singapore.

2Twist 1

🧩 TWIST 1

Go back to the base facts and add these facts.

Suppose the Supply Contract also contained clause 18:

“Each party submits to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the Singapore courts in respect of any dispute arising out of or in connection with this contract.”

Korsak still applies for a stay. It then sues Rimbun in Elbonia for a declaration that it is not liable for the beetle damage, in contract or in negligence. It does not ask the Elbonian court to stop the Singapore action.

How would your advice differ, and can Rimbun obtain an anti-suit injunction against the Elbonian action?

ℹ ASSUME
  1. Elbonian law reads “submits” in clause 18 as Singapore law does.
✔ ROUND 1 · WHICH MENU BOXES?Note the boxes you would tick, then tap to compare.

Write from these boxes

  • A4
    Says "non-exclusive": Singapore courts. Clause 18 is a Singapore clause that says “non-exclusive”, and Korsak still objects to Singapore. Per Shanghai Turbo, “submits” waives objections, and both candidate laws read it that way.
  • E7
    Strong cause: starter and nature of the test. Korsak is now the party breaking a promise, so strong cause replaces Spiliada for the claims within clause 18, with the burden on Korsak.
  • L5
    No clause: implied choice. There is still no law clause, but a Singapore court clause is a heavy pointer to an implied choice of Singapore law. That changes the Ralli answer.
  • G4
    Singapore non-exclusive clause: is suing abroad a breach?. A Singapore non-exclusive clause, and the counterparty sues abroad. Suing abroad is not ordinarily a breach, and Korsak asks for no order against the Singapore action.
  • G7
    SCORECARD · Vexation or oppression, and injustice to the respondent. With no breach, Rimbun must show vexation or oppression. The Elbonian action mirrors part of the Singapore action, and parallel proceedings alone are not enough.

Decoys: tempting, but wrong on these facts

  • B2
    CCAA applies and Singapore is the chosen court (s 11). Tempting because clause 18 names the Singapore courts in a contract signed after 1 October 2016. Wrong because it says “non-exclusive”, so s 3(2) deeming does not apply and s 11 is never reached.
  • G3
    Contractual ASI: a Singapore clause is breached. Tempting because Korsak sued abroad despite a Singapore clause. Wrong because clause 18 contains no promise not to sue elsewhere, so there is no breach for a contractual injunction to restrain.
  • G9
    ASI in a CCAA case. Tempting because there is a jurisdiction clause and an injunction. Wrong because the contract is outside the CCAA: clause 18 is expressly non-exclusive.
  • A6
    No label: "the parties submit to the jurisdiction of ...". Tempting because clause 18 says “submits”. Wrong because A6 is for a clause with no label, and clause 18 calls itself “non-exclusive”, a label that gets its ordinary meaning.

⚡ Twist 1 · 1 of 4A4
How does clause 18 change the test for Korsak's stay application?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Shanghai Turbo, Singapore takes the contractual approach: “submits” means consent plus a waiver of objections to Singapore's jurisdiction, so any stay application is an attempt to escape clause 18. Whether the clause carries the waiver is for its proper law; here both candidate laws read it the same way. “Non-exclusive” displaces s 3(2) deeming, so the CCAA does not apply. The negligence claim falls within the clause's wide words. The loan claim arises under the Equipment Agreement, which has no clause: if clause 18 does not reach it, Spiliada still governs that claim. Korsak's witnesses and Elbonian law were foreseeable when it signed (Per Vinmar), and in Shanghai Turbo such factors, even with related foreign proceedings, were not strong cause.

With no breach, Rimbun must show that Korsak is amenable (it was validly served here), that Singapore has a sufficient interest (clause 18 arguably supplies it), and vexation or oppression, which justifies an injunction only in the clearest of circumstances. 📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes and what stays

    Clause 18 now submits both parties to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the Singapore courts for disputes connected with the Supply Contract. Korsak still applies for a stay, and it sues in Elbonia for a declaration that it is not liable for the beetle damage, without asking the Elbonian court to stop the Singapore action. Clause 18 says “non-exclusive”, so s 3(2) deeming does not apply and the CCAA is out. Service on Mr Seet stays as it was, and the Equipment Agreement still has no clause; what changes is the test for the stay, possibly the proper law, and the route to an injunction.

  2. 2
    The stay: strong cause on Korsak A4E7

    Per Shanghai Turbo (CA), Singapore takes the contractual approach: “submits” means consent plus a waiver of objections to Singapore's jurisdiction. Whether clause 18 carries that waiver is for its proper law, and the Assume list makes both candidate laws read it the same way. So Korsak's stay application is an attempt to escape clause 18, and per Vinmar it must show strong cause, a higher hurdle than Spiliada. That covers the timber claim and the negligence claim, which falls within the wide words “in connection with” (Per Fiona Trust); whether clause 18 reaches the loan claim is arguable (Allianz v Goh Andress), and if it does not, Spiliada still governs that claim. Korsak's witnesses and Elbonian law were foreseeable when it signed (Per Vinmar), and in Shanghai Turbo such factors, even with related foreign proceedings, were not strong cause, so no stay is likely for the claims within clause 18.

  3. 3
    Proper law again: clause 18 as an implied choice L5

    There is still no law clause, but per Pacific Recreation submitting to Singapore's courts implies Singapore law, the chosen court being presumed to apply its own law. This is a heavy pointer, so Korsak, which wants Singapore law, will probably establish an implied choice. Rimbun replies with Art 4 of the Hague Principles: a court clause is not in itself a choice of law, so stage 3 still decides, Elbonian law governs, and the base split between the Ralli readings stays. If Singapore law governs, Route A no longer applies to the Elbonian ban, but Ralli still does: Esben's rule bars the claim, and on the frustration reading Singapore law frustrates the contract. Per Ryder Industries the readings then no longer differ, so the timber claim fails.

  4. 4
    Anti-suit injunction: no breach, so vexation G4G7

    Per Shanghai Turbo and C&Y, suing in Elbonia is not ordinarily a breach of a Singapore non-exclusive clause, the parties having accepted parallel proceedings. Seeking an order there to stop the Singapore action would arguably be a breach, but Korsak seeks none, so there is no contractual injunction. Rimbun must show amenability (Korsak was validly served here), sufficient interest (clause 18 arguably supplies it) and vexation or oppression, which justifies an injunction only in the clearest of circumstances (Per Kirkham and UBS v Telesto). Per UBS v Telesto, parallel proceedings and the risk of conflicting judgments are not enough alone, especially under a non-exclusive clause, and natural forum alone never is (Per SNIA). Without something more, such as bad faith or a far advanced Singapore action, the injunction is probably refused.

3Twist 2

🧩 TWIST 2

Continue from Twist 1 and add these facts.

Rimbun did not seek an injunction. In Elbonia it applied to stay Korsak's action, relying on clause 18 and on Singapore being the more appropriate forum. It lost, and then filed a defence on the merits, which Elbonian procedure did not require.

After a full trial on an expedited timetable, the Elbonian court held that Elbonian law governs the Supply Contract and declared that Korsak is not liable to Rimbun for the beetle damage, in contract or in negligence. Korsak pleads the judgment in the Singapore action, where all three of Rimbun's claims are still pending.

ℹ ASSUME
  1. Rimbun has no office, staff or assets in Elbonia.
  2. No appeal was brought, and the judgment is final under Elbonian law.

  • H6

  • H7
    Defences to recognition and enforcement. Rimbun will say the Elbonian action broke clause 18. That defence needs a breach, and suing abroad does not ordinarily breach a non-exclusive clause.

Application questions · twist 2

⚡ Twist 2 · 1 of 4H6
What can Korsak do with the Elbonian judgment in the Singapore action?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Recognition needs a judgment on the merits, from a court with international jurisdiction, final and conclusive, with no defence. There is no money requirement, but only a money judgment for a definite sum can be enforced at common law. Korsak pleads the declaration as a shield against the negligence claim for the beetle damage, between the same parties. Rimbun may reply, per Gonzalo Gil White, that liability was decided under Elbonian law alone; that is strongest if Singapore's rules locate the tort in Singapore. Part 3 of the CCAA is only for the court chosen in an exclusive clause.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J7.0.2 :: Recognition Only

Where [party] pleads [the X judgment] as a shield, or to bind [other party] on [an issue], J7.1.1–J7.1.3 must be met and no J7.2 defence apply, but there is no money requirement (J7.3).

⚡ Twist 2 · 2 of 4H4
Did the Elbonian court have international jurisdiction over Rimbun?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Rimbun was not present in Elbonia, so the question is submission. Its stay application, on clause 18 and forum grounds, is open: per IGCF a stay is a protest, but on Henry v Geoprosco's logic it accepts jurisdiction, and Nimbus assumed Henry without deciding. Here that does not matter: per Malaysia Marine, filing a defence on the merits is submission, and Elbonian procedure did not require it. Per Vizcaya Partners, even choosing a country's law is no implied submission to its courts.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J7.1.2.4 :: Claimant or Merits Defence (+)

Per C&Y and Malaysia Marine, [debtor] submitted by [suing in [X] (including related counterclaims or set-off against it) / filing a defence on the merits].

⚡ Twist 2 · 3 of 4H8
The timber claim is still pending. Does the Elbonian ruling that Elbonian law governs the Supply Contract bind the Singapore court?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Merck, a foreign ruling on governing law can found an estoppel, and per Chong (seminar) governing law is not so sensitive that Singapore must decide it itself. Per First Laser, the ruling must come from the final trial, as this one did, and it is immaterial that Elbonia's choice of law rules differ. It was necessary, not collateral, as the declaration covered liability under the Supply Contract. Per Gonzalo Gil White, there is no identity of issue where it arose under different laws in the two courts; per Chong (seminar), that bites only where Singapore's rules would pick Singapore law, and clause 18 arguably makes them do so. So the point is open: on First Laser, Elbonian law binds; on Gonzalo Gil White, Singapore decides afresh. It matters: Elbonian law keeps Korsak liable on the frustration reading of Ralli, while Singapore law frustrates the contract. So Rimbun relies on the estoppel, and Korsak resists it.

📄 Pre-write, word for word · J7.3.2.4 :: Governing Law (+)

Per Merck (HC, not appealed) and Chong (seminar: governing law is not so sensitive that Singapore must decide it itself), [the X ruling on the governing law of [contract]] can found an estoppel, but per First Laser only if decided at [the final trial], not on [a stay application] decided on a good arguable case.

⚡ Twist 2 · 4 of 4H7
Can Rimbun resist the judgment because Korsak sued in Elbonia despite clause 18?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Per Prof Chong's answer scheme, the defence needs a breach, so the clause must contain a promise that was broken. Suing in Elbonia is not ordinarily a breach of a Singapore non-exclusive clause. Per C&Y, a debtor that submitted to the foreign court probably loses the objection in any case. Whether the defence exists at all is undecided, with arguments both ways. A judgment obtained in breach of a Singapore anti-suit injunction is refused on public policy grounds, but none was sought.

📘 HOW THE ANSWER RUNSTry Round 1 and the questions first.
  1. 1
    What changes and what stays

    Rimbun sought no injunction. It lost its stay application in Elbonia and then filed a defence on the merits that Elbonian procedure did not require. After an expedited full trial, the Elbonian court held that Elbonian law governs the Supply Contract and declared Korsak not liable for the beetle damage, and Korsak pleads that judgment in Singapore, where all three claims are pending. The judgment goes to the merits of those claims, not Singapore's jurisdiction over them, and it does not decide the loan claim.

  2. 2
    Recognition only, at common law H6H1

    The judgment is a declaration, not a money judgment, so it cannot be enforced at common law, but it can be recognised, as recognition has no money requirement. The Elbonian court was not the court chosen in an exclusive clause within the CCAA, so Part 3 does not apply and the common law decides. Recognition needs a judgment on the merits, from a court with international jurisdiction, final and conclusive, with no defence. This one followed a full trial and is final under Elbonian law, so the live points are jurisdiction and defences.

  3. 3
    Submission, and no clause 18 defence H4H7

    Rimbun had no office, staff or assets in Elbonia, so the question is submission. Its stay application, on clause 18 and forum grounds, is open: per IGCF a stay application is a protest, but on Henry v Geoprosco's logic it accepts jurisdiction, and Nimbus assumed Henry without deciding. That does not matter, because per Malaysia Marine and C&Y a defence on the merits that local procedure did not require is submission. The clause 18 defence, whose existence is undecided, fails anyway: per Prof Chong's answer scheme it needs a breach, suing in Elbonia was not ordinarily a breach of a Singapore non-exclusive clause, and by submitting Rimbun probably lost the objection (Per C&Y). No Singapore anti-suit injunction was breached, so public policy does not help either.

  4. 4
    What the judgment decides here H8

    Recognised, the declaration is a shield: Korsak pleads it as res judicata against the negligence claim, like the slides' foreign declaration of non-liability. Rimbun may reply, by analogy with Gonzalo Gil White (an issue estoppel case), that liability was decided under Elbonian law alone; that is strongest if Singapore's rules locate the tort in Singapore, and if they locate it in Elbonia the claim fails at limb 2 anyway. On the timber claim, per Merck and Chong (seminar), the ruling that Elbonian law governs can found an issue estoppel, as it came from the final trial (Per First Laser) and was necessary to the contract part of the declaration. But per Gonzalo Gil White there is no identity of issue where it arose under different laws, and per Chong (seminar) that bites where Singapore's rules would pick Singapore law, as clause 18 arguably makes them. On First Laser, which makes Elbonia's different choice of law rules immaterial, Elbonian law binds and Korsak stays liable on the frustration reading, though Esben's reading still bars the claim; on Gonzalo Gil White, Singapore decides afresh, and if Singapore law governs, every reading defeats the claim. So Rimbun relies on the estoppel and Korsak resists it.

4Scorecards: weigh the factors

Prof Chong rewards applying facts to factor tests. Sort each fact, then answer the verdict question. These use the base facts unless a line says “Suppose”.

E4 Sort the factors: Spiliada stage 1 on the base facts

Each line is a fact offered at stage 1 of Korsak's stay application. Which way does it point? Lines marked “Suppose” are extra facts for this card only.

Rimbun is a Singapore company, and Korsak an Elbonian one.
Neutral or little weight. A claimant based here and a defendant based in the other forum cancel out. J4.1.2 :: Parties: Neutral or Counterbalancing
Korsak's mill workers, who processed the timber, live in Elbonia. Both courts have video link.
Neutral or little weight. They are Korsak's own employees, not third parties, so their location counts for less, and video link reduces it further. Students often mark this for Elbonia. J4.1.2 :: Compellability Reduced
The Elbonian state inspectors who passed the first shipment cannot be made to testify in Singapore.
Points to Elbonia. Non-party witnesses who cannot be compelled here point to Elbonia, if Korsak shows their evidence is at least arguably relevant to its defence. It is: they passed the timber that Rimbun says was untreated. J4.1.2 :: Witness Compellability
Elbonian law governs the Supply Contract, and the Equipment Agreement chooses it expressly.
Points to Elbonia. Governing law weighs where the dispute turns on law, as it does here: what the ban does under Elbonian law, and the taint. An express choice adds weight. J4.1.2 :: Governing Law: When Weighty
Mr Seet signed both contracts at the Jurong office.
Neutral or little weight. The place of contracting is neutral unless formation is disputed, and nobody says the contracts were not made. J4.1.2 :: Events: Contract
Suppose: the court locates the negligence at the mill in Elbonia.
Points to Elbonia. The place of the tort is prima facie the natural forum for that claim, unless it is fortuitous. The mill is Korsak's base, so it is not. J4.1.2 :: Events: Tort
Suppose: the court locates the negligence in Singapore, where Korsak marketed the timber and the stock was destroyed.
Points to Singapore. Then the place of the tort points to Singapore for that claim. The contract claims, which turn on Elbonian law, still point to Elbonia. J4.1.2 :: Events: Tort
Suppose: Rimbun keeps its bank accounts and its auditors in Singapore.
Neutral or little weight. Only links relevant to the dispute count. A bank account and auditors here are disregarded. J4.1.2 :: Quality over Quantity
⚡ Scorecard 1 · the verdictE4
Taking both stages together, what is the likely result of Korsak's application?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

Korsak bears stage 1. Residence cancels out, the mill workers count for little and the place of signing is neutral. Elbonian law, which governs both contracts and matters to the ban and the taint, and the non-party inspectors point to Elbonia. If the tort is located in Singapore the balance is closer, and Korsak must still show that Elbonia is clearly more appropriate, not merely as good. At stage 2, delay is disregarded unless egregious, and in Grains and Industrial even alleged delays of over 10 years failed, so the six-year wait fails. Singapore rejects the Australian test, which asks only whether Singapore is clearly inappropriate.

L6 Sort the factors: The objective proper law of the Supply Contract

Each line is a connecting fact for the Supply Contract. Does it point to Elbonian law or Singapore law at stage 3, or does it carry little or no weight? Lines marked “Suppose” are extra facts for this card only.

Korsak mills the timber in Elbonia and loads it on board at an Elbonian port.
Points to Elbonia. This is Korsak's whole performance, and the place of performance carries great weight. C2.4.3 :: Critique of "Equal Weight"
Rimbun pays the price into Korsak's bank account in Elbonia.
Points to Elbonia. Rimbun's performance is there too. The place where both parties perform is usually the strongest argument. C2.4.3 :: Application
The price is in Singapore dollars.
Points to Singapore. Currency is a supporting factor, and a Singapore dollar price points to Singapore. It does not outweigh the place where both parties perform. C2.4.3 :: Application
Mr Seet signed the contract at Korsak's Jurong office.
Little or no weight. The place of contracting matters little unless performance is also there. Students often give it full weight. C2.3.2 :: Residence, Business, Purpose
Rimbun is a Singapore company with its warehouse in Jurong.
Points to Singapore. A party's residence and place of business count as a connecting factor. C2.3.2 :: Residence, Business, Purpose
Korsak is an Elbonian company and runs its sawmills in Elbonia.
Points to Elbonia. The other party's residence and business count too, and they point the same way as the performance. C2.3.2 :: Residence, Business, Purpose
The Equipment Agreement, a related loan between the same parties, chooses Elbonian law.
Points to Elbonia. A related transaction supports the law where both parties perform. Here it points the same way. C2.4.3 :: Application
The inspectors and mill workers who would give evidence all live in Elbonia.
Little or no weight. Where witnesses live is a Spiliada factor for the forum question. It says nothing about the law the contract is most closely connected with. C2.4.2 :: Wrong Factors
Suppose: the price were in US dollars instead.
Little or no weight. The US dollar is a common trading currency, so it points to no one country and carries little weight. C2.3.2 :: Language and Currency
⚡ Scorecard 2 · the verdictL6
On the base facts (no “Suppose” line), which law is the objective proper law of the Supply Contract?
1–4 choose · ↵ check
⚖ THE LAW · LAW REVIEWED

The test is the closest and most real connection. Korsak's performance and Rimbun's payment are both in Elbonia, the strongest argument, and Korsak's base and the related loan point the same way. The Singapore dollar price and Rimbun's base are real pointers but are outweighed, and signing in Jurong counts little. Courts do not declare ties (Per Lew). The characteristic performer test comes from Rome I, which Singapore uses only by analogy.

5Remember

🧠 FOR THE EXAM
  • A never-registered company trading from a fixed office here: s 376 fails, so prove Adams v Cape presence; O 7 r 4 also needs permission and Rosenberg (power to contract, and a link to the action).
  • Served here with no clause: Spiliada, stage 1 on the defendant; own employees with video link count little, non-compellable non-party witnesses and a governing law the dispute turns on count more, and delay fails unless egregious.
  • Where the proper law is also the law broken, run Route A first, then Ralli on each reading: Esben's rule and frustration under a foreign proper law give different results.
  • Tainting Step 2 is unresolved: Singapore principles as the lex fori, or the proper law of the contract sued on; give the result under each.
  • A defective product claim in negligence: the careless act (Vibrant Group) against where the product was marketed (Distillers; Castree v Squibb); the exception fails where that place is the defendant's home and the place of the act.
  • A Singapore non-exclusive clause makes objecting here a breach (strong cause) but not suing abroad (vexation, where parallel suits alone fail); a voluntary merits defence abroad is submission, and an estoppel on governing law is open where Singapore's rules pick Singapore law.
