LAW302 · META GAME · LEARN FROM THE ERRORS

Mistakes to avoid

Across both prompts the checks found about 130 legal errors in Gemini's work (32 wrong, 77 misleading, 24 unsupported), besides several hundred smaller fixes of precision, gaps and style. The most common error by far was an open point stated as settled: Gemini picks one side of a (±) block and drops the other route, so the result holds on one reading only. The second was invented or mis-cited authority, mostly in its “in depth” notes. Its self-reviews and its “verified, no overlap” claims found none of these errors. Treat Gemini's text as a first draft: the rules below are the ones to learn.

1Where a defective product tort happens

✗ WHAT GEMINI WROTE

The tort happened where the product was made (or where the careless act was done), so that place is settled as the lex loci delicti and limb 2 fails.

✓ THE RIGHT RULE

Per Vibrant Group, negligence is located where the act was done, which points to the place of making. But for product liability the tort is where the product was marketed without the warning, not where it was made or where the damage occurred (Distillers; Castree v Squibb). Locate the tort both ways and give the double actionability result under each route.

C3.3.2 :: Negligence: Focus on the Act (Product liability)

Why it matters: Location decides whether you run a local tort or double actionability and the flexible exception, so one route only loses half the analysis. · Seen 6 times, in mx-01, mx-02, mx-09

2A stay application abroad as submission

✗ WHAT GEMINI WROTE

Applying for a stay in the foreign court was not submission, stated as settled, with Nimbus grouped with IGCF.

✓ THE RIGHT RULE

The point is (±). On Henry v Geoprosco's logic a stay application accepted the foreign court's jurisdiction. Per IGCF (PC), a stay for arbitration or on forum non conveniens grounds is a protest, unless the debtor sought more. Nimbus assumed Henry is law without deciding. Give the result on each route; where the foreign court could only have jurisdiction through submission, say so.

J7.1.2.4 :: Stay Application (±); J7.1.2.4 :: Setting Aside on FNC Grounds

Why it matters: Submission is often the only ground of international jurisdiction in a judgments question, so the whole enforcement answer turns on it. · Seen 9 times, in q1-10, mx-09, q1-08

3Judgment given in breach of a jurisdiction clause

✗ WHAT GEMINI WROTE

The foreign judgment cannot be enforced because it breached the clause (sometimes citing an invented “s 32 Choice of Court” rule).

✓ THE RIGHT RULE

Per C&Y no case decides it. For the defence: damages for the breach could be recovered here anyway (Union Discount), REFJA s 5(4)(b) gives an analogue, and it fits party autonomy; UK CJJA s 32 is only a comparison. Against: no Singapore authority recognises it. Per the March 2026 scheme it needs a breach, so the clause must have promissory content; per C&Y the debtor loses the objection if it submitted.

J7.2.6 :: Breach First (±); For the Defence (−); Against the Defence (+)

Why it matters: It is an argument both sides must run, not a rule, and submission usually kills it. · Seen 7 times, in q1-06, q1-10

4Issue estoppel on a foreign ruling about governing law

✗ WHAT GEMINI WROTE

The foreign ruling on governing law binds Singapore (or: raises no estoppel), with no hedge.

✓ THE RIGHT RULE

Per Merck, a foreign ruling on governing law can found an estoppel, but per First Laser only if decided at the final trial, not on a stay application. Different choice of law rules do not matter per First Laser, but per Gonzalo Gil White there is no identity if the issue arose under different laws in each court. Per Chong (seminar), on the narrow reading identity fails only where Singapore's rules would select Singapore law.

J7.3.2.4 :: Governing Law (+); J7.3.2.4 :: Different Choice of Law Rules (±)

Why it matters: A Singapore clause or Singapore law in the facts is exactly where the narrow reading bites. · Seen 6 times, in mx-01, mx-02, mx-09

5Ralli only catches a later ban

✗ WHAT GEMINI WROTE

Ralli does not apply because the ban was already in force when the contract was signed; Ralli needs supervening illegality.

✓ THE RIGHT RULE

Run the three readings, because the results differ. Per Esben, Ralli is an independent conflicts rule catching supervening and initial illegality alike, and per Prof Chong arguably preferable. On the frustration reading Peh Teck Quee declined Ralli where the ban pre-dated the contract. Per Ryder Industries it matters only where the proper law is not Singapore law.

C2.10.5 :: Basis: Three Readings (results differ, so run them)

Why it matters: A pre-existing ban is a favourite fact pattern; dismissing Ralli on one reading throws away a whole route. · Seen 5 times, in mx-01, q2-07, q2-12

6Status quo ante turned round

✗ WHAT GEMINI WROTE

Refusing recovery preserves the status quo, so the illegality defence should succeed.

✓ THE RIGHT RULE

Per Esben (provisional supporting points), rejecting the defence restores the status quo ante. Then test it on the facts: if the claimant kept what it received (machines delivered and kept), repaying the deposit restores nothing.

C2.10.7 :: Supporting Points (provisional)

Why it matters: Getting the direction wrong reverses the answer on reliance as a defence. · Seen 5 times, in q2-07, q2-12

7Reliance on the illegal contract as a defence

✗ WHAT GEMINI WROTE

Illegality bars causes of action, not defences, so the guilty party can always rely on the contract; or: letting the seller keep a deposit for delivered goods stultifies comity.

✓ THE RIGHT RULE

Per Esben, the defendant may rely on the Foster or Ralli arrangement against an unjust enrichment claim unless the outcome would stultify comity. It does not where reliance merely explains the payments; it does where it gives effect to the illegal performance. The “causes of action, not defences” point is about the ex dolo malo maxim. Per the Royal Boskalis majority, a defence akin to enforcing an illegal claim was refused.

C2.10.7 :: Stultification; C2.10.7 :: Royal Boskalis: Defence Refused

Why it matters: The test is the outcome, so the answer must say what relying on the contract would actually give effect to. · Seen 6 times, in q2-07, q2-12

8Skipping proper law illegality, or one proper law only

✗ WHAT GEMINI WROTE

Lemenda (or Ralli) decides the case, with the proper law illegality box left as a decoy although the proper law is open.

✓ THE RIGHT RULE

Per Kahler and Zivnostenka, illegality under the proper law bars enforcement (Route A). Where the law broken may be the proper law, run Route A first. Where the objective proper law is balanced, give the result under each candidate law.

C2.10.1 :: Route A: Proper Law; C2.10.1 :: Framework: Foster vs Ralli vs Lemenda

Why it matters: Order matters in Question 2: proper law before illegality, and Route A before the foreign illegality routes. · Seen 6 times, in q2-07, mx-02, q2-08

9Tainting Step 1 taken as met

✗ WHAT GEMINI WROTE

There is a relevant foreign illegality, so Step 1 of tainting is satisfied.

✓ THE RIGHT RULE

Step 1 asks whether the act breached foreign law or whether Singapore would enforce Contract 1 (Surewin), which can turn on the Ralli reading. Per Ryder Industries not every breach counts: an LLS prohibition qualifies per Magdeev after a balancing exercise, and a Lemenda breach is unclear (Prof Chong). Flag the threshold, then assume it met.

C2.10.6 :: Act or Transaction; C2.10.6 :: Sufficiently Serious

Why it matters: Flag-and-assume is how the scheme handles an unclear threshold; stating it as met loses the marks for the debate. · Seen 4 times, in mx-09

10The Lew grave-injustice caveat

✗ WHAT GEMINI WROTE

The grave-injustice caveat applies and decides the formation dispute (or sends it to the lex fori).

✓ THE RIGHT RULE

Lew left open “a very small caveat, very rarely applicable”, whose effect is no contract under any law, not the lex fori; per C&Y use forum public policy instead. Argue it for the party bound by silence and give the result either way.

C2.6 :: Grave-Injustice Caveat

Why it matters: A formation hypo invites it, but it is an argument, not a settled exception. · Seen 3 times, in q2-08

11A deemed-exclusive (s 3(2)) clause and anti-suit injunctions

✗ WHAT GEMINI WROTE

A contractual ASI (G3) is a decoy because the clause is exclusive only by deeming; or the CCAA box is a decoy although s 3(2) deems the clause exclusive.

✓ THE RIGHT RULE

Per s 3(2) CCAA an unlabelled submission clause is deemed exclusive unless the parties expressly provide otherwise (but not where the facts call it non-exclusive). For an ASI the point is (±): per Chong's scheme the clause gives sufficient interest and the ASI runs on vexation, and Singapore “will likely grant the ASI”; per C&Y breach is arguable, but breach is contract interpretation under the proper law.

J1.2.1 :: Deemed Exclusive (+); J6.5.3 :: Deemed-Exclusive Singapore Clause (±)

Why it matters: Both routes to the ASI must be run, and the vexation route needs vexation while the breach route does not. · Seen 4 times, in q1-16, q1-10

12The basis of O 7 r 4

✗ WHAT GEMINI WROTE

O 7 r 4 rests on s 16(1)(a)(i), stated as settled.

✓ THE RIGHT RULE

Arguable. Per Beranek, O 7 r 4 rests on limb (i): the principal is deemed present through its agent. Per Yeo, it addresses absent principals, supplies its own nexus and needs permission, so it fits limb (ii). Flag the debate in a line and say whether it matters on the facts.

J3.0.2 :: Beranek: Constructive Presence; J3.0.2 :: Yeo: Where the Defendant Is

Why it matters: Whether Adams v Cape presence must be proved depends on which limb applies. · Seen 3 times, in mx-09

13Presuming foreign law is like Singapore law

✗ WHAT GEMINI WROTE

Foreign law was not proved, so it is presumed the same as Singapore law, even for a civil law system “quite unlike Singapore's”.

✓ THE RIGHT RULE

First ask whether it was pleaded. If not, per Brownlie Singapore law applies in its own right. If pleaded but unproved, the presumption of similarity applies only where it is fair and reasonable to expect material similarity; per C&Y not for a civil law system lacking universal principles. Otherwise the party with the burden may simply lose (EFT Holdings).

C1.6.3 :: Not Pleaded: Default Rule; Pleaded but Unproved; Nature of the Presumption; Limits

Why it matters: Who loses on unproved foreign law is a quick, reliable mark when the facts are silent. · Seen 3 times, in q1-16, q2-12

14Invented or mis-cited authority

✗ WHAT GEMINI WROTE

Full case names and sections that the course does not use: “Tao Commodity Trader v Jinan Iron and Steel”, “6DM (Holdings) Ltd v Aeon”, “s 32 Choice of Court”, s 18F SCJA for the High Court clause rule, the Sayers minority splitting the issue in two, burden of proof called substantive.

✓ THE RIGHT RULE

Cite as the pre-writes do: Tao Commodity; 6DM. A post-2016 “Singapore High Court” clause includes the SICC under s 2(2) to (3) CCAA and O 2 r 2(1) SICC Rules; s 18F SCJA presumes an SICC clause exclusive. The two-question approach in torts belongs to Kahn-Freund and North, not the Sayers minority. Per Re Fuld's Estate (No 3) the burden of proof is generally procedural.

J5.2.2 :: Exclusive or Not? (s 18F SCJA); C1.6.1 :: Burden of Proof; course handout

Why it matters: A wrong name or section costs credibility in an open-book exam; only cite what the pre-write cites. · Seen 7 times, in q1-02, q1-05, q1-06, q2-04, q2-06

15Rules applied outside their scope, and facts or dates that do not fit

✗ WHAT GEMINI WROTE

The serious question limb applied to a defendant served in Singapore; a lease of land treated as inside the CCAA; a ban called “later” though it came first; a default judgment for damages on a claim that sought only a declaration.

✓ THE RIGHT RULE

Check each rule's trigger facts before applying it. The serious question is a service out requirement (PD para 63(2)). The CCAA's s 9 exclusions come first (J1.2.4). Read dates against Ralli, the FLPA and the CCAA. Make sure the judgment you enforce matches the claim made.

J3.1.1 (PD para 63(2)); J1.2.4 :: Excluded (−); the hypo facts

Why it matters: Under time pressure the facts trip you more often than the law; one date can flip a whole route. · Seen 6 times, in mx-09, q1-04, q1-10

LAW302 · META GAME · GEMINI PROMPT v2 · PLANS

Gemini's plans for the next batch, checked

With prompt v2, the third prompt on each side (“PROMPT C”) lets Gemini plan its own batch first. Gemini sent the three plans below and is waiting for the reply “go”. Each was checked against the pre-writes and the Menu. Instead of a bare “go”, paste the message under each plan into the same Gemini chat: it says go and lists the fixes.

1LAW302 Question 1 plan (q1-22 to q1-26)

Gemini's claim: Five “verified” Question 1 hypos (q1-22 to q1-26) that cover 30 of the 33 A6 thin spots, with no overlap in party names, industries or fact patterns with the bank or the past papers, every Convention, limitation and filing date aligned, every open point flagged, and nothing off the syllabus.

q1-22 · Banyan Logistics v Torvald Shipping needs fixes

A Singapore cold-chain logistics firm sues a Ruritanian shipping line under two contracts: a 2019 carriage contract whose clause names the SICC with no label and is governed by Ruritanian law, and a 2020 warehouse lease with an exclusive Singapore High Court clause governed by Singapore law.

Issues

  • A1 Starter: what each clause promises. Gemini orders it, but it is a starter that belongs in ok.
  • A6 The carriage contract's clause names the SICC with no label, and Ruritanian law governs it.
  • A2 The warehouse lease gives the Singapore High Court exclusive jurisdiction, and Singapore law governs it.
  • B1 CCAA gate for each contract. The carriage contract passes the date row (Singapore, 1 October 2016) but fails on s 9(2), carriage of goods. As planned, the lease fails too: s 9(2)(k) excludes any tenancy of immovable property.
  • B4 Outside the CCAA: the carriage contract goes to the SICC Rules and the common law. A router, so it belongs in ok.
  • B2 s 11 for the lease: Singapore must hear it. This works only if the CCAA applies, which a lease of land defeats.
  • F1 International and commercial: Torvald's place of business is in Ruritania, and both parties submitted under the clauses.
  • F2 Primary SICC jurisdiction under the carriage clause. Whether that clause is exclusive turns on s 18F (Prof Chong against Yip), which matters little for exercise.
  • F3 A post-2016 “Singapore High Court” clause includes the SICC.
  • F4 Service in Ruritania without permission under O 5 r 6(2)(a).
  • F5 Exercise under O 2 r 3, not Spiliada.

Dials

  • Carriage Contract signed on 10 March 2019, governed by Ruritanian law; its clause names the SICC and does not say “exclusive”.
  • Warehouse Lease signed on 5 June 2020, governed by Singapore law, for storage in Singapore; its clause gives the Singapore High Court exclusive jurisdiction.
  • The Convention entered into force for Ruritania on 1 January 2018. Torvald is based only in Ruritania.
  • Under Ruritanian law an unlabelled clause is non-exclusive and implies no waiver of objection.

Trap. Treating the 2019 carriage contract as a CCAA case because it post-dates 1 October 2016 (missing the s 9(2) carriage of goods exclusion), or running Spiliada in the SICC instead of O 2 r 3.

Twists

  • Twist 1: Banyan files the lease claim in the General Division and asks for a transfer to the SICC over Torvald's timely objection (F7: every party's consent under O 2 r 4(4), consent doubly deemed under r 4(7), against the art 8(5) recognition risk).
  • Twist 2: Torvald sues in Ruritania on both contracts and Banyan asks the SICC for anti-suit injunctions (G3, G9, G10: strong reasons modified by O 2 r 3(2), and s 18F).

Gemini: six SICC and clause thin spots and the untested s 18F debate outside the CCAA. Real value: the carriage half is new. Section 9(2) takes a post-2016 SICC clause out of the CCAA, and s 18F then decides breach in the injunction twist; the Mixed plan's mx-07 also uses the s 9(2) carriage exclusion, but for a High Court clause at common law. No hypo has yet asked J1.2.4's exclusions, J5.1.1, J5.2.2, J5.2.4 or J6.3.1.3, and F1 and F4 have no questions. The lease half and both twists largely repeat q1-05 (s 11 for a post-2016 High Court clause; a transfer over objection, with the art 8(5) doubt; injunctions from the SICC).

✗ FIX BEFORE GEMINI WRITES IT
  • WrongA lease of warehouse space is a tenancy of immovable property, and s 9(2)(k) CCAA excludes “any tenancy of immovable property”. As planned, the lease is outside the CCAA, so s 11 (B2) does not apply, and Twist 1 fails: outside the CCAA a transfer needs no party's consent (O 2 r 4(4) applies only in CCAA cases), so deemed consent under r 4(7) and the art 8(5) risk never arise. Fix: Make the second contract a services agreement with no land and no carriage in it, for example the claimant repairing Torvald's containers at its own Singapore yard, not a lease of land or storage of goods in transit. Keep the word “exclusive”, the “Singapore High Court”, Singapore law and the 2020 date. J1.2.4 :: Excluded (−); CCAA s 9(2)(k) as printed in the Week 10 combined notes; J5.4.2 :: Every Party's Consent (must write)

q1-23 · Sovereign Timber v Kovacs Timber and Mr Kovacs needs fixes

A Singapore furniture maker sues its unregistered Elbonian timber supplier, which runs a showroom in Singapore, for breach of a supply contract. It also sues the supplier's Elbonian director, served abroad, for inducing a Singapore distributor to break its resale contract.

Issues

  • A1 No jurisdiction clause, so no one is in breach. Gemini orders it, but it is a one-line dismissal that belongs in ok.
  • D2 Kovacs Timber is not registered here, so s 376 is unavailable. It is present under Adams v Cape through its showroom and is served on a visiting director under O 7 r 2(1)(b).
  • D4 Mr Kovacs is in Elbonia, so he must be served out on the three requirements.
  • D5 Gateway for Mr Kovacs: (c) necessary or proper party, with the company as anchor. Gemini ties the inducement to the same timber so that a common question is arguable.
  • D7 Serious question against Mr Kovacs, proved separately because (c) is neutral.
  • E1 Two tests and two burdens: a stay for the company served here, forum conveniens for the director served out.
  • E2 Kovacs Timber's stay: stage 1 on the company.
  • E3 Mr Kovacs: the forum burden stays on the claimant.
  • E4 Stage 1 factors: Elbonian law, and port inspectors who refuse to give evidence by video link.
  • E5 Stage 2: no legal aid for foreign companies, US$2 million security for costs, and a rule that discounts foreign company witnesses. The first and third have rows in the pre-writes; security for costs has none.
  • E9 An SICC International Judge trained in Elbonian law: a factor, never decisive.
  • F6 Transfer to the SICC. No one applies for a transfer, so nothing plants it.

Dials

  • Supply Contract made in 2025, governed by Elbonian law, CIF Singapore, with no jurisdiction clause.
  • Kovacs Timber is not registered in Singapore. Since 2023 it has leased a showroom at Sungei Kadut, where a salaried manager signs orders without approval. The claim is served there on a visiting director.
  • Mr Kovacs lives in Elbonia and allegedly induced a Singapore distributor to break its resale contract for the same timber.
  • Elbonia is not a Convention State, gives no legal aid to foreign companies, requires US$2 million security for costs, and discounts foreign company witnesses unless corroborated. Its port inspectors refuse to give evidence by video link.
  • One SICC International Judge was trained in Elbonian law.

Trap. Invoking s 376 CA for an unregistered company; merging the stage 1 burden on Kovacs Timber (served here) with the claimant's burden against Mr Kovacs (served out); or treating the Elbonian-trained International Judge as decisive at stage 1.

Twists

  • Twist 1: the claim against Kovacs Timber was time-barred under Elbonian law before the Singapore claim was filed (FLPA ss 3(1) and 4(2); D7; stage 2 through E5 and E10).
  • Twist 2: Mr Kovacs's inducement and the distributor's breach took place in Elbonia, so stage 1 points to Elbonia and the claimant's second bite arises (E6, framed as “Konamaneni vs Oro Negro”).

Gemini: the service-in, Spiliada and service-out thin spots in a two-defendant split. Real value: the proper party gateway with Prof Chong's common-question point, the legal aid and evidence-rule rows of stage 2, and the FLPA's effect on a stay have never been asked. The split itself (one defendant served here and one served out, so the burdens differ) is already asked in q1-16 (base question 3). The presence facts copy mx-09 (and mx-02), an unregistered company's presence with an officer served on a short visit is q1-02 Twist 2, and the SICC factor, limitation at stage 2, the second bite and the anchor claim repeat q1-02 and q1-03.

q1-24 · Helios Robotics v Veridian Dynamics needs fixes

A Singapore robotics integrator sues its Utopian software supplier over a defective update, serving it in Utopia by courier under the contract without the court's approval. The contract's asymmetric clause lets the integrator sue anywhere but contains no submission by the supplier.

Issues

  • A7 Asymmetric clause without a submission limb: Helios may sue anywhere, Veridian only in Utopia, and nothing says Veridian submits.
  • A9 The tort claim for the defective update falls inside “arising out of or in connection with” on a broad reading (Fiona Trust).
  • B1 CCAA gate: the clause is asymmetric, so it is outside the CCAA (CHLOE V), though Utopia's date (1 October 2015) passes.
  • B4 Outside the CCAA: the common law decides.
  • D9 Clause 19 allows service by international courier: is that service out without approval under O 8 r 1(3)?
  • D4 Service out on the three requirements, needed only if r 1(3) does not apply.
  • D5 Gateways, on the same alternative route: (d)(iii) for the contract claim, (f)(ii) for the damage to robots in Singapore.
  • E1 Which test, and who bears the burden.
  • E3 Gemini: forum conveniens with the burden on Helios. That is right only if r 1(3) fails; if r 1(3) applies, Veridian bears the burden on exercise.
  • E4 Stage 1 factors.

Dials

  • Master Agreement made in 2023, governed by Singapore law.
  • Clause 18 covers all disputes “arising out of or in connection with” the Agreement: Helios may sue Veridian in any competent court; Veridian may sue Helios only in Utopia; nothing says that Veridian submits to any court.
  • Clause 19 allows service of legal process by international courier.
  • Veridian is based only in Utopia. The Convention entered into force for Utopia on 1 October 2015.
  • Helios serves by courier without O 8 approval, and Veridian applies to set aside.
  • Utopian law upholds asymmetric clauses. A defective update coded in Utopia damaged robots in Singapore.

Trap. Putting strong cause on Veridian although clause 18 has no submission limb, or applying s 12 CCAA despite CHLOE V.

Twists

  • Twist 1: Veridian sues Helios in Utopia and Helios seeks an anti-suit injunction in Singapore (G1, G5, G6, G7). Veridian's suit breaks nothing, and Gemini would show why G5 would bite “if Helios had promised to submit”.
  • Twist 2: Veridian instead sues Helios in Arcadia, in breach of its Utopia-only promise, and Helios seeks an injunction here (G8, framed as “Akai vs UniCredit”, and s 4(10A) CLA).

Gemini: A7 (no questions yet), D9, G5 and G8. Real value: only the O 8 r 1(3) point is new: whether a courier clause allows service out when the contract names no court for Helios's claims and Veridian does not submit, and the burden that follows. No hypo has asked J3.1.5's three readings of “allowed” or J4.0.2's “Existence Not Disputable” row. The asymmetric clause with and without submission, and the applicant's own injunction application as a breach, repeat q1-07; the foreign-clause injunction repeats q1-06 and the Mixed plan's mx-08 Twist 2; D9 and G5 already have two questions each, though each is ordered by only one hypo.

✗ FIX BEFORE GEMINI WRITES IT

Twist 2's injunction to protect a foreign court's clause is q1-06's base (G8) and the Mixed plan's mx-08 Twist 2 (a Utopian clause, a suit in Arcadia, a Singapore injunction). Fix: Keep the base on the new point (the next fix) and replace both twists with one new twist (the fifth and sixth fixes). q1-25 · Beacon Offshore v Njord Salvage and Mr Lindqvist needs fixes

A Singapore offshore contractor sues a Ruritanian salvage firm in Singapore for a negative declaration under a towage contract with a Singapore non-exclusive clause. The Ruritanian firm sues on the merits in Ruritania and asks the Ruritanian court to stop the Singapore claim.

Issues

  • A4 Towage Contract: a Singapore “non-exclusive” clause governed by Singapore law, so it carries the narrow waiver of objection.
  • A5 Support Contract: a Ruritanian non-exclusive clause, which no one breaches by suing elsewhere. Its role in the plan is not stated.
  • B1 CCAA gate: neither clause is exclusive, and a clause that says “non-exclusive” is never deemed exclusive under s 3(2).
  • B4 Outside the CCAA: the common law decides.
  • D6 Beacon's claim is for a negative declaration.
  • D8 Singapore clause, defendant abroad: Njord is served out, and any forum objection by it here would be a breach.
  • G1 One injunction analysis per foreign proceeding: Njord's merits suit, and its Ruritanian application to stop the Singapore claim.
  • G2 Amenability: Njord was served out but has no office or assets here.
  • G4 Suing abroad under a Singapore non-exclusive clause is not ordinarily a breach; seeking a foreign order against the Singapore claim arguably is (Sabah against UBS v Telesto). The anti-anti-suit block (J6.5.1) sits under G11's pointer, which the plan does not list.
  • G6 Sufficient interest for the vexation route.
  • G7 Vexation, with the 25% interest as Njord's juridical advantage.

Dials

  • Towage Contract signed on 10 March 2021, governed by Singapore law, with a Singapore non-exclusive clause.
  • Support Contract signed on 15 May 2017, governed by Ruritanian law, with a Ruritanian non-exclusive clause.
  • The Convention entered into force for Ruritania on 1 January 2018. Njord has no office or assets in Singapore.
  • Njord sues Beacon in Ruritania on the Towage Contract and asks the Ruritanian court to restrain Beacon's Singapore claim.
  • Ruritanian law treats non-exclusive clauses as purely permissive, with no implied waiver.
  • Mr Lindqvist, Njord's chief executive, who lives in Ruritania, is a co-claimant there.
  • Ruritanian law awards 25% statutory “punitive” interest.

Trap. Applying s 3(2) CCAA to the 2021 Singapore non-exclusive clause, treating Njord's Ruritanian merits claim as a breach of that clause, or failing to split the merits claim from the Ruritanian application against the Singapore claim.

Twists

  • Twist 1: the Ruritanian court refuses Beacon's stay on natural forum grounds (H8: per Lakshmi, a foreign natural forum ruling raises no issue estoppel against a Singapore anti-suit application).
  • Twist 2: the Towage Contract's clause is an exclusive Ruritanian clause signed in 2021 (B3: s 12 applies, and the risk that Mr Lindqvist cannot be joined fails s 12(1)(c) under 6DM).

Gemini: A4, A5, G4, anti-anti-suit injunctions and Lakshmi. Real value: the Sabah against UBS v Telesto debate (the last row of J6.3.1.2) and the contractual anti-anti-suit injunction (J6.5.1) have never been asked, and A5 is a real thin spot. q1-01 Twist 1 already keys a foreign order against the Singapore claim as an arguable breach. The rest repeats q1-01 Twist 1 (the same split, the same no-breach point, amenability with no presence or assets, a foreign juridical advantage), q1-01 Twist 2 (s 12 for a post-2018 exclusive Ruritanian clause), q1-06 and q1-09 (Lakshmi), and q1-05, q1-10 and q1-27 (6DM fragmentation). A4 and G4 are no longer thin.

✗ FIX BEFORE GEMINI WRITES IT
  • Gap filledThe base repeats q1-01 Twist 1 almost exactly: a Singapore non-exclusive clause under Singapore law; the Singapore claimant serves the foreign party out; the foreign party sues in Ruritania and asks the Ruritanian court to stop the Singapore claim; and the questions split the two proceedings, find no breach in the suit, test amenability with no presence or assets, and weigh a foreign advantage (triple damages there, 25% interest here). Fix: Keep only what q1-01 did not ask. Model the foreign step on Sabah: Njord asks the Ruritanian court to stop Beacon enforcing a contractual right in Singapore (for example calling on a guarantee), and does not sue on the merits. Key it both ways: a breach (the English CA in Sabah; and, where the foreign order would stop the Singapore suit, the handout and Prof Chong (seminar)), founding a contractual anti-anti-suit injunction (C&Y); or, as UBS v Telesto and C&Y read Sabah, vexation, so plead vexation too. q1-26 · Serangoon Textiles v Dalziel Holdings needs fixes

An Arcadian machinery supplier enforces in Singapore an Arcadian default judgment for damages, 20% statutory interest and an order to return 12 looms. The debtor is a Singapore textile company that was served at its stand at an Arcadian trade fair.

Issues

  • H1 Regime: no clause and no treaty, so the common law. Gemini assumes Arcadia is not a Convention State.
  • H2 The four requirements; a default judgment is on the merits.
  • H3 Presence: a 10-day trade fair stand, served on day 9, where the sales director signed orders (Dunlop v Cudell).
  • H4 Submission: a failed stay application in Arcadia on forum grounds, then no further part (Henry v Geoprosco against IGCF).
  • H5 Final and conclusive though an appeal is pending, as the judgment is res judicata under Arcadian law.
  • H6 Money orders against the order to return the looms; severance.
  • H7 Defences: intrinsic fraud, with the genuine inspection report held in Singapore since 2023.
  • H11 20% statutory interest payable to Dalziel: not penal, as it is paid to a private creditor (Sang Cheol Woo).

Dials

  • Supply Contract made in 2022, governed by Singapore law, with no jurisdiction clause.
  • The claim was served on Serangoon's sales director on day 9 of its 10-day stand at the Arcadia Textile Expo in May 2025, where he signed orders.
  • Serangoon applied in Arcadia for a stay on forum grounds, lost, and took no further part.
  • Default judgment in November 2025: US$1.5 million damages, 20% statutory interest payable to Dalziel, and specific performance to return 12 looms.
  • An appeal is “pending in 2027”; the judgment is enforceable and res judicata under Arcadian law meanwhile.
  • Arcadia is not a Convention State. Serangoon has held the genuine inspection report in Singapore since 2023.

Trap. Dismissing a 10-day trade fair stand as no presence (missing Dunlop v Cudell), assuming a pending appeal defeats finality, enforcing specific performance at common law, or allowing intrinsic fraud without checking diligence.

Twists

  • Twist 1: Serangoon holds a later Singapore judgment that it owes nothing under the Supply Contract (H7: per Merck an inconsistent Singapore judgment bars recognition, earlier or later).
  • Twist 2: Dalziel moves to enforce against Serangoon's warehouse in Arcadia, and Serangoon seeks an anti-enforcement injunction here (H10: Sun Travels' exceptional circumstances, and why knowledge and delay defeat it).

Gemini: every Group H thin spot (H2, H3, H5, H6, H10, H11). Real value: the pending appeal, specific performance beside money orders and severance, and 20% statutory interest paid to a private creditor (J7.1.3, J7.1.4, J7.2.4, J7.2.5) have never been asked, and H3 and H5 are real thin spots. But the stand at a ten-day foreign trade fair, the stay application abroad followed by no part, the default judgment and the report-held-for-years fraud copy q1-08; the stay-as-submission point is also asked in q1-10 and mx-02; and the Merck and anti-enforcement twists repeat q1-09 and q1-06. H10 is not thin and H11 is cold.

The stay-as-submission point is also asked in q1-10 and mx-02. q2-18 · Kinta Timber v Silvano needs fixes

A Singapore timber importer sues its Ruritanian supplier in the General Division for failing to deliver hardwood after Ruritania bans raw log exports. The contract has a floating choice of law clause that turns on which party sues.

Issues

  • L1 Proper law starter and its scope. Gemini also lists subsequent conduct, but no fact plants it.
  • L3 Floating clause (“Ruritanian law if Seller sues, Utopian law if Buyer sues”): void if the lex fori tests it (Shanghai Turbo HC), valid if the objective proper law tests it and that law is Ruritanian (or Utopian) law, which permits such clauses (The Iran Vojdan). If void, skip Stage 2.
  • L6 Objective proper law scorecard, needed on both routes.
  • M1 Illegality routing across three laws: Utopian, Ruritanian and Singapore.
  • M2 If Ruritanian law is the proper law, the ban is illegality under the proper law itself, and Foster and Ralli are not needed.
  • M5 If Utopian law governs, Ralli decides the export ban, and its three readings give different results.
  • K6 Utopian law pleaded but not proved on damages.

Dials

  • Contract signed 10 January 2026; delivery FOB Port Ruri, Ruritania, in April 2026; price in US dollars, paid in Singapore.
  • Ruritania bans raw log exports on 1 March 2026.
  • Clause: “Ruritanian law if Seller sues, or Utopian law if Buyer sues.”
  • Floating clauses are void under Singapore law and valid under Ruritanian and Utopian law.
  • The ban voids the contract under Ruritanian law; Utopian law does not treat it as frustrated.
  • No evidence is led on Utopian law on damages.

Trap. Treating a ban that came after signing as Foster, or jumping to Ralli before asking whether Ruritanian law is the proper law (M2).

Twists

  • Twist 1: the seller may instead deliver processed timber from Utopia, so a lawful alternative removes Ralli (M5).
  • Twist 2: the ban has been in force since 1 December 2025 and only Silvano knew of it: Foster against Silvano alone (M3) and initial illegality under Ralli.

Gemini: drills the two biggest hot-box gaps, L3 and M5, together. Real value: a floating clause decides the proper law, which then decides the Ralli result, and the base can ask Prof Chong's seminar point that reading (1) defeats a Singapore buyer when the supplier's own State bans the export. The twists add nothing new.

q2-19 · Portside v Mr Goh and Nordik Chartering needs fixes

A Singapore company sues an Elbonian charterer for specific performance and lost sub-charter profit under an unsigned charterparty on a Singapore standard form. It also sues the charterer's Singapore director on an oral guarantee he gave in Elbonia.

Issues

  • K1 Characterise the charterparty claim, the guarantee claim and the remedies.
  • L5 Implied choice of Singapore law from the Singapore standard form and a linked Singapore-law port agency contract.
  • L6 Objective proper law as the fallback, and the guarantee's own proper law.
  • L8 Formal validity of the oral guarantee: the proper law or the place of contracting will do (AQCEL).
  • K2 s 6 CLA (“no action shall be brought”): procedural under Star City, with the functional view in the alternative.
  • K3 Remoteness of the sub-charter loss is substantive (D'Almeida Araujo). Gemini also lists “caps”, but no cap is planted.
  • K4 Specific performance, which Elbonian law does not give.

Dials

  • Negotiated in Elbonia in March 2026 on a “Singapore Maritime Association” form; no choice of law clause.
  • Loading in Elbonia and payment in Singapore; linked to a Singapore-law port agency contract.
  • Mr Goh gives an oral guarantee in Elbonia; nothing is signed.
  • Elbonian law: oral guarantees are valid; no specific performance; the sub-charter loss is too remote.
  • Singapore law: s 6 CLA needs signed writing; specific performance and the sub-charter loss are available.

Trap. Treating s 6 CLA as a rule of form that Elbonian law, as the law of the place of contracting, can satisfy, and missing its procedural “no action shall be brought” wording (K2).

Twists

  • Twist 1: a written memo is signed later, but Portside sues four years after default and Elbonia's period is three years (K5: FLPA s 3(1) and s 6(2)).
  • Twist 2: an express Elbonian law clause was put in solely to avoid UCTA (L4; K7, s 27(2) UCTA).

Gemini: targets the L5, K2, K3, K4 and K5 thin spots. Only L5 and K5 are thin. The real gain is s 6 CLA, the forum's own writing rule, as the main point (the mirror of q2-06's foreign writing rule), and the Golden Acres point in Twist 2.

q2-20 · Kallang Robotics v Marlow Automation needs fixes

A Singapore-incorporated company whose whole business is in Ruritania sues a Ruritanian contractor in tort in Singapore over a software failure. Singapore law gives no claim for the loss, Ruritanian law does, and the Ruritanian limitation period has run.

Issues

  • N1 Double actionability; the burden flips when the claimant relies on Ruritanian law alone.
  • N2 Limb 1 fails: Singapore law gives no claim for this pure economic loss.
  • N3 Locate the negligence: act and damage both in Ruritania.
  • N4 Limb 2 is met under Ruritanian law.
  • N5 Red Sea: displace a lex fori whose only link is incorporation, so Kallang relies on Ruritanian law alone.
  • N7 A Ruritanian-law clause excluding consequential loss is raised against the tort claim (Sayers; North).
  • K5 s 3(2) FLPA applies the Ruritanian two-year period; s 4(2) undue hardship in Twist 1.

Dials

  • Kallang has only a registered office in Singapore; all its warehouses and staff are in Ruritania.
  • A Ruritanian-law maintenance contract excludes consequential loss.
  • The failure was in January 2024; the claim was filed in Singapore in July 2026, two and a half years later.
  • Singapore law gives no direct tort recovery for this pure economic loss; Ruritanian law does.
  • Ruritanian law upholds the exclusion clause and has a two-year period for tort claims (Singapore: six years).

Trap. Assuming limb 1 always passes when a Singapore company sues here, or applying Singapore's six-year period under double actionability.

Twists

  • Twist 1: Kallang missed the two-year period because Marlow hid the bug logs (K5: s 4(2) undue hardship, Recovery Vehicle 1).
  • Twist 2: the faulty update was uploaded by an engineer travelling in Utopia (N3; N5, third law).

Gemini: the untested combination of N2, N5 (Red Sea) and K5. That is right and valuable: limb 1 failing, a claimant relying on the foreign law alone, and s 3(2) FLPA in tort. But the facts conflict, and Twist 2 copies q2-05.

q2-22 · Crestline Media v Ardent Fabrics and Ms Koh needs fixes

A Singapore media agency sues an Arcadian textile company on an advertising contract formed by clashing standard forms, one of which also names the UNIDROIT Principles. It also sues the company's visiting employee for a careless statement at a Singapore trade show.

Issues

  • L1 Proper law starter; non-state rules cannot be the proper law.
  • L7 Battle of the forms: Dornoch, Yeo, Art 6(1)(b) Hague Principles and Lew.
  • L3 A one-sided election right in Crestline's form.
  • L9 Choosing a law against incorporating the UNIDROIT Principles as terms. Gemini adds “capacity”, with no fact behind it.
  • L6 Objective proper law if neither form's clause survives.
  • K8 Fundamental public policy against the Arcadian rule that voids comparative advertising.
  • N9 A tort committed in Singapore still runs double actionability.
  • N6 Party autonomy in tort, and whether Ms Koh, a non-party, can rely on the clause.

Dials

  • Forms exchanged in January 2026: Crestline's chooses Singapore law with an election right; Ardent's chooses Arcadian law plus the UNIDROIT Principles.
  • Ms Koh makes a careless statement at a Singapore trade show in February 2026; it is relied on in Singapore.
  • Singapore law: the last shot wins; one-sided election clauses are void.
  • Arcadian law: knock-out rule; one-sided election clauses are valid; comparative advertising is void as unfair competition; no tort liability for trade-show statements.

Trap. Going straight to the objective proper law on a battle of the forms without Dornoch, Yeo and Lew (L7); or assuming a local tort skips double actionability (N9) and that a non-party can rely on the clause (N6).

Twists

  • Twist 1: Ardent emails a variation, “Arcadian law; accepted unless you object in 5 days”, and Crestline stays silent (L7: silence and the Lew caveat).
  • Twist 2: Ardent's managing director signed after Crestline's agents threatened his safety in Arcadia (M7 extreme duress against economic duress under L9).

Gemini: the remaining contract thin spots (L1, L3, L7, L9) with K8, N9 and N6. Only L1 and L3 are thin. The base battle of the forms and Twist 1 repeat q2-01, while Twist 2 (extreme duress) and the non-party point are new.

mx-06 · Banyan Robotics v Krono Precision needs fixes

A Singapore robotics integrator sues its Ruritanian supplier in the General Division for failing to deliver automated assembly arms after a Ruritanian export decree, serving it by courier under the contract. The supplier resists jurisdiction, pointing to a 2016 unlabelled “Singapore High Court” clause and a floating choice of law clause.

Issues

  • A6 Unlabelled “Singapore High Court” clause signed on 15 March 2016; Gemini's Assume list says Ruritanian law gives it no promise.
  • B1 CCAA gate: the clause predates 1 October 2016, Singapore's Convention date, so the CCAA does not apply.
  • B4 Outside the CCAA, so the common law decides.
  • D9 Krono is served by courier at its Ruritanian head office under a contract term, without approval (O 8 r 1(3); NW Corp).
  • E1 Which test: served under r 1(3), Krono can attack only exercise and bears the burden; with no promise, plain Spiliada, not strong cause.
  • E2 Spiliada stay, stage 1 on Krono.
  • E9 An SICC International Judge trained in the foreign law: relevant (Rappo) but only a discount (IM Skaugen).
  • F3 A pre-2016 High Court clause gives the SICC no primary jurisdiction (O 2 r 2(2)).
  • F1 International and commercial, for the transfer.
  • F6 Transfer from the General Division: is the SICC “more appropriate” (O 2 r 4(1)(c))?
  • L1 Proper law starter.
  • L3 Floating choice of law clause: which law tests its validity (the lex fori or the objective proper law).
  • L6 Objective proper law if the floating clause fails.
  • M1 Illegality route for the August 2026 Ruritanian export decree.
  • M5 Ralli Bros and its three readings; Gemini's Singapore-law dial would make Krono source the arms from its Utopian plant.

Dials

  • Contract signed on 15 March 2016, before 1 October 2016.
  • A contract term allows courier service at Krono's Ruritanian head office.
  • Ruritanian law: the jurisdiction clause has no promissory content; floating choice of law clauses are valid; the August 2026 export decree makes the contract void.
  • Singapore law: implies a duty on Krono to source substitute arms from its Utopian plant.
  • Banyan sues in the General Division and asks for transfer to the SICC.

Trap. Treating the pre-October 2016 clause as a CCAA clause (B2) or as giving the SICC primary jurisdiction (F2), and putting strong cause (E7) on Krono although the clause carries no promise under Ruritanian law.

Twists

  • Twist 1: the contract is signed on 15 March 2018 instead; Banyan files directly in the SICC while Krono sues in Ruritania (B2, F2, F4, F5, G9, G10).
  • Twist 2: Banyan adds a negligent misrepresentation claim for accuracy statements made in Utopia and relied on by Banyan's board in Singapore (N1, N3, N4, N5, N6).

Gemini: 16 thin spots (A6, B4, D9, E1, E9, F1, F3, F4, F5, F6, G9, G10, L1, L3, M1, M5) and four open points: the reach of O 8 r 1(3), floating clause validity, Ralli's three readings and s 18F SCJA. The s 18F point does not arise in this hypo. F3 and M1 were never thin, and F6, G9, L3 and M5 no longer are.

mx-08 · Marigold Textiles v Norden Chemicals and Vespera needs fixes

A Singapore textile maker serves its Utopian dye supplier out of Singapore for defective dye and for inducing its Arcadian dyeing contractor to break an exclusivity promise. The supplier says a lobbying side-deal taints the supply contract claim.

Issues

  • A5 Non-exclusive Utopian court clause.
  • B4 Outside the CCAA: the clause says “non-exclusive”, so there is no s 3(2) deeming.
  • D4 Norden is served out of Singapore: the three requirements.
  • D5 Gateways for the contract claim and the tort claim.
  • D7 Serious question to be tried.
  • E1 Which test: plain Spiliada, as neither side breaches a foreign non-exclusive clause.
  • E3 Forum conveniens on service out, burden on Marigold.
  • E4 Stage 1 connecting factors.
  • E6 Second bite: Norden is state-owned and Marigold says the Utopian courts are not independent.
  • L1 Proper law starter.
  • L5 Implied choice of law from the Utopian court clause.
  • L6 Objective proper law: delivery at Tuas and payment in Singapore.
  • M1 Illegality route for the lobbying side-deal.
  • M4 Lemenda: influence over Arcadian officials, against Arcadian and Singapore domestic policy, valid in Utopia.
  • M6 Tainting of the Supply Contract claim by the side-deal.
  • N1 Double actionability for inducing breach of contract.
  • N3 Locate inducing breach (Metall: where the contract was broken and the claimant injured).
  • N4 Limb 2 under the law of that place.

Dials

  • Supply Contract: non-exclusive Utopian court clause, no governing law clause, delivery at Tuas and payment in Singapore.
  • Norden is state-owned; Marigold alleges the Utopian courts are not independent.
  • Side-deal: an Arcadian agent is paid to lobby Arcadian officials for quotas; it offends Arcadian and Singapore domestic policy and is valid in Utopia.
  • Norden, acting in Utopia, induced Vespera to stop dyeing in Arcadia, in breach of Vespera's exclusivity covenant with Marigold.

Trap. Treating a foreign non-exclusive clause (A5) as triggering strong cause (E7), locating inducing breach (N3) where the inducement happened rather than where the contract was broken, and missing the second bite debate (E6).

Twists

  • Twist 1: Norden holds a Utopian judgment dismissing Marigold's Supply Contract claim on the merits; Marigold's appeal in Utopia is pending (H1, H2, H4, H5, H8).
  • Twist 2: the Supply Contract has an exclusive Utopian court clause instead; Norden sues Marigold in Arcadia and Marigold seeks a Singapore anti-suit injunction (G1, G2, G8).

Gemini: thin spots A5, D4, D7, E3, E6, G8, H5, L5, M1, M4 and M6 (11 listed; its table says 9) and four open points: the second bite, Lemenda as a taint, “Akai vs UniCredit” and finality pending appeal. The third is framed differently in the pre-writes. E3, M1, M4 and M6 were never thin, and L5 no longer is.

Say Tamarind has no office or agent in Elbonia and whether it was served (natural justice turns on notice). The declaration cannot be enforced, and recognising it fails for want of international jurisdiction. The breach defence needs a promise and, even with one, no case decides it: argue both ways. q1-10 Twist 2 asks about a default money judgment, so put the weight on the declaration and notice.
11. mx-08 base: drop Vespera as a defendant and from the title (J3.1.1). Drop the lobbying side-deal too: q2-07, and q2-21 in the Q2 batch, already drill that chain, and M4 and M6 are well covered. Give the proper law work instead with a substantive Utopian rule that limits recovery but does not deny the breach, so gateway (e) holds either way, for example: “under Utopian law the loss of Marigold's export orders is too remote; under Singapore law it is not” (C1.4). Order A5, D5, E3, E6, L5, L6, N3, N4, N5; ok B4, D4, D7, E1, E4, E5, K3, L1, N1, N2. Give the contract date.
12. mx-08 tort (C3.3.2; J3.1.2): with the inducement in Utopia and the breach in Arcadia there is no (f) gateway. Put the inducement in Singapore (on a one-day visit, Norden's director persuades Vespera's director at a meeting here; Norden has no office or stand here) and say Marigold's loss was suffered in Arcadia, so Metall places the tort in Arcadia, not where the inducement happened. Make Arcadian law bar one head of loss Marigold claims (for example, lost profits), not the tort itself: that head fails if the tort is in Arcadia, and the exception fails as Arcadia is not fortuitous, though Marigold can argue Boys v Chaplin's interest analysis (C3.3.3; C3.9.1; C3.6.3). A total bar would repeat q1-03 and make the gateway turn on an open point.
13. mx-08 second bite and implied choice (J4.2.3; C2.3.2): the debate is Konamaneni and Fentiman against, and Lewis v King, Metall and Spiliada itself for; Oro Negro and IM Skaugen (CA) left it open. It arises only if Marigold fails stage 1 (balanced factors are enough: Sudarga). Use an injustice fact other than state ownership and biased courts, which q1-03 uses. The Utopian clause is a heavy implied-choice factor (Pacific Recreation) but not in itself a choice (Art 4 Hague Principles): key L5 as arguable; Stage 3 points to Singapore, where both parties perform.
14. mx-08 twists (J7.1.3; J6.1; J6.5.3; J6.2.6): in Twist 1, say what Utopian law says about a judgment under appeal, or key both routes, and give the dates. In Twist 2, say Marigold has not sued Norden in Singapore and seeks only the injunction, and give Norden a registered Singapore branch so it is served here as of right (an injunction claim alone fits no gateway clearly). Make Utopia and Arcadia Contracting States well before the clause, say whether the Arcadian court has ruled on art 6 and whether Utopian courts grant anti-suit injunctions, and order G1, G2, G8, G9: the Convention row (“Foreign Contracting-State EJC; Other Contracting State Suit”) is what q1-24 cannot ask. Key Akai (go to the chosen court) against Chong's seminar reply that Akai is old, especially for a Convention State, plus the “reasons to come here” and the C&Y rebuttal. Do not cite UniCredit, which the pre-writes use only for arbitration.
Then write mx-06.

How the check ran: every new or rebuilt hypo had a review and two adversarial second checks (answers; facts and boxes). Every hypo's notes and walkthrough were written against its law-reviewed file and then checked by a separate agent. A high-level sweep (18 Nov) then compared all 24 hypos on the key rules and open points: submission by a stay application, issue estoppel on governing law, the Ralli readings, reliance as a defence (Esben), where a tort happens and the flexible exception, the forum burdens and strong cause, the s 3(2) clause and the CCAA and SICC dates, O 7 r 4, the presumption of similarity and the FLPA. They agreed except in three hypos, fixed and marked “Consistency sweep” on q1-04, q1-06 and mx-02. Two near-duplicates (q1-27 and mx-09) moved to Additional practice.
